I put yes for recommending Tera because the game itself is pretty fun, I had a decent amount of hours in it within just a few days but right now I'm analyzing what makes the game good and what makes it...not as good.
So for one, the story.
Some people really like if they can get into the story of an MMORPG so that their actions have more weight to it, in Tera however, I couldn't seem to find myself able to care about what the character was going through or what the other characters were trying to do. I was just...following quest markers and killing monsters because the quest told me to. I think the only reason I wasn't as interested in the story as I should have been was because it's basically all the same washed story for each character, unlike a game like Maplestory where each class has their own story, though they do align at times, they have personality.
In Tera...the characters just seem more like ideal models. Not to mention some of the animations are goofy for the 'story' cutscenes (which I have skipped for the most part due to my low-end PC)
Pros about Tera, I think that the combat is very fun especially when playing with other people. The satisfaction you get after succeeding in defeating a boss that took you (and probably your party) a while to defeat is just as good in this game as it is in any other MMORPG. There's one thing that I think is a little concerning but I don't really mind because it encourages the players to work together, is that it's rather difficult to be a 'solo' player. Some people prefer to take it solo, some prefer to play in a party, personally I'm okay with a little bit of both.
If a game were entirely solo, when it was meant to be with multiple people, of course the game would get stale after a while. I'm not entirely sure about the Tera community but from what I see, for the most part there's every type of person on the internet that you can find on this game, as with many games. Although, it is very frustrating when you look forward to doing a dungeon with your friends or something and then you disconnect from the server, the team can definitely work on fixing those servers or at least latency issues.
I like the fact that the loading screens don't take 50 million years as you wait in anticipation to see if you crash or not.
The settings for low-end PCs actually work unlike other games where they lower the quality but then do nothing to fix the fps drops, also you can adjust how far you are able to zoom out from your character which is definitely appreciated because some of the enemies are so...overwhelming that when you're playing a class as small as an Elin sometimes the default zoom out isn't enough (tbh I keep this at the highest settings because while my character is nice and all, I'm more focused on seeing the enemy and, well, defeating them.)
TL;DR
Tera is fun, but it's far from perfect. 6.5/10

For instance I usually play with random characters against 3 AI. I had the Troll. I killed one of the other characters and forgot to loot ALL the items (my own fault, hit the button to quick) and the Devil's Minion CPU player swooped in and grabbed it all including the follower that reduces the Peril of Plane's requirements by 1 die. OMG.
The Devil's Minion made to the the Crown of Command, because he made it there so early he only had 5 STR and 6 CRA. I got EXTREMELY lucky and grabbed the poltergiest as a follower on the right side of the outer region of the board. Along there was "The healer with 2 free heals " (thankfully I got turned to Good along the way!) and "The Shrine", next to them was the Forest. So since I could only move one space it was great that I could keep moving back and forth between these spaces healing myself and trying to bump up my craft at the Forest. I also had spells of one Counterspell, one Random, and one Temporal Warp. I was going to use the Temporal Warp when I finally started making my run to the Crown! I made a huge mistake by going into the Village and not realizing it ditched the Poltergiest! OH NO!
Since I had 10 STR and 5 CRA, I decided to make a run for it. The Devil's Minion rolled BADLY on quite a few Crown spells. I luckily made my way all the way to the Crown with 11 STR from figting one monster along the way and cashing some in.
So the Devil's Minion had 5 lives, I had 4. But I definitely had the upper hand from a mathematical standpoint. So what does the Devil's Minion do when he fights me, he picks STR!! WHAT IN THE. I was afraid it was going to be a race to 0 to see who could roll luck (he COULDN'T beat me in STR 11 vs 5, but he had a chance in CRA 5 vs 6). So I whittled him down to 1 health, and THEN he finally lets loose with a CRA attack and actually wins. I beat him the next turn.

I tried to like this game, I really did. Trying to enjoy the atmosphere of the game was a challenge. Running everywhere trying to figure out where to go. But the one thing that killed the game for me was the puzzles. The damn puzzles.
In any of the Penumbra or Amnesia games, which this game seems like its trying to be a spiritual successor, the puzzles in those games were fair and solvable. Gave you a good amount of informtion & hints to solve them. Made you think and they were fun to solve, without taking you out of the atmosphere of the games.
However, in Doorways Holy Mountains of Flesh, the first few puzzles have very little information to very vague hints, breaking you away from the excellent atmosphere of the game. Puzzles done wrong? This game is an excellent prime example of how you do not program puzzles and supply little to no clues on how to solve them.
This is a Walkthrough kind of game. Which means you have to watch someones Lets Play. Skimming through someones video just to see how its solved. Which makes you feel like you're cheating and that you're really stupid. Then you find out that when they're trying to find the solution, they needed help or look it up themselves.
I cannot recommend a game that breaks you away from the atmosphere due to its unforgivable puzzles. The rest of the game however is superb. But when it comes to the first Doorways game, it was a great game. Was scary, excellent atmosphere, and it managed to grab the attention of the player with ease. This game provides puzzles that frustrate and breaks you away from what the original game provided.
I will not say do not buy the game. If you like hard as nails puzzles, like in the old Silent Hill days, then this is your game. A word of warning however, when you get stuck (and you will get stuck often), do not be ashamed to use a walkthrough. Because this game alone literally frustrates you enough to look for one.

I first played this game on the Gameboy Advance and I really enjoyed it. I wasn't sure at first if I wanted to play through it again but I'm very glad I changed my mind. This version surpasses the Gameboy Advance version to me. I've only beaten it on Normal and only unlocked 72% of the achievements but here's a list of my pros and cons.
Pros
-Wide variety of characters with their own abilities (although the mages kind of overlap minus the summoner Rydia). You'll get to play as Yang the Monk who whoops♥♥♥♥♥and Edward the Bard who sucks♥♥♥♥♥ You'll also get to use a Dark Knight, Dragoon, Paladin, Sage and others.
-Great story, the DS version adds cutscense that add to some missing parts of the story from the previous versions of the game. Plus, the voice acting is great, (pretty sure Kain is voiced by the same actor that did Gaara from Naruto).
-Lots of things to do, I beat the game in about 22 hours but there's also a hard mode and more things to do in the game, such as hidden ultimate weapons, secret bosses and an annoying rabit thing that I missed the achievement for doing all his damn things.
-Summoning. I love summoning in a Final Fantasy game. This version they're called Eidolons and they're pretty sweet. You got your usual, Ifrit, Shiva, Ramuh, Chocobo that come with your summoner when she joins and some sweet hidden ones like Leviathan or Bahamut. The hidden ones are fun to find and are well worth the search and grinding neccesary to acquire them.
-Combat, you can either have Wait or Active combat. Both are like what they sound like, Wait you get a chance to figure out what to do when it's your turn and Active keeps the battle going. I preferred active as it made things go by quicker and made the battles a bit harder.
Cons
-Back to the variety of characters, you won't get to choose who you use. It's set who you will use when and where and that's why this is a like and dislike. It means I won't have to worry about leveling up all of my characters to stay close to the same level but what if I wanted to see if Edward stops sucking? Or bring someone else to the final boss other then the ones I'm supposed to use? It's not a huge gripe since I liked the five characters I had to take to the end but it still is a gripe.
-Now I've only played it on Normal so far but I found the game to be a bit on the easy side. When you bring up the menu to start the game, there is an option to Continue. I thought this was for a quicksave but actually, it brings you back to where you were when you died. I got to one treasure chest guarded by a tough monster and instead of taking it back to when I last saved, it continued me right next to the treasure chest to try again. This isn't a huge con but it doesn't make me feel worried about going into a fight with low hp, cause I know I'll be able to continue right where I just was and try again.
-Can't skip cutscense. I pushed every button I could and I had to watch them no matter what.
Overall
-I had alot of fun playing this game. I liked the characters, the story kept me interested and the game was challenging to the point where grinding was needed in order to keep going. I might take a break before trying hard mode but for now, I enjoyed my time with Final Fantasy IV. My rating for this game is a 9/10.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Surprisingly polished, DuckTales Remastered is an incredibly pleasant re-make that manages to positively change a classic.
…
Back in the early 90s, platforming games were made for just about every Saturday morning cartoon that existed. Honestly, there’s a game for the Biker Mice from Mars, I swear. However, the Disney franchise games were always a step above, and DuckTales was no exception. Most people who have played the original probably remember the tough difficulty (being “Nintendo Tough”) and the fantastic soundtrack (“The Moon,” in particular). There really wasn’t a plot, the main objective was to just travel around the world, grabbing treasures as Scrooge McDuck while pogo-bouncing off the heads of enemies with Scrooge’s cane…which is probably one of the most bizarre standard attacks to exist.
 
This remastered version, made by Way Forward, makes a few sensible changes while retaining all the things that made the original fun. Pogo bouncing can be made easier with a menu option, and the levels have been tweaked to require specific objectives to complete. Overall, the game’s difficulty has been turned down a notch, and even includes difficulty options. The soundtrack is a near-copy of the original, and the original voice cast makes a reappearance, which is awesome.
 
There’s an actual storyline to the game now, and each level is punctuated with moments of character interaction that makes the game essentially feel like a multi-episode storyline from the cartoon. I personally really enjoyed this extra touch, and it really makes the game feel new. If Way Forward could keep this quality level and attention to detail going, I would love to see them tackle a few other Disney projects, such as Darkwing Duck or TaleSpin.
 
I wouldn’t say the game has a large amount of replay-ability, but the achievements are all reasonably obtainable, and there is an unlockable gallery of development art and music that can be purchased with money earned from treasure pickups. It’s fun to play through, and keeps forward momentum without being annoying or frustrating.
 
Recommended to fans of the original game, or someone looking for a weekend platformer. Way Forward has done a great job with this re-make, and from the positive updates and improvements

Alright, I absolutely love hard games. Really, big fan. But there are two types of difficulty: the one that when you lose you feel like you are getting better, on your way to win next time, and the one that is just random, stupid, annoying and sometimes due to unresponsive controls.
Ducktales is more of the second type. There are lots of annoyances for losing, you are sent back to the stage selection screen and you need  to press start and select skip at least 3 times in order to skip the cutscenes you already saw. Plus, you lose all your diamonds, and as a game that encourages the player to explore to find them, it's pretty annoying having to go through the same exploration to get them again. Imagine playing Metroid and losing your upgrades after dying. Sort of closer to that than Mega Man, where you don't actually lose that much, you just go through the linear stage again.
Some stuff are pretty random and require straight-up memorising patterns, and sometimes the controls are not very responsive. I'm not saying it's completely bad, it's just a dated type of difficulty that aged poorly.
Now to the good part, I'm absolutely in love with the boss fights, those are usually the highlights of any game for me, and in this one, they don't disappoint. The level design is pretty good, not amazingly perfect, but good enough. There are a decent amount of secrets throughout each stage, which makes exploring interesting, you'll find yourself searching every inch of the stage for treasures. The environments are PERFECT, I found myself smiling stupidly with every new stage and enemy, everything looks absolutely gorgeous. The soundtrack is also incredible, and that's something I don't usually even notice in games.
Overall I'd say Ducktales Remastered is a decent 2D platformer with top-notch graphics and soundtracks, but prepare to get pretty annoyed after some free-deaths it throws at you.

Tharsis is quite in interesting game about dice, cannibalism, and teaching metaphysical aliens what it means to be human.
While the game seems hard at the first glance, after a couple of playthrough you come to realise how you're supposed to play. The only two problems I really have are:
-The lack of contents, but with the price it actually is I won't list it as a negative thing.
-The ending (spoiler alert: it makes sense, but I think they hid the actually meaning way too deep inside the story to be easily understood).
If you don't want to be spoiled, don't read further.
Explanation about the story:
So Tharsis is set in the same universe as Laserlife, a game about a dead astronaut found floating in space by an extremely advanced alien lifeform who doesn't completely exist as a physical being. The dead astronaut is in fact the one who gets ejected into space in the beginning of Tharsis.
At the end of Laserlife, the alien understand the hardship and the sacrifices the humans endured, and since Tharsis also feature a metaphysical alien at the end (with one ending ending with the sentence "The anomaly... It knew".), then it means that they are a single entity.
So now, it would mean that they tried to make the humans survive no matter what, because that's what humans would do isn't it? Putting them in an infinite loop of suffering, but with the hope of surviving at the end.
But since endless suffering isn't something human they chose to destroy the anomaly at the true end, sacrificing themselves but putting an end at that loop.
(Reminder: Laserlife and Tharsis are game about symbolism whereas Bit trip runner was about Minimalism)
TL; DR: Not so hardcore, just bear it until you get good, need more content and the story should be less hidden.

A lot of people are going on about how this game is actually very well balanced and fair and not about luck or RNG at all.  There's a lot of math to back up those assertions.  I'm not going to dispute that because it's sort of missing the point.  The main question is;  is the game fun?  The answer to that is 'no, it's not' unless your idea of fun is pretending to be a probability and risk analysis computer.  I've watched the playthroughs of people with long winstreaks and the thought of spending 2-3 hours of my time deciding the probabilities of every possible outcome of every possible decision isn't appealing, it sounds like drudgery and work.
I would ask for a refund but I played the game for more than 2 hours before I decided that if I did win (however unlikely) then it would ultimately be more because of luck and not skill.  I simply don't have the time or patience to get my abacus out and decide if I should roll the dice or not.  Play FTL if you want a roguelike in space, that game is actually fun.

Few things before starting the review:
This game was reviewed using a code sent by the developer.
Warning: This game is only suitable for ages 18+, the topics and images are quite disturbing and not suitable for anyone under that age.
Masochisia is a disturbing horror point and click adventure game that covers the topic of domestic abuse, but will you want to play this game for yourself ?
In Masochisia we play as Hamilton. Hamilton is growing up in a strict home where his family abuses him constantly. One day he finds out that he will grow up to become a psychopath. Is it possible to change fate ?
Masochisia is a simple point and click adventure game in the vein of Year walk, where you walk from side to side, pick up items and solve puzzles. This game doesn't have difficult puzzles and it's more story driven.
The atmosphere in Masochisia is beyond fantastic. The game sets up this mood that will make you feel uneasy the entire time of playing, making you feel something is following you the entire time you're playing.  The mood is built on the soundtrack and nature sounds. What feels like a relaxing tune can quickly turn into something far more sinister building up on the anxiety you will experience playing the game.
The game messes with you the entire time you're playing and pretty much the entire time you will feel chills running down your spine from the incredibly disturbing imagery. The entire time you're playing the main characters sanity descends into madness and the game changes along with his sanity. Not to mention the game leaves you "notes" after you finish playing it.
I finished Masochisia in 2 hours and 30 minutes. I felt that this was the perfect amount of time and I enjoyed every single second of this story.  Apart from the one playthrough, you can try and do other playthroughs and ask the characters you meet along the way different questions and get different responses which maybe will reveal something or open up more questions.
The game has one major problem I dislike. The save system is broken. When you load in you lose every item. Meaning if you Restart an act or if you load in a game in the middle of an Act, you will lose two items and you will have to pick them up. The good thing is that the items are always the same and they have the same spawn every time so you can quickly find them, but I still wish if you load in you get the items and you don't need to backtrack to get them.
In the end Masochisia is insanely disturbing and I would say it's one of the scariest if not the scariest game that came out in 2015.
As stated at the start of the review this game is not suitable for anyone under the age of 18. If you can handle the incredibly disturbing story and imagery, this game is a must play.
Final Rating:
9/10 - A must own

One of the first games of the psychological horror kind that actually didn't need a ♥♥♥♥ing spoken word of dialogue in the entire game to have such a damn profound effect. This game is INCREDIBLY ♥♥♥♥ed.
It deals with a lot of dark seated♥♥♥♥♥♥ Things that nobody wants to talk about or think about, but as humans we do, as much as we regret and abhor it. It deals with a "protagonist" who ends up finding out what kind of monster he will become. The game is apologetic. It does not hide itself and it does not coddle. The feeling of oppression that exudes from this game by the atmosphere alone is a pretty god damned good indication of the concept of depression and the related illnesses. It speaks of the human condition upon dealing with our thoughts we do not want to think or actions we do not want to do.
It will make you feel uncomfortable. You may not even want to continue, considering some of the♥♥♥♥♥♥it asks you to do. But there's this innate curiosity- Maybe, somehow, some way, you can make it all okay. According to the developer, there are multiple endings. But you have to be extremely careful on what you say and when you say it. You have to choose when to use items and when not to. It very subtly tells you what kind of path you will end up taking, and whether or not you can stop it.
It's a very, very short game. I got the first ending within an hour. But believe me, this man knows what it's like to have a battle within your own mind. He understands what it feels like. This game has spoken volumes about the concepts of mental illness and the struggles of depression. Also the battle of keeping your head on your shoulders and being in control of your own existence.
I get headaches sometimes when I'm in periods of extreme tension or distress, and this game made me feel that, even though it wasn't obvious. This is a sign of a very well made game. Even though he said that people that suffer from depression probably SHOULDN'T play it (But all of you know me anyhoo)
This is a very, very good game if you're into psychological horror point and clicks, and I hope to see more from this man. Excellent work. 8.75/10

I bought the Euro Truck Simulator 2 pack for $19.99 when it was on sale, and I found this added to my library a few days after I got the pack. This game is very good to pass the time, and has decent graphics. However, it is not so much of a simluator as a game and there is no free-roam capability (but you can still drive anywhere while playing a mission). This is simular to Euro Truck Simulator 2 in the way that it is very picky; you get points docked for not turning on your blinkers while switching lanes, and the controls can sometimes be a challenge around corners. I recommend you should go through the controls before playing your first mission, because they don't tell you on their own. Another thing: You can't manipulate the camera. Most of the time, the camera is fine, but when driving in the neighboorhoods where there are a lot of trees, they get in the way of your view. The camera sometimes tries to move to help but usually doesn't make things better. The traffic lights also seem to be rigged; they don't stay green if you're approaching them. This annoys me a lot when I'm driving in the city, where there are 5-lane roads that are completely empty, and I am speeding down one towards a green light, which suddenly turns yellow (for what seems like a fraction of a second) and then red. 200 points lost for a traffic light offense. I loved this game when I was a teenager and I remember it sooooo well, but it's a shame it's not free roam, well unless y'all choose 2 :P. The passengers and braking is a bit annoying, but  I think the bus games after this have gotten better, but at the same time... slightly worse. Confusing?

NOTE: Review based on digital retail release that I have completed.  Not the Steam version.
A classic from SCS.
The game is basically broken up into bite-sized missions where you take a specific bus type on a single route, picking up and dropping off passengers in a variety of locations and weather conditions. Early missions are usually under five minutes, steadily increasing over more advanced tiers. You're scored in real time along the way for obeying common traffic rules and docked points for upsetting your passengers (breaking too hard, running lights, etc.) along the way. At the end of your route your score is tallied and put in a high-score table.
Presentation-wise, the graphics are dated (technically), but since it's a '07 title it takes next to nothing to crank all the settings up to 11, giving the game a clean, inviting look. It comes off as super charming, with a vivid and colorful pallet.  The constantly-updating UI overlays just scream classic SEGA sit-down arcade racer fun.  Overall, the game has a very unique look that gives it a lot of personality.  And because it's going for a more cartoonish look, I think it's aged FAR better visually than older SCS truck-sim titles of the same period.
Finally, the game can be very challenging as you get further into the missions.  Obeying traffic laws while keeping your passengers happy and on time takes strict focus, which tests your meddle over longer 10 & 15+ minute routes.
I think Bus Driver is a hidden gem from SCS that could be too easily overlooked based on the screenshots.  The game is a ton of fun, more arcade in nature than the simulation that SCS is known for.  Great for short-burst gaming or prolonged sessions.  It's got a nice price tag too.
SCS has a free demo for it on thier website.
Play it with a 360 pad if you can.
If you enjoyed ETS2 and are curious to try some SCS history, you can't go wrong with Bus Driver.

For this price "Bus Driver" delivers and not only passengers, but a nice and relaxing gaming experience for those who want to play something else besides shooters and strategy games.

Doorways Prelude was absolutely wondeful back in 2013 - it was very much the pace setter for a great number of indie horror titles which followed, and was steeped in originality and genuinely chilling content. For a low-budget horror game, it was basically flawless.
Its sequel, Underworld, threw away every ounce of ingenuity and decided to copy all the other horror games - we had a bunch of Slenderman-esque chaser sequences and that nightmare 'maze' which might go down as some of the worst game design I've ever suffered.
Unfortunately Saibot just ignored any critical comments from those who'd been disappointed by the sequel, and provided no support or answers.
Ergo I was wary about going anywhere near them for Holy Mountains of Flesh, especially after the early access version had been merely 'ok' and had failed to actually follow on from the previous game at all.
I needn't have worried - I took the risk on this, needing something new to play, and so far it has erased the memory of Underworld, and while not quite reaching the heights of the original, comes pretty close.
Once again you are private investigator Thomas Foster (brilliantly voiced I have to say) of the psychic detective agency Doorways, and once again you are in the mind of serial killers to find out what really happened. Sort of - that part of the original game doesn't seem as well fleshed out (pun not intended) and you don't really feel like you are in their mind now, but more an observer looking into some parallel dimension where these crimes and their echos still exist.
But the horror, feel, look, and general psychological immerson from the original games is back, and while you will rarely be terrified here, you will find yourself engaged. Everything Underworld got wrong is erased here, and there are some really good moments in this, with the feel of the mountainous village of hell really working well - you feel like you're in a hell, and it's intense.
I have not finished the whole game, but thus far I'm pretty impressed by what I'm seeing here.
Saibot's customer care could be a lot better, and their consistency is lacking, but when they get it right, it really is worth your time.
EDIT (13/08/16):
I have now fully completed the final retail version, and have to admit Saibot rectified everything they got wrong with both customer care re: Underworld and the flaws with the game itself, and really did produce a fine third chapter in Mountains of Flesh, a fitting end to the series.
They really listened to us during Early Access and incorporated a great deal of the constructively critical feedback to make the final game a polished and thoroughly enjoyable game, and I cannot speak more highly of their hands-on approach this time around.
Holy Mountains of Flesh is a psychological horror, and lacks contrived jump scares, instead going for foreboding doom. It works brilliantly as it did with Prelude, and they even added some cinematics to give us even more story.
This is one of those times where promise in Early Access is truly delivered on with the final retail game.
If you like good horror, and accept it's not marquee budget, you could do far worse than both this game, and its whole franchise. Just go easy on Underworld!

Computer opponents don't have much strategy besides accumulating stats and items. They perform like mediocre bots in the single-player training missions of an online FPS. A human player would wipe the table with them every time, except the AI appears to get a boost via favorable die rolls and card draws, likely to disguise its lack of real strategy. The first few games this doesn't matter much, but after dozens of games it sucks the enjoyment out of it.
If you have 3 friends willing to play the game with you, I'd buy this game in a heartbeat. If you're going to fill in with computer players--and especially if you just want to play single-player--this is probably a pass.
For that reason--plus constant problems connecting with servers resulting in interrupted games--I have to give this game a no vote even though I generally like it. It's not a horrible purchase, just know what you're getting into.

I almost never buy a game rated as low as mixed, for I think Steam ratings are inflated anyways, but I gave this one a chance. Here's why: Negative reviews tell a lot more about the game than positive ones, and the negative reviews here tols me this game could be good.
See, there's this new kind of gamer, bred by the industry's 'no kid left behind' policy that, no matter what they do, even if they randomly click around, they will win in a single player game. That's not a credo upheld by board games. This sort of game aims to give you a challenge, even if you are good at it. When that sort of a player meets this sort of a game, there is frustration. To me, 'challenging' is a good quality, so I gave it a look.
So, knowing nothing about the game, I lost 8 straight, then won, with 1 crew with 1 health surviving, then with full crew with full health or thereabout on 10th game, all within the first hour of play. Yes, normal mode is fairly simple when you know what you are doing. The odds to win is lower on hard more, of course, and it took 20 odd games to beat it. So this is like a game of minesweeper, you play to the best of your ability and even then, you only win some of the time. That's far better in my books than a game you win all the time, get bored, and throw away.
The aggrevating thing is that people who know nothing about balancing a game whine about broken balance all the time. This is no different. What is a letdown for me is that there is not enough content yet, but the 'missions' thing seem to be a promise that there is more to come. Tharsis is an amazing turn-based strategy game for a number of reasons. And I'm here to tell you why. The story is you and your crew on a space mission to Mars, when things go wrong...horribly wrong.
You're in control of four crew members, each with unique special abilities. Each crew member rolls dice to try and meet a total objective cost for a broken module, so you can keep flying. The mission takes 10 weeks, (10 rounds) and your crew will face a bevy of challenges from lack of oxygen to malfunctioning water supply for the food garden.
There have been many dissenting reviews of Tharsis by the Steam community. People are often enraged at the fact that the game has a lot of luck, and it's too difficult and random because of that. Unfortunately for them, they do not have the strategy skill set or the patience to enjoy the game.
This game is essentially a cooperative board game in video game form. There are a few underlying strategies that will carry your crew to victory. The key is finding them. And the journey to find them is a rewarding, albeit sometimes frustrating one.
I lost my first 8 games of Tharsis. Then I won my next two. Not randomly, but by the strategy I had discovered. I happen to be a veteran strategy board game player, so I probably found the strategy quicker than some. But when you fail 8 times, and you finally figure it out and make it to Mars, beaten and bruised, the taste of victory is oh so sweet.
If you like strategy games, this is an excellent one, rich with theme that will have you clinging to  your chair wondering if your crew will survive the onslaught of perils. I rate this game an 8.5/10.

Masochisia is a narrative driven, point-and-click, psychological horror game. I can safely say I've never played another game I'd described using the same terms.
Masochisia is NOT a fun game to play. At all. And I mean that, entirely, as a compliment.
GAMEPLAY
You navigate the dark, hauntingly beautiful world by either mouse or keyboard. You can traverse by going left or right, and by clicking to go to different areas. There is an inventory for a few items you come across as you play (helpful hint: click and drag to use items). You also get access to "pills" and other non-inventory items. There are not many puzzles, as this game is mostly story and dialogue driven, but the few it does have are well done. A big puzzle, in particular, had me stumped for a little while. But, to be honest, I'm not a good puzzle solver, so you might find it all very easy. Just know, while there is some exploration and some puzzles, that is not really what this game is.
GRAPHICS/MUSIC
The art style is a real highlight. Combined with sparse yet effective sounds and music, the mood of the game is perhaps its biggest strength. I recommend watching the trailer - it gives a good idea about the art and mood.
STORY
This is what you are buying the game for. And it will not be for everyone. It is very dark and depressing and unrelenting in that tone. I most enjoyed how the game played with ideas of fate and your (in?)ability to change it. It breaks the fourth wall (in-game and out!), it provides moral conundrums, it tells a true story, and it always knows where it wants to go. The story messes with your mind, it challenges you not as a gamer but as a human being. While not for everyone, it is a very good and well told story.
VERDICT
I won't spoil anything, but I do need to talk around the ending. Masochisia has a very bold ending. I can see many people being frustrated with how it ends. Others might see a kind of audacious brilliance. I can say, if narrative games appeal to you, and the oppressive themes and dread-filled mood don't turn you off, then you should absolutely play to the end. Just know that when you're done, you will be asking uncomfortable questions about your own self.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!

First off, this game met one of my prerequisites immediately: Looking like it was made in 1991 for MS-DOS or the Commadore 64, and this game fits it better than a condom. This Android port originally made for tablets, despite what some may say in forums, is a great port to PC and although simple, is still incredibly fun. Initially the graphics reminded me a lot of a recent release called “Ultionus” but the gameplay however is incredibly unique. Deep Dungeons of Doom takes a bunch of elements and blends them all together to create a playing experience like no other. I love everything from the painstakingly perfect pixel graphics,  intense and spectacular soundtrack, all the way down to the deep, rich and in-depth story straight out of the times of King Arthur.
Deep Dungeons of Doom is what I would call a “Timing Based” dungeon crawler. Meaning you can’t move your character on the screen and you only have 3 actions, attack, block, and use item. Simple and straight forward controls, my only complaint would be the lack of controller support, but I can only hope that will come in the future. Starting out is pretty basic, but it takes a short period of play to get the timing down for blocking and attacking enemies. You face your opponent in a turn based style, but battle is very much real-time. Seemingly simple at first, Deep Dungeons of Doom ends up turning into an involved and intricate game that continues to keep your mind at work and make good use of your keyboard skills. You can cause extra damage if you attack an enemy while they are attacking, but be aware; it works both ways, so watch out. The fighting isn’t as cut and dry as it seems. During boss battles, like the first dungeons boss Pitch Black, you need to learn his secret before being able to inflict any damage. Each enemy has a unique attack and block pattern, so stay on those toes and attack when they aren’t blocking, and block while the enemy is attacking.
You will meet monsters and you will need skill and tactics to defeat them. You will find weird and wonderful treasures along the way. Most will help you, but some might not. You may choose to play as a Crusader, a Witch or a Mercenary – in fact each one might well be required if you are to successfully complete your quest – but knowing when to use each one is something you are going to have to figure out for yourself. – Deep Dungeons of Doom
The whole point of the game is to clear dungeons and build the characters stats with special items and skills. After completing the first dungeon you are given missions to complete with the Crusader. Once the first dungeon is cleared you are then able to view the map, this is where you can visit the shops and are able to purchase potions and upgrade your skills. The first skill upgrade for the Crusader is “Holier Than Thou” which gives you +5% Miracle Heal & +1HP. In the dungeons you find Altars, these Altars are where you exchange gold for enhancements. Usable items make up a large part of gameplay and are essential to success… most of the time. Some items like “Contract of The Vampire” that gives you +1HP & deals +2 normal damage to your opponent have nothing but positive effects, but others like “Devils Contract” where on use you pay 8HP but receive +60% resistance to all, +6 attack & +6 agility for 3 floors have some negative effects as well. There are also equipable items found in random chests after you defeat an enemy in a dungeon, or in shops when on the map. Items such as “Sturdy Sword” gives +1 attack while equipped, or even better “Ring of Magic Cure” which requires 2 magic but gives +2HP per floor. With continued gameplay you unlock 2 other playable characters, also upgradable. This gives the game a bit more “depth”, using magic with the Witch and swift moves with the Mercenary, combining items with the heroes passive skills makes for an even better chance of victory.
The soundtrack stays true to the 8 bit era, composed with astonishing perfection. Songs don’t get overly boring or repetitive they actually keep you interested and are pretty catchy fitting the game perfectly. Graphically Deep Dungeons of Doom is brilliant with incredible pixel art capturing the essence of the original games we call retro that paved the path before it. The cut scenes are awesome with beautiful 8 bit graphics to tell its incredible and strong story line. The death animations are on point, imaginative and gorey as hell. I don’t usually promote games made for the tablet and ported to the PC, but in this case, its was done perfectly. I’ll be honest, I had no clue this was originally Android based that’s how good the gameplay in Deep Dungeons of Doom is. This is an incredibly fun game, and for the price completely worth it. Not only does it have several hours of gameplay, but the “replay factor” on this game is huge, because remember those dungeons do get deep.

I have been enjoying city builders ever since I have started gaming. This game get's me back every now and then. Sometimes because new content is available, but mainly because it is just the only game around that can scratch an itch no other game can scratch. There are tons of possibillities to create and design your city. CIty growth is however somewhat tricky as you are continuously improving the infrastructure and a balance between industry, commercial and living areas. Every time my addicative Cities: Skylines period starts I tend to find a new way to balance these three out and test how my residents interact with the layout.
The expansion packs:
I love most of the expansion packs. It seems to me that After Dark is an absolutely must have, I can't imagine to play this game without it. Snowfall is a decent pack as it is extensive and most importantly; it brings trams into the game. I havn't played the Snowfall maps a lot as it seems to snow all of the time. It doesn't compliment the dynamic feel a weather system should have. I might be wrong on this one, as I havn't played a single Snowfall map long enough. Mass Transit is something I adore, it give you a lot of important public transport opportunities that enhances the game greatly. The blimps are however useless as they can que up a huge crowds when placed in prominant places without having the capacity to manage these amount of people. The buildings for busses, ferries and trains are however a must have. Lately I have been giving the disasters and green cities expansion packs a go. Green Cities doesn't realy pop out as an expansion pack but it gives a welcome addition to the otherwise poluting ways of life. As polution plays an important role in how you design your city I am somewhat surprised how this was not build into the main game. Lastly, natural disasters is absolutely fun as it brings in unpredictabillity into the game. I had to set the frequency to 25% however as at 50% my city was barely recovered as the next disaster hit the city.
What I have missed:
As a played the Simcity series as a kid I have always enjoyed the feeling of connecting with other cities through trade and communicating with them. The cities you build in this game are somewhat self sustaining super-cells. Missing raw materials, inhabitants and tourists are imported through your infrastructure. Thes boats, planes and trains mention where they originate from but that's it. Maybe a bidding war to obtain a prestigious HQ of an admirable company, or have other cities request a connection to a specific part of town might add to a feeling of interaction. The game somewhat leaves you with the biggest question in life; are we alone?
Furthermore, I would love to see a better interaction with your inhabitants. They seem to be pleased with every change I make or  lack in the capacity to think for themselves. Maybe an expansionpack where the inhabitants of your city can start fundraisers to build a park or protest your lack of response to a disaster?

Legends of Azulgar is a real-time space strategy title that gives you either overhead third-person point-and-click or close-up (six o'clock high) third-person steering control of spacecraft.  LoA has some neat features going for it - ship hulls and stations are completely constructable from prefab parts (so it's not really a voxel game) granting an element of creative control that you don't get in a lot of similar space strategy games.  It's also free, which basically means "stop reading this review and try the game yourself."
However, the game in its current Early Access form is very incomplete.  Pop-up notifications need to be click-exited, which is annoying when your mouse is used for steering and shooting (so just to get the notification out of the way, you have to steer and shoot at it).  There isn't currently any kind of targeting system; you literally steer your ships in the general viscinity of targets and they shoot at whatever is closest, which gives you very little control in combat beyond the single ship that you control directly.  The ship and station editor is very hard to work with, at least at first, as nothing seems to want to place quite where you want it.  The Tutorial gives you exactly zero help on how to work with the editor controls.
Further, the game crashes constantly, mostly on loading screens, or more annoyingly, as you hit Finish in the editor.  While the visual assets are very good and well-detailed, it would be even better if I could run this game at higher quality without the client crashing at startup.  Somebody else said "push every button until it works" and that applies to pretty much everything in this game, including the resolution and quality options (i.e. "try everything until one works").
I'm giving this game a Yes recommendation because 1) it's free and 2) there's a lot of original content that will be very fun to work with once the controls and camera get a little love.  However, I'm not happy with publishers that release unstable clients, and this is very close to the buggiest Early Access game I've downloaded on Steam.

This is a well done solitaire/progression type game that has been done many times before and since.  There is a mobile version of this game too, though I haven't played it.  The object is to get past each "level" by removing all the cards from the board.  You do this by placing cards that are either one higher in value or one lower on the visible stack.  The level boss is trying to reduce your health to zero by using various abilities against you.  You have abilities to counter these attacks, or to manipulate the deck to your advantage.  You need a certain type of energy to be able to use your abilities, but you gain energy through regular play.  This game is turn-based so no frantic clicking is involved, and there is a fair bit of strategy to using card skills.
My main complaint with the game is the randomness of the card draw, like in solitaire, will have a big influence on your winning or losing a level.  Sometimes you'll get the "right" cards and breeze through a level, and other times you'll be at the mercy of the RNG.  The game never feels unfair though.  I didn't have any sense that the game was cheating - it's just a luck of the draw.  I like this game and continue to play it while listening to podcasts or music.

The "meat" of the game is gauntlet-type journey, with 18/28 battles and final boss. A single successful run takes anywhere from an hour to three, luckily there's option to save & quit. And you'll have to do plenty of runs to unlock and complete everything. I've spent well over 60 hours so far and I still have few deck types that I didn't complete Elite difficulty with yet. If you like puzzle, strategy and/or card games then you should enjoy your time here.
The presentation from graphics standpoint is high quality. The artwork is great, there's some love and work put into everything, starting from animations, to user interface, cards (both front and back), icons and enemies. I can't say too much about the music
but the sound effects are nice
) and also serve an informative role, giving you some feedback on your/enemy actions.
Does the game has issues?
In windowed mode I've noticed few problems - tabbing out can break the sound completely, from time to time your cursor will do weird things
. Still, that's just a minor annoyance in my opinion since it can be fixed by pressing "Windows" key. Though for the sound you have to save & quit.
After about 5-10 hours I figured out that there are some items and spells that I always wanted to have, which made chaining long combos (and Gold earning) so much easier and fun. Since then, all my late-game inventory looked very similar. Luckily different deck types with unique spells force you to adjust, at least a bit. Later on, the passive abilities of enemies will also make you change things around. I mean, I still played over 50 hours since I figured out the meta and I'm no masochist. So this is not that big of a deal, you'll just find yourself ignoring some of the items/spells, there's still enough variance.
There's an elephant in the room though,
. Solitairica can be cruel with RNG
, sometimes it'll decide that you're supposed to lose and there's nothing you can do. For me, it usually happens when I have a massive surplus of Gold that I decided to spend on hourglass(es) (a revive feature, gives you another shot when you fail). In other cases you have to guess what sequence the game wants you to follow, because it's the only one leading to victory. There are also some, when the game holds your hand and it won't let you lose
.
This is really noticeable when you use deck types that give you a good control over the board, especially the Acrobat deck, which allows you to see the 2nd row of cards, always. With Acrobat deck the RNG is tuned very tightly, leaving you almost no room for error to counterbalance the passive ability mentioned earlier.
Despite the bad parts taking majority of the review I still would recommend the game, especially on sale (it gets up to 75% cheaper). Even at its worse (when RNG takes over) you can, in most of cases, prepare yourself and continue your runs. There's plenty of fun to be had, potentially dozens of hours before achieving everything. Great time-waster and "just one more fight/run" game.

The Blackwell Legacy is an old-school point-and-click adventure game, and it's definitely true to the adventure game roots, though with an added twist: in addition to solving puzzles to advance the narrative, you also collect clues and piece them together in order to solve the mystery.
You're a medium whose job is to help wandering spirits pass on, and I personally enjoy the combination of the detective story backdrop combined with supernatural elements: the detective part makes the game feel grounded in reality, and the supernatural elements add a sense of dread, of things being off-kilter.
The game has an incredible amount of (really quite good, in my opinion) voice acting, some memorable character designs, and some good dialogue. For a narrative-based game, there is a surprising lack of clunky or stilted dialogue in this game; people think and speak like ordinary human beings.
The game is not without its flaws. A few of the puzzles can be difficult, particularly for people not experienced with adventure game logic. The ending is a little cliche, and I personally was disappointed that
, but some of his well-written dialogue at the end of the game more than made up for that. The game is a little short for its price -- maybe three hours -- so you might wish to get it on sale if you can, But all of these shortcomings are ones that I'm willing to overlook due to the overall high production quality of the game.
I really can't say enough for how well-designed Rosa and Joey are; from their visual appearance to their animations, their dialogue to their personalities and voice actors, it's all really high-quality work, and quite frankly more games should put as much effort into their characters' verisimilitude. Ancillary characters are given the same treatment but with a lighter touch -- just enough to give us a sense of who they are, but not so much that we feel overwhelmed.
The game also has an interesting commentary track from creator Dave Gilbert, which is sure to prove helpful to anyone thinking about creating their own adventure game.
I recommend The Blackwell Legacy -- especially if you are a fan of old-school adventure games, detective stories, supernatural yarns, or all three.

Do you like text-heavy Point & Click Adventures with
few puzzles? A story that has you trying to piece everything together for days after you've played through the game? Psychological horror that'll most likely force you out of your comfort zone? — If yes, then this game is for you.
Masochisia is a game that plays a lot more like a Visual Novel interspersed with some walking segments rather than an old school Point & Click Adventure or a Telltale-inspired game. It's not for its gameplay that you want to buy this game; you want to buy it for its twisted story, its deranged characters, and the way it'll mess with you. While the game does use jump scares, the true horror of the game aren't the monsters that are hiding in the dark. Oh no, the horror lies somewhere else entirely.
If any of that sounds appealing to you, then I can only urge you on to immerse yourself in this dark tale.
In case this is important to you:
How long will it take you to play through this game?
How many endings does this game have?
Is the story linear?

FULL DISCLOSURE: I was given a press copy of this game prior to release. It is your right to disregard my opinion based on this fact, but I assure you that this has never affected, and WILL never affect, the way in which I construct this or any other review I write.
If you'd prefer a video version of this review, have a look here:
PRESENTATION
Its visuals are entirely appropriate. I really liked the style and designs of the characters, they lended to the overwhelming atmosphere of, just, pure dread. And I’m serious when I say that; you feel like you’re drowning when you play this game. But next to all that, there were a lot of moments when I noticed that the visuals and music seemed quite pleasant. And in many ways, that made the game feel even more disturbing; 95% of the game is seen through this old TV screen style filter, so even when you feel that everything you see and hear are not disturbing, there are still elements - like the TV filter - that remind you that things are not quite right. I’d say the one thing that takes away from the atmosphere, is that maybe 5 times throughout the whole hour and a half experience there are jump scares and they don’t really fit into what is going on. This game works best when it’s being psychological with you, not when a wolf-man jumps out of the trees.
MECHANICS
Mechanically there is very little to say. I already mentioned that the game plays more like a visual novel than it does a “game” so be aware of that before you purchase. There’s some puzzles, and you often have to remember details from earlier in the game but, honestly, I though pretty much all of it was very simple. I figured everything out almost immediately because the game does hold your hand. It telegraphs the answers to puzzles pretty unsubtle-ly, which wasn’t a big issue for me but it may very well be an issue for some people.
STORY
But I wasn’t in the game for the puzzles, I was in for it’s twisted look at human psychology, and it does not limit itself to behind the screen. The game is entirely dark. There is no bright light, and I mean that in the sense that there’s no hope, almost anywhere in this game, and it is specifically designed to wear you down. That in itself will be enough to make a large number of people unwilling to continue with the game, and I think understandably so. But the game is trying it’s hardest to put you inside the mind of the protagonist, and in some ways put the protagonist inside of you. This game challenges you; it challenges your morality, it challenges the decisions you want to, or do make, throughout the game. It criticizes you for trying to justify the actions you will probably take when you play, and is ultimately unfair in the way it tells its story, and I mean that as a compliment. It sets you up for failure at the very beginning of the game, and it uses some really sick tools to send you its message. It also breaks the fourth wall in a lot in ways that are really inspired and cool, and really helps to make this experience a memorable one. I did feel that sometimes the dialogue was kind of up it’s own♥♥♥♥♥and melodramatic; I got a little sense of that, but I do feel it fits with the tone of the game and the person you’re playing as. And that’s all i’m gonna say about the game. I think I’ve given you enough information that you know whether or not you would like it, but the question remains; is it priced reasonably?
VERDICT
The game is $8 and I think that’s pretty bang on, if not, maybe a couple dollars too expensive. You’ll really need to judge that for yourself; but I think it’s pretty obvious that if you're the right kind of person I’m definitely recommending this to you. If what I’ve said in this review seems appealing, then I have to say you won’t be disappointed spending that $8. As I said, it’s only an hour and a half long but one; I think that length fits, and two; I think there’s enough quality that the brevity doesn’t matter too much. Really if you're playing this game, it’s for the experience, it’s for the psychological ♥♥♥♥-ups that it does well, when you finish it you will feel like you’ve been THROUGH something and that it’s had a relatively profound affect on you. I can’t say that none of that is due to raw shock factor which is a little cheap, but it’s the combination of shock, atmosphere, design, music all the elements of the game that really give it this force that hits you in just the right places to make you feel worn-down, upset and disturbed. There’s no way around it, this game makes you feel like crap and it might have something to do with it being called Masochisia. The only thing that really brings it, in my opinion, away from that goal is the unnecessary jump-scares. I recommend this to anyone who feels like this is something they might enjoy, and I have to say, I’m one of those people. I guess I should put it like this: If you enjoy being compelled, feeling strong emotions or challenging yourself, then you’ll like it. I’m tempted to say it’s not even entertainment -- there is little chance this game is going to entertain you in the usual sense of the word.

This game is solid, but not for everyone. Think FTL (a Sci Fi Roguelike game with a couple unlockables), Defense Grid (Polished/under one hour), and Texas Hold Em (Intellegent Gambling/Risk Taking) all mixed up into one.
Bullet Points:
Beatable: Yes
Fun: Yes
Thoughtful and Interesting: Yes
Polished: Yes
Great Soundtrack: Yes
Good Casual puzzel game: Sort of (I find it relaxing)
Can be dominated and beat game after game: No (the random disasters presents a challange, but thats the point right?)
The Basics:
Its a very simple, stream lined game that you are not going to beat every time. If you dont have a mind for theory crafting/making careful desisions or bets, you will likely never beat it. A win can take about 45 mins ish not rushing. They are adding additional "missions" apart from the base game in the future. However, aside from achieving higher scores and achievements, the game includes unlockable crew that you can choose from in the begining of the game that all adds replayablility.
Game Summary:
The game takes four crew on a modernish spaceship and pits them agaist disasters. 10 turns in the game, 1 to 3 disasters spawned each turn, each disaster eating away at ship health or crew health each turn they go unresolved. Each crew member can only work in one room a turn and uses a number of dice to "repair" the room along with activation of room abilities, research, and class abilities. The dice thing kind of threw me off at first, but I like to gamble, so I adapted quickly.
The Bad Reviews:
This game is going to generate hate. Dark Souls/FTL hate. I am excited to see future content for this game, but it seems some people are being burnt after only an hour of playing. For the most part, I believe alot of the people who are hating on this game think that each character's dice is worth six whenver they go into a situation, thats a bad gamble. Some people might also be ingnoring or under vauleing each character's or room's ability, leading to frustration. It only takes a game or two to learn all these though and figure out combinations that are very successful.
Conclusion:
I have played the game through 7 times I think and have beat it twice, the second time with a full crew. Still have hard mode, crew to unlock, and whatever additional content they add. Worth it for me, but again, maybe not everyone.

It's also not going to make everybody happy, because like the boardgames that to some degree inspire it, it has a complex set of rules that you need to understand. Some people will play this game, lose badly, and angrily declare it was pure luck. These people, I suspect, don't have the patience to enjoy what is an amazingly well-balanced and skilful game, if you can understand the rules.
Once you start understanding the order to tackle rooms, the importance of crew abilities, the right time to use assists, and the right time to ignore dangerous rooms, an incredibly intricate game emerges - it's brutally hard, and there is some element of RNG, but it rewards skill, gets better the more you play it, and is one of the finest roguelikes I've ever played.

Its a good looking, easy to learn survival game with a strong theme. But that's all it has. You can be 5 days in, no situations, good food supply, high health, low stress and a well maintained ship. Day 6 starts with 3 situations, more damage potential than your ship has hit points and events which require 6 research points to prevent your crew dying on basic rolls.
This wouldn't be too bad, but there is a lot of this before you unlock any additional characters. So you grind and grind to unlock things that let you grind more. There is no real sense of accomplishment in this process either. Most turns you either got there because you had dice to spare or you lucked out. In other roguelikes, particularly the similar space themed FTL, it gives you an unlock for even getting half way through a campaign. Not here. You have to stick with the grind, learning very little about situation management along the way aside from tips that are not hard to work out yourself.
The worst part are the events. They're almost totally random. This would be ok if you maybe had a maximum of 2 events per turn. Usually you get 2-3, and require dice rolls totalling around 50 to complete them all. If you beat half that total, expect 30 on the next turn and so on. The feedback loop means that if you make a mistake, any mistake at all, its game over. If you do well, chances are its not going to matter. The research system seems to be the mitigating factor, athough you often require banking 4-6 specific dice in order to use these power-ups. Imagine playing a game like Left 4 Dead without the AI director. Just endless hordes of zombies to bash you until you die, and if you do get a MedKit, why not throw in a tank into the mix? My point is if the events were less random, and just showed a glimmer of hope for completing a day, the system would be less frustrating. Instead once the game decides to shut you down it just does it, no matter how well you've done up until that point.
There are more strategies available for beating the game when you have more characters available as synergy is clearly part of how to use the crew effectively. Using the Captain or Medic to provide small boosts to the team work well if the team is grouped together. Over the course of the game this can lose effectiveness as these crew work better when the group is at full size. But this is the part of the game that holds most weight in the strategy elements of the game.
The dice rolling aspect is a nice feature. Out of a potential 30 points, crew members can score an average of 17-18 points when fully functional. Penalties on these dice are strong. One prevents you re-rolling the dice, another removes the dice entirely and the third deals damage to your character. These penalties can vary in frequency and strength. One may remove a dice on any of three numbers. One can deal 3/6 damage to a crew member on a given number on a single dice roll. These can only be mitigated by preparation, and that preparation means you must sacrifice rolls earlier in the game. It adds a lot of frustration to the game, especially since the easiest difficulty still requires these large costs for single use effects.
Many players have proven the game is beatable, and beatable by method. This shows that despite the randomness of the game there is a layer of depth and strategy in there. It just requires a good grind to get there and that just isn't fun. With each playthrough I don't look forward to getting a little bit further every time, because that isn't how the game works. It isn't designed to be fair, its designed to make you feel hopeless and it works.
Will I play the game more? Yes I will. Is it beatable? Yes it is. Is this for everyone? No, its not. That said, a small amount of tweaking could make the decisions in the game more meaningful, more rewarding and/or less punishing when you do well. It doesn't need much, but the bit that is wrong is just holding the game back from a recommendation. Its not completely unfinished (though not all of the content is in the game yet) but it needs some attention, especially in the events department. Going from winning to game lost in a turn is not fun, needlessly sadistic and far too common. But if you like that kind of thing then this is your game. Otherwise, stick to FTL.
* Post Review Edit * After beating the game on Normal I realise just how important it is to get a lucky break just to start the level on good terms. Some runs are just fubar from the start while others can help well with the first few days. Having the right event in the right room can carry you through the game, and its about forcing these events to remain open. However, getting these events in the first place is luck of the draw, but the longer you get through the campaign, the more likely it becomes. It didn't feel like an achievement to beat this one. I also had to use the synergies of the other characters to beat it. The Doctor and Mechanic just can't cut it, especially with their abilities being so weak. In all my review isn't really affected by the end game. It just reinforces the point the game needs attention.

If you can stand the RnG, then you find a game with an interesting story and lots of replayability (the cutscenes are different depending on the make-up of your team and how many people make it). The RnG can also be controlled through mechanics in the game and a good use of stategy.

So, I've seen a lot of reviews that say the game is impossibly hard.  I will admit, it is very difficult, and luck plays a big role in the outcome.  Good planning and strategy will only carry you so far.  It is not impossible though.  I lost my first game on turn 4 because I didn't really know what I was doing, won my second game, and lost my third game because of one exceedingly unlucky roll in which I got three fours to come up out of my five dice, killing my captain, stopping him fixing a damage to crew which killed a second person, followed by all of my between round choices involving damaging crew members, which killed a third person.
Wasn't anything I could have done about it without precognition, was pure bad luck that I lost.  But it was fun.  It was a big thrill to roll the dice and know that so much was riding on it.  And the loss was quick.  This isn't one of those games that strings you along for 20-30 minutes making you think you can limp along when you really can't.  When you lose, you lose, and you start the next try.
Despite all I said about luck, stragety is very important in the game, and can add a big boost to your chances.  Proper use of crew's abilities, especially the captain's it seems, will allow you to help mitigate a large amount of the luck that occurs.  So sure, in the end, it is a roll of the dice if you win or not, but you can do a lot to set up how many dice you have, and what else you can do in addition to just rolling the dice.
You'll lose, a lot, quickly, and sometimes despite the most flawless of planning and execution, but the games are quick and fun, and the knowledge that so much rides on your roll makes it very exciting.

This is more or less a neutral review, take the thumbs down as "Game Targets A Niche Audience". There were some very good and some very bad choices made in the development of this game, and most of them seem to have been conscious design decisions. So far I'm enjoying it, but I cannot recommend it overall. If you saw a youtuber or streamer play this and then actively chose to come to this page, you're probably already in the target audience. If you've played the board game Red November, this is kind of single-player that, except full of despair.
I'm going to start with the intentional reasons you may not enjoy this, because they are dealbreakers if these are not your thing. If they are your thing, consider these to be pros.
-Tharsis is not necessarily a fair game. You will lose early and often, and a few of these losses will be entirely out of your control. My very first game was a loss on the first turn because of some bad dice rolls. That particular situation hasn't come up again, but it is always a possibility.
-Tharsis is /NOT/ a fair game, and it is not forgiving of mistakes. Most turns are a struggle to survive, and any given turn can negate all of your progress. Certain events can hurt your crew members if you roll a certain number. You will roll that number three times in one go and oneshot your doctor. Between each turn you get a choice between various "side projects" for the crew, which usually have a positive effect and a negative effect. There is very little more frustrating then struggling to keep your ship's health ahead of the incoming damage, only to have both options have a negative effect of losing two ship health in return for positive effects that are not useful in the moment.
-To be absolutely clear, Tharsis is not a fair or straightforward game. The basic mechanic for success relies on dice, and plays out much like a euro-style worker placement boardgame. There are certain actions called research projects that can help you overcome insurmountable events, but you only have access to a random group of three at any given time, assuming you have the available dice to use them. There is skill in leveraging your odds and order of actions, but ultimately you are just rigging the game as best as you can and then hoping for the best.
-There is more depth and strategy than will be apparent on your first couple playthroughs, but the game is not going to give you any hints to that. The ingame tutorial, and the video tutorial, are insufficient as to letting you know what the hell you're supposed to do.
Things you might like about Tharsis:
-Game mechanics perfectly convey the atmosphere. You are controlling a crew in a near hopeless situation, and goddamn does every new event make you feel that. I'd almost rather label this as a playable parable, rather than a game. You aren't maintaining your ship through a rough patch, you're fighting to pull your crew out of the jaws of hell.
-Every turn past the first feels like a victory. This comes with the territory of unforgiving games, but when your decisions pay off and you come out ahead it's immensely satisfying.
-The strategy is there, even if the game doesn't tell really you that. Once you pick up the mechanics you can plan your actions to make the most of what you have, as long as your willing to let those plans change as disaster strikes every turn.
There are a few genuine design issues that could use fixing.
-Once a die is assigned for repairs, research, a module action, or a crew ability,  you can't undo it. From a game perspective it's irritating because this is a strategy game, not an action game, and I would prefer to have a "Confirm" option after all my actions are assigned. As it stands, your actions autoconfirm, and then you need to confirm that you're sticking with the actions you can't change anyways at the end of each crew member's deployment. Storywise, it feels a little weird since in-game each turn takes place over the course of a week. A few times I've dragged a 6 to the research bar when I mean to drag a 5, leaving me unable to effectively repair the event that's about to destroy the ship. In game terms, my captain fixed a snack instead of putting out the fire in the greenhouse.
-Sometimes you will know full well there's nothing you can do to salvage your game. A crew member will die, or your last critical roll with fail, and you know that within a turn or two it's game over regardless of further action. When that happens, you'll need to wait for all the events to resolve, then wait for a cutscene to load so that you can skip it, then wait through the side project phase, and wait for all the new events of the next turn to be determined, and then you pull up the options and quit to menu to start a new game. Low iteration cycles are important for difficult games to be just difficult, and not frustrating, so an option to start a new game directly at any point would be a great quality of life change.
-About those cutscenes. Yes, they are skippable, but they happen between every turn, and they are static. It takes a couple seconds before you can skip them, and you will be skipping at least the first few after a game or two. Their static nature also pulls a little bit of the "despair" factor out of it. If you make a bad decision on turn two and fail to fix the "Minus One Health To All Crew" event, and your doctor fails to heal your one-health specialist, whose dice were critical to fixing the engine fire and could not be spared to spend the turn in the med bay, then in the next cutscene the captain will still be pleasantly surprised at how well the crew is pulling together and how there might still be a chance for everyone to survive.
That's Tharsis. It's by no means unwinnable, but you'll need everything you've got to pry victory from the jaws of defeat, and sometimes everything you've got isn't enough.

The Blackwell Legacy is the first game in the Blackwell adventure game series. It is made in the style of 90's point and click adventures which is a totally valid choice. Graphically it's low-res pixellated characters and backgrounds. It isn't as detailed as a Monkey Island 2 or so, but it's good enough.
You play as Rosangela Blackwell, a young woman living in New York and writing for a paper (if I remember correctly). You're aunt Lauren just died after years living in special care in a hospital. She was Rosa's last family member and all this kicks of the story on a somewhat somber note. Soon enough though things get interesting when you learn more about her family's past and end up meeting Joey, a ghost. He compells you to solve a mysterious death and it just goes from there.
The characters and world building are the strong suit of this game. Legacy is a rather short game, but is all the better for it. It gives you a taste of what the Blackwell series is about. It has solving cases, banter with Joey and learning more about the Blackwell family.
Puzzle wise it's quite easy stuff, but I welcome that. I find that really challenging puzzles usually hamper the pace and flow of adventure games, especially if they have compelling stories. There's also a nice commentary mode you can enable, but it does really mess with the flow of the game, so it's best to enable it on a second play through.
All in all I can recommend The Blackwell Legacy to any point and click adventure fans, and those who enjoy mystery stories.

The game is fully and nicely voiced, and specially Joey, he's really amusing to hear.
I believe this to be the shortest game in the series (3~4 hours long), but even if it wasn't the introduction of a franchise i'd still recommend it because it was memorable. As a game on its own, I guess considering the date it was released it's really good!
I'm just going to say as time goes on this series gets better.

4.  Battles are really slow, because the fps caps at about 15.  Obviously this game wasn't really suited for PCs (Basically a lazy port).  I feel like the battles run better on my DS game sometimes.
Honestly, I'd recommend the DS version still, and if you're a 2D purist, go for the GBA version (I don't care for the RPGMaker tone that the PSP version has, but different strokes, different folks there).  If you can't get your hands on either copy, you're stuck with this.  Despite it's flaws, it's still really good, and I actually love the 3D version a lot.  And this is coming from a person that still has the original copy of 'Final Fantasy 2' from the old SNES days.  I just hope Square stops giving very lazy ports of games to Steam for a quick cash grab.  If you own the DS version of this game, stick with your DS version.
Now I'm just waiting for the cash grab that is TAF...
Edit:  Just to say too, after playing a little bit of my DS copy compared to this one, normal mode?  WAY easier than the DS version. While in my DS version (Which was on a new game+, so I had bonus augments to boot!), Edward died about 6 times and Rydia died about 3 times, and that was only to Mount Hobs!  So they toned down the damage in this version and 'hard mode' is the original difficulty of the DS version, I'm assuming.  Either way, if you found the DS version difficult, the normal version will be enough for you.
Stick to the SNES version.

Fantastic solitaire style card game with a rogue-lite twist.  As you play the game you collect elements which then allow you to make special moves - e.g. destroy cards, reveal cards, change facing cards to make removing the next highest/lowest card easier, and so on.  You take turns with an AI opponent who is attempting to defeat you by removing health points.  It's as easy to grasp as Windows Solitaire, but there's a surprising amount of tactics in here.  There is a bit of grinding: it's a rogue-lite after all, but I found the basic gameplay loop to be so fun and entertaining that I didn't feel annoyed by it.  There's obviously RNG, but I felt the balance is good.  As you progress, you collect "coins" that you can then use to unlock new decks (that have different focus on each of the elements on the cards), or enhance abilities of existing decks.
For me it is one of those "casual" games that you suddenly realise you've just played for four hours straight and it's now 2am.  At it's price point it represents great value if you're looking for a fun twist on the classic solitaire card puzzle game.
