text: just.. why.

The writing is unedited and quite odd in particular places (and the story abruptly ends in every route; no resolution, the story is simply incomplete). I know everyone keeps banging on about this, but its plot points are essentially a rehash of Katawa Shoujo's, set in America, with an even more annoying next-door neighbor. The theme of feeling listless and directionless (like a piece of driftwood in the sea, the title actually fits quite well) is only occasionally brought up and abruptly dropped so Matt can throw around dated-at-publication slang (which has only gotten more and more cringeworthy as time has marched on). The main character is unrelatable and treats his initial love interest like garbage, and then the narration implies that she deserved it. The dialogue is terribly, terribly stilted and, once again, the writing is
unedited. It's as if they had never read over any line they had written even once once it was put in the script. The "friendly and helpful"
rich ♥♥♥♥♥ comes off as manipulative and shallow. The explicitly-unlikeable Taryn is the only side character given much depth, and even then she's wildly inconsistent, coming off as very grounded and stable in some scenes, and incredibly unhinged in others
Spending time with the characters engenders hatred, not warmth, in the reader. Character design isn't too awful, but the art is inconsistent (clearly drawn by different artists with nothing in the way of art direction) leading to confusion where one may not be entirely sure the girl in the CG is the same girl represented by a given sprite. There are dozens of minor nitpicks, such as two characters sharing the same first two letters and the same "color" for their name (Matt and Marcus) which can lead to confusion when you're speed-reading or skimming over the text, as you're likely to do, considering the story is rarely gripping. Marcus' jacket is a sickening color of banana yellow. Having a Mexican drug cartel be pulling off jobs in
is certainly a weird choice, and, honestly, between the jacket and the cartel, I was firmly convinced the author had set the story in the cocaine-fuelled 70s or 80s until someone pulled out a smart phone. Frankly, if it had been, it would have given the story more character. Bad characters are given too much spotlight, good characters aren't given enough. The novel is such a mess I can't even organize my thoughts on it.
And, again, it's a retread of
plot points and themes. Any particular instance where you can draw parallels between
and
might have been a coincidence, but when you put every single instance of them together, the odds of it all being a big cosmic joke drop to "astronomically low." Taryn's sprite is Emi minus the hair ties and plus legs (the scene where you meet her is almost the same set-up with Emi, only it becomes even more stereotypical), Yuuko fulfills Shizune's role, May is Misha, Matt is Kenji on a drug cocktail. . . need I go on? But still, even giving them the benefit of the doubt, they damned themselves by including an out-and-out reference to Katawa Shoujo. In a conversation with May and her friend, they point out that, while her pink hair is silly, it isn't ridiculous, or in any way "spiral-y." So, not only do you fairly brazenly take their concept and execute it pretty poorly, you also have to take the♥♥♥♥♥♥
Now, I can tell the writers gave it a good college try. The sprite artists did their job pretty well, even if many of the poses seem unnatural and some (all) of the fashion choices of the guys make you want to claw your own eyes out. But, even with it coming out unpolished, unedited, unfinished, dead-in-the-water and dead-on-arrival, you can tell that the team, at one point,
about it.
But just because it's someone's baby doesn't mean it doesn't fail to accomplish what it set out to. Ultimately, you can't find any theme or deeper meaning in almost anything in this novel. It feels like the creative leads were toddlers sitting in a shopping cart, grabbing items off of the shelves, and the mother, here representing the rest of the crew, was unwilling to tell them no, that's too much, put some of it back. There's a whole lotta stuff in this novel, but nothing substantial. You could say, "Hey, well at least the finished it!" but the truth is that they haven't. It doesn't end, it just
.
If I hate the game so much, why the hell am I recommending it?
Read it with friends. Set a side a few hours, have each friend choose a character (or three; the writers never learned that you need to trim your cast list or you end up with a very large, but very shallow, pool of characters) and pick the friend with the best voice to be the Narrator, crack open a bottle of something icy cold, and let the sweet memories make themselves as you watch a team of struggling "visionaries," a few competent artists, and maybe one semi-competent writer do their absolute damnedest to dig the hole they've found themselves in ever deeper. For added entertainment, give each character some stupid, out-of-place accent.

I'm with dollarluigi on this one. No idea why there are so many downvotes for this VN. I get that it ended abruptly, and is unfinished, but I for one really enjoyed reading it. Honestly, a negative review because it wasn't finished seems counterintuative. If it was poorly written, you'd think folks would be happy it ended. It's the fact we all wanted to read more and find out what happens that left us feelinga bit negative, but that's because it was a great visual novel, ergo should be upvoted to encourage the developers to finish and keep producing gems like Driftwood. Anyway, off soapbox, onto review.
Moderately short (~5 hours of read time for me) visual novel about a young man who has to change schools for his senior year of highschool after an incident in his hometown. Not a kinetic novel, but there aren't a lot of choices if that's your thing. Focuses on his meeting and interacting with a number of memorable characters at his new school and the budding friendships (romances?) he develops. Very well written, butis clearly unfinished at this time, though it looks like there is hope for a second chapter.
Pros:
Artwork - Well drawn, cute characters. Really nice cut scenes and animated bits. Sprites were
obviously drawn by more than one artist, with different styles, but not a huge deal.
Background art was nicely done.
Cost - It was free, and a lot better than many VNs I've read that cost a lot more for a whole lot
less.
Story - It was easy to become attached to the characters, and care about what happens with
them. Descriptions of scenes and people was well done and really emeshed the reader in the
story.
Neutral:
Music - I usually don't play with the BGM going, but did in this case. Overall fit the story well.
Cons:
Text - When the text appeared at the bottom of the page, it often was hard to read due to the pale backgrounds and the
text being in white..
Ending/unfinished - Really left me wanting more. These guys put out a quality product, if unfinished. I for one hope they
are able to finish it at some point. It would be a shame for this group to give up based on the number of negative
reviews.

Honestly, I'm shocked - shocked that so many people don't like this visual novel. I'll admit what caught my attention and convinced me to play was Marcus' situation with getting shot in the shoulder, going to the hospital and having to transfer to a new school made me think of Katawa Shoujo, so I decided to give it a shot. Well, it was totally worth all the time I spent playing.
At his new school, Marcus meets plenty of interesting characters like Matt and May who greatly contribute to the game's humor, which honestly, is one of the reasons I liked the visual novel so much. Not only that but the game has an enjoyable atmosphere that most visual novels don't really have. Even in an incomplete stage, it manages to be one of my favorite visual novels.
The graphics might not be as good as some of the other visual novels out there, but they still work and fit well and aren't unpleasant to look at. For music, not all of it stands out but there are more than a few really good tracks. Honestly though, I don't get how people don't like this; it's one of the better-written visual novels. I guess some people wouldn't know what good writing is if it bit them in the face (I mean, how else would Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Dual Destinies, the worst Ace Attorney game have gotten such positive reception?). Anyways, Driftwood is DEFINITELY worth the time spent playing it.

You know in WRATH OF KHAN where Spock says Khan lacks a 3-dimensional sense of battle? Do you wish a whole game was that? But in a whimsical meathook roguelike universe? I love Flotilla very much.

I like the random events that make up your story, but I do not care much for the gameplay. If I had to recommend another one of their games I would say pick up Atom Zombie Smasher over this Unless you like space battles in turn based maneuvers that is.

I bought this game during the 2017 Steam Sale, and I already have 0 regrets. The story evolves as you play, linking later interactions to things you did earlier- but ultimately it's just a tiny little bit of polish to link the real parts of the game together.
The actual beauty of Flotilla lies in the atmospheric, engaging combat. Every 30 second 'turn', you instruct your ships (starting with two, but I've so far had up to four, of at least five different varieties) as to where they should move, how they should be angled at the end of the 30 seconds, and who they should prioritise firing at. Each of these three things becomes vital, as ships are near-indestructible on the front and top armour, mildly vulnerable on their sides, and incredibly vulnerable on their rear and underside. Positioning is paramount, and it's a dance you have to play in predicting how the enemy is going to move so you can counter it with you own.
The whole battle sequences are set to soft instrumental music, which is the perfect atmosphere for narrowly avoiding certain destruction, or for cringing as your clever movement accidentally turns one of your destroyers into a battering ram. For the second time that game.
Ultimately, if you like the gimmick of turn-based orders that play out in real time, you'll love Flotilla. It's one good idea executed perfectly, and that's all I wanted it to be. 10/10

Who will like this game: People who liked Amerzone but didn't play either of the first two Syberia games. Maybe someone who like Postmortem but not the follow-up Still Life (or, maybe someone who like Still Life 2 better than Still Life).
Who won't like this game: People who loved the first two Syberia games.
Let me begin by saying this isn't a "bad" game. It's a solid mediocre. But I cannot recommend it for the same reason I wouldn't recommend Fable 3 to anyone or the Godfather 3. It tarnishes the image of the previous two installments.
The biggest strength of this game is that it does well in showcasing Benoit Sokal's artistic and imaginative legacy. The sense in being in a world not quite our own is still present in this game, and there are still beautifully creative animals present. As a standalone game, this might be a nice addition to Sokal's repertoire.
Now the bad. First and foremost, the voice acting is god awful (at least in English). It feels like back in high school, when you were reading a play as a class, and that one kid really wanted to read the lead role's lines but couldn't quite figure out how to respond to the rest of the dialogue. The inflections are often wrong and the cadences are off. Moreover, there are only about five voice actors, and they don't really change their voices, so it gets more annoying than hearing the Winnie the Pooh guy in every hold in Skyrim.
Second, the controls are weird. While the first two games were made for PC, it's clear this was primarily made for consoles, which really screws up the puzzles.
Finally, this is the game that nobody (should have) asked for. In Syberia, you get a wonderful tale about a young woman's tranformation of character as she encounters a world very different from her high class New York attorney life. It didn't need Syberia 2, but there was a lot of talk about mammoths, so the second takes you from meeting Hans Voralberg finally to the money shot of mammoths emerging from the Syberian planes. So what about this game? There's no Hans, no mammoths, no journey inspired by wonderment. Instead, you've somehow ended up sick in the middle of Russia (how?) and are going to help the Youkols with their snow ostrich migration. That's the story. It feels like being cheated after the epic journey that took place over 1 and 2 (most of the story of 3 takes place in the same town as well).
If you feel like you need to play this game for closure, wait till it's on sale, but I would recommend avoiding it so it doesn't taint your memory of the first two.

If this were the Kobayashi Maru, this review would be different but that's not what this is being billed as. Here's my suggestion; go onto your roof and balance a board out over the edge. weight down the end on the roof with approximately 30 medium-sized sleeping cats. Now go out onto the edge of the board and play yahtzee. Maybe enough of the cats will stay napping on the board that you won't fall off or maybe they'll bugger off tipping you into the abyss. I'm seeing too many negative reviews saying that this game is unbalanced, ill-designed, too hard, too RNG-heavy, etc. I want to briefly adress those concerns for those who are unsure about buying the game.
Yes, the game is hard, but not impossibly so. Most of the negative reviews would have you believe that everything boils down to luck, that even if you play perfectly you will still get screwed by RNG - and this is simply incorrect. This game is about managing dice rolls. The rolls themselves may be random, but the gameplay is brilliant in that it offers a ton of ways to play around randomness. You need to strategize and figure out how to make your chances better. The game's rules and mechanics are deceptively simple - you can pick it up and instantly think that you've learned all that there is - but being able to see all your options requires experience. During my playtime, I gradually learned how to play more efficiently and cleverly, how to cleverly manage some of the frequently-overlooked mechanics (like using/generating assists or refreshing research options at the right time), when to take risks and when to play safe... Now with 20+ hours under my belt, I can consistently beat the game. In short: The game is not that hard. It's easy to learn, and hard to master; but mastering it is very rewarding.
If you are not up to the challenge of mastering it, don't buy this game. If you like strategic thinking and risk management, give it a shot. Just know that you will lose many games in your first few hours - but if you learn from your mistakes (and don't blame RNG when you take an unwise risk and it doesn't pay out) you will get better and start winning consistently.

The Blackwell series is one of the best point and click games/series I've ever played. The puzzles are solid and require genuine thought and problem solving. In almost every case, I found the solutions satisfying and got a real sense of accomplishment from working through them.
The story is just as good as the mechanics. You and your ghost companion have to solve murders and other supernatural puzzles, and help the spirits involved move on. It is a pretty unique story idea, and works very well for a point and click game because you can go back and forth between your human character (who can interact with objects and talk to people) and your ghost character (who can walk through doors and walls, but can't really interact with anything).
Not only are the individual stories in each game good, as the series moves on, and as you work through each episode a bigger story starts to emerge. There is always a sense that the story is progressing, both in terms of the individual case you are working on, and also in the broader context.
I wish all point and clicks would take a lesson from the mechanics, story, pacing, and all the other great things about the Blackwell series.
The only negative thing I have to say is that the individual episodes of the series can be quite short in some cases. Think of this as an episodic game rather than a standalone one.

Also, Scrooge doesn't sound as energetic or enthusiastic as he probably should for the situation (demanding his nephews be set free or narrowly escaping death), but it's still pretty  awesome that the original voice actor for Scrooge (now in his 90's) voiced it.
Gameplay wise, it's the same as the original, with some tweaks. A 2D platformer with a pogo-cane attack. There is a extra heart powerup hidden within each level, as well. I played through the game on "easy" and found it very easy to complete (you have unlimited lives). I can see it becoming a challenge on the harder difficulties, though, since the bosses are by far the most challenging parts of the game.
I really enjoyed it, and would recommend it to people who enjoy oldschool platformers, and ESPECIALLY fans of the original NES game.

However it has a few negative things, that cause massive frustration. And its not about the difficulty of the game.
First of all - the game is easy EXCEPT when dealing with floor spikes. You see, the hitbox for the character is much bigger against spikes than the character sprite suggests. You will walk close to land spikes and get hurt despite the fact you are not physically touching them.
Second - Some jumps are artifically difficult, because the character for some reason bashes his head in places. You will get frustrated the most about this in the last level. The game is basically very easy UNTIL you hit the very last level, where the difficulty IS THE SAME AS OTHER LEVELS but has a few STUPIDLY SETUP places where the jump is hard to make due to the glitchy hitbox. Not to mention you have a limited amount of lifes to handle it and you cannot replay the other levels to stockpile. So if you fail on your first attempt you will be beating the last boss several times over.
Third - The amount of Cutscenes is overbearing. The dialogue is nice and funny, but when you have to replay the game - boy, will you skip a ton of them. 3 Cutscenes in a row, 3 minutes of gameplay, cutscene, cutscene 1 minute of gameplay, Cutscence. Get used to this - this will happen.
I used to play this game on the old NES. I love how they added a story to this game, but I prefered the old version when it comes pure gameplay. This one has two extra levels, which is nice BUT the weird spike in frustration at the end is really stopping me from giving it a positive score.
Overall? You have to decide.
I am not lying about the cutscene intensity - they are everywhere and YOU WILL feel it. The game is VERY SHORT. If you would be skipping Cutscenes all over, a proficient player can beat this game in an hour. I recommend getting this on a sale. Otherwise, seriously, it is not worth the price.
I'm sorry to the guys at Wayforward. I really love the graphics and humor and music of the game. But it has these small itches that frustrate you during the game.
You have been warned dear reader.

Let me first go over what I dislike about this game but why I still recommend it.
1. The best features are all locked behind DLC which to me is absolutly absurd. We give♥♥♥♥♥♥to EA all the time about stuff like this, but at least their DLC for Simcity included things you felt were not meant to be part of the base game. It felt like an expansion rather than randomly added features. There is no good reason why natural disasters needs to be locked behind a DLC.
2. This is a great city builder. Yes, that is actually one of the reasons I dislike it because it's too much city builder and too little sim. Despite all the crap SimCity had gotten, it was actually a lot more fun to me to play it, till you got to the game breaking bugs of course.
3. This can sort of go along with number 2. Progression sucks because there really isn't any. Your progression takes the form of milestones but it just feels very arbitrary.  Liek if you had it all unlocked in the beginning it honestly would make no difference. SimCity also did this pretty well. You could upgrade your buildings, and unlock different specializations. I also loved the concept of making different cities that accomplished seperate tasks. Cities Skylines largely lacks this sort of thing.
4. It's not very unique and I would argue is actually quite bland. Nearly every city feels and looks the same. It just gets very boring after a while.
5. It's way too damned easy. This goes back to number 2 as well. It's too much of a builder and too little of a sim. It's nearly impossible to fail in this game.
So why do I recommend the game still? Well, if you can get over the above issues, it's actually a pretty great game either way. I havn't played any of the DLC yet, so some of those may circumvent some of those issues. It's a pretty game. If you liek building cities, you will like this game no doubt.
I do think the game is overreated though. I think SimCity failed so badly that what happened is the bar was set very low so this game seems amazing in comparison. The whole DLC thing is also a let down. It's expensive as♥♥♥♥♥♥if you want all the DLC. It's nearly as bad as the sims games.

Cities: Skylines is an amazing new take on the city-building genre. I played SimCity, and didn't like where EA took that series after Will Wright left Maxis. I was really hoping that the SimCity would capture that same look and feel of the best game in the series, SimCity 4, and while updating the old ways and making them better, but sadly, even with all the improvements in graphics and different gameplay elements, SimCity did not feel like a true successor. That's where Cities: Skylines shines.
As soon as I started up the game and got to the main menu, I enjoyed what it had to offer. Cities: Skylines feels very new and unique in it's own way. It's doing it's own thing with city-building, and it doesn't feel like a ripoff. It's very easy to play and learn, and that's one thing I like about it. I can jump in my city at any time and start up where I left off with ease, and it runs pretty smoothly as well.
Another thing I like about the developers is that they keep releasing content for the game, and I find their support of their game superb. I never have felt like I got that with EA's games. Even with Spore, there were a couple DLC packs and then that was that. No more support for another great game that could have been even better with further support from Maxis. The developers at Colossal Order Ltd. are very supportive and helpful when it comes to playing Cities: Skylines. I'm happy with the final product, and even happier that they choose to further support their game by releasing new expansions and updates to improve upon the base game, and finally, the fact that user-made content is appreciated and encouraged by the developers themselves. That is a huge plus in my eyes.
I rate this game 5/5, 10/10, and 100/100. Very good work, Colossal Order Ltd.. Keep it up!

A brilliant little space strategy game with full 3d movement and choreography.

One of the few space strategy games that actually operates in three dimensions. This game is designed for replayability and has short, randomly generated encounters. If you want homeworld-like strategy challenges in an FTL-sized package, look no further.

is a turn-based highly tactical space fleet simulator with a simultaneous turn resolution. I wrote the word "simulator" intentionally because this game allows to move ships in full 3D just like in the real Space.
It has been 6 years since the release, and the game pretty much represents what indie games were felt like back then. Visuals are very minimalistic but have a certain style and looks fine even today. Low-poly ships, asteroids and debris are complemented with comics and choose-your-own-adventure segments to narrate an action between tactical fights. The game is light-hearted with cheeky humor, maybe sometimes over the top. Classical piano music and game sounds won’t immerse you into a grimdark space battle, but serve their purpose.
Yet all this is an addition to the key game element – tactical space combat. The game disrupts the flow of a space fight every 30 seconds and allows a player to plan her actions ahead. Each ship can receive one of four possible orders and move in a straight line along any of six axis. While a ship can take a lot of damage in the front amour, the other parts are much weaker. This makes Flanking a priority tactic, which very fun to execute in a three-dimensional space. There are also various upgrades for ships to create a progression throughout the plot. Even today, when the space theme blooms and shines, it’s hard to find many space opera games with same level of simple controls and freedom of movement.
As I said, the game represent what the indie games looked like back than. A charming and small product is built around single idea, which it delivers rather well and satisfying. Of course, by the modern standards the game is too short and too unpolished and should have a multiplayer and… But hey, six years have passed. And the
is still available.

It's on sale at the moment and may be one of the best strategy games I've played in years- simple, fun, quick to play but with loads of depth - I won't claim to be good at this game but from the moment the classical soundtrack kicks in through to that final last missile that decides the fate of your battle, this game captures the wonder of space warfare (from my dreams at least) perfectly!

Slow-paced and interesting strategy game. Kind of like Frozen Synapse but way simpler and with six degrees of freedom... and a roguelite.
Engagements have an interesting dynamic where shots against armor do almost nothing, while shots against no armor are devastating. FIghts often play out as a protracted ballet of positioning and repositioning, until a single mistep leads to a sudden, violent conclusion.
The rouglite aspect is kind of meh. Runs can be a little too random: sometimes not much happens, sometimes you see every single cool thing the game has to offer in one playthrough. But I still thinks it's worthwhile.

The main story is extremely basic, but as you move through the universe you'll meet crazy characters, creatures, make friends, and make enemies. Every play will be different
Flotilla has a unique and striking presentation that works quite well, and gives the game a special flair you won't find anywhere else!
This is one of the better Blendo Games' the company has to offer...

Mostly just really boring and tedious to get through, with a few moments of immense frustration.  When Frogwares' Sherlock Holmes games are less janky than yours, you got some problems.
Level design - A lot of the areas to explore are huge compared to the original 2 games but there's very little discover or do in them.  There's one area that's made up of like 15 screens but only 4 of them have anything actually in them.  That doesn't stop the developer from hiding critical, difficult-to-spot items around those areas though, so sometimes you will travel in circles for several minutes only to realize the thing you needed was hidden under one of 50 random benches in the environment.  This makes it so if you get stuck, it's often way better to just open up a walkthrough and read ahead to where the item is hidden rather than waste your time.
Puzzles - Puzzles are straight from the 90s point-and-click philosophy of design.  They're often not explained at all (or poorly explained) so you spend a lot of time just going "what the ♥♥♥♥ does the designer want me to do here?"  When you do encounter an obvious puzzle, it's mostly just laborious to complete.  Follow a set pattern and turn 10,000 knobs in a specific pattern.  When you screw up the pattern, you get to start at the beginning again.  The game isn't even consistent with how it presents UI or icons, so it's hard to even tell what you CAN do in a puzzle.  Once I realized I had completed an entire puzzle backwards because of this (not going to spoil where).
Controls - I started off with M+K but switched to controller 30 minutes in because I was having a lot of trouble navigating the environments and controlling interactive objects during puzzles.  This didn't work all the time though because the controller can't highlight all the interactive objects on screen unless you run up to them and it's possible to situate the camera in a way so you can't interact with the thing you want to interact with (it's weird, but trust me here).  I ended up using both controller and M+K in different spots whenever one of the wasn't doing the job.
Voice acting and translation - Holy crap, I think the original games were better than this and that was 20 years ago.  There are points where the voice acting is so wooden I thought it was being read by a computer (i.e. Sarah).  This is mostly just distracting, but it becomes frustrating when people give you clues to complete puzzles that end up being misleading because of translation issues.  One time a character told me to turn a wheel on a ship's bridge.  I was like "okay, I'm on the bridge and I can't interact with anything."  Took me about 10 minutes of wandering to realize he meant the wheel was on the ship's DECK.  I had to take a breather after this.

UBisofts decision to take a one year break from the yearly releases of an Assassin's Creed game was a wise decision.  The yearly releases were taking a toll on the game making every game seem way too similar and also causing fatique among the fanbase.
Flash forward to 2017 and the release of Assassin's Creed Origins and we see a very different but also very familiar game like its predecessors.  Much of the annoying tropes (e.g. infiltrate and eavesdrop or follow a suspect etc) of the game have been removed and new gameplay mechanics have been introduced.  But even with these changes it hasn't altered or changed the very distinct 'flavor' of the Assassin's Creed world.
The game is now a huge open world divided up into provinces and you're free to roam anywhere in the world once you finish the initial inroduction of the game.  The game for better or worse has become a RPG, introducing experience points and skill points used to access a 'Skill Tree' system to further improve your characters abilities.  Hundreds of quests not related to the main story are also a new part of the game helping you to gain experience points but also helping to flesh out ancient Egypt and make it feel more alive.
The fighting system has also been totally overhauled. Gone are the days when you could counter almost every attack and with very little effort instantly kill your opponent. The new fighting system is much more involved making you block or dodge out of the way of your attacker and than counter attack.  Although the combat can be more frantic it makes for a heart pumping and rewarding affair.
The beauty of the world is truly something to be seen.  This is one of those games you use to show off your new graphics card!  The Assassin's Creed series has always been known for the incredible worlds that have been realized and Assassin's Creed Origins has raised that bar.  The graphics quality are simply stellar and the level of detail is mind blowing.  Especially when many people who play the game may never see half of what is in this world!
The story is done well and the protaganist 'Bayek' is a likable and believable person in the world.  Dealing with a personal tragedy only to unearth an incredible conspiracy.,
Assassin's Creed Origins is not only the tellings of the beginnings of the Assassin's Order but also serves as a solid foundation for future games.

For more info:
Walkthrough part 1
This VN drags on, spends a lot of time on mundane activities, and never reaches a satisfying conclusion.

Cons:
1. inconsistent character art juuuuust enough. It isn't like Fullmetal Alchemist and Vampire Knight characters running around together on the same page, but it's just enough that anyone can really feel an almost uncanny-valley effect of it. And at times, it's actually staring me right in the face it's so inconsistent.
2. Grammar issues of the 4th kind, though few and far between... such as not quite on every bottom-text panel... but enough to where you'll be able to see one or a few each time you boot up this game.
3. Clearly others don't share this opinion with me, but I HATE the whole "wall of text" thing that this is and Katawa Shoujo did. However, this did it so flipping much. At some point, I just clicked through the big blue wall and didn't read any text because it was so frustrating. Walls of text in VNs are not fun. They take away from the character art, background art, and at times even drown out the music, just to put in a bunch of text that they really could have put in on the original bottom-text panels. No walls are ever necessary. I'm looking at you, Trump. (Cheap trump jokes are cheap, I know.)
Pros:
1. ... Uh. OH! Background art was gorgeous.
2. Despite being inconsistent altogether, the character art itself was actually just fine. Didn't come across any weird incoherent pixel monsters or anything like that. It passes. (Emphasis on "passes".)
3. Characters are fine, too. MC is clearly a guy that the other reviews here don't wanna cut any slack, but he was shot and forcefully moved from his home school to a new place. The fact he's timid and critical about his new location and the people he meets shows he's reserved since he just went through a pretty traumatic situation at the start of the game. The fact he isn't really a fan of his parents for moving him, is normal. Would you like it if your parents moved you from your city and all the friendships you built up? The hippie science teacher, Mr. Mallard, is fun and likeable. Nice guy. Yuko is also a very helpful female cohort to Marcus (MC).  Matt and Elric seem like stock characters wearing human skin though, but the game knows this and doesn't put them in a lot of situations (other than to be sidekicks) so I really just have blocked them out at this point. They're there for some side fun.
So as you can see, I'm pretty conflicted about this game. It's got a few good things to it... and it's got quite a few bad things to it. But, I've been told to just round down when it comes to a situation like this. So, if I gather that my feelings on this game are ambivalent, as my list of pros and cons demonstrates, then it actually is just a bad game.
Therefore, I don't reccomend this.

At first, I was going to say that, despite its issues, the amount of work put into this free VN is commendable. However, I eventually learned that this was backed on Kickstarter, so there's really no excuse.
By "the amount of work", I mean the few pros of the game: its length, decent amount of CGs and animated opening. They're still followed by cons, though: the sprites and a bunch of CGs look very different from each other, to the point you may not recognise some characters at first. Story-wise, they waste too much time describing meaningless things and the prologue is dispensable.
Now for the characters. Our protag, Marcus, is an ungrateful brat to his friends and family, and seems to instantly hate, look down on or be freaked out by everyone he meets. Some of the other characters are nice, but most are based on anime tropes and it's like the writers tried too hard to make them quirky.
We also have issues on the technical front. Borderless white text on semi-transparent blue text box often makes it hard to read. Despite changing the settings, the Skip button still skipped over everything, not only previously read text. No History button either. And last but not least, due to the lack of a CG gallery, achievements or an ending list, you're never really sure whether you've beaten the game or missed any endings.
As much as I'd like to support free VNs, I can’t recommend this one. Writing is nothing special, art is inconsistent, and technical issues kept me from playing through more than 2 routes. It's still free though, so it won't hurt to check it out unless you're super busy. 3.5/10

This visual novel is greatly underrated. It seems to me that many reviewers compare it to AAA-tier visual novels, which in this case is unfair, or nitpick it. For a first visual novel, the amateur team has done a good job. After a relatively weak start, the story picks up and the characters' personalities (although a little bit cliché) are interesting enough to catch your attention. However the male characters are pretty bland and one-dimensional with one or two exceptions. This VN stops after Act I, which leaves you to want more. It's unfortunate that the ending is very abrupt, I would have preferred a partial closure. Instead all the plot points are left hanging, and I'm sure they are continued in the upcoming sequel.
The art is top notch, the BGM is forgettable but doesn't sound like it's out of place. The script is decent enough for me to recommend it. Nonetheless the comparisons to Katawa Shoujo are justified, I can definitely see the similarities. Even though Driftwood pales in comparison, I suggest you should give it a go.

Nah... Savage is a really boring game... It's mostly you versus bots the whole game... The pace of the game is slow, there is no jumping and no flavour to the game. The objective of Savage is to destroy your opponent's Stronghold before they destroy yours. There are 2 opposing factions, 1 Human 1 Beast. Humans use range weapons while Beasts use melee attacks. You can choose to play either from a Real Time Strategy perspective where you are a commander doing extremely mundane chores like telling worker drones to mine minerals and building crappy buildings to unlock unit types.
In my opinion, it is far simpler to use the Beasts as the map is very big and the Beasts have the ability to dash.
Conclusion, it looks good on the ad but it fails to deliver.
1. The Behemoth
Very good wind-up action where you lift up an entire tree, then bring it crashing to the ground. That's the same creature in the ad. That's the only good thing in the game.
1. Boring
There are dead zones in the map where you can just run to and ignore the fighting with no consequence.
2. The K.O.N.G.
Junk. It moves so slow and it has a blind spot directly in front of its legs.
3. Bob the Builder
Such slow build speeds and why do you have to build them in the first place? The buildings are rubbish. Electric, fire and chemical? Why not call them red, green and blue? Why do you need to build 3 different buildings at all?
4. Low Player Population
It was all bots, bots and more bots.
5. Unlocking Unit Types
OMG... You actually have to unlock the support unit called the Chaplain by building a Monastery. This is similar to playing Team Fortress and having to wait for the Medic class to be unlocked.
6. Lousy Commander Actions
If you have played Battlefield's Commander position or Natural Selection's Commander Position, this is a total borefest. You have no way of killing the enemy, it's purely Bob the Builder.

However the entire series builds up to a disappointing and almost nonsensical conclusion that will sour the overall experience on top of many unresolved plot lines and convenient storytelling. The payoff isn't worth it, and retroactively breaks the semi-good times there are to be had.
Personally speaking, what the series needed for a recommendation from me was a solid ending. Not good or amazing, but something that tied all the loose ends up. Instead its poor ending tips it over onto the other side of the fence and amounts to a disappointing adventure.

Rodina is sorta-kinda to space games what Kung Fury is to movies. Maybe that's being slightly too generous, but I guess I'm thinking in terms of direction. It's a throwback to a nostolgic art form that takes advantage of modern technology to produce something spectacular. Or at least, that's how you need to approach Rodina in order to appreciate it fairly. The truth is, anyone who is spoiled on Bioware games and the like complete with all interactions and audio feeds being fed to the player via *cough* audio may not like the fact that the storytelling in this game requires a lot of context switching from gameplay to patient reading.
That said, the lore (which, again, must be read) is surprisingly well written, it's witty and sometimes filled with sarcastic humor while at other times helps immerse the player into the backstory of this universe. And by universe I mean solar system, and by solar system I mean planets surrounding a sun that themselves are surrounded by asteroid belts. And by this I mean you can seamlessly fly around to any of these and interact with them. No cutscenes. Everything is linear. There is travel scaling (such as "gears") so that you don't have to sit around for hours, but you're in complete control. You can land on an asteroid (which is where the game starts) or on a planet and get out of your ship and pick up ship upgrades, ammo, and electronic debris that typically contains radio transmissions that populate this lore I've already spoken too much of.
Learning how to play is apparently supposed to be part of the fun of playing. I found discovering the mappings with my Xbox 360 controller and/or tweaking them to be a slightly arduous learning process, but in the end I'm quite happy with gameplay controls. Changing gears using the controller while approaching soil by using a L-trigger + L-Joystick-Down combo is a rather scary, clunky process, but adds to the immersion, I suppose. Mapping to D-Pad up/down would be easier, but feel too arcade-ish.
Between landings, you must evade and/or fight alien sentry drones and other alien ships that are keeping a watchful eye over the planets and the loot. You're armed at first with a machine gun with infinite ammo, but as you pick up planetary loot you can equip other types of weaponry such as missiles and blaster guns. The game seems to support the Xbox 360 controller just fine, which has proven to be my favorite way to play the game, and let me just say that the space combat, while simple, is quite a blast. It's like the 1990s game Freespace, except less fluff, more action, and you can fly to planets and land and walk around, so Freespace has nothing on Rodina.
The game performs a quicksave whenever something important happens such as entering atmosphere or entering battle, which is great because I hate having to redo things that I succeeded doing before. Speaking of "entering atmosphere", any time you approach a planetary surface you must sit through 60 or so seconds of your craft being on fire during entry. It dramatically adds immersion. Unfortunately, there aren't nearly enough things on the planet's surface going on to make atmospheric reentry a worthwhile game "feature", so it does get a bit old after the 20th landing for a loot pickup.
You can walk around inside your ship, making the game feel a lot like a throwback notion of Star Trek at times, but with it being so big it feels rather lonely and non-interactive at times, since you really are all alone. There are some computer consoles you can interact with, but for the most part everything in your ship is Minecraft-style decor. There's a ship interior designer interface where you can redesign the rooms. I find all that distracting, to be honest. I'd rather more gameplay elements be added.
Sometimes your ship can catch on fire (as in, the engine room or your bridge). When this happens, you have three options (that I've found). 1) load a savegame, try to avoid what caused it to happen [lame .. and I'm guilty of doing this most often], 2) grab a 20th century fire extinguisher hanging from the wall and try to put it out by hand (LOL .. honestly this is kind of funny, no ceiling mount sprinklers or anything?), or 3) if you're in space, run to an operations computer console and hit the Emergency Open All Doors button to let all the oxygen out. You yourself might get sucked out into space if you do this, so position yourself where you won't. It's a cool concept. This is GREAT content, by the way, the game author is on the right track!
I hope that people are buying this game and the creator(s) are building up some good cash flow to put back into the game because the help this game needs more content at this point than one person (or a small handful of people?) can do alone. That is to say, the game isn't a AAA game worth $59, but at $15 it is a wonderful way to spend an evening or two, way more interesting than a movie night at the theater.
Features I hope get added: flora, land creatures, body of self w/ switch to 3rd person view, some more complex space situations than drones and fighters (i.e. a mothership to take out Star Wars style), more interaction with the ship's interior objects, some "good guys" beyond lore to join the player as A.I., and multiplayer support.
The soundtrack quality is spectacular.
I'm guessing I'm only about a quarter or so into the "story", if you want to call it a "story" (again, it's a sandbox game with some lore delivery triggers as sequential radio transmission / journal pickups), but I can't help but wonder if my character is himself an android. How else am I out here on my own with no memory?

Okay, let's get one thing straight. This is NOT homeworld. I know it looks like a simplistic indie version of it, but it ain't.  This is one of those "Choose-your-own-adventure" books from the 80s. but with a massively-simplified 3d game built in.
You start off at the beginning with a fixed amount of 'moves' (14), which equate to picking 14 planets out of 20 or so, and have to make the best choices in each situation.    Similar to 'deal-or-no-deal', there's no actual strategy to your next choice of 'planet', you just have to pick planets one after the other until you run out of them.  At each planet, something happens, (the box is opened, if you like).  You have to make a choice, and you either come off better, worse, or unchanged.
I quite enjoyed those "choose your own adventure" books, so this game kinda grows on me.  Each time you play, you get a slightly different set of choices, and therefore outcomes.   I've tried a few different options, and the results are pleasing, and sometimes marginally funny.  Mostly. however, you're left wondering WTF that was all about.  If you do remember those books, you'll remember they were designed to be played during a lunch hour, or  break time. You could rip through an 'adventure' in about 15 to 20 minutes, and once you knew the book, you could scan the text, note where you were and move on, doing each page in a few seconds.  With some of the two-person book sets, where someone was 'chasing' you (Dual-master series, for example), you could very quickly have a chase through the landscape.  That's exactly how this feels.  You play a 'game' for no more than about 20 minutes, maybe 30 if you take your time in the battles.  Each 'game' is wholly self-contained, and when you start the next one, everything is reset, and you play over.   Many of the situations repeat verbatim, so when you're playing you see a picture, pick out a word, like "pirate" or "slaver", and immediately pick the outcome you want, without reading the rest of the text, note the outcome, and move on.
By and large, the game is completely random: There's no ramp-up or anything. When you arrive at a 'planet', and are told to fight, you may be up against easy, medium, or hard at any stage. So, a lot of the negative reviews talk about how hard the game is because you can meet more powerful enemies right at the start.  Well, yes, that's true, in the same way that if you're playing any game, it's only challenging if there's a bigger monster to fight.   However, flotilla has one pro and con in the same 'feature':  There's one strategy that works really well.  It's pretty obvious when you think about it, but I won't spoil it.    There are lots of other strategies as well, but as with most space games, like Homeworld, there's not a whole heap of stuff you can do in open space warfare.
To counter this weakness in the genre, Flotilla has an overlaid 2d-ism on the 3d: Ships have 'tops' and 'bottoms', which means that there's an asymmetry in the usual turning battle you get.   The only thing I'll say is that as long as you have two ships, you should have no problem with battles in this game, more and you're sorted, fewer (i.e. 1 ship), and you have a long fight ahead, which is probably only going to end one way, death.
The game feels like a first project:  Very simplistic art, simplistic models, sound clips taken from other games or stock sources, one or perhaps two music tracks.  However, it's been nicely polished, and you don't get a sense that it's 'raw' or anything.  The bizarre animal images, like deer wearing uniforms, is just absurd, but ultimately ignorable.  In the same way that you ignore the features of the face cards in a card game: It's what the image and its text represent as a positive or negative to your 'game' that matters.
Some of the 'positive' effects allow you to upgrade your ships. Some of the upgrades appear marginally useless, whereas some really affect your life expectancy in the skirmishes.  You get to realise which pretty quickly.
I'd recommend this game if it was on sale for less than (say) £3 or £4.  It suits people who like quick skirmishes of space ships, and have an absurdist sense of humour.  Don't get it if you're expecting a serious story, or subtle combat like Homeworld.

An update and more in depth review(sort of) for anyone who is curious I still play this I simply don't recommend it as it is nearly impossible for new players to get into. It uses a player driven economy which is completely ruined by a combination of bots and monthly "lucky" boxes. It has an optional vip now on top of the pay to win junk and cash grabs from the equipment boxes. It is possible to procure these through in game economy but good luck with that, for a non paying player you are looking at a three year wait to get your first quality equipment piece unless you eat sleep and breath RO.
I have played off and on since shortly after the Dreamcast was announced to be canceled by sega and I was seeking out an alternative to the defunct PSO. I came to RO in the second beta testing phase since my old emachine couldn't even handle this game at that point. I have a few more hours of experience on record than steam may suggest. I launch through the client rather than steam to avoid connection issues from the bootstrap for steams interface but it is convenient to download this on steam since I play everything else on here.
If you are a returning player you already know about the resentfull love we hold for this game and it likely sounds silly to bash the publishers of a game I actively play but they mess up a lot. Though I love the community manager and a couple of the active gms they have no say over anything but events. There is a lot to hate but anyone who has a nostalgic tie to this game knows there is no avoiding coming back to it again and again. It's like a wicked,abusive lover who holds a special place in your heart despite all the bruises and broken bones you suffer when it comes home drunk and angry.
I have tried to get people in to this before but it is simply not beginner friendly any longer. The doram race helps a little but I am sure they will be nerfed even more soon enough. If you catch it during the once in a blue moon janeway leveling events you will be able to get a foothold by making a geneticist. Otherwise it is a truly long term and agonizing time investment unless you are so rich you use money as wallpaper.
Mechanically the game is ancient,made in a time before questing in mmos was a means of progressing. You click cute little monstrosities and wait for them to die, then grab up their gibs to hauk to npcs. You eventually gain new skills to aid in killing them faster and so on.
The graphics are dated and buggy on most up to date pcs(still praying for that directx update so i can stop seeing black,distorted textures and clipping tiles in some maps) but the artistic design makes it able to sustain due to how adorable most things are(there are of course some disgusting monstrosities,and the occasional phallic-like worm creature,just wait till you see hodes after reading this) but it is charming and pleasant if you like anime or manga art styles.
Audio is actually suprisingly good, the music in many maps is really good but it gets repetitive and you'll likely prefer to listen to your own music collection or silence while playing but it is good for the most part.
The community is mixed, there are some truly toxic individuals but there are also some amazingly nice and pleasant players as well, par for the course of any free to play community. The community staff are nice and do their part to keep things interesting when they are permitted.
The class system was revolutionary at least in the US when the game first launched in beta, It sported a Final Fantasy 5/Seiken Densetsu 3 style class advancement system that still continues to branch and expand to this day.
The biggest negative is the player driven economy mainly due to the lack of any auction house structure. They added one but botched the transaction fees so severely nobody used it. You have to use kiosks to vend and players tend to be insanely greedy. The only way to get anything on a budget is to be fortunate enough to meet someone who has the things you need collecting dust in their storage. This makes it very irritating to start for the first time or to have a fresh start in this kind of game. It is possible to never invest a dime on the game,however the time factor will be a good portion of your life to be able to gear up even adequately.
Overall it is a great game if you enjoy a grind and have the time and patience to go through some infuriating moments to get a foothold. Most people will want to stay clear.

Syberia 1 and 2 were among the first games I've ever played, I feel strongly about the series. This looks at Syberia 3 in the light of the previous two games.
Syberia 3 is a beautiful game in its own right. The game has a superb atmosphere and visually it is absolutely stunning. You get the Sybeia-esque melancholic and slightly dystopian vibe as you make your way through dialpidated hospitals, forgotten ships or abandoned cities. The challenges you are faced with are quite creative and unique, with some puzzles even worthy of its predecessors. However, the way you interact with your inventory has changed (you can no longer combine two items in  your inventory together), which I feel has limited the creativity of the solutions. Also, mostly you get challenges from the people arround you, as opposed to through exploring your environment.
The story involves the Youkols, which you encountered in the previous game. It aims to be mystical and immersive, and many times Kate is surrounded by lots of characters. Unfortunately, the voice acting for these fails at times  (e.g old-looking, ample-fronted Russian lady ends up speaking with the voice of an American teen). All in all, the story is not nearly as beautiful and emotional as with the previous games. It is no longer an emotional voyage.
The way you move changed as well since the game is 3D- you control Kate either by clicking os using wasd, but it can be slightly clunky and frustrating at times. Moreover, there are still a few bugs in this game that can occasionally be annoying.
The big thing you don't get, in my opinion, compared to the previous games - is Kate herself. Kate's personality is not shining through as it did before, due to the lack of commentary on things/items around her. There's also the fact that the player now has dialog choices, and can occasionaly control how she approaches other characters in the game.
This is a game worth playing, if only for the breath-taking scenery and atmosphere. It does a good job of continuing the series, even though on certain points, such as story and character development, it does not live up to the previous games.

Tharsis isn't a game you play to win. Rather, it is a game that you play merely to consistently make the best choices with the tactical scenarios and dilemmas presented to you. Every action comes with a cost, and the game is about carefully weighing the net outcomes of every action, the roll of the dice, and some tactical gambles you make on your own volition.
Players can use several mechanics to augment their attempts to save the Tharsis.
1. The first is research. The research pool allows you to put dice in it in order to get special abilities, effectively allowing you to "save" dice to get special abilities in anticipation of a rainy day. These special abilities can be reshuffled at the cost of one die, or when used, the individual slot refreshes.
2. Every one of the ship's modules have a special ability, ranging from repairing the ship and replenishing food and dice if you roll enough of the same die, to one off bonuses that can help you get out of a sticky situation, such as removing stress from one team member, healing to full health, or maximising squad assists to negate environmental traps (void, injury or stasis that applies to specific die results).
3. Crew members have special abilities that can be handy at the right moment, such as moving throughout the ship without taking damage, replenishing assists, reducing stress, adding die and a few more.
4. At the end of every phase the crew's stress levels are calculated, and low stress crew provide sensible "tactical" packages that will affect your next turn.
Every bonus comes with a drawback however. Healing a squad mate to full may mean using a valuable dice that rolled a 5 to heal him instead of contributing towards reducing damage that's destroying the entire ship. Getting more food may mean sacrificing ship integrity. Replenishing assists may mean sacrificing a crew member as that lethal gas leak remains unfixed, so that another crew member gets the chance to safely fix the re-entry vehicle.
Expect a lot of mission failures, some of them right at the beginning of the game. However, also expect many brilliant saves. Expect the making of hard choices and solving difficult dilemmas, as you drive the crew to reach planetfall at all costs, up to the point of cannibalising the dead, or euthanising the weak or dying for food.
Tharsis is a game of mathematical dilemmas and tactical options that come with a cost as you struggle to survive, like playing a chess game with the board itself always changing and in a way that stacks the odds against you, where you must use all your ingenuity to merely consistently make the best decisions with the scenarios presented to you. Recommended if you like unforgiving but winnable quick games that you play mostly for the difficulty.

As others have pointed out, Tharsis is a game where your odds of success are significantly influenced by your luck (or lack thereof). However, this alone does not mean there is an absence of strategy or planning. The game is based around making decisions, calculated risk-taking, and developing contingency/backup plans around the various dice roll outcomes that can happen - those are the skills that the game encourages you to develop. If you choose to play this game, yes, there will be times when you get unfavorable dice rolls, but there will also be times when the dice fall your way too. Based on my playtime, the dice rolls seem random, not weighted to make things more easy or difficult for you (although I have yet to try Hard mode).
Regarding other aspects of the game such as presentation, graphics, sound - these are all solid, although ultimately unremarkable.
If I had to compare this game to another, I'd say it feels somewhat similar to FTL. If you enjoyed that game, you might like this one too.
TLDR; Luck is involved, but it's not the sole factor that decides games. The core gameplay concept is fun, and the game is worth a try.

It is easy to recommend this remastered version of DuckTales.  The devs have taken the levels and layout from the original 1989 version and expanded them to enchance the gameplay even further.  The graphics, music and story have been recreated and even surviving members of the animated series lend their voices.  New areas are included in the original game's levels and bosses are given new patterns.  The game even comes with two new levels exclusive to this version of the game.
It certainly is a nostalgia trip and I would highly recommend it to fans of the original, but I would also recommend it to any fan of 2D side scrollers.  It is quite difficult, which makes it enjoyable.  Various difficulties are included and despite the game being quite short, it does offer some replay value if you attempt the Extreme difficulty.
I recommend picking this up in a sale and experiencing a remastered version of a great NES game.  It will at least occupy you for a couple of hours!

For a platformer, this is definitely worth checking out if you're looking for a challenging, old-school throwback.

I've been hearing a lot about the Blackwell series and their creator, Wadjet Eye Games for years now. As a genuine lover of adventure games, I've always been curious and expectant. This old school, Sierra style adventure game promised to give me a good time and snatch a spot in my list of memorables, I could tell even with one look. Now that I found some spare time to explore the world of Rosangela Blackwell, I am not disappointed.
As you may have guessed so far, Rosangela Blackwell is our heroine. She is a shy, misanthropic yet smart young woman who lives in New York City, all by her lonesome. She writes book reviews for a local newspaper and tries her best to avoid any social contact. She is a silent one, who prefers a quiet and uneventful life, in her quiet and uneventful apartment. Passing of her aunt - and her only living relative that she knew of - marks the beginning of a drastic change in her 'not so silent anymore' little world. Following strange headaches and flickering lights, Joey Mallone makes an appearance and pulls a "Ghost Whisperer" on Rosa. Yes, Joey is a ghost - or rather a ghost guardian, self-titled as "The Blackwell Legacy" - who's been appearing to Blackwell women for generations now and drives them to help lost souls find peace. So, Rosa's actual story begins.
This first game in the series serves as an introduction rather than a full throttle game. We learn about Rosa, Joey, get clues about their backstory and solve a simple, exemplary case real quick. It's more like Ghost Whispering 101. It's a cute game, with some deadpan humor and interesting story waiting to be built more elaborately in the future. Puzzles are ordinary, and with some attention to detail nothing would excuse you on being stuck. You collect clues, combine them and make appropriate suggestions to appropriate characters to progress.
The game also contains a commentary option that appealed to my taste, in sense of presenting behind the curtain information about the development process, straight from the mouth of the horse, namely Dave Gilbert. I found his statements, apologies on recognized mistakes in either the development or story purposes, personally given thanks to visual and recording artists particularly charming. Any error or annoyance that I may point out, is already recognized and explained by Dave Gilbert himself, so... nothing for me to be distasted about anyhow.
I'll be looking forward to the next game in the series,
to discover more about both Joey and Rosa. If you are into adventure games also, I recommend for you to give some attention to
whence you wonder what to play next time. It invoked pleasant memories of classic Sierra adventures like
or
, and rewarded me with further expectation.

The Blackwell Legacy is the first chapter of the Blackwell series: you play as Rosangela Blackwell, a freelance writer who suddendly discovers she has the supernatural power to see and exorcise ghosts. Rosangela is accompanied in this journey by a ghost named Joey who has been acting as the family's spirit guide for decades.
-well-written and mature story
-Rosangela is an interesting character in her own way, she's pretty asocial, lacks confidence and struggles to come to terms with her powers. She's far off from your run-of-the-mill heroic protagonist and this makes her more real and likeable. Joey is also quite charming and offers several moments of humour
-fully voice acted
-good soundtrack
-while graphics show their age there's no denying most of the places you'll explore are quite detailed and well crafted
-the notebook and its puzzles (where you check clues and try to link them) work well
-comes with two commentary tracks, both giving pretty interesting insight into the game
-no resolution options, graphics look as old as they are
-voice acting is so-so, there's also a few instances where audio wasn't properly mixed leading to character voices being slightly too low or loud
-pretty short and linear
-can get a tad too verbose at times
As a first chapter The Blackwell Legacy is a pretty strong one, giving you lots of information on your past, your family, the powers at your disposal and letting you test them during the investigation: the case you'll be trying to solve is quite interesting with a decent ending setting you up for the rest of the serie.
The game might be a bit lacking in challenging puzzles and is a bit more focused on dialogues and investigations rather than giving you alot of chances to interact with the things and people you'll meet but it works and it works quite well.

Note: First, there may be spoilers below. Also, this game is NOT listed as early access, so I am reviewing it as a completed game. That said, I recognize that this is also only the first act (Although it also doesn't mention this in the description), so I wont comment on the abrupt end.
We'll start with music, as the music is quite good for the most part. The only problem I had was that there are several scenes without any background music or sound effects.
The Art is good as well, but there is clearly more than one artist, if I had to guess I'd say three, and they are not attempting to merge styles at all. The result is that there is a vast difference between characters art in CGs, sprites, and what I will call psuedo-CGs, each of them having their own very unique style. The opening animation looks great, but also has it's own even farther unique art style. Some character sprites look rushed as well, most notably the uncle. The game is in 4:3, which seems like a strange choice, but they were probably just following default RenPy. Many of the characters names share the same color, which can get slightly confusing.
Writing - The writing is decent in most places, great in some places, and strange or downright awful in some others. There are lots of filler sections too, such as the main character describing what kind of sandwich he got, then describing how it was rewarding but eventually bland. It's just a side thought that doesn't add to the story at all. Lots of the writing follows this trend, where you will have lots of main plot dialog, but in the middle of sections it'll just detour to some random irrelevant side thought. The idea is probably character development, but knowing that the main character ordered a turkey sandwich and only sort of enjoyed it doesn't develop his character at all.
And on to the story itself - The story is the main area this VN falls apart for me. When I read a VN, I try to put myself in their shoes, thus a good VN to me is one where I can relate to the main character and their experiences. The story starts out with the main character getting shot. This is a pretty clear parallel to Katawa Shoujo, which I assume is their main inspiration, where the main character is also hospitalized and had their old life and new girlfriend left behind in lieu of this new learning experience. The trouble for me is the scenario, which involved a 'Mexican Drug Cartel' (In Boston for some reason), robbing a bank, and pausing in their getaway to attempt to murder the main character. This seems very out of place to me. This is then followed by the 'overprotective' parents deciding to send their child a hundred miles away to live with his uncle, that no one had seen since the main character was a kid, and described in game as a drunk, lazy, unreliable has-been. That's not parents being overprotective, or even regularly protective, thats just parents finding an excuse to abandon their child with a relative. So already, the backstory is filled with very little that helps me relate to the main character or his problems. After this, your character moves to Martha's Vineyard and enrolls in the school. Up till this point I probably would have recommended this as a free one-off VN, but this is where it goes off the rails for me. At this point the main character meets Matt. Matt may be the most poorly scripted character I have ever read. He is clearly written solely to be the main comic relief, but he does so by communicating in nothing but bad teenage slang, no matter how out of place, inappropriate, combative, or completely racist it comes across, and the strangest part is that very few other characters even bat an eye at it. This is where I lost the story, after this point is was obviously writtin with very specific people in mind, and I am clearly not the target audience. The only character whose motivations I could understand was Taryn, naturally combative and accuses the main character of being a low-life despite obviously not being one, an attitude she probably picked up from the rest of the male characters being terrible people constantly. At a certain point I just skimmed through the rest.
I think my earlier point sums up my thoughts perfectly. In the end, this game is clearly written with a specific audience in mind, and not I, nor any of the people I know fit that group, and thus I can't recommend it.

It's honestly hard for me to decide if I should recommend this game, assuming it will be further developed. Knowing that Steam differentiates between overall reviews and latest reviews, I think I will go with a "no", focusing on how the game looks in its current state.
What is available right now is the first act of the game, and it ends pretty abruptly - to the point where I actually assumed the game bugged out and moved me back to the intro. The fact that the ending animation had credits indicated it was all as planned at this point, but still, the story was just cut out of a sudden, which didn't fit an end of a whole act in my opinion.
The writing is... mediocre. I actually 'played' less than what Steam says, because a few times I just went away from my PC to do something quickly and didn't come back for a while, as I forgot the game was still running - with games that keep me interested all the time it's usually the other way around. There are a few typos and grammatical errors, which in my opinion is a very bad thing to have in a text-based game officially published anywhere.
I never considered the visuals to be important in the VN genre, but I have a few complaints here. The quality of graphics isn't very good, but that's OK, what bothered me is the inconsistency and some of the designs. The characters in sprites used through most of the game can look different from when drawn in a group scene, and from how they're portrayed in the cinematic - and you don't have to pay much attention to notice it. Some of the designs can also be a bit... weird. The default pose of the first female character introduced into the game was so unusual it was actually distracting.
The sound, which, in fact, is just the music, is pretty OK, simple, but sounds good most of the time. One or two pieces didn't seem like they were written to be a perfect loop, even though they were used as such.
One last thing is pretty technical - I couldn't seem to find a way to view the log or go back a scene. That means that if I accidentally pressed space, whatever I didn't read was gone for me forever - or until I decided to play the game again from my last save. I think that and the abrupt end of first act is what made me not recommend the game, even though it's free and you can't really lose anything but time trying it out. That being said, I think it has potential to be at least entertaining and am curious how will it be developed.

Overall, Driftwood is a really good game, but it's pretty boring in the beginning.It becomes truly interesting on day 3 or 4(when characters' routes start).There are 5 routes, and probably the biggest pro of Driftwood is that routes are indeed different from each other.80-90% of text in each route is unique, there are only a couple of scenes that appear in nearly every route, and even these scenes are slightly different each time.In many other visual novels 60-90% of text is the same in every route, so Driftwood lets you to feel that your choice of route actually matters.And you don't have to click "skip" every 2 seconds when you are trying to read another route.
About music and art.Music is pleasant and soothing, but nothing extraordinary, except for a few tracks.Great backgrounds, sprites are really nice for the most part.A lot of CGs, but they are of moderate quality.There is a terribly amateurish mistake about CGs though.Sometimes characters on CGs look different from their sprites.The only difference is hair color, you will never confuse characters because of this, and I think it isn't critical, but still, it's very amateurish.You can see an example of this mistake on screenshots 1 and 3.
You should also know that the game isn't finished, there is only act 1 for now.Still, completing all routes may take some time.15-25 hours, I guess.

So, I bet you're here because this game is on sale for basically dirt cheap.
I can tell you with total confidence that this game is worth every penny of the full price.
If you like strategy games and roguelikes, this is for you. It's short and sweet, with unbelievable replayability, and quirky humor splashed over what would most likely otherwise be a somewhat depressing and gritty world. Think if Star Trek went on a bender, and every episode featured Q. That is this game in a nutshell.
On the gameplay side of things, it works like nothing else I have ever seen. The game map is sort of like in FTL, where you move from system to system on linear but branching paths. However, the battles are where things get a little crazy, with a turn-based combat system on a full 3D plane of movement. The depth of planning and strategy you need to put into every move is unbelievable, because if you forget to move a part of a ship in a particular way, that could easily be the end of you, or if you don't check your movement from other angles and directions. Also, something I normally don't appreciate in games but has to be mentioned here because of the complexities, the tutorial in this game is nice and straightforward. It teaches you the ins and outs of combat quickly and in good detail.

Rodina has a lot going for it; it could be one of the best space sims ever made, and it's not a complete game.
The controls are intuitive and easy to learn, which is remarkable.  I've played Elite: Dangerous and spent the first hour going in and out of the options screen.  I spent the first hour of Rodina exploring asteroids and planets and engaging Xenos in combat.
That's the best part here -- no lengthy tutorials, no flight schools, just jump into your ship and go.
The physics model is good, the stellar system is huge, and so far, it's a lot of fun to explore.  I can't wait to see what the developers will add, and add they must, because there's not much to do right now.
I would like to see less inertia in the physics model.  I like flying sideways and backwards, especially in combat, and I've noticed that downshifting from cruise mode to combat mode slows the ship down.  I would love it if the developers would implement zero gravity onboard the ship, but I don't expect that to happen.  Of all of science fiction, artificial gravity seems to be extremely commonplace, yet it is probably the most fictional element present.
Finally, what I'd really like to see is facilities that spawn NPCs, good and bad, and the ability for NPCs to expand operations by building more facilities.  If you want to wipe out the NPCs, you've got to wipe out the facilities that spawn them.  I recall playing Freelancer and Privateer and wondering how busy the shipyards must be as I cut my bloody path through space.
The bottom line, it's a great game, easy to play and lots of fun.  Let's hope they keep it that way!
