A fantastic game.
Yes, it is a game that relies on the throw of a dice, therefore, obviously, there will be a very huge random element.
However, there are a lot of options and opportunities to mitigate the negative impact of a bad dice throw.
Make use of your assists and research options!
Having your crew die horribly and your ship break apart is part of the experience.
I've made it to mars in my third try. Now on to hard difficulty...

I really like it.
of course, sometimes all kinds of♥♥♥♥♥♥is gonna happen around the ship and it will look impossible to fix everything. But there's a way... Most of the time. It might sometimes be a long shot, but hey, it's a flight to Mars.
So, For example, you have this fire in the greenhouse, 29 damage to fix. Also, you get injuries when rolling a 4, a 5 and a 6.
And it does 2 dmg to your ship hull every turn. And your ship has only 2 hull HP's right now.
Well, it looks grim to say the least.
And of course, this isn't the only event going on. So, what to do ? Well, you could rush all your crew to the greenhouse and most surely kill them all trying to get those 29 points with rolls.
But no, you have to think laterally.
So, there's this other event in the maintenance. This one looks better : only 10 dmg to fix, and maybe void effect when rolling a 2. (void makes your dice disappear, rending them unusable for anything)
Now we can see the starting point for a solution to our problem in the greenhouse.
Let's send our mechanic there and roll some dice. With a bit of luck, he will avoid rolling too much 2s. Ok : a 1, a 5, and two 4. Those two four are interresting : in this room, we can use dice of equal value to increase the ship's hull HP. The first two equal dices giving 2 armor, a third one adding one more armor point.
Ok, so now the fire in the greenhouse won't destroy the ship. Not on this turn at least.
Our mechanic isnt done yet. Let's use our 5 to reduce the damage in the maintenance room, and the 1 on research.
Now it's turn for the Captain to work. Let's make him join the Mechanic in maintenance. He ate some food at the end of last turn, so he can throw five dices. Ok : a 2, a 3, two 5, a 6.
A 2 : void. But we had one assist point, so it doesn't take effect. No more assist points though, so we gonna need to build up some more later if we want to throw dice in the greenhouse without risking too much injuries.
With a 4 we could've finish what the mechanic started with his dices and and add a third dice to the hull HP, but no luck.
But with the 5 we can finish to repair whatever was broken in here, so that's that.
Now the only place to use the remaining dices is the research bar, let's do it : with the 1 from the mechanic and the 2, 3 and 6 from the captain, it's almost full, and we already have 4 points to spend on research bonus. Wich is good, because with two more points, we could unlock a sweet 28 damage repair bonus for one room.
Now the solution is clear : Build some more assist points to avoid injuries in the greenhouse, completing the research bar to get the bonus. The place to do that is the Laboratory. Let's send our Specialist there.
She only has two dice to roll, meh, but there's no event going on in the Lab, so we can rolll the dices safely.
Now it's all down to luck.
She might get a 4 and a 5, allowing us to complete the research bar right now on this turn. We could then send our fourth crewmate in greenhouse, use the bonus, and try getting 1 more point with dice rolls to finish the repairs; but with injuries on 4, 5 and 6, it could be very dangerous for him.
Or she might get a 1 and a 6. The 6 can be used to get 3 more assist points, but the 1 would be useless.
Or she might get two 5. With that we could still get the assist points we need, and the other 5 would be directed to research, to be completed next turn.
So that's it. Of course, you might be overwhelmed by terrible events all over the ship on this next turn. Or it could go well with only minor events, giving the time you need to fix the greenhouse and maybe even grow some food for the turn after that ...
Luck is important in this game. Be Lucky, be clever, and you might just make it ... for better or worse.

At this point I cannot recommend Tharsis. It is an incomplete product that shows promise of a great game, but does not yet deliver. I will update my review if this changes.
Tharsis is a dice game, which brings a certain kind of randomness into the game play. Now many games provide dice mitigation and manipulation to stabilize the game play, Tharsis doesn't. Instead it opts for a more poker-like approach where a single roll is not really relevant, your overall strategy is (i.e. you might loose some battles, but you still strife to win the war).
This would be fine, as long as the challenges were generated in a controlled manner. Unfortunately they are not. The game has no issue with generating "unbeatable" challenges for you, my personally most hated are "sniper" -- 3 orange dice of the same value, meaning it will one-shot pretty much anyone attempting the challenge and "black hole" -- high number with a 4,5,6 void dice.
Apart from this, game UI needs some small tweaks and the game overall needs more content for its price (but that is apparently coming).
I do believe that if some of the game mechanics were tweaked and made more transparent, the game would become a great casual time-waster of mine, but right now, I will go back to my board game collection instead.

Tharsis
Most people would say, this game is an RNG simulator and oddly they are not wrong. You are at the mercy of the dice and if you love rolling 1's like I do. I'll most likely lose... But I think that is the main attraction to this game on any level, watching as you make harder and harder choices. People die, more and more hazards start happening. There is a bit of strategy involved, like eating your fellow crew members... tasty!
When you start a game, you lose one of your crew members right off the bat, then things (randomly) start going to♥♥♥♥♥♥on your ship. Your job is to use what crew you have, and fix those problems by rolling the dice. The only thing I feel is so incredibly broken is the "void" rolls. Each "problem" comes with random sets of numbers you can't roll, some are injury, some lock your dice... But the void one is the worst. If you roll any of the void numbers, you lose those dices.
I had one problem where I couldn't roll a 1, 2. And a 5... Plus 3 for injury.
That means I could only roll a 4 and 6, come on! The RNG Gods were not with me! ._.
Like I said before RNG simulator.
Pro - Challenging gameplay, cannibalism, Each crew member has their own skill, Each part of the ship has its own benefit.
Con - You can't just give up, RNG Sim, void dices, some of the "problems" heavy handedly hard.
Verdict - If you are one of those people who doesn't mind losing 95% of the time, pick it up.

I read many of the "Helpful" reviews on here and found myself discouraged to try a game with a very alluring and topical concept.
Journey to Mars and try to survive while your ship goes through some malfunctions while you utilize the skills and abilities of the crew.
Now, before I toss my opinion into the wind, know this. For the past 4 years I've been playing board games every Saturday with a group of friends, so I'm quite familiar with things NOT going my way, and leaving my "Abilities" to chance part of the time. That being said, this is a game that doesn't entertain you like a rail shooter. You're not going to be better than your friend at getting head shots. This game is built for you to feel the desolation and helplessness of the vikings discovering Greenland. You're making this voyage with what supplies you have and HOW you use them is based on failing at the game a few times. You likely will not win right out of the gate. Take time to learn how to manage resources and better mitigate potential damage.
"In war, sometimes to take their life you have to lose an arm."
If you wanted each of your crew members to be Master Chief, don't play this game.
If you want to use your intellect to manage resources, mitigate damage, maintain sanity, and lead a crew of trained astronauts to Mars, pay for the game and discover something new. After all, HL3 isn't confirmed, and you're probably tired of playing COD.

(MAJORITY PLAYTIME BASED ON PS4 VERSION)
Flip a coin, or buy a lottery ticket. Your only goal is to call the correct result. Do you want to call heads or tails on a coin flip, or would you rather attempt to buy a winning lottery ticket?
Tharsis is a game of luck, which means putting the odds as much in your favor as you can. You can't guarantee a coin flip, but your odds are a hell of a lot better than the roll of a die or picking a winning lottery number. When given the choice, you want to flip a Heads rather than roll a Six. Right out of the gate Tharsis throws you meaningful decisions and makes the consequences of each one clear. You need to choose which approach to take, from Brute Forcing repairs to gambling on Research bonuses, to Fixing Under Fire. Whether to take a big risk on week 5 that could end your game early, or to play it safe until you can't play it safe any more. Whether to try and fix every problem, big or small, or to let lesser problems rot and get some crucial prep for whatever hell the next week wants to throw at you.
You can never guarantee success in Tharsis. The most you can do is make the best choices to stack the odds in your favor.
Good luck.

While I generally prefer games that rely more on skill than chance, this was one game that I’ve always really enjoyed, but often cursed the roll of the dice or a card draw. (The hate part of things relates to how long the game can go on for.)
A while back, I received a copy of the digital version of the game. This version appears to have the same “board” as the 2nd edition, but I believe it’s based on Fantasy Flight Games “Revised 4th edition“, since the character and card images are the same. (Also, the expansions match.)
For those that haven’t played the game (or don’t remember much) here’s a summary:
The board layout is three circular regions – Outer, Middle and Inner. Each player selects a character (randomly) that has different starting stats and special abilities. Strength is used for physical combat, Craft for psychic combat. Players have a number of lives, and a bag of gold. In your turn, you roll a dice (d6) and move that many spaces (locations) around the board. Each location represents a place (such as) – plain, forest, wood, shrine, chapel, graveyard, tavern, village, city. Most locations require the drawing of an Adventure card, others have a dice roll to see what happens. The cards may be an enemy or monster to fight, an object that can be kept, a follower who may assist you, etc. Some may allow you to gain Strength, Craft, Life, or Spells. Combat is 1d6 + Strength (or Craft) + item/follower bonuses vs the same roll for the creature. A win means a trophy, else lose a life. Players build up their characters (increasing stats, buying/finding items, etc) and move towards the centre of the board, hopefully gaining a talisman along the way. In the inner region lies the Crown of Command, which is used to drain the life of all other players in order to win the game.
My game box states playing time as “1 Hour plus” and I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game take less than two hours. (Playing the digital version with AI opponents is quicker than with real people, but still takes a while!) This is mostly because of the great amount of time required to build up a character to a level that can enter the Inner region and progress (without dying or being pushed back to middle/outer region). This, and the chance of losing nearly everything with a bad dice roll (or unlucky card draw) is the games biggest down-side. The game play is very much one based on chance. The only skill is in good use of items, spells, and special abilities. There is a lot of variety with characters and cards – it’s also a large board – so every game is very different.
The two main “changes” that I’ve noted in the digital edition (compared to 2nd) are the Fate stat (which allows re-rolls, FANTASTIC addition!), and the ability to increase Craft by trading in defeated spirits (psychic combat monsters). In 2nd edition, you could only trade “strength using” monsters. (7 Str points of creatures for +1 character Strength)
It’s extremely faithful to the board game. The graphics are very well done, and everything runs smoothly. You can play with 2 to 4 players, with those players being AI run, or actual people. The game speed can be adjusted, various “house rules” can be turned on/off, and it saves games. It’s really nice having the game track all your bonuses, and you can click on any board space to get detail on that location, as well as check what cards (objects and followers) any other player holds. It’s got a tutorial mode and good “help”. Overall, I’m very impressed and I can see myself playing a lot of this over the next month.

Ahh, DuckTales: Remastered. Just as a sidenote, I never did play the first one on the SNES. But yeah, as a Disney fan and generally wanting to play light-hearted cartoon-y games a lot, I was excited for this one. Having it gifted to me, I decided to hop straight into this and found that the presentation was fantastic. The visuals are top-notch, pretty much having been remade for this HD remake of the first game, and the music even better. With a New Game option awaiting me, I decided to go for that (and picked Easy mode, mind you!) but went back to explore the other menus later; there waiting for you to pick is a Gallery of sorts, which can also be accessed via the main game's "world hub"/level selector. Options for game configuration are there and play time. That, and a leaderboard which was quite fun to look at (how do people get through the game that quickly?)
As for the actual main game itself, I loved it despite a few small flaws. The character models look brilliant and most of the time, work really well with the backgrounds. We start with a small cutscene and an opening level in the bank where you play as Scrooge McDuck (voiced by the original VA, who just so happens to be around 80, I believe) and you save Huey, Dewey and Louie from the evil (and a bit ditzy) Beagle Boys. In the process, you get to know about the main storyline; get 5 artifacts from around the world and then you'll have lots of treasure (or something like that). Woo hoo!
So what do I think of the 5 levels after this? Pretty good. All different, long and have a great boss at the end for you to tackle, all while getting to know the hilarious Launchpad, 3 boys and Webby who tag along for the ride. Although, cutscenes aren't the best (but are skippable) as they don't show the character's mouths moving when they speak. Another flaw to the game is the sometimes dodgy platforming; whether it's cheap deaths from the weird jumping mechanics or taking a bit of damage when you really feel as if it's not your fault, WayForward definitely could have improved this. It just doesn't feel as great as the Mario platformers, for example (then again, most platformers don't).
So after the next 5 levels (including THE MOOOOON, of all places. But I didn't see Princess Luna, so this is set after MLP season 3 apparently, heh heh heh), you get to save the 3 boys again and try and retrieve the treasure at Mount Vesuvius where you end up defeating Magica and also competing in some weird "escape the volcano" level that really felt bad, as sometimes Scrooge just wouldn't grab onto the ropes and wouldn't jump properly - and that kinda let that down for me, until I realised that there are a few tricks to get it right.
Pros:
+ Great level variety
+ Voice acting is top notch
+ Art is fantastic, so is the game design
+ Good difficulty at times
Cons:
- Cutscenes aren't the best
- Sometimes dodgy platforming
- Length of game isn't great, despite decent replay value
Overall, pretty good game. 8/10 for me. Would (get gifted, but otherwise) buy again.

There's been a trend in recent years to cash in on nostalgia in a big way.  Take an old game, give it a little bit of polish, release it again and rake in the dough.  Sometimes it's welcomed because its handled respectfully, while other times it's a shallow cash grab.  I am very happy to say that this is NOT a cash grab.  If anything, DuckTales: Remastered is an example of how a updated re-release should be done... mostly.
So, as per the usual formula, let's talk about the good to start.  First and foremost, the core of the original NES game, what made that game a beloved masterpiece, is still there and fully intact.  Scrooge still has his bizarre pogo stick ability that is as inexplicable as it is fun, and the levels still stick to the same general layout, even having the same locations for pickups.  The game's tunes are also the same, save for being performed by real instruments rather than an 8-bit chiptune processor.  If you thought the Moon theme was catchy in chiptune, wait till you hear it now.
Of course, that's not to say the game is just a graphical update without any other changes.  DuckTales: Remastered adds some new content to the game, most of it welcome.  While the levels are mostly the same, there have been some minor alterations and changes, most for the better in terms of level flow.  Bosses in particular have been changed up so that they have more than the same single attack pattern to work with, making them far more challenging (though not unfairly so) than their pushover NES incarnations. There are even two additional levels: an intro training level and a final boss level, both with new soundtracks that fit in quite nicely with the rest of the tunes.  The final level in particular was a surprising addition, and is far more satisfying than the original game's "go through this level you already beat" concept of a final level, albeit with a caveat I'll talk about later.
Probably the best thing DuckTales: Remastered brings to the game are the fully voiced characters.  Rather than just relying on canned sound effects and clips from the show, the game actually uses newly recorded lines from the original voice cast (minus the ones who, tragically, are no longer with us).  Yes, this includes Alan Young as Scrooge, sounding surprisingly good for being 92 years old.  Scrooge obviously has plenty of time to say a variety of things, what with all the pogoing and gathering treasure and whatnot, but the other characters get plenty of time to speak, too.  Mostly this happens during cutscenes that occur between and sometimes in the middle of the levels.  These cutscenes are true to the original series, and do a great job of explaining some of the more inexplicable parts of the original NES game; why was Bubba Duck frozen in ice, for example.
Cutscenes aren't without downsides though, which brings me to the next part of the review: the bad. As I said, cutscenes can happen in the middle of levels, which can get very tiring on repeated playthroughs of the game.  You can skip them, but it does take a few seconds to do so, and quite a few are placed such that even that can be a noticeable interruption.  The game also has some serious issues with recognizing all but the most common monitor resolutions, and really didn't like my 16:10 monitor at all.  I was able to get around it by manually altering the game's ini file to use my specific resolution, but it's still something that could have been handled better.  The most maddening thing for me though is that in keeping true to the core of the original game, much of its buggy movement behavior was kept in as well, especially the random things that could cause Scrooge to stop pogoing for no easily apparent reason.  Any fan of the original NES title won't be surprised, but the movement quirks could have been ironed out without angering most people, or at the very least with an optional toggle as was done for the requirement to hold the pogo button while bouncing, a.k.a. "Hard Pogo Mode".
The only other thing I can add about this game is only arguably a downside, but I found it somewhat negative all the same, that being the significantly increased difficulty of the final boss fight (and beyond) compared to the original game.  It's not impossible by any means, but it's still quite the jump in challenge.  I'll freely admit it had me frustrated for a little bit.
Despite the few bad things in this remake, there's clearly far more good things to say about it. Ultimately though, DuckTales: Remastered is a bit of a victim of time, with its gameplay style not nearly as popular by today's standards, not to mention the waning popularity of the DuckTales franchise.  That said, it's still a solid platformer with a lot going for it, and very little going against it.  Fans of the original game will love this update, and people who have never played either can get quite a bit out of it, too, but you might want to watch a few episodes of the original show first.

The plot, the characters, the music, the professional voice acting. I've heard of the Blackwell saga before so I decided to get the whole series when I saw it on the summer sale. I've yet to finish the 4th chapter, but the first three have already proven their worth.
If you enjoy investigations, adventure games, ghost stories and moving experiences, get the game, or rather, the whole series. If you're not quite sure, get just this first one and give it a try. The chapter's finale is very intense and finishing the game will have your thoughts provoked for quite some time.
The puzzles are challenging yet not irrational or overly complicated – you need to listen to the dialogues carefully and pay attention to the envioment, but there's no excessive pixel hunting or other annoying elements you may hate in other adventure games. You can always consult your sidekick for a clue and this whole thing works very well and yet it doesn't feel artificially implemented.
Finishing the game takes about one or two afternoons, the story is very fluent and the universe and its rules are very likable. The stories of each chapter are connected, but since this is the very first chapter, it will also work on its own without you having to play the other chapters. I'm pretty sure you'll get them anyway once you finish this one as, even though you may not realize when playing, you'll miss the characters once you finish the game and you'll want more and see how the story continues.
tl;dr: get the game, at least on a sale, enjoy it, get the rest of the series

Blackwell Legacy is the first in a series of point and click adventure games. It has the elements you’d expect from a point a click: investigating items, finding clues, talking to characters, combining objects and puzzles.
The story I found to be a bit strange but surprisingly I was ok with it and wanted to press on to find out what happens. You are on assignment in a dorm suicide and in the process meet up with a family “friend” that is with you throughout the game.  Now that I’m looking back on it, there’s a lot of death talk that goes on, but…that’s part of the story and certainly isn’t a bad thing!
The puzzles are not hard so you shouldn’t get stuck and the game is relatively short. You’ll be able to finish it in a handful of hours.
The game was released in 2006 and does have a few graphical/audio stutters and some crashes. Be sure to save often. I do see an auto save system which is much appreciated!
One gameplay gripe is that an action cannot be canceled once clicked. For example, I may click on the elevator to leave a location but want to cancel and click somewhere else. You are forced to go into the elevator and back out into the map and then go back in.
+Open “winsetup” in the SteamApps -> common -> Blackwell Legacy folder
+Graphics Driver = Direct3D 9
+Graphics filter = 4x nearest-neighbor filter
+Somewhat interesting story
+Classic retro graphics are done well
+Dialog is well paced (and skippable if you want)
+Characters fleshed out well
+Unlockable blooper voice acting reel (first time I’ve ever seen this in a game)
+Game commentary
+Music didn’t match the scenes I was in a few times
+Can’t cancel an action once invoked (read my explanation above)
Blackwell Legacy is a very nice, short and interesting point and click adventure game. I’d recommend it if you can grab it in a bundle or on a Steam sale.

Solitairica is a rogue-lite card game with RPG elements and a cool story thrown in there. It features procedurally generated attacking monsters and you must battle them using cards and spells yo ugain from your cards.
The graphics are pretty standard for a 2d card game. The art is beautifully drawn and colorful. The whole game has that spooky atmosphere.  The enemy monsters are very adorable and drawn pretty good.
The music in this game is very good and I like listening to it while playing the game. The music has that Halloween/spooky theme going on as well.
The way Solitairica works is the basic concept is you have a bunch of cards on the screen and you have a deck and one card in hand. You must select a card from the top which is one number lower or higher than the card in your hand. You must do this to all the cards and finish all the cards on top. Once you finish them the level is beaten. There can be other tasks too but mostly you will see are missions which tell you to clear the cards.
So the basic card gameplay is similar to numerous card games found on Steam such as Faerie solitaire etc. but this game features RPG elements. You have elements on your cards which can give you abilities which will help you beat levels. You also have enemies in this game and every enemy does something different so you have watch out for their attacks which can do a lot of things. Every monster has a different strategy, some do more damage, others keep adding things like freezing or burning the cards You have an energy bar which when depleted you will lose the game.
Every time you lose a battle against an enemy you’ll have to start the adventure again from the start. They will give you runes though which can help you buy better decks and upgrades. Once you upgraded the decks you can have much better chance of beating the enemy in the next run. There’s a total of 18 levels and every one of them feature a different monster. The game gets pretty difficult in the later levels so you can expect to play the game a few times in order to build a better deck and to have a chance against the later monsters. This game can get pretty addicting if you’re a card games fan.
A very addicting and fun solitaire/RPG/Rogue-lite game which will keep you entertained for hours. It has that “just one more game and I am off” thing but you never leave it. I recommend this game, it’s pretty fun.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Solitairica is solitaire wrapped up in a fantasy setting, complete with magic, weird enemies, and a strange sense of humour.
There's no introduction to provide a backstory, but it seems that for some reason it's up to you to fight the armies of Stuck through 18 levels of the Blandlands, to confront some sort of sinister evil. Each level has you fighting a strange creature, many with a humorous twist, by completing a hand of solitaire.
Graphics - Graphics are functional, with some humorous touches. Each group of levels in the quest has a different static background image over which the main game is played. Your opponent for a hand is shown at the top, represented by a deck of square cards, and the normal playing cards that make up the hand are displayed at the centre of the screen. You are represented by a heart, showing your life points.
Cards and abilities are animated, and it's the abilities that shine as far as the graphics are concerned. Some of these (such as the beards) are very odd indeed, but should elicit a chuckle or two at least.
The interface between battles is big and cartoon-like, with icons that are easy to understand and use, and some nice simple animations showing your progress and your next opponent. Graphics options are minimal, only allowing resolution and windowed / full screen selection.
Sound - Sound effects are good, with various effects for magical spells and abilities, and appropriate sounds for button feedback and card movements. There are a few musical flourishes at various points in the game, such as when winning a level or losing the game, but during battles there's a notable lack of background music that leaves the game feeling a bit empty.
Gameplay - As mentioned, your job is to battle through the 18 levels of solitaire that make up The Blandlands in order to confront the evil that awaits you in the castle at the end.
The basic solitaire rules are implemented, but what makes the game interesting is the introduction of various special powers, spells, and items that reduce or improve your ability to complete the hand. As you play through you'll no doubt die (by your opponent draining your heart's life points to zero), which puts you back at the beginning again. Never fear, though: each death earns you 'wildstone' gems, which are used to improve your deck or purchase a new one for your next attempt.
Between levels you can spend coins, earned through completing levels and getting long chains of cards, on items and spells to improve your chances. There's not a whole lot of variation in items, though, with most being of the "begin with +x" in a certain value variety. Similarly with the enemies you fight: there's only a relatively small number of enemies you're likely to encounter at each stage, sometimes enhanced by one or more abilities. It's hardly the "horde of ever-changing enemies" and "wide variety of items" that are promised in the game's description.
The promised 'rogue-like' features come in when you die and return to the beginning of the game. At this point you can spend wildstone gems you've earned on upgrading your card deck (up to three upgrades per deck), or purchasing a new deck. I wouldn't really call the game 'rogue-like' based on this, but it's a nice feature nonetheless.
Pros:
+ Good sense of humour
+ Cute graphics and sound
+ Simple to learn, but fun and addictive
+ Items, spells, and deck upgrades keep you coming back for more
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Crashes to desktop with 'fatal error' on occasion (but it seems to save turn by turn, so you don't lose anything)
- Repetitive, especially in the early stages of each game when you tend to encounter the same enemies with no special abilities
- Lack of background music during battles leaves the game feeling a bit empty
- Some grammar errors (e.g. "no where" instead of "nowhere")

A visual novel, being a type of novel, has writing as its most important vehicle for telling a story and presenting its content to the reader; the graphics are a non-essential bonus. The authors of Driftwood, however, are either blissfully unaware of this, or have a vastly overinflated opinion of their writing skills.
The writing in Driftwood is riddled with numerous grammatical errors, even down to such basic things as its/it's (and the possessive in general), then/than, your/you're, etc. In addition, spelling is frequently a problem, not to mention poor sentence structure and vocabulary--in some instances it's even obvious the author doesn't know the meaning of a particular word.
The character art is amateurish, wildly inconsistent between the sprites and various CGs, and rather poorly shaded; some of which you can see in the screenshots. Some of the characters also have utterly ridiculous poses. The background art is pretty decent though, and there's a good variety of it. Ditto for the music.
Combine all of the aforementioned flaws with an annoying protagonist who often gets "offended" at perceived "insensitivities" and wants to punch other characters to teach them a lesson, and you get a VN which breaks immersion so much that it's nearly impossible to enjoy. Oh, and it's not even finished.
3/10 -- Dear devs, please at least pass high school English before trying to write again.

I WAS going to finish this game and write a funny review about it because, in all honesty, it IS a pretty funny game, albeit entirely unintentionally. However, I found that every time I think about going back, I felt this lump in the pit of my stomach, begging me to reconsider. Was it the fact that Driftwood is written in insipid, leaden prose? Filled with banal observations that are passed off for insights or emotional depth, while possessing neither? Or is it the fact that what starts off a romance VN is "MC, teenage boy 17 years old, gets shot in Chicago gang violence because he witnessed a robbery and is left dying in his girlfriend's arms"?
Part of the "it's so bad it's good" genre is acclimatising to the trauma you're being subjected to. The first time you watch The Room, Tommy Wiseau's seminal film about Tommy and a red Room, the first 15 minutes is hilarious. However, as the movie progresses, laughter is replaced by something more like morbid fascination. You start asking yourself just what it is you're watching, who it is, why it is. You peer beyond the obvious artificiality, to look at what the work says about the people who made it.
When I peer behind Driftwood, I see very little. It's a pale Katawa Shoujo imitation, written by someone who felt a commitment to a kickstarter for what had only really been a hobby project between his friends. It's rather telling that the options menu background is a drawing of the dev group ca 2014. It's kind of like how someone scrawls their name over a custom map in an FPS, gauche as heck - but worse than that here, it's sad. The troubled development of this game has been no secret, and it seems the team split long before the release now in 2016. (If one can call it that, as this is just Act 1 of 2 - though nowhere is this advertised on the store page.) The CG seems to have been put in as some kind of memento by the main creator, or perhaps a lazy leftover.
That's what makes Driftwood such a deeply uninspiring game to play, and gives me that lump in my gut. Once the laughter subsides, and you dig deeper, there's not a whole lot there other than the broken ambitions of an unambitious VN.
It's bloody funny before that realisation hits, though.

I struggled to force myself to become--and remain--engaged with this dating sim. I could forgive the slow start if it weren't for the unlikeable protagonist, illogical thought processes of the characters, completely unnatural conversations, overly descriptive sentences, and the writer taking too long to get to the actual point. I'm not sure which parts I'm supposed to find funny. All I know is that when I did laugh it had more to do with disbelief than anything else. The premise and much of the plot feels almost entirely lifted from 'Katawa Shoujo', another free dating sim you can find online. Even several of the characters are like copies of those in KS.
'Driftwood' tries too hard to be edgy at times. Or perhaps it is an attempt to have the kids seem 'authentic'. I'm not sure. All it did was make me cringe. The game also doesn't handle the social/emotional issues it brings up very well at all, in my opinion. Especially when it attempts to have somebody sound as if they know what they're going on about. If that's something that will frustrate you, you might want to skip this visual novel. It happens a fair bit in a variety of ways.
The best part of 'Driftwood' is the music; I enjoyed some of it. The art is not what I'd call wonderful but for a free to play VN, I wouldn't say it is a complete disaster. I know about the Kickstarter ($8000+) and although I don't know much about game development, I wonder whether the budget is represented by the quality.
As it stands, I put this at about 3/10. 'Seduce Me the Otome' has god-awful writing as well but at least there's voice acting and the actual plot is intriguing enough. 'Katawa Shoujo' has many faults but still, I think it can offer all of what 'Driftwood' attempts and delivers it in a much less disappointing manner.
I can't recommend this game to anybody lacking a certain amount of patience. Since it's free I think that it is worth trying out if you have time to waste. You may find you like it. I personally have to give it a negative review. It failed to grow on me and I don't think I'll attempt any further playthroughs.

Rouguelikeish space combat game with great writing. Become a karaoke champion. Fight space pirates. Help hitchhikers. Acquire cargo. Sweet.

DESCRIPTION
Flotilla is a short to medium length space strategy game. In comparison to similar games, it was made before FTL (and served as minor inspiration for FTL) and after the first two Weird Worlds games (not cited as an inspiration for Flotilla).
You are the captain of two identical small ships to begin with, always the same two ships. You have been told you have seven months to live. You jump around a procedurally generated starmap just like FTL and Weird Worlds, at each jump you encounter a random event. It can be a multiple choice question, a free item or ship to add to your flotilla and of course it can be a fight.
You'll enter a fight with your full flotilla, which will be every ship you managed to get during that run. You will fight the opposing team in 30 second bursts until one team is completely annihilated. Back on the map, after a certain amount of time has passed, the game ends and you get your final score.
PROS
The combat: Every time someone makes me play a game and says "it's art" they're not always wrong but they usually are. Well I'm putting my nuts on the chopping block, this is art. You point out where on the X, Y and Z axis you want your ship to travel too, you decide if they'll be firing and who they'll be firing at. Then you press play and it plays out for 30 seconds, everyone floats in their allotted directions firing at what you wanted them to. In the background plays classical piano pieces, Prelude in D-Flat Major by Chopin etc. as this is going on. Then when the 30 seconds are up, silence.... and you plot the next moves and press play again. Shielding is actually proper shielding, you hit the light coloured areas you're hitting a shield, chances of scoring an actual HP lowering hit are slim when you do that, you hit a non-shielded area such as the rear or underside then you'll likely cause damage. I play out these battles in the background all evening while I'm working on other things, it's a relaxing experience and it's very difficult to get flustered. To me this is the best part of the game it does what FTL and Weird Worlds couldn't do for me, fit into the background rather than command my undivided attention.
The characters and setting: Rastafarian Cats, Bandit Penguins it's got an interesting mix of anthropomorphised characters, humans too. Each character is offset against a very fitting musical theme. After every jump in the star system you find yourself asking "what the hell was that about?" which definitely seems to be the developer's intention and I think they pulled it off. I find it even more interesting than the lore in FTL.
The Mystery: Outside of the ships and ship upgrades, nothing is explained. Every decision can come back to haunt to you in a branched off event, this was done to excellent effect in FTL two years later as well, Flotilla's handling of events is terser and shorter but far more representative of the whole game story. For example each jump you make and what happened gets written down in a Captain's log which reflects your ending score.
CONS
Reduced content: The game is small. It's a real shame that it likely won't see the updates and DLC that it so richly deserves. From a standpoint of pure common sense it's just not viable for Blendo Games to return to the development of a 4 year old game, especially when it's a one man team and the popularity of this title pales in comparison to their other titles, such as Thirty Flights of Loving. As opposed to other games where the community would like to see PvP/Co-op multiplayer, updated art assets, expanded story or even a sequel just for the purpose of milking their favourite game dry even when it's not the best decision, that is definitely not the case with Flotilla. This game gets the green light on PvP multiplayer, especially online, the mechanics are screaming out for this addition to the game it would work incredibly well, online co-op fits in just as well (note: Local co-op is already available). Another well-fitting feature would be modding, Flotilla is built from a small pool of "what is fun", to pull this off the developer reduced the graphics to very simple geometric shapes and made the game all about travelling to the location, then fighting in the location. As for the fighting itself, you move, you roll, you fire, you turn your shields in the direction of oncoming fire, you direct your fire towards the non-shielded areas of the opponent. A modding community could work with the whole game, even if it was just pure XML (similar to Dungeons of Dredmor) after only experiencing 5 hours of the game you could extend it straight away.
Un-pruned areas: The developer has been very honest about the state of his code on Flotilla, undoubtedly being his first commercial game it's likely that large swathes of the code didn't lend itself to decent re-use and as a result it would seem that a few screw ups here and there that detract from the overall enjoyment of the game can't be as easily fixed as you would think. Certainly not as easy as if he wrote the game today with his current experience. An example is controller support, this game has it but in a very old-fashioned way, you can't use the gamepad in single player, but a second player can use a gamepad in addition to the first player using keyboard and mouse in local co-op. The Beam Frigate's AI can get stuck quite a lot and just not move, making them sitting ducks, it typically happens when there's too much going on in the frigate's vicinity. You start with two of what is arguably the best ship in the game, it's so fast it can take on almost anyone, my opinion may change after a few more games in hardcore mode but for now I would say that other starting configurations and balancing things more favourably for the opponent would have been a great improvement also.
SUMMARY

When I saw so many negative reviews, I hesitated to buy this, but having played and enjoyed 1 and 2 I was keen to play this one. I was eventually tempted by the recent sale price.
The FAQ thread pointed out that up to date graphics drivers were essential, as it happens I recently updated mine. I played using an xbox 360 controller.
I have played this to completion over a leisurely 23 hours and I have had no crashes, and only one or two brief laggy moments, nothing that spoiled the moment.
There are some character control issues, Kate will become stuck in unexpected ways and occasionally walk through some scenery, nothing major though.  At some scene changes the transition point is a little tricky and you have to be careful and slow to avoid returning back to a previous scene without wishing to. At certain moments the camera angles are awkward, they can be worked around, but it could be better.
At one point the view from outside the ship was missing most of its textures for a certain funfair scene making it look mostly invisible.
There was also a bug, again in the fairground section,  where a significant and already utilised item reappeared in my inventory. I had quit the game and returned to it the next day, this confused me somewhat but I ignored the presence of the item and played on, and everything worked out perfectly well. It has to be said though that the save system could be better so you can create one or two sequential backups. I suspect the incredible reappearing inventory item might have been save related.
I see that upon initial release the bugs were more numerous, so obviously a patch or two has improved matters.
When I first started playing the game I felt a more thorough preliminary tutorial might have been a good idea. It took me half a minute to realise that the on screen prompts are colour coded to the xbox controller buttons and that also you sometimes click once, and other times click and hold, whilst using the left joystick to say open a drawer or pull a bolt or lever.  Also I didn't immediately realise that you can use the right stick to change focus to different items of interest, and they are sometimes indicated by just a single white dot so I missed that at first. But after about ten minutes of trial and error I managed to figure it all out, thereafter the controls were straightforward enough to use.
Yes the graphics are somewhat dated I suppose but I've been gaming for 20+ years so perhaps I'm a touch more forgiving on that one. The same goes for the English soundtrack not lip-synching exactly, the original language being French I think, but for me that's no worse than watching a good dubbed foreign film.
It is clear the game should have been tested better/longer before release, not an uncommon issue these days sad to say.
As with most point and click puzzlers some of the puzzles are infuriating because insufficient information is provided leading to too much guesswork. Mostly though the puzzles are fair and satisfying to solve.
Having said all that, and generally speaking, I enjoyed my time with this third episode. A few people criticise the story, and maybe it would have been better if it were not exclusively based around the plight of the Youkol. The enemy and its machinations should have been fleshed out some more. I also agree with others that they could have paid a bit more attention to the voice acting choices and accents here and there.
You might want to wait for the price to drop a little, and check out the forums to see what issues there may still be and be sure to read the FAQ thread, it seems that some systems have a harder time running the game than others, and some people have had more serious save file problems.
None of the minor bugs I personally encountered spoiled the game for me, so for the price I paid I am content, I enjoyed the game, and I would like to see part 4 realised in the future.

Great Idea. Bad execution.
If this were a real board game, it would be broken.
Watch the designers' videos. It's interesting that the lead designer goes on ad nauseum about his design inspirations, because he succeeded in ship design, and failed horribly in character design. I find it painful to watch the character animations. (Also, the music is absolute torture.)
In the systems designer's video, he references King of Tokyo and Craps (of all things) as justification for the use of actual dice in this simulated board game. Great, dude; so why didn't you bother to study more appropriate game models when working out your mechanics? Games such as Elder SIgn, Alea Iacta Est, Yspahan, Arkham Horror, or Pandemic?
Here's the thing with a game like this: There has to be some inkling of hope for success. It is definitely important to keep this kind of game challenging, but this game in particular suffers from balance issues (which is a shame - read on).
In bg design, we have an ongoing debate about the win:loss ratio of this kind of game, and its effect on replayability. On average, the consensus among designers is that the players should win one in five to ten plays in order to avoid frustration and want to ever again take the box off the shelf.
This game sets you up to fail regardless of any concern for your experience beyond the mere process of playing. It's not challenging; it's rigged.
I've played ten times now, and from the very first turn of every game, I
had any hope that I would succeed. I'll probably sit down one more night and play through another ten times, just to get a better idea of the trends, but here's where I think the design is fundamentally flawed: Initial setup and escalation curve.
The odds are too steep coming out of the gate, and there are never adequate opportunities to prepare for the next challenge(s). I understand the need to keep the pressure on the player, so I don't lament the lack of opportunity to get ahead or on top of the progression, but the most consistent experience I have at the beginning of every round of Tharsis is that there's no point to try to continue the game. It is obviously hopeless at every turn. This is a critical failure in the area of balancing.
Designers, you have to let the players have some hope! In all but one of my playthroughs, I looked at the (obviously random and arbitrary) dice allocations at the start of game, and felt there was no point to even beginning the game. Did you even playtest this thing, or did you just write some automated script to crunch the numbers? You clearly put a lot of thought into the process, but failed to adequately consider the experience. (A common failing among bg designers.)
Ultimately, I think the
of Tharsis is delightful, and the
of Tharsis is fun - I really enjoy the dice allocation mechanic, the hard decisions, and the thematic challenges.
But the game is broken in setup and balance: FIx that, and Tharss would be an excellent game.

Ahh, DuckTales: Remastered. Just as a sidenote, I never did play the first one on the SNES. But yeah, as a Disney fan and generally wanting to play light-hearted cartoon-y games a lot, I was excited for this one. Having it gifted to me, I decided to hop straight into this and found that the presentation was fantastic. The visuals are top-notch, pretty much having been remade for this HD remake of the first game, and the music even better. With a New Game option awaiting me, I decided to go for that (and picked Easy mode, mind you!) but went back to explore the other menus later; there waiting for you to pick is a Gallery of sorts, which can also be accessed via the main game's "world hub"/level selector. Options for game configuration are there and play time. That, and a leaderboard which was quite fun to look at (how do people get through the game that quickly?)
As for the actual main game itself, I loved it despite a few small flaws. The character models look brilliant and most of the time, work really well with the backgrounds. We start with a small cutscene and an opening level in the bank where you play as Scrooge McDuck (voiced by the original VA, who just so happens to be around 80, I believe) and you save Huey, Dewey and Louie from the evil (and a bit ditzy) Beagle Boys. In the process, you get to know about the main storyline; get 5 artifacts from around the world and then you'll have lots of treasure (or something like that). Woo hoo!
So what do I think of the 5 levels after this? Pretty good. All different, long and have a great boss at the end for you to tackle, all while getting to know the hilarious Launchpad, 3 boys and Webby who tag along for the ride. Although, cutscenes aren't the best (but are skippable) as they don't show the character's mouths moving when they speak. Another flaw to the game is the sometimes dodgy platforming; whether it's cheap deaths from the weird jumping mechanics or taking a bit of damage when you really feel as if it's not your fault, WayForward definitely could have improved this. It just doesn't feel as great as the Mario platformers, for example (then again, most platformers don't).
So after the next 5 levels (including THE MOOOOON, of all places. But I didn't see Princess Luna, so this is set after MLP season 3 apparently, heh heh heh), you get to save the 3 boys again and try and retrieve the treasure at Mount Vesuvius where you end up defeating Magica and also competing in some weird "escape the volcano" level that really felt bad, as sometimes Scrooge just wouldn't grab onto the ropes and wouldn't jump properly - and that kinda let that down for me, until I realised that there are a few tricks to get it right.
Pros:
+ Great level variety
+ Voice acting is top notch
+ Art is fantastic, so is the game design
+ Good difficulty at times
Cons:
- Cutscenes aren't the best
- Sometimes dodgy platforming
- Length of game isn't great, despite decent replay value
Overall, pretty good game. 8/10 for me. Would (get gifted, but otherwise) buy again.

There's been a trend in recent years to cash in on nostalgia in a big way.  Take an old game, give it a little bit of polish, release it again and rake in the dough.  Sometimes it's welcomed because its handled respectfully, while other times it's a shallow cash grab.  I am very happy to say that this is NOT a cash grab.  If anything, DuckTales: Remastered is an example of how a updated re-release should be done... mostly.
So, as per the usual formula, let's talk about the good to start.  First and foremost, the core of the original NES game, what made that game a beloved masterpiece, is still there and fully intact.  Scrooge still has his bizarre pogo stick ability that is as inexplicable as it is fun, and the levels still stick to the same general layout, even having the same locations for pickups.  The game's tunes are also the same, save for being performed by real instruments rather than an 8-bit chiptune processor.  If you thought the Moon theme was catchy in chiptune, wait till you hear it now.
Of course, that's not to say the game is just a graphical update without any other changes.  DuckTales: Remastered adds some new content to the game, most of it welcome.  While the levels are mostly the same, there have been some minor alterations and changes, most for the better in terms of level flow.  Bosses in particular have been changed up so that they have more than the same single attack pattern to work with, making them far more challenging (though not unfairly so) than their pushover NES incarnations. There are even two additional levels: an intro training level and a final boss level, both with new soundtracks that fit in quite nicely with the rest of the tunes.  The final level in particular was a surprising addition, and is far more satisfying than the original game's "go through this level you already beat" concept of a final level, albeit with a caveat I'll talk about later.
Probably the best thing DuckTales: Remastered brings to the game are the fully voiced characters.  Rather than just relying on canned sound effects and clips from the show, the game actually uses newly recorded lines from the original voice cast (minus the ones who, tragically, are no longer with us).  Yes, this includes Alan Young as Scrooge, sounding surprisingly good for being 92 years old.  Scrooge obviously has plenty of time to say a variety of things, what with all the pogoing and gathering treasure and whatnot, but the other characters get plenty of time to speak, too.  Mostly this happens during cutscenes that occur between and sometimes in the middle of the levels.  These cutscenes are true to the original series, and do a great job of explaining some of the more inexplicable parts of the original NES game; why was Bubba Duck frozen in ice, for example.
Cutscenes aren't without downsides though, which brings me to the next part of the review: the bad. As I said, cutscenes can happen in the middle of levels, which can get very tiring on repeated playthroughs of the game.  You can skip them, but it does take a few seconds to do so, and quite a few are placed such that even that can be a noticeable interruption.  The game also has some serious issues with recognizing all but the most common monitor resolutions, and really didn't like my 16:10 monitor at all.  I was able to get around it by manually altering the game's ini file to use my specific resolution, but it's still something that could have been handled better.  The most maddening thing for me though is that in keeping true to the core of the original game, much of its buggy movement behavior was kept in as well, especially the random things that could cause Scrooge to stop pogoing for no easily apparent reason.  Any fan of the original NES title won't be surprised, but the movement quirks could have been ironed out without angering most people, or at the very least with an optional toggle as was done for the requirement to hold the pogo button while bouncing, a.k.a. "Hard Pogo Mode".
The only other thing I can add about this game is only arguably a downside, but I found it somewhat negative all the same, that being the significantly increased difficulty of the final boss fight (and beyond) compared to the original game.  It's not impossible by any means, but it's still quite the jump in challenge.  I'll freely admit it had me frustrated for a little bit.
Despite the few bad things in this remake, there's clearly far more good things to say about it. Ultimately though, DuckTales: Remastered is a bit of a victim of time, with its gameplay style not nearly as popular by today's standards, not to mention the waning popularity of the DuckTales franchise.  That said, it's still a solid platformer with a lot going for it, and very little going against it.  Fans of the original game will love this update, and people who have never played either can get quite a bit out of it, too, but you might want to watch a few episodes of the original show first.

Simple, absolutely charming point and click game with a wonderful story and endearing characters. Puzzles were clever and really require you to think outside the box in a way you may not be used to, which I appreciated.
That said, the puzzles make up only half the gameplay. The other half exists in the form of extensive dialogues with other characters to which you can respond in various ways. This mutliresponse/multiquestion gameplay is difficult to explain beyond that- it's often more complex than the basic style of dialogue tree you'd see in other point and click games, and as such would seem possibly seem trite in another game, but The Blackwell Legacy manages to immerse you on a higher level than many point and click games, again thanks to its immensely charming presentation, and for a $5 price tag (possibly much less if you grab it during a sale) it's certainly worth a try.
My only complaint would be that it's suuuuuuuper short- I was expecting it to take around ten hours and it took half as long.
Ultimately, despite its brevity and the fact that it often tends towards being more of an interactive experience than a typical game, The Blackwell Legacy proves memorable, engaging, and endearing to the point that it's almost impossible not to like, and will certainly leave you hankering to play the other games in the series.

Cute and amazing story.
I really got the feel of old JRPG, build items, battle, trying to understand the alchemy (items making), and trying to understand the battle mechanic. It's fun to get the feel of old JRPG yet with nice graphic and voice acting.

(TL;DR)
is a fun JRPG. The core mechanic gameplay of the gameplay is making items with the best possible combination of traits. The game also features well-balanced battle system. The game also has remarkable soundtrack which is what defines the identity of the series. While the story is not bad enough to keep you entertained for a while. Therefore, it is recommended to have it in your game library.
The main thing you will do everytime is crafting items with best possible traits by combining materials that have the desired traits, which is the identity of the series. These materials can be found by loot from defeating enemies, by gathering materials from place to place, and by making prerequisite items. The materials you get from gathering is different for each time you get it as the game has Day and night time system. As for the crafting, it has a lot of depths so you need to do some thinking and planning to make it works as you intended.
The game also offers you quest system which is very common in all of RPG games. The quests could be hunting, gathering, and making certain materials. These quests mainly net you money while there is certain requests that will also net you tickets as a bonus. This tickets can be traded for rare items. These quests also have time limit but don't worry about missing any quests because they will appear again after sooner or later. Basically it is a fulfill-and-reward quest system.
As for the battle systems, it is a well-balanced mechanic. The game offers you to be able to choose difficulty throughout the entire game anytime, so you don't have to worry enemies that is too strong if you play it on easy difficulty, although it is recommended that you play it on at least normal difficulty to not bore you. Every characters in your party have their own unique skills so you could do some strategic approach and it is a plus for the gameplay aspect.
The story mainly involves the main protagonist, Sophie, and her book companion
, Plachta. Plachta lost her memory so Sophie must help Plachta to regain her memories by writing a lot of alchemy recipes on the book. The story involves not only the main protagonist and her companion book but also her friends who will support her.
The story is simple and yet kind of heartwarming. There is good amount of comedy skits that keep you smile. The development of each character although is not much, but it is enough to keep the story more entertaining. But I believe they could have done it better than this one.
I think the visual aesthetic or the graphics is not bad. The town where the protagonist lives feels like not lively enough because there is not enough background people. It's just kinda empty. As for the technical graphics, I think it is not enough. The lighting is NOT good enough to make it feels more impressive(or perhaps am I asking too much?).Therefore, I think that it could have been improved more better.
The soundtracks are magnificent and fit the mood of the game. This is what I've been wanting to say for a while.  The town, eventhough visually is not lively, the background theme compensate for that. And as for the battle theme, I think it feels kind of happy and upbeat. Fits the game theme. They really did a remarkable job on this one. The 'Great Soundtrack' tag was there for a good reason. I even listened to the soundtracks everyday on YouTube. The soundtracks of the game series are like a treasure trove. Kudos for the sound team behind this. So it is a BIG plus for the soundtrack aspect.
I really love this game especially for the soundtracks and the gameplay. I think this game is for everyone who loves JRPG genre. Although not all people have the same taste, but I still think this game is a worthwhile for those who wants a refreshing game. Therefore, I recommend this game.
I'm looking forward for their next installment which I will buy when it's on sale.

I got attracted to this game because the amazing graphics and also the fact that I can GATHER and MAKE stuff, like LOTS AND LOTS of stuff! However I was not willing to toss $59.99 on a game that I might or might NOT like. My friend ended up getting this for me as a birthday present and I fell in love with this game! Also, if you're like me who tried to play this with a keyboard...I suggest you not, its wayyy simpler with a controller...unless you get used to the controls very quickly.
The good parts....
I can gather, I can fight monsters, I can run around, I can upgrade/create new items, and the graphics are so stunning. The storyline is a little bit mediocre since I played so many games already, but everyone is so cheerful and adorable. There is even voice acting in the main dialouges for lazy people who do not want to read. You can take this game at your own pace, play a little here, a little there, no rush. You can recurit other characters after interacting them a few times and pick your team. You can make bombs, materials, healing items (food), metals, etc and enhance your wep/gears. Also the damaging items you make can be "customized" with traits and are actually USEFUL in battle, not like a complete waste of time. Game's system is pretty easy to understand for one who played MMO/turn based combat/gathering type games like these. Art style, skill effects, landscape, etc are very smooth and impressive.
The not-so-good parts/TIPS...
-You cannot walk through or jump over blades of overgrown grass, small rocks, and things like that.
-It takes a while for the blacksmith+clothier to give you options to make better gear and to enhance them (not SUPER long, but a while)
-Some monsters only appear at night (for good or for better)
-Sometimes the storyline is kinda boring (the voices are cheerful and nice tho)
-NPC have limited merchandise.
-You unlock more stuff to do with artisians the more you talk to them (don't forget to do that!)
-Not all monsters are listed when pressing "Y" on the map, some you have to encounter before it shows there. Item drops are not displayed, so it can be confusing to remember what drops what.
-It doesn't tell you what materials can be found where in your alchemy book, nor what item qualify as which catergory.
Despite the downsides, this game is definetly a 8.5/10 for me, great game, great graphics, minor issues that are tolerable.

Atelier Sophie is nothing I would recommend to the average person, because it is a game which requires endless grind and kinda like nothing else. For me grinding isn't something terrible and that's the reason I could enjoy it over the most part. But in the case of Atelier Sophie the grind didn't led to something special.
Let's be honest here. The characters are all flat. If you think this is sad, then you need to know that the story is also flat. There are a lot of 'sidequests'. These are giving you an understanding of each character. Yeah, they all have a background which is the most interesting part, but even with all these different backstories, they don't differ in their final appearance alot. And that's weird, because they all have a different character formative past.
The good part is the variety of different battle styles with your personal sets of the characters. It was enjoyable to fight in your constellation and synthesize the equipment for your squad.
I finished the game in around 40 hours, but only because I rushed the last bit. There is a lot you can synthesize. That's in the beginning enjoyable, but in the end the alchemy part and getting all the clues for the recipes is timeconsuming. After 2/3 of your playtime it's just annoying. I skipped a lot of recipes because of that. It's not even needed to do all these to finish the game.
Even for me the grinding in this game is getting over the top. I want to compare this to the Hyperdimension Neptunia Grinding, which is also a big part of this series. Anyways it was for me fun in the Neptunia games, because you know why you grinding this much (grind for far better equipment as example). But in Atelier Sophie you don't know why. You know it's the gameplay of the game and it's somehow important, but there is no reward in sight.
I finished the main story and I am happy I did. Also if you getting ill (like me in the last week) it's a simple gameplay to just cure yourself with time. So yeah if you are a person who has patience and want a simple playstyle where you can chill and don't need to have a lot of awareness, this is your game. If not...well...then it isn't what you want to play.
TL;TR: Good battlesystem, endless grind, less story! Be a calm and patient person to enjoy this game. If not I won't recommend this to you.

The ultimate crafting game, throwing random things into a cauldron, to make something completely different from the materials used.
Being a fan of the Atelier series, I really enjoyed Atelier Sophie and it's slice of life story. Overall I liked it and is an okay port for the PC.
Well to go into more detail, Atelier series never been about it's story, just the slice of life or daily life of Sophie, the main Heroine. Sophie is a beginner Alchemist that finds a book in her home left over by her granmother, whom passed away and.... Well if i type anymore I'll basically spoil the story.
Atelier Sophie: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Book, begins the new Atelier series with the theme Mystery. There are very few changes over the course of the Atelier series, its still a heavy focused crafting game with cute anime characters.
Some things to note, day and night cycle, performing actions now consumes in game time, well more like a clock, since there is no time limit. Massive changes to the battle system, such as 4 active party members, assist actions are now based on turn order, chain attack (attack command may now do more than 1 hit), all party members may equip alchemic items (though a bit limited) and Sophie may use skills in battle (Something Alchemist heroines couldn't do before).
Like every other Atelier since the Dusk series, the sythesizing or crafting system changes once again, but I rather not go into too much detail about this, since this is the heart and soul of Atelier games and wish not to spoil it.
Now to point out some bad parts, heavy focus on the crafting system, seriously this game is really about crafting from making new weapons, armour, bombs, heal items, enhancing gear and trait properties of materials gathered, everything is about crafting, not too much of a bad point for long time fans, but might be a bit overwhelming for newer PC players.
No new game +. Yea this kind of shocked me when I found out, which really lowers replay value.
To sum this up, I liked Atelier Sophie and the new changes, if you liked the previous Atelier titles, then I don't see why you won't like this one. For newer players:
Do you like anime?
Do you like crafting, combining, and finding items (I suppose experimenting, as well)?
Do you like simple and normal lifestyle stories?
If all yes, may be worth trying out Atelier Sophie. If you're looking for more intense save the world story or goal driven, action packed, fast pace type games, this is seriously not the game for you then.

Rainbow Six Siege is an odd creature.
Do I play this because I enjoy the gunplay?
Sure.
Do I play this because I think the destructable environment is a neat addition to an FPS?
I suppose.
Do I play this because as I sit in the objective room, with bated breath, as explosions go off in distant rooms and I watch as the clock slowly ticks down and I see that the fight has quickly gone from a 5V5 to a 2v4 and my last living teammate is across the map, only to rush over to the objective and die before reaching it as well? Left in a 1V4 I can feel a tingle in my arm, my chest is hurting, my brain is overclocking, trying to calculate every footstep and every sound in an attempt to find where the enemy is about to appear next.
Survive.
Thats all that is running through my head, the objective is simply another tool I use to locate my enemies, Its coming around the corner, that insatiable bloodlust of 4 overconfident players, come to finish me off and win the game. I can hear it, FEEL it. Suddenly, there is a silence. Minutes pass by. Days. Months. Where have they gone? When will they strike? I know they are there, they wait for me to lose my focus. 15 seconds remaining
14
My chest is throbbing
13
My eyes are burning
12
My arm is dying to move, even a millimeter
11, 10, 9, 8, 7
THE BEAST APPEARS

Did you see that trailer for No Man's Sky? Have that space exploration itch located in the most awkward spot? Well this is the closest thing you're going to find that can reach that itch.
Rodina is set in a single solar system Occupied by 4 life size planets, over 400 gigantic asteroids, and 15,000 tiny asteroids. All of them are teeming with loot, lore, and a hostile alien race. It is up to you to ensure that Humanity can colonize this new system safely before they arrive.
In Rodina, your ship, is YOUR ship! You can set the layout of your ship however you want and furnish them as you please. Make your bedroom, bathroom, engineer room, and your bridge. There's even a Tile set made entirly of Holoscreens, which project the outside area on the walls in 3D, making it perfect for cockpits and/ or observation decks, so that you may gaze upon the stars.
Space combat takes some getting used to, but very satisfying as you unleash hell on alien fighters and watch them hurl towards the surface of the planet in a fireball of glory!
Space exploration is a tad bare bones at this time. You find a marker, destroy any hostiles gaurding it, land, grab the Datasticks (lore), Encryption Keys (story progress), and any special weapons ammo, and repeat. Although you can exit your ship, and explore the surounding terrain, theirs not much to see other than some amazing vistas on mountain tops and HUGE canyons. This is my only gripe in the game, however the Developer is very active in the community and is working on fleshing the game out.
Did i also mention Mod support? Can anyone say, kestral ship mod? :P
all in all, for $15 you're getting alot for whats available right now. This game is a little bare right now, but already has more heart and soul than any Triple A game that iv'e played in awhile. There's a 60 minute demo for you to try out, please try this game out, this is a must have for any space buff out there.
P.S. The soundtrack is amazing too. It feels like a mix of Intersteller and Firefly. ^_^

The joy of this game is in the playing, not the beating, of it.
I think it's a shame that, as of the time of this writing, this has "mixed" reviews. I can see where it would not be everyone's cup of tea but there is nothing wrong with the game. The content is fine for the price and I experienced no technical problems.
There is no fun in making a decision that you always know for a fact will work out. That's how a lot of game puzzles are, pull the right lever and the door will open. This is not like that and the very fact that the game occasionally has anal sex with you against your will via the dice and/or the troubles that befall your ship is what keeps the game fresh and replayable. If this game only had the one mission it comes with and there was one, solid, foolproof strategy to use to win every time, it would be all but pointless. It's not a pure gamble, there are definitely good calls and bad calls but nothing is guaranteed. You always feel like you're "getting away with it" and that's fine because the fun of it all is making those decisions, figuring out the best possible strategy under the given circumstances. That's where the game is and that never ends because the circumstances are never the same.

- a "resign" button for when you are mathematically defeated because it only adds insult to injury when you have to play out a turn that is impossible to win
- random events that benefit rather than harm (at least in "easier" game modes)

I assume you are here trying to find out what redeeming qualities positive reviews have to counter the bad stuff said in the negative ones. Let's get started.
Firstly,
, simple but strategically deep (do not let anyone tell you otherwise). The randomness of the events do keep you on your toes, but preparing research items, saving food and fixing the ship ahead of time is possible, and I would say necessary.
Secondly,
They are not detrimental to this game. Take into account that this very same game with a 1 in 3 or 5 win ratio, would have almost no replayability value. Unlockable crew members are nice to try out, only got two of them so far and they do change the way you play, but trying to beat the odds are what make me want to play again and again... and again. I just finished my 14th game in less than 6 and a half hours. Take into account that I took my time to think every move the first three or four games, and I went AFK with the game open a couple of times.
Having said that, I found no reason to call the difficulty "punishing" as many others have (even in positive reviews). If you’d prefer to keep having a bad time then skip this review.
Not gonna lie, I was pretty frustrated the first several rounds I tried playing this game. I couldn’t make it three rounds before having to serve up some Iktomi tenderloins. I kept trying to devote all of my dwindling resources to repairing the damaged compartments, but that quickly revealed itself to be an exercise in futility.
Ladies and gentlemen, I have seen the light, there is another way.
How? Food. Get it.
So far as I can tell, food is the key. Food production allows you to replenish the dice that decrease every round. The more dice you have the easier it is to fix modules by deducting their sum from the damage, or by using them to conduct research which can fix modules that have damage greater than the sum of the dice.
Just because there a compartment is flashing red does not mean that that is the only place you can send a crew member. The star in the background washes out all signs of the ship. Click the ship info tab and that will reveal other areas that you can send crew members. Were I to have known that from the start that would have saved a ton of headache.
Yes, there is an undeniable element of chance built into the game, but you do not have to totally give yourself up to it. Produce food, research wisely, and survive.
Once I figured that out the game became much more enjoyable. It is a grim story, but there is hope. Enjoy!
Now that that is out of the way, I must give props for the design and soundtrack, it’s very well done!
-GPB

I don’t do game reviews, but this game needs a balanced review.
The vast majority of negative reviews focus on the fact they played a game and couldn’t win. If this argument was valid than games like Nuclear Throne, VVVVVV, N and Spelunky should have very poor ratings.
The next assumption is, that it takes luck to win the game. Currently a streamer has a winning streak of 17 games and he’s still going. That would be impossible if luck the primary mechanic of the game.
And finally - Tharsis is not “Brutally hard” at all. It is quite possible to win 4 out of 5 games on normal level. It does require thinking, planning and an understanding of probabilities. But this is exactly what a rogue-like dice game should be about.
The mechanics of the game are quite diverse. You’re controlling a crew of four astronauts. Each of them has up to 6 health points and up to 5 dice. Your ship has up to 8 health points and 7 modules where crew and negative events can be located. Your mission is to bring the ship and at least one member alive on Mars.
The dice in this game are your action points. Once you deploy a crew-member into a module, you roll his dice and decide how to spend them. The dice are spent to remove the negative events that threaten your ship, to enable special features of each ship, to enable special abilities of your crew-member, or deposited into research bar that enables special actions.
As an added complication, each turn begins with a choice between two or three options. These will give you more dice but reduce health, repair the ship but increase stress levels of your crew, in various combinations. If your crew has high levels of stress then the choices will get worse. So you should manage that as well.
The whole game now revolves around managing your resources and prioritizing the threats. Although it seems like you’re quickly overwhelmed with problems, if you make reasonable choices, you will likely land on Mars.
If this sounds like something you like, then don’t worry about negative reviews and get the game. There’s enough videos around to get a good feel for the game-play and you can always get a refund.
