I tried a new strategy on my 6th game, after 2 hours of play consistently hitting a brick wall at triple events, and handidly won. There are a handful of resources to manage in this game: the ship, morale, food, and indirectly the positioning of crew members. The most important resource, and perhaps unfairly way too important, is food. Every other resource is most efficiently gained with excess food by spending excess dice on the locations and this isn't communicated too well. Eat immediately and generate food on your first few turns, even if you have to leave a crisis, and the rest of the game is easy as you'll be able to keep every crew member above 3 dice.
The game is not impossible and I tentatively recommend it for presenting themeatically brutal choices. Replayability is also a large concern, as it appears weak with a dominating strategy. The balance can be made more dynamic, perhaps easing up when necessary, and increasing if not. My first win actually had all crew members survive with 0 stress, full bellys, and even a fully repaired ship.
The risk management is mostly fine, the only thing that screams unfair RNG is rolling injury hazards. The rest of the game is difficult resource management, with food perhaps trumping the rest a bit too highly.

This is essentially a 3D story-driven point 'n' click adventure with puzzle elements. It has been receiving a lot of bad Press since its release a few days ago. Here's my take on it.
You play as Kate Walker, who wakes up in a medical clinic having been rescued from somewhere in the previous game (which I haven't played). In the bed next to her is Kurt who has lost a leg. He turns out to be the very important Ostrich Guide of the dwarfish Youkol people, who are in dire straits without him, as he is desperately needed to oversee the impending Ostrich Migration - these are very large ostriches with woolly-mammoth coats. Kate spends some time trying to escape from the clinic, then sets off to sort things out, travelling to various places, talking to various people and interacting with various objects on her quest to achieve... I'm not quite sure what, even though I'm halfway through the game.
It's a series of long cutscenes/dialogs strung together by tasks and puzzles of the type you'll be familiar with from any decent point 'n' click game. A lot of time is spent passively watching the story unfold and/or the next task explained via these cutscenes, which are totally devoid of any kind of humour. The dubbing is worse than a 1970s kung fu movie, with mouths flapping independently of what's being said. The voice acting is pretty good though, they at least sound like proper conversations instead of stuff being read off a sheet, which some games are guilty of.
Sometimes during a conversation you have to select between 2 or 3 different responses but they have zero effect on the storyline, apart from eliciting different reactions from the other character, resulting in the same outcome. Waste of time if you ask me (or push me, or cajole me...)
Controller layout is good and the on-screen button prompts make everything very easy and intuitive, but the right-pad is a little clumsy for targeting interaction points and I often found myself reaching for the mouse.
There are no manual save slots in this game, it's all auto-save and you can play only one game at a time. If you want to stop at a certain point in the game and save it for later while you start another new game, you can't do that.
The minimum graphics requirement is a GTX550Ti which just happens to be exactly what I have (along with i7 + SSD). Scenes take quite a long time to load - so long, in fact, that when I first started playing I thought it had crashed. Character movement is laggy - there's a delay before you start moving or when you change direction, which is a minor (but constant) irritation and causes you to bump into things.
I had no problems at all with my Steam controller, it works perfectly without any adjustments. With that said, I have to talk about the right-pad camera control. There really isn't much of it. I've played other 3D games where you can turn the camera around 360 degrees, look straight up in the air etc. but here there is only a tiny amount of manual camera movement available. 95% of the camera work is auto-controlled, and this causes it to constantly switch to the opposite direction as you pass between rooms or through doorways and suchlike, so one moment you're holding your left-stick to the left, and then you must suddenly switch to the right to keep going in the same direction. The aforementioned lag exacerbates this problem so, until you learn how to deal with it, you're grappling with a rubber band effect, bouncing back and forth between rooms. It's bizarre.
There's talk on the discussion forums about Denuvo being the cause of poor performance, with cracked games showing huge performance gains. Since I've never played a cracked game and wouldn't know (or want to know) how, I can't confirm or deny this. However, what I will say is that as a Unity game, this should be a slam-dunk for a Linux version, but I've been denied the option of playing the game on my preferred OS due to the (Windows-only) Denuvo, so that's my personal gripe about it.
There are two options right at the start of the game: Voyager (easy) mode, which I selected, and another harder mode for Syberia veterans and point 'n' click experts. I think this is the same game but with fewer prompts or indicators. You can't switch mid-game either, so choose carefully.
For the past few weeks I've been playing some very tough, challenging puzzle games, and I've also played my fair share of 2D point 'n' clickers (Daedalic, Double Fine titles etc). In comparison, there is very little challenge here, at least in Voyager mode - you can decide for yourself whether that's a good or bad thing. All you need to do is wander around for a while and interact with whatever you find (within quite a restricted area usually). Apply a bit of trial and error, follow the (rather obvious) prompts and it won't take long to solve. When you encounter a puzzle, more often than not it involves lining up or matching a set of patterns/objects/whatever. It certainly doesn't reinvent the wheel.
The price tag is pretty steep, I wouldn't want to pay it. I'd be happy with it at 50% discount though. There's plenty of content, probably around 20 hours' worth, plus maybe some replay to collect remaining achievements.
I've done a lot of complaining so far and by now you probably think I hate the game, but it's not all doom and gloom. None of the problems I've mentioned have major game-spoiling consequences, they are all minor annoyances. The actions are comfortable and intuitive once you get used to the quirks. Graphics are nice to look at, albeit slightly dated in places. Good music here and there. Puzzles/tasks will get you thinking for a few minutes and provide some interest but I wouldn't say challenge. Vaguely interesting characters. Storyline is certainly abundant if not entirely gripping.
All in all, there's enough entertainment to persuade you to continue playing, and ultimately that's what counts.

I have been a fan of the Syberia series since I played the first one. When I finished Syberia II, I couldn't wait for a sequel, and now that it's here and I have played it... well...
The Good:
The story is amazing, the characters are interesting, the puzzles entertaining (although I didn't find them as hard as the ones in the previous chapters) and it absolutely feel like a proper Syberia title. I even like the new visual style (even if a lot of people are criticizing how "dated" the model and textures look) and the amazing music, which fits really well with the gameplay. The French voice cast, from what I can tell, is actually pretty good, so for you people out there who dislike the english dub as much as I do, play it in French with subtitles (which is the language they probably based the lip movement of the characters on).
The Bad:
The first thing that I was displeased with was the lack of an Italian language dubbing, which was present and very well done in the past chapters (yes, I am actually italian and I speak Italian). The second thing was, as I said before, the English dub. My god... just awful, it really made me want to quit the game. If you want to hear how bad it is, well, just go on YouTube and listen to the English trailer for the game. I'm baffled that Microids didn't care about having a good english voice cast to do the voices: the english language is one of the most spoken languages in the world, in my opinion doing a poor english dub means doing a poor job in making english speaking people caring about your product.
The Ugly:
This game was released unpolished and full of bugs. It seems to be a very common practice nowdays, because we have updates, and we can fix everything later... hopefully. I can't say that I was happy spending 40€ on day one and receiving a product so full of bugs and glitches.
Where do I even start?
The movement is jerky, both with a controller and with mouse and keyboard (no, wait, ESPECIALLY with mouse and keyboard. A little disappointing, since the older titles were point and click, and they were made for PC, but I guess they did this to have an optimized interface for the console releases). Sometimes I get stuck when I try to open doors or walk on stairs, having to rock the analog stick back and forth to free myself.
There is a noticeable delay from the moment I press a button or move and the moment the action happens on the screen, and this can be really annoying in the long run.
The game has huge framerate issues and freezes momentarily in certain areas. Now, I know that my system is not the best, but my PC meets the minimum requirements, and I am playing at the lowest graphical settings; besides, a friend of mine has the game on a PS4 and he lamented the same framerate issues. I think the culprit of this might be the anti-piracy system (Denuvo), which is known to cause performance issues on games.
Other occasional graphical issues include broken animations, disappearing skyboxes, being teleported out of rooms (it happened on the ship) and object models twitching. I was also able to interact with speech or observation points that were still there despite the fact that the character or object they were related to was long gone.
I REALLY hope they will be able to fix these problem soon, and provide the product that should have come out on day one.
However, even with those issues, I will still recommend Syberia 3. Just wait a little while to buy it, so Microids can fix at least the most annoying bugs.

I haven't played the original Talisman. This game takes hours to complete. The online games take even longer. Despite the length, most people who you play with online are super friendly and super fun to play with, which basically ends up making the length an advantage (more time = more fun). And the game itself is amazing! It's like playing a full scale MMORPG (an RPG if you don't like online play xD)! It's a game, a board game, that truly does require a huge amount of strategy. It's not just "roll you dice, move on, get to the end first", it's about thinking of where to go, what to do, how to get what you want and so on. And it's not very straightforward either, it's quite complex and utterly wonderful in all aspects. To sweeten the pot, it even has several modes and expansions to make sure you never get bored of playing! A 5/5 game if I ever played one.
EDIT: I must admit that after a while, the game does get quite boring and repetitive. If you can find a group of players and form a group (relatively speaking) to play, then sure, it'll give you hours of enjoyment without fail! Besides, considering how long a game takes, you'll probably end up playing it once or twice a week, in which case it'll provide you with years of fun!
One thing I have noticed, however, is that the community has died down quite a bit. Ever since the "free weekend" ended, the number of games in the lobby is three in the maximum and that's in the European server (which, ironically, is the busiest). Once again, if you've got a group of friends to play with every once in a while, I'd recommend this game without a single moment of hesistation!

A charming game best played with friends but can also be played alone.  The price is a bit higher compared to other games in its genre but its well worth the price since the amount of content this game has greatly makes up for it.  There are currently 120 levels and 4 zones with each level having anywhere from 1 to 5 sublevels.  Each level has keys that you collect to move on to the next level along with items called litho-stones.  These litho-stones are collected to finish off puzzles to earn equipment that give different stats to help make going through different levels easier.  For instance theres a bag that gives you extra oxygen to reach places further out to get rare collectibiles and a hat that protects you from bat guano.  There are also pet companions you find which have different abilities to help you and your friends such as a dog that can dig for collectibles and a parrot that can resurrect your friends from a long distance.  The game does have limitations to how many times you can use these items and companions to help balance out the game but this can be increased based on leveling up these items which is done just by completing stages and wearing them.  On top of all that there are also 40+ quests you can do to allow you to earn even more items and companions.  If after all that the price still scares you then think of all the laughs it will give you to watch your friends make fatal mistakes and plummet to their death!  It is a for sure pick up if you want a fun and challenging co-op game (its up to 4 players).

In this review, i will talk about three of the reasons that i recommend this game : The history behind the game, the tryout and my actual gameplay.
1) The history : Nostalgia. Oh nostalgia...
A lot of gamers don't know but Spelunker Party isn't the first game of this serie. In fact, i think it's the third game (Spelunker on NES, Spelunker HD on PS3 and Spelunker Party! on Steam and Nintendo Switch). I played both the three games and they were just that good. One can't be compared with the others cause of the gap of time between each title and their graphics constantly changing makes them a different game each time. However, the main mechanic and story was always respected, making the game easy enough to follow. So for nostalgic fans like me or complete newbie, no one will be penalized for that point.

I tried the game at a friend's house on the Nintendo Switch. The controls were fine despite the shape of the controllers on the console. When i heard that the game was on Steam AND it was playable with the Xbox style controller, i jumped to the occasion and decide to buy the game for my own good. It actually took around 30 to 45 minutes of gameplay before i took my decision... Talk about quickness.

When i started playing alone on my computer, i realised that the game was quite challenging but a lot, LOT of fun. Spelunker's staying power is something of a mystery: It started in the C64 and NES era as you playing the absolute most pathetic cave explorer ever conceived. This was back before platforming conventions had been established, so this was not even a cute gimmick. You just died if you took a fall more than half your height, into a tiny pit, trying to hop off a rope without treating it like a careful six step embark/disembark process. Hell, your biggest enemy as bat guano. Bats pooing on you, killing you in one hit. The whole affair was nearly spiteful, behind the cutesy music, the game HATED you.
And yet it came back, an HD reimagining on PS3 with slightly less outright hatred (Rope/ladder disembarking is no longer a crapshoot, even if the falls are still as brutal.). Then a F2P, multiplayer-centric take on it on PS4, with some slight MonHun style grind and collection to round that out.
Spelunker Party is a sequel then to that F2P version. MP Lobbies, cave selection, a bit of grinding, but no microtransaction nonsense. Of course, they never advanced beyond the incomprehensible C64-era item pickup icons.
After all that, Spelunker still loves to kill you, but it doesn't really hate you any more. The dungeons are fairly short, so a game over won't cost you a lot of time; enough to make it not an instant retry indie game but not enough to feel punitive. The entire affair ends up feeling rather charming; the deliberate pace of it, stopping to make sure you hop over every pit carefully, dodge bat guano, climb each path for keys, bombs, flares, or meta-loot. The game's love of killing you ends up giving Spelunker its own unique pace and gameplay. It does not end up like IWBTG or similar masochist platformers; the pace is too slow, and it does not often throw you into long sequences without a break demanding fast reflexes.
Spelunker will not stay dead. On paper, it sounds like it shoould, but if you give it a chance, I think you will discover why it has such staying power.

Here's my first review,
Pros:
- The controls are smooth and natural
- The graphics match the style of the game
- Unique gameplay
- A variety of characters and playstyles to choose from
- All of the maps are balanced and enjoable to play on
Cons:
- Complex for beginners (how the resource system works, what you should be focusing on, etc)

- Hard to read Minimap (It's hard to find what exactly is under attack on your minimap.)

The 3 skins you get are only usable on the human team, you get 3 keys for random drops, the fire footsteps are alright but could be more visual and noticeable, the other taunts and such are okay. Looking forward to future updates and work done on the game.

Do you take pride in being an SCV worker drone?  Harvesting resources & constructing buildings day in & day out.  Or do your aspirations reach higher, to a blood-soaked field strewn with fallen foes?!
by
is the place for YOU to discover where you fall on
The first Savage was the one & only successful example of genre blending FPS hack 'n' slash + strategic RTS gameplay that I'd seen anywhere.  Its sequel -
- strayed from the appeal of its predecessor in various ways.  But this most recent "resurrection" is so true to the original (which I poured countless hours into) it seems virtually unchanged outside the obvious visual update (Unreal Engine 4) plus a few minor alterations.  I'm happy with this because
always had a winning formula.
The player community however is vocal in its disapproval of each & every perceived flaw.  The devs appear to be watching this feedback closely, making frequent & meticulous adjustments to the game during these days shortly after the official launch, for everything from bug smashing to balance.
never seemed big on marketing or publicity & I can't help but wonder if that's a factor in why the community has always felt small to me.  I hope Steam will put attention on this one & help it grow, because a game like this is heavily dependent on a thriving player base.
Speaking of that, there are typically three to five populated servers per mode (Standard or Advanced).  So far I haven't had trouble finding a decent game to join, but I'd be more comfortable with stronger numbers.  Teams are 16 vs. 16.  Standard mode = AI Commanders, whereas Advanced mode = player Commanders.  Obviously the former lacks the complexity & richness of gameplay that a fully human match can offer.
It doesn't help that server issues occasionally impede the ability to jump right into play: A server clearly has available slots yet returns a message that it is "full."  Or you'll see network errors, bugs, etc.  Server filters can't be saved for when you get booted back to the home screen, either; annoying.
Aside from that however, the game runs admirably well in its current state; my slightly older machine has no difficulty with frames per second or stability while settings are high.  It does look & sound great!
Initially, accuracy in the 1st person view (ranged weapons) felt somehow off - not as responsive or accurate as in the original game; melee hit recognition felt different too.  The snap-to-target aiming for healers is usable, albeit a bit jittery.  But as I played, all this quickly became very natural & now I'm mostly pleased with combat.
In combat, winning strategies involve protecting friendly siege, targeting enemy siege & knowing when & where to establish forward garrisons.  Following the Commander's orders always helps.  Most fundamentally, one
get practice with each race's unique mechanic: Humans can block (mitigating damage & briefly stunning if timed properly); Beasts can leap (opening avenues for flanking attacks & evading projectiles).
Obviously one of the biggest draws of this game has the potential to be a drawback:
Commanders.  Rolling with an experienced Commander is so fun.  The match is exhilarating & victory sweet!  An unwitting or inexperienced one (or worse, an intentional troll Commander) leads to a frustrating, uninteresting match - win or lose.  It does happen sometimes, but believe it or not the majority of the time things work out just fine.
A cash shop exists but rest assured, it has no Pay to Win components.  The "Loot" screen at match end shows who (if any) earned what.  Just like in
, you occasionally earn loot crates to open with cash shop keys for a random cosmetic equippable.  Some cool looking armor pieces.  Take it or leave it.
In my opinion,
had a vision that became an awesome experience.  Yes, some situations feel one-sided or odd, but that effect stems from the same thing that makes Savage great:
How many competitive multiplayer games have you enjoyed?  In how many of those did Team A look
to Team B?  Not too many developers are brave or determined enough to experiment with something different.  Credit where it's due, this one did.
Definitely thumbs up.  I recommend this to any fan of FPS, RTS or action genres.  My word of warning: just know what you're getting, & also be aware of where the player community/population currently is.
TIP: Turn off motion blur - this graphic setting (which I normally enjoy) should be lowered or even scaled down to 0%; it's unhelpful when trying to whip around & block or leap during a fast-paced fight.
TIP: Learn to use every single item!  They make or break your strategies, rendering seemingly impossible feats doable (with considerable practice).
TIP: Practice commanding with the AI - the place to learn the ropes as Commander is absolutely not in Advanced mode.

Tharsis is missing something vital: a button on the game screen that says "I give up." Because in 99 out of a hundred games, you will want to do just that as the RNG, halfway through though frequently much sooner, tells you in no uncertain terms that you no longer have any chance at all of winning. What masochist would keep playing under such circumstances?
Obviously the single incentive to keep spending time with this evil little slot machine is the hope that drives any gambler: "Maybe this time!" That's it.
Fair enough. But when the main draw of a game is the endless drudgery of trying and failing again and again, at least make it quick and easy to abort and start over instead of forcing us to quit because the escape key doesn't respond except at the end of a round. There's a reason one-armed bandits are operated with a lever.

You want to get to the center of the board crossing through two "rings" of board tiles to get to the tower where you take control and cast a spell that slowly kills off the other players to win.
After a game is finnished you claim XP and level up to the next level where you can get bonuses to the pawn you pick for the next game.

I'm all for keeping a good mechanic if it works, but TERA just throws the same tired MMO game mechanics at you while providing significantly less content than their competitors. An uninteresting story pushes you from quest objective to quest objective. I always give MMO stories a shot so I read the story and kept up with it for a while, but it's so dreadfully dull that I lost interest and just wound up following my mini-map and looking at the quest tracker.
The saving grace of TERA and what you generally hear people rave about is the combat which, admittedly, is fun. However, it's being outdone by other MMOs that are doing real-time combat better. Gone are the days when real-time combat in MMOs was a novelty, and TERA hasn't put forth changes to stay competitive. The only thing they really seem to consistently put forth is a new revealing outfit you can buy with USD on their store. Let no one say that their revealing outfits are unfair, though, for in TERA you can make women
men wear equipment that shows off all the right skin in all the right places without requiring a much higher ESRB rating.
I digress, if you're looking for an MMO with real-time combat that's more engaging than this one, try Black Desert Online or Elder Scrolls Online. Hell, even DC Universe Online has more interesting combat.
One thing that is great about this game is that it's beautiful. Three cheers for their art team because they really know what they're doing. The visuals are stunning and I often found myself stopping in my tracks to turn off the HUD, adjust the camera, and take a well-deserved screenshot. On top of that, I found the game to be very well optimized, with settings you can adjust to make it optimize in real time, so even lower-end setups can get some pretty nice visuals.
All in all, play a different MMO if you're like me and your trolled the web for something to fill that MMO void you feel. If you're looking for quick suggestions, I would say give Black Desert Online a try, and maybe DC Universe Online if you're into the comics and all that. If you're a Tolkien nerd, try out Lord of the Rings Online. And, of course, you can always go back to WoW but, to be frank, you're probably here because you've given up on WoW.
Happy searching.

Spelunker Party, if your familiar with the HD version the majority of the gameplay is already known to you, some new system around cosmetic items and level selection stuff aside.  Everyone else, read on!
Spelunker Party is based off of Spelunker, that game some of you may regard as some ancient relic if you know of it at all with the highly regarded weakest character in video games, the spelunker.  A man capable of destroying his life from simple missteps half his height that destroy his legs and all chance of survival, to needing a rapidly depleting oxygen tank to breath at all.  A character who braves deep ruinous caverns to grab treasure and try to keep smiling while everything turns into a living hell around him.  Spelunker Party keeps this man and his flaws intact, while giving him some friends who also suffer similar vulnerabilities to play as.
Spelunker at it's core is a platforming game that requires precise timing of your actions, from given only a split second of thinking time to work around a passage of instant death traps to running from giant boulders through a cavern composed of just platforms to jump across.  Simple snakes and hidden pits require your full attention as your ability to jump is only just enough to bypass such things and mistakes lead to lost lives. Jumping from a rope onto an incline the wrong way is a good way to perish. Flares you launched to rid yourself of bats and their deadly guano ended up falling on you on your way back with the treasure and burned you alive. You will struggle and try to endure and the game offers great personal satisfaction for your troubles.
The series likes to pride itself on it's difficulty, and while it's still largely intact here, you are also given items to find and equip that augment your abilities, such as your bombs having a larger blast radius, or recieving protection from a single type of trap/enemy to stave off death for one or two hits.  Such items also gain experience and level up through usage, increasing the bonus they give.  While some of this is just for personal comfort, the game does expect you to use certain equipment to uncover secrets through abilities they give, such as a dog you can travel with is capable of digging up hidden treasure.
While the core of spelunker is alive and well in spelunker party, it does have some caveats in it's design, namely certain secrets can only be obtained through multiplayer.  Cooperating with other players is sometimes the only to progress to certain secrets, such as someone needing to stand on a switch which creates platforms across a wide pit for someone else to run across.  If you are intent on getting everything in the game, be sure you have people to work with.  The game does have local and online multiplayer.
------------------------------------------- Update---------------------------------------------
While I'm aware that there is a piece of equipment that allows you to press switches from far away, you still need other players to actually perform all the quests in the game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
As for some technical points, you can't remap controls within the game, and you will want a controller ready for this.  The game boots up with the steam Big Picture Mode UI - not necessarily fullscreen, you can always play the game in a window but the UI will remain in the overlay.  While playing multiplayer if you encounter any cutscenes after a level you will be kicked from any group you were playing with.  If you lose all your lives in a level while playing multiplayer and no one manages to revive you, you will be booted from the group you are playing with, if this happens to the host then you will be dealing with a hopefully minor annoyance of host migration.
Despite it's faults, this is a game I greatly enjoy, and intend to put many more hours into it.  Multiplayer also allows for a great amount of entertainment - for the full experience turn Friendly Fire on in the lobby creation settings, your not doing it to intentionally kill eachother, it will just happen and it will be the magical misery that will cause you to howl with pain and laughter.
P.S.  If using a dual analog stick, be sure to click in the right stick during multiplayer, it will save you a lot of eye strain.

Fantastic Game.  A very tricky blend of RTS/RPG/FPS.  If you've played the first two, then you'll most likely have some high expectations.
I find that the game returns to the origins of the first game without a lot of the additional features of the second (Demons).  They basically took the first game and analyzed how it could be better.  They've added BOT support so that your team is never completely outnumbered or ridiculously stacked against.
The Human Commander was really the make/break point for a match in the original.  They took this concept and added an AI commander that is reasonably balanced and performs fairly well and at an even pace.  This allows for much better matches that aren't won/loss within the starting minutes of the game.  They still have Human Commanders, but this is in the "Advanced Mode."  The AI Commander can be found in the "Standard Mode."
They also updated the theme from the original as it was somewhat silly to have a Nomad with a machine gun (repeater).  The humans now have more of a Sci-Fi feel and the beasts are as good as ever.  I also feel that there have been some improvements in the control and hit boxes of the characters overall.
Top of all that off with much better graphics, and you have Savage: Resurrection.  All in all, a fantastic game that can certainly hold your attention.  I highly recommend this game.

I came to this game expecting to judge it against No Man's Sky - I've been waiting for a seamless space navigation game for a while, and NMS was the best offering I had seen. After playing Rodina, I'm certain I'll be judging NMS by how well it stacks up to Rodina.
The combat is straightforward, but fresh. It doesn't feel like Freelancer or EVE or any other space game, it prioritizes momentum and special weapons. It seems to hinge on the "stickshift" mechanic, which works excellent with the flow of the combat/navigation, and ties everything together well. The places you visit are varied enough, but will definitely feel flat and boring after a few hours of seeing the same crevasses, blank textures, and lack of surface features save for a heightmap.
Building your ship is also rewarding. After I realized that the ship was definitely bigger on the inside than it was on the outside, I decided to fix that. I'd spent too much time getting lost in the default ship anyway. In about five minutes I had a sleek interior that was sized approximately to the actual size of the ship, and looked fine. Maybe a bit bland, but the editor controls are decent enough. I could recognize some amateur tile-and-entity selection/manipulation mechanics, but with a little ironing out I'm sure it'll be fine.
That makes the game sound pretty lame, I know. It's early access, and seems to be progressing apace. But what really sold me was the story.
Look, I'm not one to hype up story-games, especially not when it's done in a "find game item, read blurb, find game item, read blurb" format like this. But my mild interest in the story turned to appreciation near the end (no spoilers), which tied together the reason you (the player) existed, why you were different, and what was going on. Very rarely do I feel like a story explains why the player acts how he does (players are crazy, we don't act at all like normal people in the real world), or why he knows nothing about the universe that everyone else has been living in. Rodina explained all of that beautifully with one single twist, and I'll recommend the game if for no other reason than to encourage someone to have that "whoa, cool!" moment that I did
My biggest gripe is that the re-entry mechanics are a little frustrating, and seem to take too much time with you just spinning around in place. In cruise mode in space, you can orbit any planet in under a minute, why does re-entry take so much fkn time? Why is my cruise velocity so low once I'm in atmo? I get that spaceflight would really be like this (especially in denser atmospheres), but game mechanics need to serve the game, not reality. If it wastes my time and makes me feel tied down, it shouldn't be in a free-roaming game.

This game has a really cool concept with a really neat story to it. I just wish I could see more of the story to tell you about. The idea here is that you're a crew of astronauts on their way to mars, your ship is hit by some space junk and all hell breaks lose. Not bad so far.
You know enter into a resource/ event planning game mode, where your roll dice to solve issues like the food room being on fire, or the engine room being broke. If you don't fix one of these events something bad happens to your crew. Be it losing hit points, sanity, dice, or the ship taking a hit. If you ship complete breaks you lose and if all your crew dies you lose.
Now with that out of the way let's look at what I liked and didn't like about this game.
Pros:
For the first couple rounds I had fun in this game. I know it was a hard RNG based game, that would require some planning to get through. My first 10 or so games went pretty bad with me only getting as far as turn 3. Soon though I start to understand how to manage the events and my resources better and i got as far as turn 6. Even though i was losing every game I played I had a plan. I was sure that the 4-5 other lock characters that you can unlock in the game would increase my chance to win. I was ok, i get it. The Devs added a way for people who can't figure out this game really fast a way to grind through objectives to unlock more characters, thus meaning a better chance to win. Neat!
Cons:
Here's the thing though that's not what those characters are. They do not simply become part of your crew as i thought, but instead replace someone on your crew. This means you are always locked at having only 4 characters. This topped with the now 20+ loses i have had in the game with little progress has really turned my opinion of the game around.I felt completely helpless to the point of not enjoying this game anymore. I could understand if the mode i was playing on was hard or something, but i was on normal. On normal and getting to the point of wondering if this game is worth the frustration. So i looked through the discussion page to see what others are planning and talking about. I got a few ideas from people but nothing different from what i had already figured out on my own. The one thing that really struck out to me though was the conversation the Devs were having there. Which pretty much went like this, "there is nothing wrong with the game, we want it to be frustratingly hard, and we do not have any plans to change that.". While I respect a Dev for sticking to their vision of their work, I can't find the ability to complete this game. Making it a must return for me and not play again. In fact I will most likely avoid this Devs in the future cause i now know what kind of games they like to make and they aren't for me. I am not the target audience. I am by no means a casual gamer but when my fun time becomes more stressful than my job or relations in the real world, then it is to much.
In the end, if you like extreme (and i can't state that enough extreme) challenges get this game. It looks like a lot of fun from all the videos i watched and my first playthrough was fun, but it claws at you over time. If you're a braver person than me this is the game for you otherwise I would skip this and get something else.

You have characters to choose from and they all have special abilities that effect game play.
The base game has plenty to choose from so don't worry.
Each player begins at a character specific start square on the outer ring on the board.
The board is made of three rings of space each with location names on them, some of these locations also have special abilities that effect your pawn.
You have 2 sums that are used in combat, strength and craft, then life, fate and gold all of which can be leveled up or chipped away at to reduce them lower that starting amounts.
You roll a random generated die and move to the tile options you come up with, than you draw an adventure card that may be a monster, loot, item or event to challenge youor the other players.
The object is to level up collecting items boosting your stats and fighting the other players, It plays just like a board game- one player after another takeing turns but as the game goes on the difficulty and struggle increases.
You want to get to the center of the board crossing through two "rings" of board tiles to get to the tower where you take control and cast a spell that slowly kills off the other players to win.
After a game is finnished you claim XP and level up to the next level where you can get bonuses to the pawn you pick for the next game.
WARNING!!
The games seem to take a long time to play through, I've played many- finnished two and both of those took longer than 3 hours to play. Lots of fun! Very replayable, lots of laughs with your friends.

What can I really say about The Blackwell Legacy? It felt like a nice nod back to the OLD point and click adventure games I remember as a kid. The interface was simple. The puzzles were easy enough to figure out, but not so simple as to be pandering. The only thing that put me off a little- at first- was the voice acting, but I quickly got acclimated to it. The good: this was a nice throwback to an earlier generation of video games.  I liked the graphics, although it's going for a certain style.  Amazing graphics, these ain't.  I liked the music in the game.
The bad: The voiceacting was so bad that my first action in the game was to go into the options and turn the voice over off.  Unintuitive actions led to walkthrough consultations (geez, why didn't I think to explore every dialogue option with a character, leave, and then immediately re-enter their room to talk to them again?).  I also encountered a genuine bug in one of the last puzzles of the game; I eventually figured out what was wrong (an item could not be picked up unless I was on a certain page in my inventory), but it was very frustrating.  I found the storyline trite and fairly unengaging.  The game is *very* short - no more than an hour and a half to two hours, even with the built-in backtracking the game makes you do.
Personally, I wouldn't recommend this game unless it's very cheap.

The port itself definitely needs some basic attention for some fairly basic things, but overall seems solid.  It took a couple launches for it to run, and once it did run it failed to recognize the Steam controller or the Dualshock. It's about a 5gb download, and the graphics resolution isn't really intended for 4k displays -- the art is as good as in the previous games in the series, but it's clear this is an up-port of a Playstation Vita level model and not the quality of models generally being used on Playstation 4 or in PC titles.

Where to start...This is one of those games that if you played it when it first came out, years would pass, you would try multiple other MMOs and realize that you keep coming back to Ragnarok. There's just a certain charm to it.  On the surface this might seem like a usual simple grind-fest, however the game is very complex. Mainly because it gives you complete freedom to build your characters the way you want (and make many, many mistakes in the process).
Want to build a battle-priest because you do not like monks? - go for it.  Want to make a full-crit assassin with the sole purpose of hunting high-def monsters? - go right ahead. The beauty is that with enough research and equipment planning you could make even the most bizzare character builds work.  Or you will fail miserably and realize that you want to try again, with a different skill-set, different stats, different cards and equipment..possibilities are limited only by your imagination.
Even though the game is quite old, it definitely held up very nicely and is worth a try.

I've noticed a big spike up of spaceship games recently, starting from no-mans-sky to elite and a few more (spike up at least in my knowledge of them)
But current Rodina and planned Rodina both seem to have their very owe special feel. I think this comes from the total freedom of movement and how you interact with everything.
For starters, I've never played a game that allows for this level of interior design, truly making a ship your own not only in feel but also gameplay.
You can go from walking on a planet to navigating your way to the toilet block on your ship to sitting in the cockpit (now in complete first person). But it doesn't stop there because you can start to fly your ship, get out of the seat, get a drink, then come back and take the wheel again but have it still moving at the same time.
It has that elderscroll level of choice where you are given a bunch of mechanics then told to have fun, and a story to hold your hand if you so choose. Which leads to chaotic stories and amusing bug discovery. Simply because the player has that power over what they can do.

I've seen a lot of good reviews for Rodina recently, which is enough to make me happy, but I noticed eighty percent of those reviews focus soley on Rodina's gameplay. Now Rodina's gameplay is stellar - don't get me wrong - but nobody seemed to point out the story in Rodina. You might not have even known it had one. That's why I'm here.
The story in Rodina is set up a little differently than most other games, being that instead of playing through a chronological chain of events, you discover pieces of it at a time. The pieces you collect are written, and I have to say, the people behind Rodina are certainly no strangers to writing. The remnants and transmissions you obtain detailing Rodina's story succeed in inducing a strange twinge of awe inside you, along with the bizarre growing apprehension of the larger scheme of things at work.
There are two kinds of story elements I suppose: the Encrypted Transmissions, and the Archive Remnants (just what I've chosen to call them). The Transmissions are unlocked procedurally, and give you more and more info on the situation the Rodina's 'Vanguard' faced (roughly) years ago. They are witty, somewhat humorous, and make for great reading. The Archive Remnants are other 'Datasticks' you collect and add to your Archive, which describe various scenarios or bits of culture pertaining to the world and life on the Rodina. Some are single pages, while others are in pieces of four or five, and the latter usually tells its own mini story as well.
Finally getting that last encryption and discovering the truth behind the Rodina and the Vanguard made something click in my head; you could say it confirmed my suspicions. To put it modestly, it felt wierd. Really wierd. The writing, and the way the story is told, coupled with the expansive solar system and seamless world Rodina had created gave me goosebumps. And let me tell you something.
I live in Minnesota.
I don't get goosebumps easily.
[EDIT] Quick developer note: Turns out the writing is done by Andrew Schurr, a friend of the Brendan Anthony (the developer)! It's worth pointing out since I want to give credit to all who deserve it. If you're still reading this, what are you doing, and why haven't you bought the game yet? If you're not sold to the story, check out some of the gameplay reviews. The writing's not the only thing Rodina has to offer you know!

Syberia wasn't supposed to play like a typical action adventure and it also wasn't pretending loyalty to point & click. Having avoided being just a copy of its shape from 13 years ago it still conserved its essence well! It had to graphically evolve (I'm ok with nostalgia but perhaps not obsessive nostalgia) and it did, with the unchanged vibe of old.
Character rendering is definitely adequate to nowadays standards; the environments slightly less so. I'm relatively pleased with the overall design, while some things just didn't seem all that important to justify a complaint.
To me, Polish translations unfortunately came off as dispassionate. :) I recognize these voices of multiple identities, living in way too many characters and beginning to sound a little repetitive AND bored. I mean, they must be!
Voice acting in English however was truly satisfactory. Kate Walker sounds lively, soulful, caring, and everything that makes for her personality and wisdom is reflected by the voice of irreplaceable Sharon Mann! She worked on previous games and she is super talented.
Most NPCs sounded decent. And did I hear Jesse Eisenberg - his voice so distinct - also as Steiner? Because the age disparity can't go unnoticed, man. Ok so it's just a minor oversight: he plays someone 2 generations (oops!) older, let's hope nobody notices!
The story is brilliantly designed and was clearly an inspired project. Like in previous Syberia gems it focuses on the high road journey of the protagonist. The moral purpose behind Kate's decisions couldn't be more relatable, personally...
It's probably just me, but I think that puzzles in all games should occupy very little space in my awareness whenever I'm solving them. I don't want to be presented these like standalone problems that have no relation to anything and are devised just to slow me down.
Syberia 3, like her predecessors, isn't like that. It has places worth going that these puzzles enable, but they are melted into the reason why you care. And while they are an integrated part of the journey, they become just things you are actually delighted to tinker with.
Syberia 3 has upheld the standard of its beautiful world, though admittedly it is less detailed when not drawn. But it's still reminiscent of steampunk, art nouveau aesthetics that visually defined first two.
Last but not least: I love that the series has quietly embraced, perhaps without meaning so, the often solitary lifestyles of the many encounters throughout it. We peek into fascinating lives organized outside of society, so often around some passion or necessity, ocasionally a need to escape... I'm happy to see the game hold onto the old traditions it created for itself and that it celebrates individualism.
I would recommend it to all, but not all will be able to appreciate it. And that is a fact I'm all right with.
I have a lot to say about it, but I'm not going to. It begged for a sequel, certainly. The future a mystery, maybe.

To start, I never leave reviews on games because I generally just... don't really feel strongly about the gameplay. I play a lot of adventure games. A lot of old point-and-click adventure games. I play and replay them.  I am a forgiving person when it comes to graphics, because I enjoy older games, and for me it's almost always more important to have a good story than it is for it to look amazeballs.
The TL;DR is this: I don't recommend this game because it's 40 dollars, and for 40 dollars you should expect a game not to be broken when you play it.  If you can get it on sale, or wait until maybe they release some patches to fix the save issues at minimum, definitely wait.  (I am not the only person to have this problem!)
I am a huge fan of the series. I loved Syberia I and II. I wanted to love Syberia III.
The good: The story is decent. Mostly. So, I suppose I don't really understand the motivation of the antagonists, and that kind of grated on me as the story went on.  I get that they ARE enemies, and I get what they are trying to achieve... but I'm just not convinced as to why they've landed themselves in this desire to begin with.
It doesn't really get better in that regard. But, some of the characters were loveable, and I did laugh quite a bit. I enjoyed wandering around talking to everyone I could, and overall I enjoyed the "journey". Despite the "why even?" of the enemies, I did feel sufficiently pressured at times to escape, so that was well done.
The voice acting isn't great (in English? Haven't tried it in other languages) but that's another thing I could get over despite all the other things.
What was surprising: Believe it or not, I didn't actually mind that you use WASD controls to move around.  There were times when it felt natural, and when the camera wasn't screwing me up, it was great.  I explain this below. It doesn't NEED to be point-and-click in my book, and this COULD HAVE been done very well. I mean, it WASN'T done very well, but it could have been.
What was bad:
Sweet mother of God, if this were Google these developers would have been fired forever.
Reasons:
My save broke when I was about 3/4 of the way through the game. Randomly. I made a point to make sure I followed directions. I waited until it wasn't auto-saving. I exited the game through the menu (Menu --> Exit). So then when I go to enter the game again, my save wouldn't load! It just hung on the black screen. I lucked out, that another user had something similar happen. Their solution was to start a new game, and load their old save from there. This worked for me too! Thank goodness. But then when I got back into the game, I couldn't leave the screen! So I reloaded again, and finally everything was okay and I could continue.
^^^^^^^^^ This is a deal breaker for me. Everything else, and I was like "Eh, okay." This is the point where I said, outloud, "Man, I shouldn't have bought this game. It's just completely and inexcusably broken." I understand save corruptions, but if you search through the forums, you'll see a lot of people complaining about that same issue. This was the point where I very nearly lost an entire save -- and you know these point and clicks. They take hours. You try to talk to all the people. You don't want to have to do it all again because your save gets corrupted.
But you have no way of saving a second copy of the file "just in case", because there is no way to manually save!! So you're just stuck hoping nothing bad happens to your only save.
Anyway, another time, I got stuck in a scene where I couldn't leave the room. The camera wouldn't follow me, there were no clickable options. I had to reload the game and start the whole scene over again.
And what even is this "autosave only" feature anyway? I don't understand why there isn't manual saving in this game. Autosaving is nice and all, but sometimes I like having multiple save files, sometimes I like to just... you know, save and go to bed and not have to wait for autosave to save my progress. The autosave is semi-frequent, but not always as frequently as one might like. And it's just silly -- this isn't a survival game, and there are no timed puzzles, so who cares if you have the ability to save on your own?
The camera controls were weird. I felt like I was playing an older Resident Evil game, or one of the early Silent HIll games... you know. Where you're running down a hallway, and they suddenly switch up the camera angle and it screws up your running? And then you run into a wall, or the monsters catch you, or whatever? It's exactly like that. How many times did I go up a set of stairs in this game, only to immediately find myself coming back down the stairs? How many times did I exit and reenter a screen?  Anyway, this was only semi-annoying, as there are no chase scenes in this game. But seeing as other games have progressed past this, I'm not sure why this was the design choice they made. Aside from maybe not wanting to flesh out the scenery in all directions in order to give full camera control to the player. Like I said earlier, it didn't need to be point and click for me. But the camera was just all sorts of screwy and I don't know that a patch would fix this.
Also, randomly? They use a lot of Russian in this game for signs and letters and documents, which is awesome! But a few of the documents ... weren't translated? Like you get this whole letter and there's just no translation, at least, there wasn't when I played. So, I got to put some of my rusty Russian skills to the test, but I imagine that would be annoying for other people.  So. Oops? I guess?

Since I had some uncertainty as to whether or not this would work on my machine given the warnings on the Store page, as well as some older reviews, here is my current setup:
i7-7700k
16gb DDR4 RAM
GTX 1070 8gb
Windows 10 64-bit
All the updated versions of I - VII work from start-to-finish, but whatever versions would launch through the Legacy launcher, don't (they immediately CTD).  This release includes the Windows version of KQVI but you can't launch it through this package, you need to install SCUMMVM and run it through there to do so (has high-res portraits as well as some other upgrades, but I prefer the DOS version).  If the "Legacy" versions CTD for you through the official launcher as they do for me, you can fix this by running them through SCUMMVM as well.  This is also how you can play the official KQI remake from 1990.
VIII is missing for some reason, I know it wasn't very popular and as such Sierra maybe thought including it in this collection would have tarnished this release, but this is definitely incomplete without it.
Further adding to the confusion at VIII's exclusion from this package is that VIII (released in 1998) was later included in the 1999 re-release of 1997's "King's Quest Collection".  The Collection version this Steam release is based on was originally released in 2006, it too excluded VIII which was a mystery as well, it's exclusion is even more mysterious now that it was updated on Steam in 2016 to include better versions than were available in the 2006 Collection release - why not add KQVIII through this update as well?
It's also worth noting the 2006 release this Steam version is based on excludes all the extras the 1997 Collection had, such as "making of" videos and more full Sierra games.
KQI and KQII are extremely simple, mostly boring adventure games, but they're pretty easy to get through with some modest annoyances here and there (the beanstalk climb is pretty atrocious).
KQIII has a ton of potential, but it's the worst of the first four, no question.  Part of the game design is to, at times, sit around for 5 - 25 minutes doing nothing but waiting on the wizard to go leave/take a nap and come back from wherever he left to/wake up from his nap.  There's even a later segment where you sit idle for ~15 minutes waiting for a ship to drop anchor.  Brilliant design, Sierra!  The manual included in this release also includes the "first wave" KQIII manual, which is a problem because the spell creation is this game's form of DRM, and that "first wave" manual had a couple typos in the spell creations - hence, if you try to beat the game with this manual alone, you won't be able to!  So, you either need to find an updated manual, *OR* just use a guide and hope it doesn't have typos itself (there are several lackluster KQ guides out there written by those with poor understandings of English who didn't do spellcheck, or were simply written in a rush and are very poorly made!)
KQIV still asks for the DRM code (references a word from a page of the manual) for some reason, but you can either look in the "manual" section of the King's Quest Collection install to find the required code, or find a copy of the manual online.  This  Steam release only contains a "cheat sheet" for KQIV DRM codes which doesn't contain all possible required entries, so there is a chance you'll need to find a copy of the full original manual online, anyway!
KQV has great art, but it also has a ton of deadends.  The desert can be quite tedious to get through if you don't use a guide, several puzzles have absolutely no logic to them whatsoever, just trial and error (or, much to Sierra's benefit back in the day, calling the hintline).
Use a walkthrough.  Save often.  V CTD'd on me once near the end, I thought it was the scene being glitched on Windows 10 64-bit, but when I reloaded the game and my save and did the scene again, it progressed fine, so it's likely some bug inherent to the original game itself.
KQVI is one of the best point-and-click adventure games ever made.  If you go guideless, remember to use the manual, you need some of the info in it to solve some puzzles.
KQVII is enjoyable as well but it has more of a Disney vibe to the art.  I'd also say it has more "horror" elements to it than V and VI, the base movement speed is quite slow so mash that + button to get it up to something proper!  I like the intro song, but the scene itself is pretty amusing.  It wasn't a surprise when I found out this is because the intro movie (and only the intro movie) was animated by the same people that did Zelda on the CD-i.
The main appeal for most people is likely going to be nostalgia, without that these games will be extremely rough if played without a guide. King's Quest Collection is a collection of almost all of the old King's Quest games before reboot. All made by Sierra. Almost. It's missing a game that was made before King's Quest franchise but was accepted as canon part of it later on: "Wizard and the Princess". But then it never came on DOS, so no wonders. Last pre-reboot game, KQ8: Mask of Eternity is also missing. It was quite a controversial one, being much darker in tone and being action-adventure based with combat. Oh, and if you run legacy launcher that is so bad that it requires patch you will get 1990 remake of KQ1 instead of 1984 original. They aren't too different however. You also need to patch legacy launcher if you want to see Windows 3.1 version of KQ6 which had these huge portraits for characters talk.
But eh. To be honest, I really don't like these old adventure games. Deaths are cool but dead ends are not. Neither are rather silly puzzles. Somethings illogical, sometimes just BS. I mean, there are some good parts but once you get one BS puzzle you start to suspect that the next one is BS one too and it just ruins everything. Plus, too tired of them after playing so many. Probably just grew out from teenager years when I was willing to accept it all without knowing better cus old. Albeit I did end up recommending Space Quests games in oldie Steam review but that's because the story itself was more original and deaths were much more amusing, making me laugh. Then again, it was extremely guilty pleasure due to nostalgic reasons, I should be ashamed. As for KQs? Just read some books instead.
Seriously, go read some books. They aren't inferior art, you know.
You know, I could write a more detailed review but I beat these games quite a time ago, year or so, when collection was taken off Steam store and only now decided to write up what I think. So here are my short opinions over these ones.
KQ1:
1984 released game. It's actually pretty cool one. It was like text adventure, you still have to write commands in, but it was graphical and you could walk around. By the way, you can use buttons like Home and PgDn to walk diagonally. Unlike other games this one is completely unlinear, you just have to get three items so there are three paths you can take in any order. From what I remember. Also, multiple solutions to puzzles make it much better. Most of BS puzzles were optional. Or at least the one that people keep referencing about Gnome's name.
It's also based off English fairy tales which is cool. Aside from part of filling the bowl. Just asking it to. I mean, we in Russia have similair fairy tale object but it's a carpet, so.
Then again, I first played Sega Master System version where you get a list of objects and actions for each scene. That's the one I recommend.
Also, the first death is best ever. Pretty much every player gets it in the first 10 seconds. It's just so ridiculous it's a classic.
KQ2:
1985 game. It's like the first game but this time it's linear and without valid multiple solution so it sucks now. Also, different fairy tales. With Dracula.
KQ3:
1986 one. A combination of oldie adventure games with prison escape genre. Do long chores for wizard and then do your own stuff while he is away. Excellent idea! But still ruined by gameplay. It's still linear in progression and meh bleh dead ends. You also find requirements for making spells in manual. And I have heard that some manuals had mistakes in them, don't remember if Steam one is correct. Also, gotta use roman numbers to turn on pages. Ha!
Also, time limit. There is limited amount of food in kitchen so at some point wizard is going to zap you anyway.
KQ4:
1988. This time it's back to almost linear. As in, there is optional path that you gotta go through to get a good ending. Also with time limits. Engine was upgraded to allow mouse control for moving but no pathfinding. Still very eh. Also, copy protection, consult with manual.
KQ5:
1990. It's now classic point-n-click interface, all in VGA. This is the part where they go from ridiculous to ludicrous as far as attepts at gameplay go. Nothing like throwing a pie at yeti being a puzzle. That's why you shouldn't give eat pie in mountains, just eat a leg of lamb that you will eat only half of instead of full pie. Yesss, I feel my mind capability increasing. I mean, people talk about satisfication when they finally solve puzzles like that but I don't get any feeling if I think that puzzle was BS. Just "Dobby is free".
At least it's charming. Owl is cool. No sarcasm.
KQ6:
1992. While the locations here are even more wacky at times, it's also more creative and writing is more mature. This one is interesting even with walkthrough. It does have few paths. One toward bad ending, another for good ending. Get all scores for the best ending. Interesting, bad ending route is much shorter. It's too bad it still has dead ends and occasionally silly puzzles. Perhaps it's on par with KQ1, albeit I still think that SMS KQ1 is still better.
Also, when you climb up a mountain in one island you need to consult with manual for solutions, yo.
KQ7:
1994. Now they decided that mature tone of KQ6 was too much and went off to unmature one. Er, I mean, kidlike. I mean, it's now cartoon styled and all family friendly. Aside from the death in desert where you turn into bones. It's like they overlooked this thing. Too bad it stole away any sense of danger with these friendly deaths. Ha. There are no dead ends now. Sadly, puzzles still don't make me happy. Furthermore, I hate settings, the plot and so on. Not only because Halloween land that I spend too much in. But it has that uncanny valley for me. As in, it's cartoonish yet so wrong for cartoonish. I mean, pulling off cartoon animation in 1994 was quite something, alright, but it wasn't there yet. Jumpy frames mixed with smoothness, flat colors, jumpy pixels. Let's say, I heard that studio that worked on Zelda CD-i took part in this. Not 100% sure but that's the best way to explain it. Also, MIDIs somehow give me depression. I don't know, man!
Intro is still pretty sweet. The theme song. But so is KQ6 one by the way.
None the less. Ehhhh. Don't know. Old adventures games. Tired of their BSs. That's the only thing I can mutter right now. None of them are really worth it here, so eh. Only if you want to experience how they were like.
Classic.

I can't hit the thumbs down button since (some of) these games are genuinely enjoyable -- so long as you fall into the small niche of people who are willing to tolerate the scummy game design associated with Sierra games. Running the games are also pretty easy: just grab scummvm and run the games through it. But there is another "but":
There are free fan remakes of the first three games. The first remake in particular is excellent, and the second is great too: they make the games much more enjoyable while not taking anything away from them.
King's Quest 7 is bad and is a waste of your time.
As such, you are essentially paying the price of a full collection, but you only get the benefit of three games for it. While King's Quest 6 is great fun, King's quest 4 is very dated -- and how good King's Quest 5 is is a topic of debate. If you have more "modern" gaming sensibilities, I doubt you'll enjoy them very much. Whether that sounds like a good deal for £15 is up to you.

Especially for King's Quest 6, since it might not be obvious that the puzzle you're up against is actually copy protection. Thankfully, they included all the required manuals in this collection, unlike in the Space Quest one.

This series is very tightly connected to my childhood, much like the Space Quest series was. King's Quest V was my first of this particular series, but it captivated me, and I yearned to play the rest, lurking around all the game shops I could, trying to find the earlier releases. I managed to end up with all of them except King's Quest I, and played them to completion. I adored them and completed IV, V, VI, and VII multiple times. I replayed the Space Quest games maybe a year ago, and though I didn't love them as much as I originally did, I definitely still have great love for them. WIth the King's Quest series, however, I don't have the same sentiments, despite having played the Space Quest games at the same point in my life and again now. Why is that? Well, I figure I'll go through each entry, both from my own time looking back on the games with my "grown-up" perspectives and opinions.
In the original King's Quest, which was the first time I've had the chance to actually play that one, it's so basic that every screen for the longest while looks to be a forest area. Very little of interest appears on screen, and all the fantasy elements just stick out like a sore thumb. I understand they hadn't done this before, but everything felt so clumsily put together. Also, whomever decided Graham's walking speed is a jerk. On slow, he moves like a sloth. On normal, he moves at a sleepy turtle's pace...and at fast, he moves like the Flash. Set it to fast, tap the right arrow key, and you will cross the entire screen in half a second. It's practically worthless because you will zip right into death traps instantly and die.
In King's Quest II, some of that forest area environment persists, but there are more interesting things to see and do, in my opinion. I had completed this one way back when. The movement speed problem is still there, but it's less noticable since there are less worthless screens in between screens of relevant things to do, from what I've noticed. It's an alright game, but just feels like a bunch of fantasy stuff tossed into a game in the place of actual writing. I'll talk more about this later in my review.
King's Quest III I actually respect more now than I did as a kid. I think I'm going to say that it has my favorite premise out of all the games in the series. You're a slave of an evil, old wizard who will kill you if you disobey him, and you want to escape by using spells against him. To do this, you must break into his secret lab, read his spell book, steal items from around the house, sneak out while he's away, visit the outlying lands and villages, and run back fast before the wizard gets back home and realizes you're missing. Then you hide everything under your bed like you're a prison inmate planning a jailbreak or something. Holy crap that's awesome. I love it. The game itself could have been a lot more interesting if original ideas had been used for the fantasy elements themselves, instead of copying Medusa and a bunch of other stuff, but again, I'll talk more about that at the end of my review.
King's Quest IV has you play as a female, and if you want an example of "girl power," this is it. Why? Because Rosella's walking speed is acceptable!!! Oh my gosh. Seriously, this is the first game in the series where the protagonist walks at a reasonable speed. I felt like this entry's premise and the fictional things you interact with were not as fun as in King's Quest III, but it's an alright game. The graphics are a huge step up as well.
King's Quest V was my entry point into the series, and graphically, it's a massive improvement. I really enjoyed the music in it as well in various parts, and it had some good puzzles. Most importantly, I felt like the environments were a huge step in the right direction for the series. There was a lot more variation in the appearance of the screens. WIth the earlier King's Quest games, I don't remember the outdoor areas well at all, but with King's Quest V, almost every screen except some of the irrelevant desert ones are incredibly memorable. There's the screen with the bear and the bees, the one with the inn, the one with the snake, the desert areas...all really memorable and pleasant to look at.
However, this game is one of the longer ones in the series, and will screw you over harder than most when it comes to getting permanently stuck. If you do buy this game, when you see a rat in front of the inn, being chased by a cat, you make sure you hit the cat with a shoe/boot. If you don't, you just lost the game. No lie. You won't find out until several hours later, and you then have to start over or load a save before you walked in front of the inn. That is just dirty, and there's a maze near the end of the game that I found to be pretty drawn out and aggravating.
The graphics are even better in the sixth entry, and are my favorite look for the series, personally. The game is divided into several very different islands with plenty of puzzles/problems to solve and some enjoyable voice acting and music. This is probably my favorite King's Quest game ever made. There's whimsy, danger, excitement, adventure, and really neat environments. Each island is highly memorable, the game has some good comedy, and there are multiple endings depending on how well you resolve things. Man, I really dig this game.
After King's Quest VI, I'm not quite sure whey they decided to go for the cartoonish look of King's Quest VII. It worked for Space Quest VI because the goofy tone didn't throw things off by changing the art style so drastically, but with King's Quest VII, it made a series that walked a line between silly and somewhat serious and just hopped too far over the cartoony/silly side of things, in my opinion. King's Quest V and VI had genuinely scary moments in them (V's witch woods with that music made me so uncomfortable in a good way, and VI's land of the dead was really creepy!), but VII feels like a kid's show where nothing is really dangerous. You can die, sure, but the game's atmosphere and monsters weren't unsettling, even though they were graphically superior. Cartoons with that art style just weren't scary. =/
Much of the series - the first four games in particular - feel like the most uninspired writing I've seen in games that actually bothered to have a plot at all. Roberta Williams, the lead writer, seems to have essentially taken the most superficial and blatant version of anything in fantasy tales, such as Medusa, the big bad wolf, princesses turned into things by witches, tiny people making shoes, a Count Dracula-looking vampire that doesn't talk and has a Dracula-style castle (of course), a large green dragon guarding a treasure, and the list goes on and on and on. She took all this stuff and just threw it in, instead of making anything new or writing anything clever with it. It's not a homage if everything is a ripoff and originality doesn't come into the equation.
With Space Quest, it's a parody, and a brilliantly done one - especially Space Quest III and IV, in my opinion. Scott Murphy and Mark Crowe seemed to realize that just ripping stuff off wasn't enough, and made their own story with the gags like icing on the cake. Roberta Williams, on the other hand, has the plot of the game as the icing, and it's a poor icing, with the piles of fantasy things just crammed in to give the illusion of creativity where there is very little. As a dumb kid, I just cared that it was colorful, had nice music, and that it kept me busy. As an adult, however, I'm put off by the laziness of just tossing in all the free folklore/mythical characters Roberta Williams could think of and writing lazy plots.
Out of room, but I do not recommend for the prior reasons.

What do you get when you take a beloved franchise with solid mechanics, like Assassin's Creed, and mix it with the open world RPG qualities of a game like Witcher 3? You get AC: Origins, which is a barn-burning return to the series. From top to bottom, this game will satisfy in almost every capacity. Top marks go to the characters and story writing which are both strong. Bayek and Aya are completely charming, believable and sympathetic, and there's no doubt that the setting makes for an amazing journey into the past of the Brotherhood to show how they came to be, a pivotal moment for the franchise which we hadn't experienced before (outside of journal entries). I'm a big fan graphic adventure games from the early to mid 90's. As such, The Blackwell Legacy, being a game developed with the AGS engine, caught my attention, and, like many AGS games, gave me a somewhat nostalgic yet fresh experience.
The real meat of most AGS games would be the story, and The Blackwell Legacy's story does well to draw you in. You play the role of Rosa Blackwell, a freelance writer living in New York, whose aunt recently died. Her aunt's death impacts her far more than she initially imagined, and it basically leads her to investigate other cases that have occurred in the area. There's far more to the story than that, but I don't wish to spoil too much. It's essentially a mystery story with supernatural elements to it. The game does quite well to flesh out a bit about Rosa, her backstory, and those of some of her friends and family. The game did try to do a huge info-dump of backstory near the very beginning, which was quite tedious, as even the game's designer admits, but beyond that, the game paces itself okay. It's the first part of an episodic series, so it obviously feels you wanting more in the end, but as a first episode, it does it jobs of grabbing you into the series.
The gameplay is standard fare for most point-and-click adventure games, where you click on areas to move your characters, and click on items and people to interact with. As such, there's not really much to talk about. Unlike most adventure games, though, you don't really spend all your time using inventory items with objects/puzzles/people you see throughout the game,. Instead, you will collect information about people and events that occur through the game, and try to combine such information to help Rosa understand them to help progress the game. It's was a bit different, and while minor, was a good touch to differentiate it from many other adventure games, like the old Sierra ones.
AGS games never really look technologically impressive in today's age; the graphics are pretty reminiscent of early to mid 90's adventure games, like King's Quest VI or Gabriel Knight. That is not to say the art is bad, though, as the artist of the game does really well to depict various places in New York quite well, like Washington Square Park. I haven't really been to much of New York in the past, but I've read elsewhere that the game does a good job of accurately depicting some of the areas there, which is cool.
The music was quite nice in some areas of the game. In particular, I really enjoyed the music at Washington Square Park, as it's rather calming, and compliments the park scenery very well. The voice acting was okay, for the most part, but I felt some characters lacked emotion in delivering their lines. The game's designer even commented that he felt some of the spoken lines didn't seem to convey the messages he was trying to send. Still, the voice acting wasn't horrible, so it doesn't really detract from the game, too much.
Some of the cons about the game include the inability to delete or overwrite saves in-game. I was surprised to see that I created 3 saves of the same name when I played, as I had thought I simply overwrote an old save. You can simply delete the save files from the actual save directory on your computer, but it's just less convenient. Also, at times, the wrong voice-overs would pop up for certain lines in the game, which was kind of strange.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend trying this game out if you are a fan of graphic adventure games.

The Blackwell Legacy is the first in the five-part Blackwell series by Dave Gilbert. This part exists mostly to get you familar with the characters Joey and Rosa. What I'm saying is this, if you are going to play the Blackwell Legacy, you should probably consider getting the rest in the series.
Before giving my score, there is one other point I should bring up: The voice acting, it leaves a little bit to be desired. I'm not saying it is bad, just that there are some issues with the over-all sound quality. Some popping, and background noise is not out of the ordinary for this game. It is not a big issue, but it can be a little jaring to hear.
Sound issues aside, the presentation of this game works well and feels like a good point and click game. However, you should only buy this if you have the money to spend on the other parts afterwards.
