To the casual observer Rodina may not seem like much, but again we know what they say about judging books by their covers.
Given the still early state that the game is in at the time of this writing it still plays and feels very nicely with some surpisingly emergent gamplay in there.  As a freform space exploration game Rodina doesn't really hold your hand or tell you what to do, and if you need that in a game you'll feel yourself wanting here.  However if this just your thing then you won't be disappointed.
Rodina strives not to be a sterile simulation and does have a neat underlying story that is worth the discovery and it really tries to immerse you into it.  On top of that being able to walk about your ship and look around and if landed go outside onto whatever terrestrial body you happen to be on simply adds to the immersion.  Granted the terrestrial bodies are pretty barren the scale of it can be bit breathtaking at times.  Look and feel asside you feel as though you have been dropped into the midst of some mysterious event and are compelled to find out what happened while at the same time trying to simply survive.
Personally I think it is the little things that make the difference and make for interesting events as you play like getting into a fire fight and the alarm going off stating that there is a fire aboard your ship as the enemy hits you just right.  I found myself having to evade the enemy first and jump away to safety before I even get up and deal with the fire on an already damaged ship.  Scrambling about trying to remember where the fire extinguishers were and then frantically spraying the fires while watching the health of my ship deteriorate with me in it makes for a tense moments as you finally put out the last of the flames and your ships health is down to 8%
I digress I recommend this game to anyone whom likes to drift about in space, and explore a solar system, while getting into the occasional firefight and maybe become part of an interesting story and make up stories of your own.

1) Pay2Win system:
It is against term of service to purchase in-game gold (zeny) using real cash. Yet it is ok to sell your warp portal energies into zeny ( which is obtained by cash). So the only way to cheat is to give money to WarpPortal.
Cash shop items also rendered many other in-game gear useless. And the only way to upgrade safely to +9 is to choke up $20-$50 in game cash for it.
2) Cheaters
There are so many bots in this game. Honestly I only see around 100-300 active players in game, and the rest are either bots, vend bots, or afkers. Also there's this thing called ragial which is obviously run by third party bot systems.
3) Lag issues and DDOS:
It's 2015 and this game is still constantly lagging and I am using 75mbps fiber optics internet.  Also their servers keep crashing very often,  and usually at the worst time of the day.
4) Immature game design decision:
For those who paid for VIP for leveling, the GM sometimes decide to change the turn in quests so impossibly difficult that only godly geared veterans can do them. In short: Buy Atelier Sophie, if it's the kind of game you like. It's amazing. But it's not for everyone.
The draw of Atelier has never been exhilarating combat but a more laid back style of JRPG play. Much attention lies on presenting likeable and cute characters and exploring the relationships and backstories between Sophie and her companions.
Then there is the actual alchemy which is pretty much a game in its own right, mixing and matching the right items to create the best bombs, killer books or whatever else you can make, as well as crafting the best equipment possible. The dollmaking system in particular is very fun to experiment with just to see what sorts of good looking or silly (or slooty) outfits you can end up with.
Combat is functional with a lot of flashy effects but not too much of a focus. There is some tactic involved with bringing party members with different strengths and setting up equipment, as well as balancing the attack and defense rolls in the otherwise fairly standard JRPG battle system.
For GUST's first port they did a fairly good job. There is a noticeable sort of lag when navigating the menu of all things but the cutscenes, general open-world gameplay and combat moves fluid even at the highest settings on my mid-range rig.
The game certainly isn't for everyone. It strikes an odd line between casual players through fairly easy standard combat and making up for the lack of excitement with character and whimsy and the super-hardcore players on the other spectrum through the high difficulty levels which necessitate a lot of crafting, making the best equipment you possibly can and using tactics effectively in combat, though the challenge hererin lies more in the pre-battle prepwork than the actual fights.
If this appeals to you at all, Atelier Sophie is definitely worth a recommendation, if only so GUST starts paying more attention to the PC market.

As a veteran of the Original Savage: The Battle for Newerth game, I'm intimately familiar with the formula this game runs on to achieve it's intense blend of Tactical RTS resource-war style objective pushing and Viceral split-second melee-focused combat. no skills, no macros, just you, a blade, and your timing stand between you and death at any given moment. team play is a requirement for success and working with your commander to achieve victory is very satisfying. the games can go for 20-50 minutes depending on how well the players and commanders sync up, which is pretty manageable as far as game times for Real-time strategy shooters are concerned.
Graphics are beautiful, with maxxed out settings being easier to achieve on most games using this kind of engine because of its optimization for lower stress on graphics cards.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys fast-paced action broken up with tactical base-building and a heavy emphasis on both player skill and team objective advancement. Some may say Savage: Resurrection is just a "resurrected" version of the first savage, but it's really about point of view, since the original savage was a diamond in the rough, with just the graphics lacking(good for their time though). I'd call this title a 4.5/5, heavily improved assymmetric Team-based RTSS, well worth the low price with no pay-to-win options.

I love the premise of this game. An RTS with actual players as teh units is something I've been wanting to play since I randomly thought of the idea when I was 12 or so. Sadly, this game does not deliver on its promise due to a single flawed system.
Ammo.
Especially when playing as a human, ammo is an ever-present, all-encompassing concern. Enemy players are tanky (which works well, since there's not really any cover to speak of,) and it takes half of your total ammo to kill a player from any reasonable distance. If your ammo regenerated, this would be fine. But it does not. Instead, to get more ammo, you have to travel back to a friendly base, hop into it, click a spawn point, and then respawn. This is moronic. It prevents players from staying on teh front line where the fun is, and instead encourages players to stay near the base with a sniper rifle taking potshots.
I hope this game gets better, because I really want to enjoy it, but for now, I have requested a refund.

Sanitarium is a great old school Point & Click game. It’s got a good story, a good hero and a great villain, but let’s start with the story.
You play as Max, after a car accident knocks him unconscious, he awakes up in a part of a derelict sanitarium going up in flames. But even worse than that, Max does not know who he is, or how did he got into sanitarium, or why is his face all
bandaged up.
He is able to escape from the burning tower of the sanitarium, by way of a taking Statue and taking him to a creepy and weird little town just what is going on? That is what Max must find out.
Now what I liked about this game. I really liked the story; it had a good bit of twists and turns. Liked the mix of both horror and fantasy.
Why’ll this game is not crap your pants scary, it well sometimes leave you with a feeling of being disturbed or creeped out. I liked the music. Liked the creepy atmosphere of the game. Liked levels going from derelict sanitarium to creepy little town to a demented circus surrounded by water.
But what I really loved was the villain, even those you can see he is bad guy right off the bat; he does have a good bit of Deep to him. Voice acting was okay for the game was okay too, but does show its age.
Now for the bad. There is really nothing bad about this game it just shows its age.
So with that said get this game if you want a creepy classic old school Point & Click game this is for you.

Five Nights at Freddy's 4 is a point-and-click, Horror survival, game created by Scott Cawthon. And is the fourth game in the Five Nights at Freddy's series.
Unlike previous Five Nights at Freddy's games, the game is not set in a security office, but in a child's bedroom. There are no cameras, and instead of "Phone Guy", the player is given on-screen instructions to help the player during the game.
The first four nights will put the player against four animatronics:
Nightmare Freddy,
Nightmare Bonnie,
Nightmare Chica,
Nightmare Foxy, and
Nightmare Fredbear, who combines the scare tactics of the previous four, solely taking over on the fifth night.
Completing all five nights will unlock an additional sixth night that serves as the epilogue, in which the four animatronics will haunt the player until Nightmare Fredbear takes over when the clock hits 4 AM.
One of the loudest games in the series, the game requires you to turn your volume all the way up to the max. That one little detail has driven away quite a few people, leaving few to get past night 1. But if you can withstand the massive screaming from the animatronics, it’s actually a very good installment to the series. 10/10

The original King's Quest is one of my earliest PC game memories, and it's also a major historical milestone (see Lazy Game Review's video on King's Quest I for the IBM PC jr.). At the time, adventure games were either text only or featured a static image, but King's Quest I allowed you to walk around & interact with the screen that you were on. Being able to walk behind objects was a big deal, as bizarre as that sounds now.
It's important to keep this in mind because the early KQ's feel very dated, so it helps to keep some perspective. As the series progressed, the puzzles, graphics, sound, and story all improved, so it also helps to not give up on the series if the earlier releases come off as too frustrating. The highlight of the series is easily King's Quest VI, since the storytelling & characters make it easy to get drawn in. I'm also extremely fond of King's Quest III, but the frustration factor may put off some people.
One major downside to most of the King's Quest games is that they often feature a "walking dead" scenario, which means that the player did something that caused the game to be unwinnable regardless of what the player does. For example, if you eat a steak before you're hungry, you won't have it later on when the game tells you that you're hungry. This would be fine, except the game allows you to continue playing without letting you know that the game is no longer winnable. With walkthroughs being easily available online, it's much easier to avoid, but it's worth keeping in mind.
Even with its flaws, King's Quest is a must-play for any adventure game fan, and has a lasting charm that should be experienced. I would also like to recommend downloading SCUMMVM, which is a program that allows you to run many of these older adventure games. It has quite a few features, such as Roland MT-32 emulation (which requires a MT-32 rom to use) which allows you to hear the earlier King's Quest games the way they were meant to be heard. It also gives you more graphics options, which lets you choose how you want to display it (the Steam version places the game up top, which puts a black border around the left, right & bottom sides, I prefer the game centered with equal sized black boxes around it). This will be a matter of taste, though, since I know some people prefer DOS Box.
I highly, highly recommend the series, as long as people keep in mind some of the downsides.

I'm just going to use this review to reminisce now. My love of this series goes back to when my brother's friend installed a floppy disk copy of King's Quest V onto our family's Macintosh LC III in 1993. I remember my grade 5 teacher explaining to me a few years later that was piracy. Well I didn't even consent to it! I was just a kid without money who loved games and learning how the world works. And I'd end up here owning it on Steam one day anyway.
Anyways, along soon came King's Quest VI from that same friend of my brother's. The series was quickly installed in my mind as well as my computer. Just overall fun excellent adventure games, with fantastic musical scores as well.
I still have dreams about King's Quest, and my own musical style is probably influenced by it.
By 1999 the family was finally equipped with Windows 95 (and a CD-ROM drive). I could finally install and run King's Quest VII, after having held and examined the box at stores for so long up until then. My parents surely thought I was gay playing that magical classic! (Not that there's anything wrong with that of course.)
I finally got a used copy from "Round Again Software", a brilliant little store that has long closed down. It was a well-stocked treasure trove of classic big-box computer games, and was also the site of Calgary's first branch library between 1913 and 1943. The Crescent Heights Branch Library, north storefront of the Hicks (Kelly) Block 1804 1st St NW.
Later that year I got the 3D and final "Mask of Eternity", which while it still had its enjoyable elements, was mostly ruined by its most perplexing and incomprehensible puzzles. It's not included in this collection of course, but I still yearn for a Steam release one day so I can hear Connor say "'Tis beyond my reach!" and "What is this, a Celestial Globe?".
I haven't really played very much King's Quest I-IV, or even touched the new 2015 game yet. I plan on giving the unofficial remakes a go next. They look ok. You can make them launch in the steam launcher instead of the ancient official games. I've done that. Is anybody actually reading this? Oh well, I still enjoyed writing it!

A Collection of 7 King's Quest titles released from 1983-1994. It's a great Inventory Adventure series that Sierra On-Line created back when MS-DOS & Windows 3.1/95/98 was still by popular demand. I grew up with King's Quest 6-7 when I was a child.
In King's Quest 1 - Quest for the Crown:
Enter the Kingdom of Daventry which was once a peaceful, rich and free of hardships land ruled by King Edward with 3 Magical Treasures; A Magic Shield which protects its bearer, A Magic Mirror which foretells the Future & finally, A Magic Treasure Chest which is filled with Gold. However, over the years, these 3 Treasures were lost thanks to those in power whos lies and deceit took advantage of King Edward's Hardships. Now, King Edward is old and frail with no heir to the throne. So calls forth Sir Graham, one of his bravest, greatest and youngest Knights, to search the land and reclaim the 3 Magical Treasures. If successful, Sir Graham will become the new King of Daventry.
In King's Quest 2 - Romancing the Throne:
Following the events of King's Quest 1, Graham is now King of Daventry but is alone ruling the Kingdom on his own & seeks a maiden to become his Queen. Not knowing what to do he consults the Magic Mirror, one of the 3 Magical Treasures & sees a beautiful woman in a Quartz Tower in the Land of Kolyma. Knowing what to do, he removes his crown, dons his Adventurer's Cap and sets off on his quest.
In King's Quest 3 - To Heir Is Human:
Gwydion begins as a peasant of Llewdor and a slave of the wizard Manannan, but ultimately discovers he is really the long lost son of the Graham (Alexander) and that he has a sister. Help him escape from Manannan's clutches & saves his sister (Rosella) and father from the ravages of the dragon (and restoring the magic mirror).
In King's Quest 4 - The Perils of Rosella:
Rosella travels to the fairy land of Tamir (after learning about it through the magic mirror) on a quest to save her deathly ill father, for which she must vanquish the witch Queen Lolotte.
In King's Quest 5 - Absence Makes the Heart Go Yonder:
King Graham has to rescue both his kingdom and family from Mordack, Hagatha's and Manannan's brother and also an evil magician, in the land of Serenia.
In King's Quest 6 - Heir Today, Gone Tomorrow:
It's Prince Alexander's attempt to save his true love, marry her, and ultimately becoming the king of the Land of the Green Isles. The magic mirror pointed him in the right direction to finding the kingdom.
In King's Quest 7 - The Princeless Bride:
The Final Adventure Game in the King's Quest Collection, this game involves the dual protagonists Queen Valanice and Princess Rosella attempting to save the realm of Eldritch from the evil enchantress Malicia. Rosella ultimately finds a romantic interest in Prince Edgar, whom she rescues with the implication that they may marry in the future. Provided that you obtain the Good Ending in order to do so.
I hope to see King's Quest 8: Mask of Eternity on Steam, because I would buy that game and play it... Kickstarter. And as an added Bonus, it's possible to install & play the Space Quest 6: The Spinal Frontier Interactive Demo in the same directory as King's Quest 7 in the King's Quest Collection: Standard Edition and not the Legacy Edition.

This is a neat little Half Life 1 mod. There's some simple physics puzzles, a bunch of varied environments to fight in, and a bunch of odd and funny quirks (like Half-Life's energy packs being replaced with...cans of beans). The level design is pretty good, and brings to life the vibe of a run-down, decaying, dystopian prison.
There's lots of neat little details. For instance, there's a soda vending machine that you can dispense soda from. If you break it, it'll spew soda cans everywhere. Then an automated voice over the intercom will mention that the vending machine has malfunctioned. Later, you'll see a glowing red alert in a control center notifying that the soda machine is broken. There's this  same weird level of detail for quite a few things strewn about the map.
The soundtrack being composed entirely of Skull and Shark (one of my favorite albums) was an immediate draw for me. It's cool to hear it in a game. However, I feel like it was not utilized enough, with large portions of this roughly hour-long experience being without music. The compressed audio files are also not of very good quality, but that's to be expected.
The main issue I had was with the combat. Wow, is it hard! I thought Half Life 1's medium difficulty was a bit too easy, and Half Life 2's medium was about right. This mod's medium difficulty had me constantly dying and relying on memorization of where enemies were in order to have any chance of beating them. Health pickups aren't too sparse, but energy is almost unseen throughout the mod.
When you fire the smg, it's hilariously inaccurate even at medium range, while the enemy soldiers wield them like sniper rifles. The 2 helicopters that are seen at the end of the mod are also amazingly accurate, gunning you down in a second flat...and that's if they don't decide to blast you with a dozen instakill missiles of doom. It seems like whatever code in HL1 that affected accuracy was tampered with in rather game-breaking ways. Regardless of what's been done, don't feel bad for picking easy difficulty...it'll probably make it half as long, but twice as enjoyable.
Overall, I'd recommend trying this if you like Half-Life and you like Lazerhawk. Don't expect it to be totally amazing, but it's decent, and it's free.

Having finished the game I can tell that its biggest strengths are the graphics and the OST while the weaknesses are the gameplay and the story.
The graphics are beautiful and detailed while the OST (specially the main menu theme) is something I will keep on listening to. Unfortunately, that's where all the good end.
As you start the game (playing only with mouse - that's how a point and click game is supposed to be played) you'll notice that the camera moves by placing the cursor at an edge of the screen. The problem with this is that as you need to click somewhere on the edge to move to another screen, then the camera moves too, which is very annoying when you need to go "down" cause then, you can only see the floor and Kate's legs, until you move the mouse to the upper part (so the camera moves)... Add to this the odd angle most cameras are placed... That's the perfect way to ruin the gameplay...
Then you want to access your inventory. You'll need to press down your mouse's wheel over a hotspot (also why are all the hotspots pointed?). Then you'll have to roll the wheel until you reach the item you want.
I guess the reason for both the problems I've mentioned is that the devs didn't mean to make a point and click game. They wanted to make a console game (that's why there was no total mouse control from the beginning)
No matter the problems I thought I'd try it because if the story would be nice... Unfortunately the story is at least indifferent. You help a group of Youkols reach a destination. Just the Youkols are so pathetic... They can do nothing on their own (how did they survive as a tribe so far, really?), they mostly make stupid comments and most importantly, wherever they camp, they roam everywhere needlessly telling nonsense or gigling...
Also there aren't so many characters to interact with in the game. There are a couple of interesting ones but then all the rest are Youkols... Add to that the the voices of the actors chose, don't fit their in-game characters at all, Kate a only couple more being an exception.
To sum it up in a few words:
If the gameplay would be fluid and the story as it is, I'd give it a thumbs up.
If the gameplay was broken like now but the story worth it, I'd give it a thumbs up.
Nice graphics and good OST aren't enough and the game lacks almost everything else.
I know the devs tried to fix the game after the initial release but they can't turn the game to what it wasn't made to be.
Sorry but I can't recommend it. Especially when it's priced at 40€!
If you want to try it, at least wait for a sale, at 15€...

Probably only 10-15 hours of the total amount of time that was spent on this game were actually entertaining and to some extent educational (there are interesting things to learn about Egypt and world history in this game).
CONCEPT AND STORY:
Concept is great and it's a very unique idea to set the game in Egypt, it totally works well with the whole Assassins vs Templars idea dating back so long.
This game starts off good, and then you get further in the story, which turns out to be quite shallow for something as epic as this title is trying to portray. Towards the end of the main quest line the story becomes weaker, characters do not get developed properly and events are sped up at times. Waaay too much grind to get little bits of story. With such big budget game and studio, could have done a better writing job! Plot twists are predictable and it's possible to get bored with the story before reaching level 20. However there is a great story chunk and a long mission towards the end of the game that picks interest up for a brief while (only until the next mission).
ART:
Amazing! This game is a great piece of digital artwork! The scenery and authenticity of the world is superb! Really neat locations and good level design. I am very excited for the Discovery Mode to come out!!! UI is good though could have been slightly more customizable because there is a big jump between Light and Minimal, it would be better to keep markers but get rid of the top bar, instead of removing it all completely.
GAMEPLAY:
Very rich gameplay experience with so many things to do. Even though both main and, especially, side quests are repetative, The game offers quite an outstanding freedom of choice in completing them. Fast travel is your king and cash is your ace! Buy maxed out version of this game to get additional points and equipment. It did save me a good number of hours of grinding to complete the game.
TECHNICAL:
Technically the game is good but not great. It is a lot that the game handles with such big world and I give respect to that. The idea and implementation of frozen-in-action character and camera rotation when an area loads is genius!
There are some minor visual bugs here and there, a couple times, the horse mount or quest related stuff would pop out from nowhere or have no textures applied to them. There are lots of cutscene glitches! And the final cutscene failed with audiosync for 90 percent of its length.
OVERALL:
Beautiful and rich world, fun to explore for some time. Shallow story, watered down with lots of XP grind and ruined with glitchy cutscenes.

I'm just gonna do a short and sweet about the game.
I love this game.  Both melee and gunplay feel great, and the battles you can have feel epic and grand in scale, even though it's only 16 vs 16.  The reasoning behind this is when the final siege happens, everyone basically funnels into one area, and you have all of the fighters trying to control the battlefield while the siegers are trying to take each other, and the enemy buildings out.  So what you have is a bunch of orcs vs humans in melee and gunplay combat on the open battlefield while you have siege rockets flying overhead and big 20ft tree wielding orcs bashing through the front lines.
People say this game is unblanced but I would say no, it's perfectly balanced.  People have a hard time coping how to play their race against the others.  You'll hear that range is hard for Orcs to deal with, or that the beasts are too powerful in melee.  However, that's exactly why it's balanced.  Orcs are supposed to ambush from higher ground, and there's plenty of places on every map to do that.  Orcs have a pouncing ability that has no cooldown, and it's only metered by stamina.  Using a Frenzy potion makes you INCREDIBLY fast because it gives the beast increased stamina regen, you can basically spam pounce for a few seconds without draining stamina.  So the strategy is to pounce from higher ground, once you get in melee, you have the advantage.  Humans can counter this by blocking your attacks, and a successful block will stun the beast, giving you a chance to counter and back away.  Beasts can also counter this bydoing a side-strafe pounce, and then pouncing forward, in order to try and circle around quickly to hit the back of the human when they are blocking.  The best thing a human can do is get some range and use a repeater(one of the very first upgrades) and you can be very effective.  Blcoking auto-switches you to melee so you can use your gun, and then block, and you can resume the battle in melee from then on out.  Humans can also save sprint to get a better distance advantage on orcs and control the fight even more.
The reason why I like this game is that there's plenty of counter-play, plenty of strategy and teamwork, and there's a good amount of paper rock scissors wtihout it being law.  The game gets constant updates, looks great, feels great, and has great strategy.  Your decisions matter and have significant impact, no matter what you do.  You can be a defender, building, repairing, and gathering, and still top the scoreboard without scoring a kill.
The only thing I wish is if you could volunteer your gold to the team pool.
The community is also incredibly hateful to new commanders.  However, commanders shouldn't be commanding until they have a full understanding of what the best weapons are for the best situations.  There's a specific build order and if you are interested in commander, it's easy to sit back as a defender and watch and learn.  Don't jump into a game brand new as a commander, because it ruins the game for the entire team because of one inexperienced person, this is why newb commanders get so much hate.

I've been a fan of this game for a long time but I'm going to try to give it a fair and thorough review. (Content warnings at the end). Despite its lack of story choices, single ending, and short play time (11 hours) I feel Sanitarium has a lot of replay value because the story is compelling, well written, and fun to come back to.
Even after all these years I think the story still stands out from other horror games. It starts out in a bizarre asylum that looks more like a castle than a mental hospital. The player character has no memory of anything before this point but seems to be a patient in the asylum. As you progress through the game things continue to get stranger and reality quickly becomes uncertain.
Amnesia is a common trope in horror and I've seen it used artlessly many times. The writers us it well here and don't expect it to do the work for them. While the main character recovering his identity is part of the story there is much more going on and far higher stakes than just his own well being.
The game has a creepy and sometimes ominous atmosphere. There are a lot of disturbing concepts and scenes in the game and much of the time what is real isn't certain. Reality seems to lie in one direction, and then another, and another as you make your way through nightmarish places all marked by imminent yet unseen threats, insanity, and disease. Over the chapters the truth is slowly revealed and it's notably different from what I find in most horror games.
On the technical side of things: the controls are clunky and sometimes irritating. I don't like holding down the right mouse button to move my character and I wish the walking speed was faster. I had some problems activating staircases by accident. There were a few times when I ended up walking up and down the stairs several times before I could escape. I found I couldn't activate objects when my character was standing behind them. The game thought I was clicking on my character and brought up the inventory instead. Cinematics are also very easy to skip by accident. Other than that the game seems to have no problems.
The game has a very basic combat system which is used infrequently. The player is temporarily given an improvised weapon and must click accurately on enemies to kill them. The combat controls are clunky but combat isn't too difficult once you figure out the trick to it.
The puzzles in the game are fairly simple; especially in early levels. In the last few levels the difficulty goes up noticeably. The types of puzzles vary a lot but are fairly standard: numerical codes, item hunts, mechanical puzzles, social puzzles, simple codes, riddles, and mazes. These puzzles are based on knowledge provided to the player in game and here are usually plenty of clues for major puzzles.
In terms of graphics and sound the game has not aged well. The graphics are pixelated and fuzzy. The cinematics actually hold up pretty well but have black lines that are distracting on newer monitors. The animations for 3D models seem good. The game's sound is tinny all round. That said, the voice acting is decent. Its seems like the actors really gave it their all and had fun doing it. The music is atmospheric and variously maddening, creepy, beautiful, and haunting.
Content Warnings and Spoilers.
There are gory scenes usually of dead bodies, medical horror, mentions of suicide, depictions of “circus freaks” and deformed people as monsters, child abuse, child death, mentions of domestic violence, cruelty to animals, and inexpert depictions of mental illness for both horror and humor.

This is not a game so much as a hobby.  Every square on the board has different rules.  Every player has different rules.  There are four different decks of cards to draw from and of course each card drawn is unique.
If you're thinking this is a role playing game where you might choose to pop over to that trader, stock up on items, then head over and kill that creature, you are going to have a bad time.  Game play is random.  Very random.  Strategy tends to be very broad and take hours to play out.  Mistakes are painful.  At its best, any one turn might have a 33% chance of something good happening, 7% bad and the other 60% of the time is just time spent.  Better maybe than real life but its hard to play with a goal of ever finishing.
And by something good I mean anything good.  You hardly ever get to do what you want.  Most often its just pragmatism: "choice a gives me slightly better odds at improving my lot than choice B, and choice C is suicide, so "A" it is."  Worst part is learning what effects what and where and when so you can tell the A's from the B's.
You'd think computerizing the gameplay would at least make things faster but it absolutely does not.  Delays are built in automatically to attempt at giving all players a chance to respond to every action. And it's unforgiving.  You'll end up missing opportunities for counter moves because there arent always hard prompts when you could take action and no way to go back if you click wrong.
Wishing for a much freindlier interface like "You just took damage, would you like to cast that heal I see in your inventory?"  "You have a spell, which player would you like to have skip a turn?" or for Pete's sake "No one can effect gameplay until the next turn, why don't we skip ahead until then?" And please plaese please do something about the end game. "Autoplay to finish? Y/N" would shorten most games by hours.

So. I designed my ship, and embased space head on. Just me against the universe full of infinite possiblilities. I could have gone flying through space forever, but what use would I be then? Rodina gives you a huge world that's bigger than it seems, and it's still in ongoing development. It gives the player an imersive story line, that you can choose to participate in. Many side stories, and a great feel of freedom.

So, first I flew into the sun.
The game didn't try to stop me, didn't try to teach me where to fly, nor did reality break and let me fly through the sun to avoid an untimely demise. Instead, my ship started to give me a warning about solar radiation, followed by my ship more or less melting in the extreme heat of the sun's outer layer with warnings and sirens blaring the whole time. After which, the game told me that I died and that was that.
So, next I few into a planet.
I melted in the extreme heat of entry into the planet's atmosphere, ignoing my ship's pleading warnings about too steep of a trajectory. I died.
So, after that I flew into an asteroid.
I blew up on impact. Then, too, did I die.
I'm not saying you will die a lot in Rodina, such as when I dove head long into a large hostile space battle soon after playing chicken with a space boulder, I'm saying that Rodina gives you plenty of opportunities to die. Not only are enemy spacecraft seeking your death before someone or something else can claim you, you've a galaxy of reality to explore physics with. No loading screens, no auto-pilot, just you and your ship against the universe.
And for those of you out there not seeking your deaths, Rodina gives you the tools, the inuitive controls, and the weapons to stay alive as well if you're that kind of person. Oh, and you can customize the interior of your ship.

As a young kid I played these games religiously. I used to write letters to Sierra asking for help and they'd respond via snail mail. That was before AOL 4.0. These games have aged as well as can be expected. Simply put, if someone created these types of games today and marketed them as 'retro', 'pixel graphics', 'point and click', 'text adventures' etc.- I doubt they would be as well made as the KQC games. The nostalgia is overwhelming, the quality of the content is priceless, and the feeling of solving a puzzle is unparalleled. If you are around 30, you probably paid $150 or more for the box set back at Media Play. The games are almost as fun today at a fraction of the price. kQV... "Look out Graham, that's a poiiiiiiisonnnnnus snake!" And KQIV? Come on, completing the game 100 points over the maximum score? KQ3, finding the right ingredients in the spell book to advance their game. KQVI, making your way into the castle for the first time just waiting for your opportunity to return. VIi, those graphics - the epic ending where the win / lose was completely random based on your computers mood. So many memories. Where is Laura Bow and the dagger of amen ra? Or mixed up mother goose. All of the ascii text games, NORTH NORTH WEST NORTH, ahh a shack in the desert. Oh the memories.

Games of my childhood always have a sweet spot with me, and this whole collection has been one of my favorites. My father introduced me to King's Quest when I was young and he bought the first 4. I remember the rather unique official cheat books which required a special marker to make the invisivle ink to appear.
But to talk of this collection, the first four were originally text driven games. meaning that you have to type in commands like "Look at woman," or "rub lamp." The first three were then later re-worked with updated graphics (but still rather dated compared to today's games). Starting with 5, gameplay shifted a little, instead of being text driven, they became what is now called "point and click."
This collection is the story of how King Graham's family came to be, basically a preface to the more recent version that has come out, in whcih Graham recalls the stories of his youth, before he became king of Daventry. The first game in this collection covers the story of how Graham became kind. The second is about Graham finding a wife. The third seems a little odd when started, but it is about the lost children of Graham and their return to Daventry. In the fourth game, Graham, getting old, falls ill and his daughter, Rosella, undertakes a quest to find a way to heal Graham. The fifth game ties back to the third, the son of Graham, Alexander, having escaped the clutched of an evil magician, has brought upon daventry, the wrath of the magicians brother. It it up to Graham to find his now missing castle and family. The sixth installment ties into the fifth. Smitten by the beauty of Cassima, the princess that Graham rescued while restoring his family and kingdom, causes Alexander to search for her. The final game finally touches upon the queen Valance and Rosella, their rocky relationship of overprotective mother and rebellious daughter, and their way back to Daventry after being magicked away from home.
The games seem to work well on my computer, running Windows 10. I do have issue with alt-tabbing out in order to check the manuals for clues as to what to do in a few of the games. Back in the day, Sierra made games that had DRM imbedded in the manuals. What appears to be flavor text is really actually important, least you die is quite awful ways. This is the only difficulty I have with the collection. Alt-tabbing on my machine, causes the program to scrunch over to the left of the screen and in rendered in shades of gray.
There is one game missing in this collection, but it's somewhat of the black-sheep of the franchise, The Mask of Eternity. It was only set in Daventry and was panned as an awful game because of bugs, glitches, and graphic rendering issues. Of the old games, thsi is the one I have yet to play and have a slight curiosity in it. I udnerstand GOG does have it for sale, but it's bundled with the last game.

Ragnarok Online has an interesting system where players have two levels, a base level and a job level, How you raise those levels is by gaining experience either by clearing quests or killing monsters, but the job level tends to level up slower. Each base level earns you status points that can be allocated into different attribute and each job level earns you job points which you can allocate into skills which the player can use.

A 1998 point and click adventure originally created by an American company known as DreamForge Intertainment which unfortunately no longer exists and later thanks to a French company known as Dot Emu (
) was ported to Steam and other mediums with achievements added.
While the game is no doubt dated graphically, the game has stood the test of time thanks to its superlative and artistic use of storytelling. Unlike cheap jump scares used in many stories today, the main story here and many of its sub plots concentrate on having the gamer enthralled with concepts teetering in the morbid and with adult themes that constantly confounds you with the creepy and bizarre mysteries that make you want to push forward and learn more.
The Main story follows a man that has stolen a male nurse’s car from an Asylum accidentally plummeting it off a cliff while he drove down a mountainous and dangerous road. Next thing you know, is that you’re simply back in the Asylum from which you were fleeing, this time in one of its Gothic towers surrounded by patients that seem to be on the loose and guards that are nowhere to be found. To add to the mystery you have no recollection exactly who you are and your face is completely rolled up in bandages. As you begin to chat with the various patients each telling you their bizarre encounter stories and delusions, you eventually find yourself experiencing those same dreams and stories first hand, even changing characters as you do so. How is this possible? Why do you have a connection with each patient in that tower?
Each sub plot will take you to a quirky landscape, filled with its own dark stories and secrets. For instance a village filled with deformed children, a preacher with a following of wooden mannequins, a circus being terrified of the sea and a god whose people no longer give obeisance too. As you gradually push forward through each, you will be rewarded with flashbacks and the eventual fill in the blank sections of memory loss. While many Hollywood such stories usually end with a cheap supernatural idea that you’re simply dead and experiencing some sort of afterlife, instead this story rewards you by exposing how the various idiosyncratic common threads of each sub plot connects to your main characters real life.
The puzzles, the randomness, the character development is so perfectly balanced that you will probably even forget your playing a point and click adventure. In short if you’re a little crazy and you like the creepy, this is a nuthouse you should enjoy. I know I did because I finally found people crazier than I.
On a side note: If you enjoy this game you should enjoy 'Stasis' it’s considered to be Sanitarium's spiritual successor. Though I must admit I have not played it myself yet. Below is the first chapter to see if this point and click horror game has a story which you might enjoy.

The vast majority of this game revolves around the following:
- 1 or more events ("bad things") occur each turn.
- All of these events involve a module of your ship becoming damaged in some way, with a consequence for leaving the module unrepaired and a certain amount of repair points required to repair it.
- Each of your crew memebrs gets a number of dice.
- You move one or more crew members to the damaged module.
- The crew members roll their dice.
- If the result is higher than the number of repair points then you successfully repaired the module. If not, you suffer the    consqeuences of leaving it unrepaired.
If you have a crew member with some dice left over, you can engage in some of the other "gameplay" on offer, such as:
- Moving your character to the food module, then rolling their dice and trying to get 3 of the same number in order to get food.
- Moving your character to the communication module, rolling their dice and trying to roll  >5 in order to reduce that characters "stress level".
- Moving your character to the medbay, rolling their dice, trying to roll >5 to heal your character.
Do you see where this is going? The entire game is the one single mechanic. Move a person to a module. Roll their dice. Either go "Yay. I did it." or "Dang. I failed." entirely at the mercy of RNG.
As a result of this, it feels to me more like I am watching the game play itself, with me just along to look at it (not helped by the fact that the game is not very pretty.)
I did not find this game very entertaining. I don't like being so heavily at the mercy of RNG. Maybe this could be  forgiven a little if there was more variety in terms of the events that happen and the actual gameplay involved, but there is so little content. It feels like Early Access.

First off, this game has very little replay value in terms of story. Every run has the same exact story, in the same exact order, at the same exact times. Expect to skip many of the cutscenes once you watch them the first time.
It's a very simple game: roll dice and hope to not get RNG'ed to death. But each character has a specific ability that you can use, and each module has another specific ability that you can use. Yes, you may get RNG'ed to death, BUT you still have to use each character to the best of their abilities, and synchronizing abilities with the order you use the characters adds a bit of strategy to the game.
This game is reminiscent of gambling in how you play it, so in my opinion replayability is pretty high. No, you don't have anywhere near a good chance at beating the game, but an entire game can take about 15-20 minutes depending on how long you spend making decisions and how far you get. It's a great time killer if you need a short diversion, and if you need to there is a sort of save feature so that you can quit out and continue later.
I would recommend this game to people that enjoy board games or if you need a short game to play between activities. Personally, I really like this game and hope that the developers release more content for it, especially story-wise. This game is NOT for strictly-strategy oriented gamers or people looking for a story, as there is a greater emphasis on the RNG aspect of the game rather than the strategy and the story can be summed up in a few sentences. Also, there are no actual upgrades either in a run or with unlocks, but there are some unlockable characters that you can use in place of the original four. I'm not absolutely sure about this last bit, but I think that the voice actor also changes depending on which characters you choose, though the story doesn't change.
If the developers add in more story this game could definitely turn into one of my favorite games because I like the gameplay and how quickly the runs end (mostly in a flaming ball of failure, but hey that's how my FTL runs work too).
A few extra issues I have with the game:
-The skip cutscene button is space instead of the mouse button or any key, which is slightly annoying in a game which only uses the mouse other than skipping cutscenes
-No option to turn off the hints, and they return every run
-The unlock requirements are a bit ridiculous, as I have beaten the game and it will probably take me another hour or more of gameplay to unlock even one more character
-No option to undo any dice allocations (Chess rules: move is not set until you take your hand off the mouse button)
-What the heck does stress do? I still have no clue.

Yahtzee!!!.... in space... no its not that exciting.
Four astronauts stranded in a space station on a journey to Mars based on a "random" signal. Will they ever complete their journey? Likely not...
Tharsis is a Dice RNG management game that plays like Yatzhee on a Space Station that looks like a boardgame.
Plays like Elder Sign but if you strip everything thats dice manipulation from it (spells, items, Yellow/Red dice, etc.) you have THARSIS which is highly unfortunate. Thats the short version of this review. Anything thats dice manipulation is too minimal while the game has no problem throwing impossible odds at you. You are at the mercy of the unchecked RNG to complete a run.
Your 4 Astronauts are aboard the Iktomi, a Space Ship consisting of 7 stations. Each stations has a benefit to either your Astronauts or the Iktomi itself if a Astronaut uses a dice that rolled a 5-6, Doubles/Triples or Free depending on which station you are. If you activate their benefits you can receive 1-2 FOOD, restore sanity to 1 crew, fully restore 1 crew health, repair your ship, etc.
Every Week(Turn) new Events(Problems) will pop up, up to 2-3, that will require your Crew to FIX it, if not they will either Damage your ship or your Crew or disable that station functionality at the end of every Week until you fix it. Taking an Astronaut to the event with their available dice at that moment (max 5d6 per Astronauts), reduce to 0 or if you cant reduce it to 0, as much as you can and then take another Astronaut and repeat till it hits 0.
Example: Event #25 pops up, Take X Crew there with 2d6(2 dices of 6 sides), your results will be around 2-12... so after that astronaut finishes you will need to bring more crew members there to help until you can reduce 25 to 0. Every Astronaut can re-roll Once, except for a Astronaut which ability adds an extra re-roll.
Everytime you use an Astronaut for an Event or for a Station, they permantly lose 1 die from their pool, this can be refill with FOOD(3d6) icons and the Oxygen Station(2d6) up to a MAX of 5d6.
While rolling to REPAIR that #X on the Events, each Event will have some "BAD" results which for every die that lands on a specific number, that Astronaut will suffer a penalty. INJURY: For each die landing on # lose 1 health, VOID: landing on a # you lose that die for that roll and STATIC: lands on a # you cant reroll that die. Assist is a resource thats used AUTOMATICALLY everytime you get hit with a penalty even if you didnt want to....
Red Blocks on Events determines the damage on your ship at the end of every turn.
That picture pretty sums up the problem with this game, unchecked balance and RNG.
Each crew member has a passive ability but when the game assaults the ship with 3 Events like shown, 32, 26 and 19, theres no passive in the world that can save you. Especially when you start rolling low and there NOTHING to manipulate the results.
Anyone that has played somekind of dice game, knows that d6 can be a wild number and without any way to manipulate results, other than reroll ONCE, knows thats bad game mechanic a reason why new boardgames dont use a dice to move mechanic. Its entirely possible to have a doomed crew on Week 2 which Ive had countless times. The game has 0 mercy, and this is on normal, on assaulting the ship with 3 events of high improbability with major INJURIES to boot.
Worst of all, again, no way to manipulate the dice, either roll high or doubles or dont get any benefit from any station or crew's ability to use, except for the Oxygen Room. which most of this are just minor.
The only thing this reminds me off is Yatzhee!! Roll... roll again did you get it? Great.... you didnt then GTFO!

Why even choose?
With so many inspiration out there and boardgames that move outside of this wild RNG, with a RNG Event system that can kill your crew from the get go with no input from you, no dice manipulation mechanics with a game that plays like Craps (Casino) and Yahtzee!!. Its really hard to recommend.
Granted, you will have fun with its aesthetics, music and Yahtzee!! Style of gameplay... and thats what I would say. Throwing X number of dice 2 times and see if you are doomed can be as addicting as Yahtzee!! and just as intriguing.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Point-and-click adventure games have always been a vexing genre to me. On the one hand, I find myself enjoying the storylines quite a bit, as they seem like that's where most of the effort in making the game goes. That's fine and all, but oftentimes, the puzzles receive the short end of the stick as far as the design attention goes. When I wrote the review for The Walking Dead game (the first long form review I did), I mentioned that one of the things I enjoyed most about the game was the fact that the puzzles made sense. They may not have actually worked in the real world, but they made enough sense nevertheless.
Most point-and-click adventure games that I've played have puzzles that don't make all that much sense. The adventure game purist's perpsective seems to be that having these puzzles adds to the gameplay, making it so that the game doesn't just last an hour and a half or whatever it may be. If this is not your position and you are an "adventure game purist", forgive the potential strawman attack, but I don't really feel like the typical adventure game puzzle should be like this. With respect to the Blackwell Legacy, it's a bit of a mixed bag.
One of the things that the game does to shake up the formula a bit is introduce the system of a notebook, in which you can link various topics to proceed in the game. There are some usages that do work and do make sense, such as linking a first name without a last name with a last name without a first name. However, there are some implementations that don't work. For instance, there is one puzzle in which you have to link two names together. I had already figured out the puzzle, but since I didn't use the right dialogue option with the right person, the game wouldn't let me actually solve the puzzle
. This had me stuck for about an hour.
Fortunately, there are very few inventory puzzles in the game, but again, those puzzles are often quite obtuse and farfetched in nature. Regarding the stability of the game, there is a way to reliably make it crash (at least in version 1.7), where if you click outside of the notebook when you have it pulled up, the game will crash. This isn't too big of a deal, but it's just something worth noting that you probably shouldn't do that. The game autosaves every time you go to the world map, so if you do accidentally crash the game, you shouldn't lose too much progress.
Apart from the puzzles, there really isn't much else to this game. Again, puzzles are sort of a mixed bunch in this game with regard to quality. However, the puzzles weren't anything that really blew me away in cleverness, so I'll give this game a 6/10 for the gameplay.
Story: The main draw of the game, obviously. The series is quasi-episodic in nature, with this being the first in the series (I really wish they introduced a numbering to the games, but oh well). It definitely does feel like the first thing in a series, but that's not to say that it's necessarily bad or unenjoyable. I found myself enjoying the characters introduced thus far, and the writing lends a very believable nature to them. The premise is quite good as well; of course, I won't talk too much in-depth on that, since that's the whole point of getting the game. Overall, I give the writing and story an 8/10 for a cast of very enjoyable characters and an interesting enough premise to base a series off of.
Graphics: A bit of an odd one. It seems to fluctuate between a few different styles of art; the facial features of Rosangela and Joey in-game don't really look anything like they do on the title screen, and nobody's facial features look ANYTHING like the ones shown in pictures. In fact, I'd go as far as saying the faces in the pictures are potentially more unsettling than the premise. None of it is bad, but the lack of a consistent art style can be a bit jarring. This is an Adventure Game Studio game, so if you can run Steam, you'll be able to run this game. Also, since this is an AGS game, there is the winsetup.exe file in the root directory of the game. Alt-Entering doesn't pull you out of fullscreen (which it fullscreens in 640x480 and looks not so great on a 16:9 monitor), but using winsetup.exe will allow you to run it windowed. With technical aspects being pointless to rate, we are left with the pretty good but still sometimes inconsistent art style, leading me to give this game a 3/5 for graphics.
Sound: They definitely have a good composer on staff for this game. There's definitely a few songs from this game that I wouldn't mind putting on my MP3 player. If I had to pick a favorite song from the game, I'd pick the intro song. It just does everything right for me. Regarding the voice acting, it's not bad for an Indie game. There were a few voices that I wasn't expecting for certain characters, but oftentimes in real life people look nothing like what they sound like, so it's not too big of a deal. There were a few lines that did feel kinda forced, but that didn't ruin my enjoyment all that much. Another issue I noted, specifically with Joey's voice actor, is that it seems like sometimes they record without a pop filter. This may not be the case, but it is definitely noticeable on a few lines. For a very good OST and some pretty good but not perfect VAs, I'll give this game a 3/5 for the audio.
Overall scores are 6/8/3/3; Cumulative score of 6.7/10. While the gameplay may not have left me with the greatest impression for puzzles to come, the story has given me good impressions for what's to come for the adventures of Rosangela and Joey. So far, I'd say to pick up the Blackwell Collection when it's on sale, but $5 isn't bad for a decently put together adventure game.

This is a 2-3hr point and click adventure, the first in a short episodic series.  As such there's not too much to say about it.  The game is broken down into a few scenes and a few small locations, so the amount of content is limited.
Setting wise, the story doesn't really appeal much to me.  I'm just not a ghost-story person, so there isn't much draw there, and the topics covered are also kind of uninteresting too.  The voice acting is passable though, and there isn't any GUI frustration.
I have a few complaints about the game, though.  One puzzle involves completing an interaction with an NPC where at the end you automatically leave the area.  The first step in solving the next puzzle requires returning to that NPC to acquire an item from her you, and you have no logical reason to believe she would have an item you would need much less what that item would be.  There is NO volume slider in the game, and with the audio set to 1/100 in windows the music was booming loud in a few places.  Some puzzles require you to combine topics in your notepad, and you can only do so at certain times and on top of that only do so a few times in the game.  Its not really fun in adventure games when the player has to bruteforce his way through a puzzle by throwing every action at every target, and its kind of dumb here where the NPC wont respond to being asked about A or B, and only to A+B.  I as the player make the mental leap easily, but it doesn't straightforwardly apply in the game.
$5 is a reasonable price point but I can't really reccomend this game on its own, as it doesn't offer much and has a few nagging annoyances.  It might be worth it as an intro for the rest of the series but I could also just see it being skippable since it just introduces the premise and I'm sure that will be summarized in the later games.  I will find out as I continue the series I suppose.
EDIT: Having played the full series, I would very much recommend it as a whole.  This first game is a bit rough, but the full package is worth it.

This is a neat little Half Life 1 mod. There's some simple physics puzzles, a bunch of varied environments to fight in, and a bunch of odd and funny quirks (like Half-Life's energy packs being replaced with...cans of beans). The level design is pretty good, and brings to life the vibe of a run-down, decaying, dystopian prison.
There's lots of neat little details. For instance, there's a soda vending machine that you can dispense soda from. If you break it, it'll spew soda cans everywhere. Then an automated voice over the intercom will mention that the vending machine has malfunctioned. Later, you'll see a glowing red alert in a control center notifying that the soda machine is broken. There's this  same weird level of detail for quite a few things strewn about the map.
The soundtrack being composed entirely of Skull and Shark (one of my favorite albums) was an immediate draw for me. It's cool to hear it in a game. However, I feel like it was not utilized enough, with large portions of this roughly hour-long experience being without music. The compressed audio files are also not of very good quality, but that's to be expected.
The main issue I had was with the combat. Wow, is it hard! I thought Half Life 1's medium difficulty was a bit too easy, and Half Life 2's medium was about right. This mod's medium difficulty had me constantly dying and relying on memorization of where enemies were in order to have any chance of beating them. Health pickups aren't too sparse, but energy is almost unseen throughout the mod.
When you fire the smg, it's hilariously inaccurate even at medium range, while the enemy soldiers wield them like sniper rifles. The 2 helicopters that are seen at the end of the mod are also amazingly accurate, gunning you down in a second flat...and that's if they don't decide to blast you with a dozen instakill missiles of doom. It seems like whatever code in HL1 that affected accuracy was tampered with in rather game-breaking ways. Regardless of what's been done, don't feel bad for picking easy difficulty...it'll probably make it half as long, but twice as enjoyable.
Overall, I'd recommend trying this if you like Half-Life and you like Lazerhawk. Don't expect it to be totally amazing, but it's decent, and it's free.

It takes an hour, it's pretty good, but it's also quite hard in some places and has a couple of unfair BS moments. Don't be ashamed of selecting the "easy" difficulty; I wish I'd done that. But if you love Half-Life SP mods, you shouldn't even be thinking twice about clicking the "INSTALL NOW" button. Go for it!

Just finished the game and all I can say is ugh. I could go on a rant but no. Just ugh is all I have to say.  This game is so poorly done it's a disgrace.

Although I've only played for a couple of hours thus far I can definitely say that it's still very rough around the edges. So much so that they probably should have delayed it further. Starting with the issues I have thus far:
- Movement/interaction: It's extremely clunky, especially on keyboard/mouse. Sometimes it completely breaks as your character moves on her own despite input.
- Camera angles: I know they probably are a staple of previous games but they just don't give any good or useful angles and are even contributing to the problem of movement. It simply would have been more appropriate with a 3rd person camera like that of e.g. Life is Strange or any of the Telltale games.
- Lip syncing: Aside from often being completely out of sync sometimes there's not even any voice at all for speaking characters.
- Voice acting: Good for some characters, not so much for others. Dr. Olga's voice e.g. does not fit her looks.
- Optimization: Frame rates can dip down to 40 and 30 FPS even on high-end hardware.
- Overall lack of polish: One example of this is in Dr. Olga's room near the beginning of the game where it's just completely silent. No sound effects, no music, not even any footsteps from your character. Sound design could really use some work throughout the game.
- Poor logic in several puzzles: It's easier with an example (minor spoiler).
Ultimately it becomes extremely contrived
These types of illogical puzzles are just tedious and should be left out in my opinion.
There are a couple of good- and potentially good things however:
+ Mechanical puzzles: Unlike in any other game I've played this is a very interesting and unique gameplay mechanic.
+ The game doesn't rely too much on previous storyline which means new players to the series (like me) can get into it. Though I was confused a couple of times who Oscar was. Like in Dreamfall Chapters, they should have added a recap video of the previous games at the start.
+ Music is good:
+ Dialogue wheel: I always love having choice in what the protagonist says. Even if it's just an illusion of choice.
I will comment further on the overall story and characterization after I've finished the game. Thus far it's unfortunately not all that intriguing for me but Kate Walker is a fun protagonist so I hope it'll get more interesting.
These were just my first few hours of impressions. Given these, I do not recommend the game currently. Especially not at €40, unless you're a hardcore fan of previous games. For everyone else, wait for it to be polished and reduced in price.
I hope none of this discourages the developers. You guys got something good going on here and with a couple of patches many of the issues could be remedied.

The graphics are mixed for me.  While the art style and choices are very nice and what keeps this as an overall positive for me, I don't get why this had to be 3D.  I won't get into it, but it's certainly not of the quality of a retail, 2017 "A" or even "B"  title.  I understand this began development in 2012, but if it has to be 3D, it should be more polished.  The best part for me so far is the score/soundtrack.  It's amazing and definitely adds to the overall experience.
On the negative, what the hell is going on with those voice actor choices.  Seriously?  Dr. Olga looks and should sound like a middle-aged Russian woman with a mean streak, but instead she sounds like a 17 year old co-op.  The Youkol boy at the beginning has the reverse issue.  It doesn't completely ruin that part of the story, but I can't understand how they could possibly think it was okay.  Also, there is absolutely zero localization for the lip synching. I really, desperately want to like this game because the story is compelling, the environment is interesting, the music and voice acting are great*, and I want to see where that goes. Like most people who have reviewed the game at this point (just after its release), I enjoyed Syberia I and II immensely and had high hopes for the next installment of Kate Walker's adventures. The hype and trailers were promising, so I happily shelled out the $40, expecting another great cinematic game.
However, gameplay is TERRIBLE. The camera angle changes frequently and unexpectedly...and changes your controls with it. Even once you get accustomed to WASD being relative to the camera rather than the character, you can't account for the fact that the controls are slightly different in each camera angle, so you have to mentally step out of the game and focus on the controls in every second. Worse, the proximity triggers for interacting with people and objects are fairly narrowly defined, so exploring a scene is arduous. Even when you're interested in the story and have a clear objective, it is nearly impossible to execute, much less enjoy.
This is also linear gameplay at its worst. Kate (your character) can walk up to a box, identify that the button doesn't work, find the instructions for fixing it, and tell you that she needs something to act as a screwdriver. You see a knife sitting on the table next to her, but you cannot interact with it until you walk away, talk to another character, and have him tell you to look around the room for a tool. In another early instance, Kate can identify a problem with  a key, inspect it and tell you what's wrong and what needs to be done...and then refuse to continue with the puzzle until she has conversed with her friends about the problem and *then* inspected the key in that order. She doesn't tell you that she needs to converse, only that she needs to inspect the key (even if you have already done so). The conversation is the same whether or not she's looked at the key, and it doesn't help her identify the problem, but the game requires that order of events. When solving puzzles, you can never be sure that your solution or instincts are incorrect; you may just be smarter and faster than the developer wants you to be.The game actually penalizes you for doing well. It's infuriating!
Dialogue is also a chore. When you choose to speak to someone, a small wheel appears with short prompts about the direction of your response. However, you can't always scroll or interact with the wheel to choose a response, and may have to reboot once or twice before the game recognizes your mouse for inventory or dialogue. That wouldn't be so bad except that you have to read the prompts, guess what that means Kate will say, and weigh how that might influence the conversation (she's being interrogated at the beginning and hooked up to a lie detector, so this is important) while your conversation partner badgers you to give them a response every few seconds.
I hope that these are issues that Microids will be able to patch in the next few months. Unless that happens and you can verify it in later reviews, my strong recommendation is not to buy this game yet. Especially if you loved the first two Syberias. Wait until Microids has made some serious patches.
*In French. The English dub is like every C-rated 1980s kung fu flick you've ever had the pleasure of viewing while inebriated.

As someone who has just finished the game I am recommending Syberia 3, however there are a lot of different things you should know before you start playing. I have listed some of these things below:
- Syberia 3 relies on your knowledge of Syberia 1 and 2
- Syberia 3 has a cliffhanger ending
- Syberia 3 was made by a small team of developers and has a lot of minor glitches
- Syberia 3 has pretty iffy controls
- Syberia 3 ocasionally has spotty voice acting and the lipsyncing has been done for the French version, even if you are playing with English voices
So why am I still recommending this game?
- The world of the Syberia games is unlike any other I have experienced in gaming
- The locations feel interesting and unique
- I enjoyed the story and characters
- I enjoyed most of the gameplay (despite the controls)
- The music is awesome
- The game creates a sense of joy and wonder that few other games can match, which made the adventure worthwhile for me

Syberia is part of my childhood. I loved the games as a kid, mostly for how they made me feel like I'm on this big adventure. While waiting for this new one to come out I (after all these years) replayed the previous games and what now I liked most about them (besides the spirit of adventure I still got) was Kate as a character.
Now about this new one. I played it on 'Good' graphical settings, with a wired Xbox360 controller and on Adventure difficulty. So far I haven't ran into any major problems.
Cons:
- At times horrible voice acting. Mostly the problem is caused by casting too young actors for old people roles.
- No manual saves.
- Can't skip dialogue.
- Some questionable animations (Kate's shoulders while walking stay still making her seem really stiff and I would advice against looking and people mouths while they speak).
- At times unresponsive controls.
Pros:
- Kate Walker is still very much Kate.
- The general atmosphere still makes me feel like I'm on a big adventure.
- Even on not the highest settings it's still beautiful.
- Music is varied and fitting.
- Puzzles are enjoyable.
- Writing is great,
- Option to choose if you want to play with hints or not.
All in all while mechanically being more of a Telltale than old Syberia's (this is NOT a point-and-click, don't expect it to be), I still am enjoying the game a lot.

A generally agreed upon lack luster installation to the long standing franchise. Don't let that title fool you, Atelier Sophie is far from being a bad game, however it also doesn't meant that it's a great game either. Sophie rests comfortably within the 'okay to good' range on the spectrum but with a lack of context to the series, the game can be a great starting place for beginners.
First, let's briefly talk about the pros and cons before talking more indepth about the game.
- The Alchemy system is arguably at it's best.
- Character models look amazing.
- The game (not the menu at the moment) run at a steady 50-60 FPS, even on average computers.
- Good old Atelier soundtrack.
- TURN BASED BATTLE SYSTEMS.
- Characters are bland, even more so in this game.
- No direction whatsoever, even with the lack of plot.
- Menu hovers below 30 fps.
- Battle system is a step down from most turn based battle systems.
The Atelier series does not have a particularly engaging battle system or story. Instead, the series relies heavily on self motivation, similar to how you would in an sandbox RPG. While there is a linearity to it, Sophie has a pseudo-sandbox in that you are free to do whatever you want whenever you want so long as you follow Plachta's ingredients. The game does little to advise you on what to do that it feels like there is nothing to do but mindlessly grind despite there being character and story events randomly placed.
Where the game truly shines, and is emphasized with this entry, is the Alchemy system. The game is called 'The Alchemist of the Mysterious Book' after all! Each item you pick up or loot has special traits and quality that influence the items you produce, with each item requiring certain catalysts or ingredients to make. The system gets complex once you realize that you can convert weapons to raw material and carry over extremely coveted traits. Suffice to say, once you figure out the ins and outs of Alchemy, you'll find that the deep, complexity is almost addicting and the desire to create the very best equips become almost an obsession. Of course, this is all optional so long as you stick to the main storyline and regular difficulty.
The battle system is an extension of Alchemy. You fight monsters to get more materials and with the new items you make you try to sweep the monsters even faster. It's important to know that upgrading your weapons and armor is just as important as building new bombs to clear mobs. There isn't much to say other than 'it's a battle system', but Sophie tries to reintroduce Offense and Defense stance that you might compare to Paradigms in FFXIII (and drawing comparisons to XIII isn't a good thing). This makes the battle system too straightforward for some, but as long as you stick around your level it should be okay at best. Luckily, Spring Wind Skylark is amazing to listen to which helps the monotonous grind a bit more easier.
Unfortunately, yes. The characters are nothing special but the designs are absolutely lovely to look at. Atelier Sophie has the benefit(?) of having two illustrators known for their aesthetics and vibrants colors that should reflect the casual SoL that Atelier Sophie tries to promote. The characters feel more like a backdrop as there are more emphasis on Sophie and Plachta, but even then it feels like they didn't do a stellar job at developing the deutagonists that well either. On my end, I absolutely love the cuteness of Sophie and Plachta acts as a very good foil and support to her antics. The duality is done relatively fine in some occasions but otherwise is just the usual JRPG fluff.
All in all, Atelier Sophie is an okay game. It has pros and cons, but I recommend you give the Atelier series a chance with Sophie. If you liked the game, know that this is considered one of the 'okay-est' entry to the series. If you can, please take a look at the Arland and Dusk series, as well as keeping an eye out for Atelier Firis which is definitely a step up from Sophie.

After a handful of plays, I've decided not to recommend this game. While it's vaguely interesting, it's massively dominated by luck rather than strategy, and plays at a snail's pace once you know what's going on.
The default Crown of Command victory mechanic harshly punishes any player trying to win, effectively removing them from the game and having them roll a die every turn to see if they get closer to winning. During this time, other players can interrupt the lead player or heal themselves, build up their strength, reset the lead player's advantage, and then walk in and win an hour later. Luckily there are houserules that deal with this (instantly winning or disabling healing when someone reaches the Crown).
They try to keep it interesting with the runes, which you earn by playing a lot. All the runes do is give you a minor, but unfair, advantage. Additionally, custom classes and cards which were easy to incorporate in physical editions are sold in relatively expensive DLC packs, leaving the core game feeling sparse.
It could be fun as a lighthearted game with friends every once in a while.

In a small town of Kirchen Bell, you play as the novice alchemist, Sophie Neuenmuller. Known for her sloppy and clumsy work, she hopes to become a legendary alchemist just like her grandma. Without a mentor, though (grandma passed away) her current alchemy skills lack the experience to do most of the recipes, and fails them every time. Until one day, a mysterious book (hence the title) suddenly starts flying and talking to her. Stunned with these events, the book has lost her memories. Sophie being the good girl she is, offers to restore the lost memories in exchange for a mentor.
