This is my very first steam review, so bear with me. At the time of writing this review, I have had zero hours played of this game IN STEAM. While I have not played this game through steam, I have played through it at least five times in the past straight from the disk. I can say without a doubt that this is my favorite point and click game. Not only is it simple, but it has a compelling story, some very creepy elements, and is overall a well thought out, and well balanced horror game.
First of all, the story of this game is very immersive. It really puts you into the protagonist's shoes and makes you want him to progress and find whatever it is that he needs to find. (Trying to avoid any and all spoilers in this) This tactic of turning you into the protagonist really compells you to progress in the game.
A good point to also make is that the characters in this game are all VERY diverse. There are a wide range of individuals in this game, and they are truly individuals. They have their own voice, action set, and personality. This makes the game seem realistic no matter how crazy it all seems.
True Horror. This game isn't a new game, obviously. It is before all of this jump scare nonsense. A lot of people can't stand them, and I am one of them. Instead of throwing things at your face, his game uses it's storyline while constantly and consistently sprinkling creepy people, places, and ideas to get under your skin and really make your heart pump.
The music in this game is very good in my opinion. It adds a lot of subtle creepy tones to the game that couldn't be attained with such a magnificent soundtrack.
You may see point and click and think "Too easy. I would be done in minutes." This isn't the speedrun kind of game. It actually has given me some difficulty. The game really makes you think about what needs to be done next.
Puzzles, puzzles, puzzles! This game has many uniquely puzzling puzzles. It has just enough to make your brain work without bringing you out of the game's atmosphere.
Overall, I think this game is very well worth the five dollars that I payed for it on sale even though I know the story by heart and all the places to click are stored in my brain. I honestly can't think of anything negative to say about this game. I have loved it for years upon years and I will keep loving it as the simple, yet eerie and enjoyable game that will stay in my heart forever.
TL:DR:
Well structured game.
Good cheap horror title.
Great character development.
Perfect music.
Challenging.
Great puzzles.
And creepy as all hell!
Thank you for reading. I really suggest this game to anyone looking for horror, point and click, casual, adventure, or creep-me-out kind of games. The developers from the past really deserve a pat on the back for this masterpiece.
EDIT: It was requested that I speak more specifically about the story in my review. Hopefully this helps some of you.
In this game, you wake up in an insane asylum after a tragic car accident. You have amnesia and can not remember your name, why you are there, or many details about your own life and the world around you. You explore different planes of reality and even fantasy to learn the details of your life and why you woke up in the asylum.
I suppose this summary kind of dumbs down the amazingly integrated and intruiging plot of the game, but don't let my horrible preview fool you. The story may seem unrelatable and maybe even boring to some of you, (Trying to figure out your past, present, and future) but once you begin to play this game, you will instantly feel otherwise. I hope this bit helps some of you decide on purchasing this game.

I nominated this game for the "No Apologies" award: even with its mixed reception, even with its self-evident flaws, ACIII still remains, for me, one of the series highlights.
I can understand why others feel different. Coming off the very successful Ezio Trilogy, with its charming protagonist and colourful Mediterranean romps, to this, where you play as a moody teen in a downbeat tale of dashed hopes and broken promises...it's a hell of a transition. I don't blame people for feeling let down.
But for me, that's one of its strengths. A series only survives as long as Assassin's Creed has done by constantly trying new things, and this game is that attitude in abundance. Any effort made to avoid staleness is to be commended, whether it works out or not.
And a lot of what's here does work. The combat mechanics are superb, building on Ezio's combo-kills to new heights of speed and fluidity. The rural setting, with its climable rocks and trees, makes free-running fresh and exciting again, bringing back a vivid sense of...well, freedom, that was perhaps wearing off by this time. And whilst Black Flag makes it feel primitive in retrospect, the naval missions still remain a series highlight.
But what I like most is something very simple: this is one of a very few stories, in any medium, to dare criticise George Washington, and the Founding Fathers as a whole. Many countries have a "founding myth", but America's is one of the most dominant in global culture, and even now so much of it remains unquestioned. A story that places the Revolution in its fullest historical context - that of the native tribes, the first owners of the land over which the white colonists were squabbling, and to whom the Patriot victory was a disaster - is something that simply doesn't happen often enough, especially in a Triple-A title like this.
That being said, ACIII does have its shortcomings. Even I'm not blind to that. It's obvious that the studio were working under a tight deadline, and the larger-than-usual portion of bugs and glitches is testament to that. The story also suffers, ultimately, with both Connor's and Desmond's plots coming to rushed, underwhelming endings, which is a particular shame considering their strong starts.
Personally, I'm willing to put that aside. The aspects of this game that work, and they work very well indeed, are more than enough to make up for the aspects that don't.

It's such a joy to hear Alan Young in peak form reprising his role as Scrooge.
DT: R isn't a long game, nor is it particularly challenging (except for the final level), but it's exceedingly well designed throughout. The gameplay is varied and the controls are refined and precise. The boss enemies in particular are very well crafted, with fun, pattern-based attacks and just the right amount of RNG to keep things interesting without being unfair.
I can definitely recommend that anyone who enjoys platformers pick this game up, even if they're not familiar with the source material. DT: R is a rare gem that's perfect for young kids but also will easily keep adults entertained and delighted.

I recently started getting more into sidescrolling space shooters just to change it up. At first glance, I really enjoyed CounterAttack. But coming from someone who plays games to relax, I can't say that it's overall enjoyable. The difficulty in the game is much too high, even on Casual/Arcade modes.
I really liked some of the ideas they've incorporated into the game mechanics. The unlockable loot system is cool, and continually gives an added edge for one of many many restarts of the game. The powerup idea is also a great mechanic, however, I think it would have perhaps been better to collect powerups during the level, and then spec your ship before the next level using what you've collected.Since it plays such a big part in your ability to pass a level, I often found myself trying to grab powerups in highly risky gunfire, else risking it flying off screen and becoming uncollectable. The majority of times I've died in game have been due to this, and it is extremely frustrating, especially in the early game levels. More important is the fact that you have a limited number of lives, and can't save between levels in most game modes. As if that wasn't enough, once you die, you lose powerups, adding even more frustration to my last statement.
I don't know why the developers went to such great lengths to make this game uncharacteristically difficult. There appear to be plenty of levels on the worldmap, and even on Casual mode the furthest I've ever gotten was stage 5. More importantly, each of those maps come with unique weapons and ship enhancements that you have to "unlock" which happens at random during a playthrough. That being said, it would have been much more fun to simply unlock levels and then be able to play them again whenever you like without having to progress through the entire story. Either that, or an automatic save (regardless of difficulty) after each level
The other issue with powerups is that they cycle through a progression, and don't carry over between levels. It is very easy to accidentally skip over the upgrade you wanted during a playthrough, and if you forget to use your powerups during a level, you lost them. There is PLENTY going on during battle without having to constantly keep an eye on powerups and manage that aspect of the game. Again, it would have been much more enjoyable to spec after battle, or even during battle by pausing and choosing where you want your upgrades to go.
I will say that if you have the fortitude to grind these levels for dozens of hours ( hard to do in a game that requires so much focus and attention to detail), it could be very enjoyable. Playing the sandbox level was really incredible, as it showed me just how powerful my ship could become. It was a sight to behold, to be sure. But I doubt the sheer amount of pain you need to go through to get there is worth it in the long run.
Nevertheless, I give it a positive review, because I believe it is as the devs intended, and the gameplay is pretty good. Plus the price point is perfect.

CounterAttack is a blast to play! Purchased it with my cousin and we were instantly hooked. I highly recommend it in it's current state, very playable and haven't ran into any bugs as of yet. An excellent shmup you and your friends will play for many hours.
~Gameplay~
A side scroller shmup that you collect power ups on the battlefield to upgrade your ship on the fly. There are two types of powerups you collect (along with other miscellaneous powers that are used right away) through out your play through; green for your primary weapon and orange for your ultimate weapon.
You have a primary weapon, which can be upgraded through out the campaign as well as a unique ultimate weapon depending on the character  you choose. While collecting the power ups, you can choose to use them right away or hold on to them until you get further down the attachment bar for more powerful attacks, but be careful! If you die, you lose all the powerups you collected, but retain the attachments you've unlocked to that point.
~Story~
There isn't much of a story. Aliens have invaded and it's up to you to save the world. At the start of each level you get a brief dialogue of the situation from your captain and some one liners from your character.
The levels range from outer space, ground level, meteor showers, navigating through space ships, and defeating bosses at the end of each level.
~Graphics~
The game is beautiful. From the planets in the background to the sheer number of enemies on screen, you will have your eyes full. While collecting powerups and upgrading your ship with new attachments, you will be covering your monitor with a ridiculous amount of bullets. I was especially pleased with how incredibly detailed your spaceship is, along with the enemies.
I tried setting the graphics to 4K with Ultra details but my rig couldn't handle it. (i7-7700k w/ 1080Ti) I was getting about 20fps. So I set the details to Very High and I was hitting 30fps. When I went to High details I was able to hit the 60fps mark. Even with High details, the game still blows me away.
~Sound~
Loved the soundtrack. There were more then a handful of times my cousin and I were getting pumped up by music while playing. It really puts you in the mode and gets your blood flowing. There is no voice acting that I'm aware of while playing through out the campaign outside of the intro. Would of have been nice to have voice actors for each character to go along with the dialogue, but the game is fine without.
~Lasting Appeal~
Through the campaign there are multiple paths you can choose to go down. Some require a certain attachment while others simply require you to choose left or right. Each character you choose has a unique ultimate weapon. Along with choosing your character you can customize your spaceship with different modules and attachments before the start of the campaign. Upon gameover you can choose to change your setup to try something different or help you in a particular mission you may be stuck on. There are a few difficulty options along with 3 game types; campaign, survival and custom.
~Final Thoughts~
If there was one negative I would say about the game it would have to be the inability to save your campaign while playing in multiplayer coop. When you and a friend lose all your lives, the game is over and the both of you have to start from the beginning along with losing all your attachments in the process. If we were able to save or have checkpoints, it would be a more enjoyable experience, but as of right now its tough going back and playing the same levels over and over just to get back to the mission the both of ya'll died at.
Overall I think this a must own title if your into the shmup genre. Not only is it gorgeously detailed, but you will be hard pressed to find a better action packed 4 player coop with a rocking soundtrack for under 10 bucks.
A really solid shmup, good visuals, upgrade system is both enriching and easy to understand, and overall I think it is a very nice game. Worth the price to be sure.

I played the original version of Savage since it's release.  To say the least, it's a unique game that cannot be compared to other games.

Commander is also something that takes some time to master.  Although the tech tree isn't nearly as expansive as something RTS focused like Starcraft 2, there is still plenty of tough decisions to make.

The critical issue is that the dice roll is not randomised. To demonstrate, perform a turn to see how the die rolls, exit, reload, and then re-do your turn to see the dice roll the exact same way. I've performed different actions and even seen the AI players get the dice rolls I would have got. It's ridiculous. The whole point of rolling a dice is to be random. Not random = not a dice roll.
The annoyances are as previously alerted to in prior reviews, mostly to do with poor AI, but I could have lived with that had the dice rolls actually been pseudo-random, you know, ceiling(math.rand()*6) or something.

Conclusion (if you want to read more):
So...the average time I'll play a game if I'm interested is around 8 hours...unless I can beat the game before that. If you see any review with +100 hours, the game is worth the play. The game is basically "Free". Hypothetically if you play 3 hours a day every day, you've spent a month playing this game before giving it a thumbs down. Not only did you get your money's worth, but this game is free. Why spend hundreds of hours on this game if you didn't like it?
First off, frame dropping. This can be easily fixed with Tera's guide from the community. Really helpful. Look it up. I went from lowest settings getting 20FPS in dungeons to 50FPS on mid. Check it out before you boot up the game to run smoothly.
2nd, if you're new to MMOs or basically playing console before you got into PC play etc, I'd highly recommend you buy an MMO mouse. Yes, pretty expensive, but what isn't nowadays? Think of it as an investment. You've spend hundreds of dollars on another game(s), so why not invest in some peripherals? An MMO mouse has 9-12 buttons on the side, which is essentially a numberpad on the side of your mouse. That helps significantly on commands. Before someone points out its simplistic space button mash, again, it's an investment. The one game that practically requires you to use all 9 numbers and ctrl + and 9 and probably macros +9 is FFXIV. Buy an MMO mouse. It will solve many problems.
There are other games similar to its combat like BnS and DSO. If you haven't played them, then the closest thing is a mix between Devil may Cry and Dynasty (samurai) warriors. This is much simpler if you make it simpler. It'll allow you by default chain combos in which you only need to initiate a special attack and follow it up with another by pressing space bar. Or you can have a harder class that doesn't chain and in which requires that MMO mouse I pointed out earlier.
There are other mmos that are free and F2P like BnS, however one would argue that its P2W but you can scurry and grind on by doing everything free. Since the game is pure skill vs. dungeon grindy armor based than skill in my eyes outweighs P2W. Star wars is free until lvl 50, so there's that arguement, and then there's other games w/o subscription like ESO and DSO that you pay once.
Originally, I was tasked to play 5 mmos mainly for its free content: ESO, FFXIV (free month only), WoW (20 lvls free), BnS, and Tera all at the same time. Typically, that's alot of mmos and alot of time I have to spend playing all of them, so bare with me as I might be opinionated for each game for their sole purpose as my time was fairly limited, and I will be updating this review for further purposes in case I play them longer. If I ranked all the mmos in the other that I enjoyed it would be FFXIV, BnS, Tera, ESO, WoW.
No offense to WoW as I hear great things about it, but it's completely outdated amongst all of them even on the highest of settings. I also didn't feel compelled to play through the easy grind just mashing buttons to make combos. I have a brother-in-law that swears to me that WoW is the greatest MMORPG of all times, but when I play it I feel like I'm playing an updated Runescape, and all I could ask him is "and you pay monthly for this?" WoW at this moment or in ayear-ish should be free. If it isn't free, than I blame those that still pay its $15 a month hanging out at cap lvl just because.
FFXIV is expensive, but thankfully in a month you can get to lvl 50 (2 jobs too) as a tank class, not DPS as you will be waiting forever (pugilist). I'm quite tempted to pay subsciption for it as there's other features like "One character to rule them all". You essentially can choose your favorite class and gender and have that class play anything. Just switch the weapon and poof you're a lancer, pugilist, hypy-dipity doo dah dancer, magic (okay, I'm forgetting all the names). Because of this, it makes the game worth a playthrough even if you pay just once for that full free month (amazon only). The battle system is quite standard. You don't really have to dodge unless you're wearing paper thin armor and there's too many of them. It's easy at first glance, but as I mention earlier, you're going to need an MMO mouse. There aren't any shortcuts like Tera. You are going to press everything, and on top of that, typing messages because "F" discord. Yeah, I said it. I'm old school. Filter your chat so you don't see all those hit points. Read my messages in the middle of the fight. This was apparent back in FFXI but not anymore.
ESO has a specially place in my heart. I had fun, especially stealing. It has alot of things going for it...solo. As a group, this is wear it lacks the most attention. Missions get glitchy and weird if you have group members that completed it already. I found myself wondering why I even grouped up in the first place. But the stealing though! I could spend hours just pilfering through crap that isn't mine and getting rid of it later because it's just the thrill of it. It's combat system is much simpler than the other ones. I actually like its extremely easy action system. If you ever want to get anyone into MMOs, this or FFXIV, but mainly this because even at highly levels the combat system is so simple it you wonder why do other MMOs have so many buttons to press.
BnS is...special. If you have fighting game experiences in your background at a tournament level, this is the game for you. I actually do, which is kinda sad. This game requires absolute skill and the skilless will just delete this game and call it bad and P2W. You can breeze on by doing everything free. It's just a bit harder like having limited carry space. You didn't need that item because you're not a horder. You ever want to talk about an MMORPG that is purely "Git gud" material? It's this. You don't need to dungeon run to get the best gear. 1v1 anyone anytime at cap lvl with the minimum required gears and still slay because I'm not all about that "I've played this game longer than you have" MMORPG.
All-in-all I recommend this game. Tera sits somewhere in the middle of all of them. I wouldn't pay a subsciption for this game at all...an neither for WoW. I'm still grinding my way to cap lvl. Amazingly fun and well crafted. Half-Life: Caged doesn't take too long to finish but it's a ride definitely worth taking. Hard difficulty is a tough but fun challenge that will take some careful planning and health conversation, which where the mod really shines in how much it can provide the player breathing room without any sort of handholding, but rather through clever designs and cues from the level itself. The visual style really compliment the level design well, along with the inclusion of custom models and textures. The new assets definitely breathe into new life on the familiar base of Half-Life. Last but not least, the synthwave musical soundtrack by Lazerhawk really sets up the mood of the entire mod, and fits all the moments throughout the game, from quiet moments to intense action.
The amount of secrets and achivements to discover also keeps the replayability up a bit, and even just the overall length of a single playthrough if one were to attempt to get all of them in a single run. Overall a really fun and awesome mod that is well worth your time. I look forward to many more mods of this quality and calibre to be created in the near future.

Now this game was a real surprise! Tharsis blends an interesting boardgame aesthetic with the tough decision-making and resource-management of the best in turn-based strategy sims. At first it seems as if the dice completely control the experience, but as you spend more time with the game it becomes apparent that the real strategy comes from learning *when* to move, *who* to move, *where* to move and what to repair when you get there, always taking into account that low dice rolls may throw a wrench into your plans. The secret is to plan your turns in such a way that you minimize the severity of low dice rolls, and celebrate the moments when the dice are kind. It's really a one-in-a-kind experience.
And that's not to mention the temptation of making use of *all* the possible meals on board as the mission progresses... once you see the possibility of eking one more week of survival by making costly sacrifices, it becomes very difficult to stop...
Highly recommended.

A challenging single player board game experience.
You face a series of events taking place during the last 10 weeks of your voyage to Mars.
Things will go wrong. Things will go very wrong.
You goal is to survive until you reach Mars.
The modules on the ship will break each turn and it's the job of your 4 remaining astronauts to fix them and keep from otherwise dying of starvation or mental breakdowns. Your astronauts perform tasks by rolling dice and most events require a certain number of points to repair which come from the value of your dies. *YES THIS MEANS LUCK IS INVOLVED* But it's not the governing body of the game mechanics, it's your descisions that come from understanding and working through your bad situation and what oppotunities to look out for.
Aside from the game systems, the atmosphere is top notch. A foreboding sci-fi survival tale. Your astronauts will appear visibly disturbed as their stress levels rise. Dice physics. A moody electro soundtrack (provided I believe by some artists from the San Francisco bay area electro scene.)
Fans of Chainsaw Warrior or Elder Sign: Omens would definitely enjoy this, but if you're looking for this to be a replacement for FTL, you probably want to look elsewhere.

Possibly one of the most misleading games of history. This is a remake of the NES classic which was made by Capcom in the Mega Man era (the original actually uses the Mega Man engine). While I must admit that I barely played the original NES game, DuckTales Remastered is an instant nostalgia bomb from the moment you press start. From the colorful sprites of all our favorite characters, to the original voices from the cartoon show, and the theme song, everything feels so perfect at the beginning. It really isn't just a "remake" of the original game, it's also a reunion for people who were fans of the show as well.
With colorful graphics, tight controls, fun gameplay, and great music, Remastered also attempts to make fans of the original game feel at home. However, with the inclusion of many pesky and intruding cutscenes, the wonderful flow of the game grinds to a complete halt. Some can be welcome -- introducing a new level or terrifying boss. But other cutscenes will activate whenever you complete trivial "objectives", which can be anything from finding a token or aiding Launchpad fix his plane. They interupt a bit too often, and while there is an option to skip these (by pausing the game during the cutscene, selecting "skip cutscene", then confirming), sometimes there's two or three back to back, making you have to awkwardly repeat the process. It doesn't help that if you Game Over and have to repeat a stage... well, get ready to skip all those cutscenes again! I understand they were just trying to add story to a game where there was none (except perhaps in the instruction manual of the original), however, it is still frustrating to repeatedly have to keep skipping cutscenes.
Despite that one flaw, DuckTales Remastered is an easy game to get into and a very rewarding one to complete. Scrooge and all his companions are back for a DuckTales encore that seemed long overdue. And I'm very happy to have been apart of it! DuckTales fans, pick this one up! Fans of the original game or just fans of old school side-scrollers in general, maybe wait til it's on sale.
Happy adventuring!!!

I have played TERA for many years (specifically started in Closed Beta). The game has gone down since it began, but overall it is still a good game. It isn't as pay-to-win as many make it out to be. If you are looking for a true action MMORPG then TERA is the game for you. If you really want to experience the beauty of the game then I suggest doing all the story quests and no dungeons unless needed till end-game. Plus you can now search for a guild based on your playstyle. Guilds are a great way to meet people, even the small guilds can be fun.

I've played dozens of MMORPG style games over the years, and most end up falling flat.  Tera, on the other hand, really gets going once you hit max level.
The game is a bit grindy once you hit lvl 65, but it's nothing like other games of the same genre.
The combat system is aim based, so you have to aim at your target to attack or heal, making the game much more involved than other big title games.
There are a few drawbacks.  First off, maxing your gear after fully enchanting it, is a huge grind for each piece.  You can speed up the process by buying mats in the cash store, but it's not a must.  Making gold is easy enough, so you can also buy the mats from the trade broker.  Another drawback is the limit on the number of dungeons you can do in a day.  Each dungeon is different.  Some only allow 2 runs a day, others allow up to 4.  These numbers are doubled if you pay the monthly fee for elite status.
All in all, Tera is a solid game, with hundreds of hours of quests, dungeons, and battlegrounds.

They shadowbanned users, banned users and removed comments/posts that are critical of them, even constructive ones, often hiding behind their tight forum rules that basically disallows criticism on the forums to be carried out against the publisher. It is akin to governments using laws that tackle public peace issues to shut citizens up when they create a uproar to criticize the government actions. How is a community as a whole ever going to have a channel to discuss things with the publisher if all they do is create a thread, stop responding to it and ban every other thread? They can say private emails, but heck, it is the input of community members discussing as a whole that matters, not just one person's perspective.

A surprisingly addictive little side/vertical-scrolling shooter game that hearkens back to the classic days of Gradius and R-type. The powerup system works almost identically to Gradius III. Dozens (possibly hundreds) of obtainable ship upgrades, a good selection of base ships, and a decent variety of enemies makes this a good time-waster. For ten bucks, it's probably one of the better choices out there for shooter fans who don't want a game that's going to require a considerable investment of time and skill to get into. It's not a bullet-hell shooter, but it'll still challenge both casual and advanced players in its own way.
A brief pro/con breakdown:
Pros:
- MANY, many upgrades and unlockables that will encourage you to play through missions multiple times to try for the rarer weapons. Seriously, an absolutely insane amount of unlockable attachments and weapons. If you liked playing around on the loadout screen for R-type, after a handful of missions there are going to be times that it'll take hours before you even press the start button to begin a campaign.
- A good number of stages split up into 3 main routes (A-la the original SNES version of StarFox) ranging from easy to hard. Some of the stages offer a fairly steep difficulty curve, but for score junkies that can be a good thing.
- The backgrounds are well-drawn and the art is pretty decent for an indie shooter game. Not up to par with later installments of Touhou or B-tier console titles, but not hard to look at.
- The music is catchy and energetic.
- The game will occasionally surprise you with optional semi-secret missions that throw a real curveball at you by changing the mode (Like putting you in a hovertank instead of a spaceship for instance),
- The game occasionally varies stage mechanics, forcing you to adapt to new rules and environments, which greatly helps reduce the 'been there, done that' factor that many shmups tend to have.
- 3 different gamemodes (casual, normal, hardcore) that allow those of us who are used to bullet hell shooters to up the difficulty a bit.
- Multiplayer support lets you team up with other people, and provides a matchmaking system that lets you create public lobbies.
- Multiplayer mode lets you hurl an absolutely unprecedented amount of ordnance onto the screen.
- Component sorting system makes managing the absolutely absurd number of weapons and upgrades much easier.
- The developer has very clearly made this game a labor of love, and actively hunts down bugs, updates the game, and playtests. The devs are very open to community discussion, and actively participate when they can. Major bugs are quickly squished and patches put out to fix them.
- Constant and steady stream of new content.
- It has that absolutely badass purple laser from Raiden III.
Cons:
- Replayability is somewhat limited by the number and types of stages. Once you get beefed up, you'll find that the earlier stages get a bit stale.
- Grinding for parts can be irritating sometimes.
- The music, while decently composed and fairly catchy is somewhat limited and you'll find yourself substituting it for something else in fairly short order.
- The part/upgrade system can be somewhat overwhelming sometimes as you quickly become swamped with multiple components.
- Some of the optional alternate-mode scenarios are a bit glitchy sometimes.
- The later levels (especially on harder difficulties) can be overwhelming and in some cases nearly impossible with some weapon loadouts. (Whatever you do, don't enter the minefield stage with a massive spread weapon. Trust me, you'll regret it)
- The story is a bit thin at the moment, and some of the conversation text can be a bit janky sometimes.
- Boss battles can sometimes be a bit underwhelming for hardcore shmup fans.
- It also has the MUCH less badass yellow laser from Raiden Trad.
If they had the rights, the developers could well have called this Gradius Online and it would have been a very well received addition to the series. Yes, that's a compliment.
Clearly the developer loves this game very much. Often, you'll see indie developers throw out games like this as a way to try to snag some quick cash, but this is very obviously not the case here. Between the open communication process, transparency and absolutely relentless drive to add new content, I think that by the time this game makes its way out of Early Access, it'll be far more than just the sum of its parts. The gameplay is somewhat repetitive (as many shmups tend to be), but with enough variation and unique concepts to not quickly become stale. If I had to ask for any one specific thing, it'd be more additional levels and maybe a level editor; I think I'd probably lose more than a couple weeks of productivity if I had the option to submit/play new levels through the steam workshop.
I received my key through a steam-key giveaway, but I've paid twice as much as the going price of this game for a fraction of the content in the past.

Everything about this game is inadequate and sloppy.
The story is pretty tropey.
A lot of the game is a massive grind, filled with needless padding.
Combat is very clunky and difficult to manuever around in, especially when as soon as you move enemies crit and slow you if not timed right.
The areas you fight in get very repetitive and the random encounters are somewhat nonsensical in terms of ecology.
A lot of the spells feel useless and lack depth.
The world map is so devoid that it is almost senseless to even have it.
The side quests are mostly fetch quests and aren't worth the time in the rewards they give.  You could kill enemies in a random encounter and get 10x the reward plus save half the time.
The thing that gets me the most is the shopping and buying equipment.....You can wear two pieces of chainmail for about 30k and it will give you the same protection as a 300-800k suit of armor.
The game has almost every aspect of a first generation game rushed out to a new console, with little planning and foresight....with massive padding so they could claim X hours of gameplay.
It has very few redeeming qualities (I actually like the chaining system).  The only people recommending this are doing it out of nostalgia and/or haven't completed the game to really see how bad it gets.

Summoner, a game that i first played at it's release on ps2. And despite being pretty dull, repetitive, graphically ugly (it was even back then), and raw it still has stayed on my mind all these years. There's a certain charm in this game. The first city stays on your mind forever.
Combat is pretty clunky, relying on timed button pressing to get chains, you can pump out chain attacks as much as you got AP. That's pretty op in the end stages. You get a party of 4 chars, and one slot reserved for your summon. so, 5 slotted party :D I never really found much use for the summons actually, and i haven't grinded my characters especially either. So the game is pretty easy on the combat-aspect. If you're looking for tactical challenge, it's not this game.
The lore is big on this game, that is really the most crafted part of this game, and a big thing that got me into this game. It's interesting, there's a lot of lore you might miss if you don't explore the game. The locations are also intrestingly crafted, the cities feel like cities. There's one dungeon that felt too boring, but otherwise the swamp palace felt logical. Not too big, not too small, something that wuold be built in the real world also.
I wuold like to see this game remade, there's a lot of potential for epic fantasy moments/locations, the island monastery, the giant waterfalls at lenele, the Urath temple.
There's a lot of flaws in this game, nothing game-breaking but annoyances like bad camera movement, clunky combat, sometimes it's really repetitive when enemies spawn when going back to other floors. underneath it all, it's a solid sotry, unique world and that strange, raw charm that somehow gets you interested, and eventually thinking about this game from time to time. With a cheap pricetag, it's a good addition if you're into rpg's.

I had well over 2,000 hours racked up on this game on my PS4, but I wanted to switch over to PC because it had better specs. I will tell you this,
With that out of the way, this game is wonderful. I would say this is my favorite Ubisoft game at the moment.
This game plays like a surfboard on a sea of f**king butter. It's so well optimized, and I barely get frame drops. Whenever I first got this game, I had a 1060 3GB and an FX-8300. It played on medium at 90FPS. The graphics are so well integrated, I barely ever see any rough edges or have any rendering issues. Controls-wise, all of the keyboard keys are relatively the same to what someone would usually play in terms of an FPS on PC, but there are some annoying keys that are kind-of out of the way. For example, the Push-To-Talk button is U, which is a long reach from my other keys, and that wouldn't be so bad if this was a game like CSGO, but since there is
much communication needed, it's an inconvinence. However, it's always remappable. It will tell you most of the keys you need to press while you're in-game (in terms of special items) so there's no real learning-curve on the game controls. Also, it is extremely rare to find cheaters in the game, but sometimes it can get a little annoying (due to the ability to teamkill) for teammates to kill you in casual. However, they are removed from the game if they kill 3 teammates. In short, the game mechanics are great.
I know that most people who purchase Ubisoft games are even just the slightest bit worried about microtransactions, but I will say that in this game, it's fairly balanced. All of the operators are generally on the same level, and depending on your play-style, it can be very easy to get good at even the legacy operators. All of the operators can be obtained through in-game currency, and depending on if you purchase the standard edition or the starter edition, it can take a little bit of grinding or a significant amount to get the operators. However, I would say that if you purchase the starter edition, you are kind of setting yourself up for a lot of grinding. All of the things that can only be obtained through real money is cosmetic items and skins. So overall, the microtransactions are very minute.
The game itself is very tense and a lot of fun. There are quite a bit of maps, each with 3 possible gamemodes (hostage, secure the room, and bomb defusal) and multiple different rooms you can spawn in. You are either a defender or attacker, with different operators designed for those roles. You can customise your weapons pretty heavily, and all of the weapons feel balanced and real. The recoil feels very real, and damage taken also feels very real. There are 5 people on either side, and you have 30 seconds in the beginning to locate the objective with small drones, which can be shot at and prevents you from locating it. This can be a game-changer sometimes, which is great, it doesn't feel like an unnecessary mechanic. You are then given around 5 minutes to do whatever the objective wants you to do. When you die, you die. You can spectate and look at cameras and locate enemies to help your teammates, but you're dead until the next round. This makes it less of a run and gun and more of a team-based game. I love that. It's so much fun whenever you can get a group of friends together. There are always thousands of concurrent players, so there's never a time (on PC yet) that I've had to wait more than 2 minutes for a match.
This game has it's flaws, but it's constantly being supported by the developers, and even after 3 years, they're still adding new content, with another year so far to go. It can be frustrating sometimes, but it feels fair most of the time. It's immersive, it's challenging, and most importantly, it's a ton of fun.

A homage to the people who remember the original, or the series - to many people, just the moon theme alone brings up memories. I don't mind paying $14.99 for a game that would have never hit the market unless someone was willing to develop it without visions of making insane profit.
I can't argue that the game is "short", for it's price, but I don't view how I spent my money as a corporate investment, I had far - far more fun completing this than I had with any other game in a long, long time.
As for the price, this game's concept isn't about "completion", it's a 2d sidescroller, and one that's meant to be replayed, I played it on every single difficulty, completing everything, as it's meant to be played - that's why it has leaderboards, that's why there's 4 difficulties, they could have easily made 5 more levels, but it would make no sense. The game was a homage to simpler times, a nostalgic reminder that despite country of residence, we share common childhood memories.
To make a conclusary remark, if you don't have a sentimental value in playing this game, just don't - and I don't mean that in a rude way, but the game simply isn't meant for you, it's meant for those who hold a sentimental value in seeing a bit of their childhood remade. The music is great, and the gameplay owes a lot to it.
Overall I enjoyed the game, a lot. And that's all there is to say. I got far more than I paid for, in terms of nostalgia.

There's one word that describes this game: AWESOME
I have played and tested so many free MMORPG's in the past few years. I have never played one that kept my attention very long, except SWTOR, but even then, it felt punishing for a free to play-er.
-VERY F2P friendly!
-Action packed combat system
-Unique classes/styles from other mmorpg's
-Daily reward system to aid in crafting and such. (No consecutive bonuses, but one each day)
-Federation rewards (These are able to be completed alongside quests in the same area. Example, you have to go to an area and open chests for a quest, the federation wants you to kill a small number of monsters along the way for a reward plus XP)
-You can use the broker (auction house) for a small fee of 5% of what you are selling. (Selling item for 100 gold, must pay 5 gold to list item) This will be eliminated if you have a membership, but itn't dire.
-The game keeps you moving all across the continent as you level up and do the quest line. Each area is unique in and of itself.
-Questing can be changed up as you level and even then you don't have to do quests to hit max level. There are categories for each section of the story mode quests, so you don't have to do any one at any specific time. You are able to unlock higher level quests through leveling, so if you want, you can skip entire sections of quests!
-Dungeons and battlegrounds, you are able to queue up for these as long as you meet the level requirements. Each is very unique and quirky. It sets a different tone to the game from the world you spend most of your time in.
-Try this game, get to level 20 to see a bit of what armor, weapons and damage you can do. It will give you a better idea than the first 10 minutes of playing.
-There's so much more to say about Tera, but if you have questions, message me!
Literally 9/10 for me, and again, it's VERY F2P friendly!

This is one of the most accessible local multiplayer games I've played on Steam: it's essentially digital air hockey. You only use the left analog stick and two face buttons, to pass and shoot the puck. When a game is this easy to play, it opens the door to non-gamers, who will love Clusterpuck. I consider this to be exclusively a local multiplayer game, as that is where it truly shines.
Amazingly, Clusterpuck supports up to 8 players. I tried this out with friends and it was an absolute blast, and we have played with 8 players several times since then. Note that if you want to do this you will not only need 8 controllers but you will also need two Xbox 360 wireless dongles to facilitate the 8 controllers. The setup is a hassle but it if you go through the setup and have 8 friends to play with on a large screen, I think you will agree that it's worth it. We played this on a 120" projected display.

It seems that the local multiplayer craze of the past few years has hit a peak recently. The genre has expanded out far and wide, and many games that would have been praised before are now plagued by obscurity and fighting amongst their talented competition. ClusterPuck 99 had been out for some time on Desura before hitting Steam at the beginning of 2015, one of five games bearing the genre’s tag released in the month of January. Steam in 2015 can be a vicious marketplace, which is why I was pleased to see ClusterPuck come out on Xbox One earlier this month. I had found the game on Desura ages ago, was eager to see what improvements had been made in the meantime, and what console specific fun I could have with the title. For better or worse, I found that ClusterPuck 99 has stuck to its roots as an insane multiplayer arena that requires swift aim and a roomful of friends.
NOTE: This review was written primarily using the Xbox One version of the game.

-It says there's a way of "buying" lives.  I couldn't figure out how though.  You don't get given any lives for completing a mission and the only one I found was a pickup.  So basically you only reliably get 3 lives than oops game over, start again.  Actually the whole upgrade thing I kinda don't get, I just slam Y every time I can upgrade something and than bask in the explosions.
-When you die you drop some of your pickups.  Yet there's a large delay before you respawn, and you always do so from the top, so they are off the screen 90% of the time before you can grab them again.  Maybe this is a multiplayer consideration, but it's pretty aggravating to see them just slip away.
-The voicework is pretty bad.  I think trying not to hear  the "humanity went down with a fight" speech you get after losing all your lives is forcing me to play better.
-Not a big fan of the "technical military-ish" names for the powerups.  Q41 and Q43?  So boring I can't even remember them for sure and which is which.
-Ships hiding behind asteroids and firing at you are a$$holes.  Because reasons.
I'm giving it a tentative thumbs up because it's in early access and it's heart is in the right place.  The last few complaints are mostly me just throwing it out there as feedback.  All depends on the route this goes, seems to be wanting to be an old school arcade game (fair enough), but that's not really my hankering.

As one of the few survivors ofthe destruction of Ciran all those years ago, Joseph has led a hard life. Now, the Emperor of the continent Orenia has invaded Masad village, his new home, looking for a young man with a strange mark on his hand - Identical to young Joseph's. Now, he must find out why the Emperor wants him so badly...
I first played Summoner in 2013, when I got it at a garage sale for my PS2. The title was enough to draw my attention, so I bought it and tried it out ASAP. The background of the protagonist, Joseph, is a sad one. The opening cinematic, after giving a bit of backstory, transitions into gameplay, and starts you off with a tutorial, which involves killing some of the afore-mentioned Orenians, referenced in-game as "Rennies." The controls are hard to get used to, as movement is controlled by mouse, but entirely possible to get used to. The lore of the world is a bit patchy in places, but there's enough there to give you a sense of the world's history. And then, there are the characters. Each of the four main characters has their own unique backstory (and I got deep into theorizing about one of them), meaning they all have their own specialized skill sets. Finally, for a game of its era, it's actually MASSIVE. Not quite Elder Scrolls massive, but still ♥♥♥♥ing HUGE. The navigation is a bit disappointing, however, as whenever you leave certain areas, such as Masad village or the Lenele Outskirts, it places you in the World Map. Traveling around the map, you have a chance to be placed in an Encounter, where you are pitted against rather powerful enemies, depending on your skills and inventory.The navigation is also disappointing because of how huge the continent you start on (Medeva) actually is. If Summoner had been made by Bethesda, Medeva and Orenia would each be the size of the Daggerfall map (approximately the size of Great Britain).
All in all, Summoner is a great game and, in my opinion, a worthwhile purchase. I give it 10 p.i.s.s.e.d off Fire Imps out of 10.

I played the original and Savage XR extensively. Savage Resurrection is actually a good game but it's so reliant on having a community and player base. Most populated servers are US and UK, so if you're not in those regions expect 200-300 ping, which was devastating in the original and in XR but doesn't feel *as* bad in Resurrection. Check how many people are still playing the game too before buying.
The main problem is how the game 'launched' without notice and with minimal marketing. I don't see any news outlets covering the game and myself as a huge Savage fan only discovered the game a week ago after it being in early access for 3 months. The point of a remake is also to surpass, or at least match, what already exists. It's currently lacking:
- Proper tutorials for commanding/duels like XR has (there is a practice mode with bots)
- Map variety (the classics are in but XR literally has thousands)
- Map editor
- Guild/Clan stuff
- Replays
One interesting addition is AI commanders for an 'easy mode' so you don't get one good and one bad commander facing each other. The AI commanders lack any kind of personality though, so it feels like being controlled by a robot (which is true but it doesn't feel as fun). Bot players act realistically enough but have weird quirks like never going siege.
Overall, it's a true enough recreation of the game but it feels like S2's first game all over again. A lot of things have been innovated in recent years to make the multiplayer experience more personal and flavourful — whether it's 'play of the game' and upvoting the top players of the match for player recognition (important for voting commanders and choosing officers in future) or faction/clan/guild stuff — and it would be nice to see these little things help build a community out of the player base.
Would recommend as it's a good game with great potential and it's honestly not that expensive. If development continues fast enough it'll be awesome, otherwise the player base will die very quickly.

Five Nights At Freddy's four I think has some sense of horror in it but most of time I play it because of it's thilling feeling for when you get jumpscared I rate it an absolute got to have. also in this game you go through five nights at your own house being tormented and haunted by the animatronics
Nightmare Freddy, Nightmare Bonnie, Nightmare Chica,  Nightmare Foxy, Nightmare Fredbear (Nightmare Golden Feddy), and finally the newest addition Nightmare. In each night Bonnie and Chica each attack from the sides of the room or Bonnie attacks from the left door, and Chica from the right. To avoid being jumpscared listen carefully for breathing from them and if you hear breathing then shut the door ( The breathing should be the first thing you would hear at the door). To not be jumpscared by Freddy you will have to check behind you on the bed by flicking the mouse to the bottom of the screen, then if you see mini little withered Freddies then leave the flashlight on until they go back under the bed. If you don't want to be jumpscared by Foxy then first don't let him get into your room and in your closet, if that happens then check the closet frequently and if Foxy is not a plushy then close the door until he is either standing straight up or he is a plushy again. Nightmare abd Fredbear are the same they will come from both sides of the room but if you shine the flashlight in their faces they will stand there starring at you, if this happens then close the door until you here foot steps which means they've gone back. After each night you get a chance to "skip" 2 hours of the night. this is known as the famous "Fun with Plushtrap" Plushtrap is a plushy form of Springtrap from FNaF 3. In FWP you have to land the possesed plushy on a "x" within a certain amount of time. Quick reminder check the doors, bed, and closet frequently to keep the animatronics from getting right in front of you in your room and jumpscarring you. I don't usually make Steam review unless the game REALLY deserve one, but I feel that I need to make one for this game in particular so here's goes my crappy review
Streets of Rogue is a pretty interesting Rogue-Lite who managed to make something very different out of his genre, you don't simply kills hordes of enemies and progress through a procedurally generated dungeon and aquire items that give you bonuses, it's WAY more than just that.
The developer himself label his game as a mix of Nuclear throne for the heavily randomly generated cities and structures, Deus Ex for the gameplay diversity through each classes and how to play them and GTA for the silly and chaotic nature of the combat.
The replay value of this game is just insane... so many classes to play, so many mutators, so many upgrade to unlock, so many possibilities on how to complete your objectives, there's even an endless mode for those who completed the game, it is just straight up insane, and the game is not even finished yet !
I personally NEVER saw a game like that in my life, and I have more than 100 games on my Steam account, the developer just managed to make something so different out of the genre and i'm so glad that he did, this game deserve your attention if you're a fan of the rogue-lite genre in general.

The game has a terrible title. Borrowing the aesthetic from a classic brawler and punning it up, really doesn't do the program justice. In the graphical presentation there really isn't anything distinctive to set this aside from the hundreds of other games lining up behind the rogue tag. I thought I was completely finished with the 'rogue' genre, that it had been clubbed to death and beyond.
Where this game shines is in the gameplay. Your approach to each job can go hilariously wrong or impressively right. The amount of planning you're willing to commit to is rewarded, as is attention to detail. Many solutions are available to each little puzzle the game generates. Controls are tight enough that you can hold your own in a fight, but can get overwhelmed when odds turn against you.
It's got seriously replay value. Each loadout completely changes the experience. The random level generation doesn't spit out duds. Making your own custom classes, choosing from included mutators, unlocking more traits and powers, all this stacks up heavy value against the indie game price point.
There's plenty here and more to come. Devs update regularly, and have already implemented local and online multiplayer. Looking forward to watching this one grow.

Please ignore all reviews calling this game "difficult." Or comparing it to FTL or calling it "rougeliek" or any of the other instances of appalling idiocy and ignorance. Rolling dice is not difficult. In fact, a monkey or a child could do it. Because that's all this game is. Beneath the intriguing premise and great presentation, this is yet another lolrandom RNG simulator that's impossible, or highly unlikely, to get to the end of. As much as I wanted to like it, two and a half hours of wasting my time on relentlessly being crapped on by bad luck is quite enough. And in this game, "bad luck" is essentially not getting perfect dice rolls for 20 minutes straight.
Perhaps the developers wanted to make this game "replayable." In that case, I submit they don't quite understand what that means. The game's story is exactly the same each time. As interesting and well done as the cutscenes are, they repeat every single time you play the game. Seeing them three or four times was, again, quite enough for me, let alone the ten attempts I suffered through. And it's not like there's any depth to what minimal amount of strategy there is. All you really do is pray to the RNG gods that a) you get a good starting board (if you don't, just Alt F4 and restart because there's no point in continuing. The game will absolutely give you no opportunity to recover), and b) that you get a not horrible draw of disaster cards and between-round events for the ~8 rounds it takes to finish a match, or "get to Mars." That's all this unfortunate miscarriage of a game is: infuriating BULL♥♥♥♥♥♥randomness presumably aimed at deranged masochists, with very little thought put into intelligent design or playability.
Since I've gone over two hours, and since I still hold some baseless hope that the game will eventually be fixed into playability, I'm not going to refund it. Not that I would review a game I've refunded on principle, or vice versa.
Edit: After two more hours of desperately trying to salvage this purchase, and 9 more matches, every single one ending in a completely lopsided loss through unfavourable RNG completely regardless of what strategies I used, I think I'm calling it a night. In the current state of things, Tharsis is just not enjoyable. A high difficulty combined with a punitive RNG system just makes the game way, way too hard to be enjoyed. Often, your dice pool is incredibly low after your second turn and you end up with ridiculous situations where you just want to give up.
For example, you must repair a module with a total of 27 points. That wouldn't be so bad, but said module also has stasis on 1 dices, void on 6s and injury on 5. So you constantly lose your best rolls, get stuck with unhelpful dices you can't re-roll and if you're very unlucky, you'll roll a bunch of 5s that will kill your crew mates. I don't want to imagine what hard mode is like, really. This isn't an isolated occurence, it keeps happening over and over when you reach Turn 3.
While the game is simple enough in term of mechanics and the visuals, as well as the cutscene help setting the tone, this game will need a lot of fine tuning before it can shine properly.

This game is tough. You will lose a lot and most of that time will not be your fault at all, just unforgiving Dice Gods who love to see you squirm. With that said, I like this game. Basically, you're the captain of a ship called the Iktomi which is on a mission to Mars. Disaster strikes and cripples your ships food stores leaving your group in a very dire situation in which it must find ways to generate new food while surviving the unforgiving hell that is space.  You will have to resort to cannibalism at points. You will manage the groups food and health while also trying to repair damage caused by unending meteoroid strikes. However, you do have ways to control what is otherwise just a random number generator simulator... For example, assists which can stop crewmen from being injured or using your dice to repair the ship, heal the crew based on someone's class. You have to survive 10 whole weeks, which doesn't sound that long but so far the furthest I've gotten is about 5 weeks in and even then, only 2 people of my original 4 made it that far. Personally, I can't wait to see what other missions they add in.
Pros:
-Addicting gameplay
-It's like an interactive board game
-Who doesn't like ripping fingernails off in anger?
-Well-drawn and voice acted cutscenes in between turns that add a little cinematic quality to the nightmare
-It's a really good looking game. I love how when you zoom up to a module you can really just sit there and inspect it.         Take all those details in!
-Cannibalism!
-Lots of managing resources is going on despite the restrictions by a RNG.
-Plenty of events that make you wonder if space really is a place Mankind should go, you know, because of all the brutal  unending death that seems prevalent throughout.
Cons:
-I don't like ripping fingernails off in anger.
-This game is really hard and sometimes it feels unfair. I'd just prefer to roll the dice myself.
-Can they make an easy mode?
-The tutorial leaves much to the player to figure it out themselves.
-RNG is lame but an almost necessary evil.
-It's not an actual boardgame that can be bought.
In summary, this game is good and pretty cheap for some quality entertainment. I can't wait to see what other missions they add in.

Clusterpuck 99 has a lot of elements that make it an ideal game to pick up and play if you regularly play video games with people on your couch. It boasts the rare ability to have 8 players play at once (if you have the controllers and USB ports to pull it off, mind you), and what it lacks in graphics, a sluggish pace, and the glaring error of no online multiplayer it tries to makes up for with its simple and engaging concept and gameplay. This simple game (with its ~4 controls) regularly creates the memorable moments that most people look for in local multiplayer games. You know, the ones where people are laughing, yelling, or high-fiving because of momentary displays of skill, chaos, or brilliance.
In my time with the game I have found that the AI, even on "hard" difficulty, are very little challenge and it is often best to give them an extra man or two to keep things stressful in the most delightful way. Friendly A.I. rarely, if ever, pass the puck which is frustrating but the developers explained that having a "call for the puck" button would radically change the game and its feel and I agree with them. However, it does make playing this game alone vastly inferior to playing with a buddy. A hell of a lot of fun can be had when you're outnumbered by A.I. and have to work together to overcome their quantity with the quality of your play.
It is frustratingly easy to over and/or under-pursue the puck and if you've played the EA Sports NHL titles, there is almost no element of the puck "magnetizing" to you if you are in proximity to it, you must make contact with the puck to possess it. This takes some getting used to, but it is by no means a deal breaker in regards to the feel of the game.
For the most part I play on the "competitive" levels because I find that there is more than enough chaos without boost squares, bumpers, and spiky death balls, but the game does feature a nice variety of levels. The zanier levels are good fun if you want to escape the feel of air hockey and sate your hunger to murder opponents by checking them into spiky death balls (it never gets old). The fact that there is a level editor supposedly on the way makes this one of those little-known games that sincerely deserves your attention.
With all of that being said, I would not have paid $10 for the game because of the lack of online multiplayer and how much there is left to be desired in regards to some of the controls, game speed, and the AI. However, when the next update rolls around and adds the level editor, more levels, and some other layers to this game it will easily be worth $10 if you regularly play with other people. If this one goes on sale again and if you're a local multiplayer aficionado, give it a look and tell your friends to bring their controllers, you're going to need them.

Camera and movement are also a very large problem, you move by using your mouse to point on the ground where you want to go. Summoner is a single player, third person RPG that is reminiscent of the Dragon Age series in terms of gameplay.  The story is told mostly through text windows and the game is not very difficult once you learn how to play it.  Get this title on sale if you enjoy older RPG's with original stories, simple mechanics, and minimal inventory management.
The story of Summoner is rather complicated.  Playing through it means lots of reading with the occasional cutscene providing exposition.  To briefly summarize: players take on the role of Joseph, a farmer living in the kingdom of Medeva.  In his youth, soldiers attacked Joseph's home village.  During the pillaging, Joseph manages to summon a demon, which not only destroyed the attackers but also the village and nearly eveyone in it.  As one of the few survivors, Joseph left his town ostracized but eventually meets a man named Yago who helps Joseph learn about his true identity.  Many years have passed since then and the game begins in the village of Masad, where Joseph is currently working.  From the northern kingdom of Orenia, the army of the Emperor Murod invades Medeva in search of a very important person.  Joseph fights his way out of Masad and heads to Lenele, the capital of Medeva where Yago is currently residing as an assistant to King Bellias.  Once in Lenele, Joseph's true quest begins as he meets colorful characters who join him and help him to understand his past.
As I said above, Summoner is quite similar to the Dragon Age games in terms of it's gameplay.  You have to talk to people to recieve quests and information.  Most quest givers are found in the main cities but if you explore levels, you often find quest givers hiding in obscure places.  There is no morality system but in several quests you have the option of choosing different dialogue lines that can merely alter quest rewards.  In other words, you almost never see the outcome of completing a quest a certain way (aside from the main quest), you just receive a different reward.  Loot in Summoner is actually one of the main reasons to complete sidequests, since certain side quests will give you powerful weapons that you will use for a long time.  Of course, you can still buy everything from potions to armor from merchants but everything in Summoner is very expensive, especially in the early game.  I recommending grinding random encounters for a bit early on, not just to improve your stats but to also collect a bunch of junk to sell.  Most of the quests are of the fetch variety but there are a few that standout.
Combat in Summoner is a hybrid of real-time and turn-based.  Once you are seen by an enemy, they will automatically engage your party and you will trade blows back and forth automatically until you or the enemy is dead.  Your party consists of four members (some of which have overlapping skills) and an optional fifth in the form a "Summon", a creature that only Jospeh can call forth.  You can pause the game at any time during combat and issue the next command you'd like each party member to execute as well as use items, switch gear, choose targets for spells, etc.  When combat is occurring and you control a melee character, you can chain together attacks with the press of a button, extending your "turn" until you break the chain.  It's sort of like playing a rhythmn game: pressing the chain button at the right pace unleashes bonus damage and special effects as you learn more chain abilities.  You can only control one party member at a time with the other party members operating on an AI routine that you can set in the character attributes screen.  Giving a bow to your thief character?  Set her to "Ranged" and she will engage enemies from afar instead of getting close.  Want your mage to focus on healing? Set her to "Healer" and she will only cast spells to heal party members when they go below a certain threshold.  This ability to choose how your party members behave is very nice becuase it allows you to instantly change a characters speciality if you need to.  And you will need to,
, in my experience at least.  That being said, the AI sometimes behaves erratically, such as targeting unintended enemies, not casting the most useful spell, or getting stuck on the environment.  There is a lot of micromanagement in the late game, requiring you to constantly switch characters to cast hero specific abilities.  I advise making at least one character strong in "Heal" and "Holy" spells for increased party survivabilty.  As Joseph acquires certaing rings, he is able to summon a fifth party member known as a "Summon".  Summons all have their own unique look and abilities and knowing the weaknesses of your current enemy allows you to bring forth a summon that counterracts their strengths.
While loot can be acquired through completing quests, great loot can also be found if you take the time to look around.  Seriously, scour every corner because loot is literally just sitting on the ground waiting to be found.  Most of your exploration will be easy though there are a few segments in the game where you can only use one or two party members for plot reasons.  There are a few sequences where you can only use the thief character for example.  The only part of the game that bothered me was a segment beyond halfway through the main quest where you must trek through a haunted forest while poisoned.  The only way to cure the poison is to reach the end of the level, requiring a lenghty slog through enemies and a boss fight you may or may not see coming, all the while constantly spamming party buff and heal spells as everyones' health constantly depletes.  The level felt too long and really killed the pace in my opinion but I made it through.  Backtracking is also something that you will do a lot of in Summoner and certain areas are also reused albeit with a different aesthetic for the most part.  This did not bother me however as there was always new loot to find.
At first glance, you may not believe Summoner was a PS2 launch title but it was.  It has not aged well but I assume you are not buying this game for it's looks.  Environmental textures are simple, characters are jagged, and animations are stiff.  But, each piece of gear looks different and even stays on you during cutscenes.  Spells and abilities all have unique sounds and partical effects.  The voice acting is nothing to write home about but it gets the job done.  You will be reading most of the story anyway so thank goodness the text is humorous and serious at the right times.  Sounds all have a canned feel to them but some are custom and fit well with the what is happening on screen.  I think this the first game I've played where the music does not fit the setting of the game but still works great anyway.  There are definitely some hummable tracks here and a few that remind me of Deus Ex for some reason.
At around forty hours for a first playthrough, Summoner provided more value to me than I thought it would.  While it's age and backtracking in the game are certainly hurdles potential buyers should consider, Summoner feels like a very casual RPG that is not too difficult to complete and does not last longer than it needs to.  The game's mechanics and inventroy system are simple and the graphics are too but it tells a compelling and original story none the less.  If you can look past the age of the game, you will find an RPG that may be more entertaining than you thought it would be.

Despite watching the cartoon daily as a kid, I never actually played Capcom's classic DuckTales on NES, so I wasn't really sure what I was getting into with this. I was really only interested because WayForward was involved, and because I'd heard stories that the NES game was actually pretty great.
Well, lo and behold, I actually loved DuckTales: Remastered. Virt did a fantastic job on remaking the music, and everyone involved did a great job at updating the levels, and, apparently, adding two new ones. The somewhat open-like gameplay that a few levels had gave me a bit of a Metroid vibe, something I was not expecting from a game based on talking ducks.
The only real negative I'd have with this game is the constant cutscenes. The writing is rather charming, like watching an old 80's Disney cartoon, but they start to get on your nerves when they play every five minutes. It's also a rather short game, as my first run of the game, on PS3, took about 4 hours. However, this is one of the few games that, immediately after I finished, I began again on a higher difficulty.
The bosses are fun to fight, the stages are fun to traverse, the music is great, and the controls work well enough. Another great game from WayForward.

I've been playing/following Assassin's Creed since Brotherhood, and, in all honesty, this is the best time I've had with one in a very long time. Don't get me wrong, all of the previous ones, at least the majority of which I've played, had something that kept me playing aside from the story. In Brotherhood, I loved trying to recruit specific assassins as Ezio. In Revelations, the new hookblade and the conclusion of the stories for arguably the most important figures in Assassin's Creed was enjoyable. In Assassin's Creed 3, the hunting, new tools, new combat, and new flow helped keep the game for me. In Black Flag, the expansion of the naval combat and the sea shanties sung by the crew always kept me sailing the high seas. I skipped Rogue and jumped into Unity, where the new more focused single-player/co-op experience brought in new ideas which were honestly needed. Then comes Syndicate, where I loved zipping around Victorian England, not as a single assassin, but two.
For all of these reasons, I stayed around, even despite my focus gradually leaving single-player games in favor of multiplayer. However, with the release of Origins, I found myself enjoying the story of Bayek more than any current multiplayer games I play. The new combat is fun and exciting, being equally engaging and needed for the series as the previous combat iterations were all generally the same and became honestly too simplistic and effortless to cut a bloody swath through 50+ enemies at a time. The stealth is still the same, but the changes according to which bow to use and the differences between them that improve with certain skills make it more deep despite still being the classic Assassin's Creed formula. On top of all this, you consider the fact that we're finally Egypt, a location which nearly the entire player community has been begging for since Brotherhood, then it's no wonder why the game has brought many back to the series.
In short, it's a great game with a damn good story, more depth than the previous titles, and a promising return to form for the series.
Now, here's hoping that the next game is set in one of the other most begged for time periods. Personally, my heart wants the Old West to show up in a Ubisoft title, but I'd be ecstatic if we finally get to run through Feudal Japan as a ninja instead.

A very enjoyable Assassin's Creed game, the setting isn't quite as interesting as the predecessors, since it's 80 percent covered in a desert. But the developers managed to make the most of it.
The story itself is fairly simple and straightforward, but it does a good enough job of keeping you engaged. Bayek is a likeable protagonist but isn't on par with Edward Kenway or Evie Frye. The other characters are pretty forgettable, and I feel like Ubisoft could have done a better job at fleshing them out a bit.
The new combat system is interesting, completely different from what we had before. I would describe it as Dark Souls Lite, it's more about positioning and timing, getting an opening to attack the enemy, rather than the easier and more repetitive combat of the previous titles.
Performance-wise the game is very demanding, but I feel like it's justified based on the experience it delivers, and not a case of a bad optimisation. And it got a pretty amazing photo mode that is porobably more addictive for me than the game itself!

Very hard, very fun game! At first glance it looks like air hockey, but it really isn't at all like that apart from the main point being to get the puck into the goal. But as you control your "character" (if you can call a red or blue circle a "character") you'll slip and slide around obstacles toward the goal. The spikes are deadly, the yellow bouncy things are annoying as hell, and your opponents can bash into you and knock the puck away from you at any time, which all combined make this game insanely hard and super fun. It's awesome to push opponents into the spikes and rush to victory, and super frustrating to push opponents into the spikes only to discover that you misjudged the distance and pushed yourself into the spikes too :P
Visually, this game reminds me of Heavy Bullets, with the same minimalistic and vibrant atmosphere. The controls for keyboard and mouse are some of the worst controls I've ever seen. Seriously, it uses "ESC" as the B button, and either enter or space as A (I never could figure out which, since it's different in the menu than in the actual game). But plug in an XBox 360 controller, and the controls are great. The fact that you slide around like an air hockey puck on a low-friction surface means you have to be much more precise than you might think, and shooting can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because your opponents don't actually have to do anything to block your shot, they just automatically catch it if they happen to be in the line of fire.
Clusterpuck is aptly named, it's one giant clusterpuck of insanity, but very enjoyable insanity nonetheless. And since it's on sale for only a dollar right now, there's no reason not to try it out! It's probably not for everyone, especially people who ragequit easily, but if you enjoy difficult games then this will be right up your alley.
EDIT: Forgot to mention, this is mainly a local multiplayer game. There is no online multiplayer, which is really inexplicable since it's a game made for playing with other people. But if you're like me and don't have friends, you can add bots to your match to play on your team and the opponent team.
