There are some major flaws with the design but if you enjoy older hack and slash rpgs this can be fun gem. Combat is mostly back and forth timed attacks with you cast/using abilities similar to Neverwinter Nights or Baldur's Gate except that there is one "chain" mechanic that lets you do special bonus attacks if you right click exactly when the blow lands. The mechanic is surprisingly deep as you gain new bonus attacks each different party member gets different ones (though some are shared). Characters are built via skill points which you pump into things like "fire" for fire magic or "sword" to up hit chance for sword weapons, each person gets predetermined skill sets which appear as they level so while there is some customization it is limited. The major draw here is the ability of the main character to summon one monster party member which is as cool as it sounds, really I wish I could just ditch the 3 other npcs and go full monster party. All the summonable monsters are unique with different traits and skills you can switch them out depending upon what kind of enemies you face. One flaw with the monster summons is no ability to set their AI.
This game does have its share or problems: no mini map notes, large empty areas, no fast travel, poor AI, respawning enemies, linear story. The combat can be fun but all the tedious traveling and looking for merchants or quest npcs or having a side quest completely disappear because you advanced the main story without any indication before hand leads to lots of fustraition. Additionally because of the enemies respawning its very annoying getting from point A to point B on top of which you cannot leave non-random encounter zones while under attack and with your party members all nearby. The game also starts slow with you lacking your "Summoner" skill till a hour or so in but if can handle the flaws you'll find a game worth playing.

My first thought when I glanced at this game was that it looked like like Pony Island's pink, gliterry, cutesy little sibling. I wasn't that far off course, but in the end
is less about the meta and more about the surprisingly smart puzzle elements that lie at its heart.
The gameplay is an ingenius combination of minesweeper and match-3, where the fundamental goal at all times is to basically find where things are being hidden. There are two parts to the game: first is the map-like area where you move between boxes, and must divine where the exit, helpful items and enemies are hiding depending on the information you get from the other connencting boxes. The second is when you actually have to fight the enemies, with the battlefield being the traditional match-3 grid. Using elements like compasses and computers you get hints as to where the enemy is invisibly hiding, so you can then explode bombs on the right tile to defeat them. Each action costs energy which you replenish by matching batteries, and at the end of each cycle the enemy gets to attack so you should also increase the duration of your turn by matching various other items. As a result you really need to pay attention on both 'attack' and 'defense' so to speak, and juggle a lot of different aspects at the same time, since focusing on only one part is an easy way to run out of health and fail.
This may all sound pretty confusing, and it does take a while before you're fully familiarised with the mechanics, but once you do the game becomes truly fun and challenging. And it  should be noted that
can be a surprisingly difficult game! The enemies get progressively harder to beat, having new behaviours like moving around on the grid in various patterns or even outright hindering you, and each 'dungeon' introduces a unique gameplay mechanic that you need to follow, some of which can make your life very miserable indeed. The dungeons can also get exhaustively big later on, although the fact that they're proceduraly generated adds to the replayablilty of it.
As for the story, it's kept simple and relatively meta, with the always fun mechanic of accessing files on a virtual computer to serve the narrative. You're a loosely-defined Glitch Witch, following your mysterious predecessor's footsteps and attacking hackers on forums. The game really does have a great presentation, cute without being childish, and the dialogue and characters are light-hearted while still being fun and witty. There are even some cool and weird secrets hidden inbetween, and while they weren't as many or as important as I had hoped, they still add wonderfully to the general atmosphere.
All in all,
is an impressively unique little game, and I'd definitely recommend it to people who appreciate some challenge in their puzzles.

There is no story to DiscStorm, just arena after arena of disc throwing madness, testing the player's skills with what they've learned in the tutorial level that teaches you all the mechanics of the game. It's just up to you to use them properly, which means your experience with this game is ultimately determined by how good you are at picking up the controls. Learning how to dodge, deflect, dash and ricochet your discs off of walls and other objects is essential for learning how to play the game. It's fast paced gameplay so it's both fun and challenging, constantly keeping you on your toes as you throw your discs like some sort of Olympian. This game doesn't have any difficulty settings, it expects you to be an expert at the game as soon as you leave the tutorial level, and it shows by how much it tests you. You're put up against not only basic enemies that chase you all around the arena, but Disc throwing enemies, regenerating enemies that come back after you die and Jason Voorhees-looking individuals with swords. But those are only the grunts; when it comes to the bosses and the mini bosses, you're given a variety of creatures based on the level you're in. You're also given a selection of four characters that all have unique dialogue depending on the level they are in, which makes it worth it to play all of them at least once.

The game used to be fantastic. It was always light on lore (as Asian games usually are) but the setting was beautiful and the gameplay engaging. I played from beta (starting as a Lancer) all the way up to the Brawler release. I'm a huge altoholic so by the time I stopped playing I had two accounts with multiples of each class, save for the female only classes of which I had none. Really loved this game and was an avid member of the RP community when it still existed.
Pros:
+Graphics and art style are pretty for a (now) dated MMO. The animations feel like they have some weight and power to them and are beautiful to look at, too.
+Races are interesting, except for the Elin. I really love the Baraka in particular. Large stone golems who are sentient.
+Awesome boss/big monster fights, feels like you're going toe to toe with a huge adversary not just a named enemy.
+Great mechanics, feels like more of an action game than a traditional MMO.
Cons:
-New classes are female only. This is my biggest issue with the game and ultimately why I left it. Decided to come back and write this review after seeing they released yet another female only class. I understand that after all this time Tera is struggling to keep its head above water and can't afford to make new animations/armour/what have you for a new class for every race and gender (at least I hope this is the case and that these aren't just blatantly terrible design decisions), but come on. I HATE gender locked classes in MMOs, but if you're gonna do it, at least even the field. This is a disgusting business practice aimed at basement dwellers who play female characters to look at butt. I'm a roleplayer (we're notorious for playing opposite genders to live out a story beyond our real life selves) and even I think this is ridiculous. Which leads me to my next issue...
-Fan service. Almost all new content designed for the game revolves around fan service. Silly, out of place items and outfits (mostly designed around females). The game is now about dressing up your female character in different ways while you do the same content over and over.

-Toxic community. Didn't used to be this way but it is one of the worst MMO communities I've ever experienced.. and I've experienced A LOT. This is even worse than the old school FF11 community. Pure poison. What's worse is, because of Elin, the game is FILLED with players who love childish anime girl themes and it is really uncomfortable. If that is your thing it is so huge here that there are probably more Elin players than any other. As a roleplayer I've known quite a few Elin who are NOT this way, and I know there are more out there, but they're the minority. Top guilds have little anime girls as their tags and general chat is a constant downpour of such themes. Word of advice: If it makes you uncomfortable don't say anything about it in chat or else you'll get savagely attacked. There is always a new player chiming in about it in Velia, who then gets swarmed.

-UI is pretty terrible and clunky. You can move it around a little but it doesn't help much.
-Game gets repetitive. More so than other MMOs this is a real grind. Maybe not in length of time spent leveling, but in regards to what you do to progress.

-Crystals and enchanting are stupid. The methods you use to improve your gear in this game are convoluted and tedious. If you die the crystals you have will likely break. To improve your weapon you gotta do the same tired Asian method of gathering a bunch of materials and putting it on your weapon with a chance it'll not succeed. Keep doing that to get to things like +15 or what have you. Black Desert does the same thing. Don't know why they think it is good gameplay.
All in all I recommend you invest your energies elsewhere. This title will bring you nothing but anguish.

TLDR; Only buy the game if it's on sale and you want to play the story. Be prepared to google search for graphical fixes.
Full of bugs:
Had to Google search for about 30 minutes to find a fix to the 'screen clipping/jittering' issue.
Game gets stuck in foreground when trying to alt-tab out and controls/movement are inconsistent at best.
'Contraints' (optional objectives for 100% sync) for main missions and some side missions are infuriating due to the above reasons.
Can get stuck in a cutscene with the save wheel spinning. Can also have other actions take place within your cutscenes causing unpredictable outcomes. (wolf attacking you during cutscene, then once cutscene finishes you get stuck in the close up camera animation as if you're being attacked.
Game can, and will randomly crash for no apparent reason or cause. Can happen between cutscenes, running around, opening menus and probably more.
Assassin recruits will on occasion remain in an area, start walking around or otherwise think there's an enemy when there isn't. Recruits can also get stuck while running to saftey, never resetting on their own and effectively forcing themselves into an 'injured' state.
Overall complaints:
Short storyline.
Be prepared to either run around A LOT or spend about 30-60 minutes per city unlocking fast travel points.
Almanac Pages (collectable throughout the two cities) can be frustrating with the movement bugs as you have to 'chase' them down.
Snow, while a nice weather change, is a garbage mechanic on the Frontier zone.
You assassin recruits are pretty useless early on, if not a burden entirely when you first unlock them.
Making money is pretty limited, and almost entirely from you hunting for pelts. The process is tedious and you have to spend countless hours running through the forests just to be able to unlock a few upgrades early on.
Lack of weapon upgrades, more or less there are static weapons that are overall better than their counterparts, which are unlocked incredibly early on.
Unrefined AI and some questionable moments in the engagement process. A group of 2 guards can be facing away from you on one side of a ship, and air assassinating a target not only behind an object but out of view will trigger them, but a gunshot at the same location won't.

Largely, this game features an interesting setting, but is largely flawed. I cannot for certain state that this game is terrible, because it isn't, but it has so many flaws, it makes the game hard to like, even for someone who has played and enjoyed nearly every other Assassin's Creed game.
To start with, Connor is largely uninteresting, which is shocking, because he had the potential to be the coolest assassin ever. I mean, a Mohawk native turned assassin, how could that possibly be boring. Well, when the character is introduced to us by playing hide and seek with his friends, that's a pretty good way to make them boring. It takes seemingly forever to get to a point where you ever start to do assassin like things, and even then, the game still feels largely boring.
The bugs, oh my, the bugs. Assassin's Creed games are largely plagued by bugs, but this takes it to a new level. From the horses getting stuck on things causing you to eventually abandon them and continue on foot, to things not appearing on the map, including entire city locations, to game breaking bugs that delete your save game, this game suffers from bugs. In my most recent playthrough, I experienced this bug, causing my save game to be deleted. Considering I was nearly finished with trying to complete the game with almost 100% sync, I was upset.
The lack of explanation of in game missions and collectables is mind numbingly annoying. The first time I played through the game, I never unlocked the best weapons and equipment, simply because I had no idea what I needed to do to get it. Eventually, I figured it out, but it certainly was annoying. Same with the assassin recruits. Although the most egregious example of lack of explanation is the “Pivot Points”. I still do not understand what to do with these. They aren’t even available until after you complete the game, and honestly once I get to that point, I am done playing, and really have little interest to try to figure it out.
The modern day stuff, as usual, is boring. This one may be the worst examples of the modern day content in the Assassin’s Creed series, since it really pulls me out of the game the most, and features long, un-skippable content that tries to explain the bizarre connection to these ancient people that is talked about in nearly every game, but is largely unsatisfying. The ending itself is definitely unsatisfying, but I will not elaborate to avoid spoilers.
All in all, I really can only recommend this game to people who are hardcore fans of the Assassin’s Creed series, or really want a game set during the American Revolution, but for most, I would encourage you to stay away. If you want that feeling of early colonial America in your game, check out Assassin’s Creed Rogue. Otherwise, if you just want a fun Assassin’s Creed game and don’t really care about colonial America, play Assassin’s Creed Black Flag. Both of these are far more enjoyable experiences.

A very small but extremely well made mod by an ex-Valve employee. Caged is a remake of a very old mod, by the same people, but with incredible use of the goldsrc engine's power.
As soon as the intro began I was already surprised by the quality of the text on the monitor and how it was readable, and (regardless of the polygons) how smooth a lot of the blocks/objects were in that particular area - I almost felt like I was playing a Source game!
A few new models
and sounds, along with fantastic use of sprites, made the mod that whole lot more visually enjoyable for an engine that was created in the 90s.
There is also a built-in achievement system that doesn't use Steam's achievements
to give it that little extra playability
Also, the qwerky and comical signs
and all sorts of minor easter eggs, that don't affect the gameplay, make it just that bit more enjoyable! Traditional, doesn't feel forced, and absolutely gives you the HL1 feel!
This is what one whole chapter of HL2 should have been if Source was never created. Fantastic mod and a great little freebie to experience HL1 again in the years it should have been enjoyed!

Sins of the Demon RPG is a pretty typical RPG Maker game, developed by Chandler Rounsley, and released on steam May 13, 2016.
You play as the character named "Kenshi", Kenshi and his 'brother', a demon-cat named "Shinto".
Kenshi and Shinto are trying to uncover how or why Shinto was turned into a demon. Because the land has been cursed by a greater demon known as "Isharul".
There only two features that stick out from other RPG maker games I've played: the pop up "extra" story stuff, which you press Q to listen to. I missed a couple of them so I don't have 100% of the achievements.
And level grinding is kinda pointless because the exp per npc kill ratio is kinda messed up (I think I articulate it better in My Thoughts video, if you care for more elaboration explanation). The key way to grow your character is by feeding them food which perminently increases character stats.
Coupled with getting junk-item-drops / trophies to sell instead of simply getting gold drops from NPC's, there are a few interesting things in Sinf os the Demon RPG, but not enough to make it stand out against all of the other RPG maker games out there.
It's a play and forget, you can expect to sink around 7 to 9 hours into the game, I don't know that you can really go much faster then that with the stat boosting requirements being the only farming I could really do to effectively defeat the final bosses.
RPG maker games are typically people's first project. I don't like going around insulting them when it's clear there was at least some effort, and not blatant story-ripping off.
While I acknowledge there's clearly sign of effort in creating this game, unless there's something new bringing people to the game (be it custom sprites, an interesting and enjoyable story, etc) it's simply going to be a play and forget.

I've bought this game and then sent it to be refund after a few hours of playing for one major flaw : lack of players.
The most players I've managed to find was around 15, in the afternoon, but I won't be able to play the game on a daily basis at that hour because I will come back home from work at that time, and it's not worth bothering with playing the game in the evening or in the morning, because the servers are empty, regardless of the continent.

The reason I have refunded is because even if the developers manage to gather a decent amount of players, the game will know an apex of maximum an year and then the number of players will go down, just like how it happened with the other Savage games. I have my doubts that the developers can maintain the number of players knowing what happened with the past games.
The gameplay is fine, great even, it's a well made RTS/RPG hybrid, but the joyful experience of playing this game will fade out pretty quick once you're stuck with playing with bots most of the time.

I had lots of fun with this game. Nobody will heed my word. Friends, listen: it's a great game. It's almost too clever, asking the player to think outside the box and grasp onto new concepts at a fairly speedy pace. It's almost too cute, giving you a pink laptop, cartoon avis with puns, and a match-3 puzzler that is anything but casual.
It's a high-concept cocktail of genres, that doesnn't bother to explain, or answer for the flavors. Beglitched all takes place on the pink computer I just mentioned, given to you, your character, by a talented, precocious - maybe genius - hacker who left a long shadow. You are exploring it because you were entrusted to it, and it should be fun. It has two interfaces, one a Bejeweled-like "fight," where you have to use one of several pieces to track down how far, and in what direction a certain enemy is hiding, before you blow them up. Outside of battle, you are a cat avi, traveling through a varying grid of computer screens which you can dive in, digging into more. This is the "adventure" mode aspect, where you get from one point to another over a longer period of time, with battles intermittently. It plays like Minesweeper, where spoils of certain computer screens are only revealed by their neighbors, so you deduce the "mines" from the desirables. Once you dive into a screen to the next level, it blurs and makes a quick "dial-up" sound. Which never gets old.
On a third, "menu" screen, you are simply clicking icons on Glitch Witch's desktop to travel into her files, where you can read her poetry and journal entries, or travel through a lost woods of folders that reset once you hit a wrong "turn." It has a voyeuristic thrill, except of course Glitch Witch always feels one step ahead of your nameless protagonist.
All this minesweeping and Bejewling is a metaphor, for something that goes over my head, but never bores with its ambient buzz. You meet other hackers, other speaking animals who are all happy to see the "Glitch Witch" again. Based on her old "forum" buddies, you can start to build a portrait of what kind of person she was, an early ♥♥♥♥♥ type who had experiments and potential with trickster trolls, fortune hunters, and others who didn't develop the sense of responsibility with their skills. The side characters are likeable and funny but slightly forgettable. Building your concept of the past Glitch Witch, and her vague present challenges the player in a way, and packs narrative as much as a short story might.
Eventually, after a difficulty curve, the new mechanics in each level are also explained in journal pieces as metaphors for what she was thinking when she created certain programs, or possibly even "spells." The "glitch" part is taken to the extreme as outside of the box thinking forces you to push the limits of what is given to you on the screen. Also, probably a metaphor, of course.
The tutorial is left out: it assumes the player can pick up how to play. This may rankle some, but please others, who don't like to be pulled down by tutorials. I didn't have a problem, because I like to get my hands dirty first; the game doesn't punish you for failing until after you've grasped the concept. But it is hard not to see it as a crafty cop out of making something that eases the player in more, to shove the tutorial to a later part of the game (when it becomes a gag or easter egg).
Unfortunately, I didn't catch on to the story elements until it was past time to reflect on the first half of the game, so I may go back to clear things up. The ending, however challenging, still teases that I haven't completed the game, and there is a techno hole in the pink laptop that I still can only speculate about, like he playfully cryptic journal entries.
Beglitched is a computer within a computer, to show how some people lived online, even before the dawn of social media. As a cultural artifcact, younger players may come to understand better the life of a nerdy person in the 90's or mid 2000's. Not many games help you view games, casual genres, or the world in a different way, so it's cool to Beglitched deliver.

I'm rather saddened by this review. I wanted to enjoy Beglitched, I really did, it's a cutesy game with a lot of heart and passion in it, and the design is clever. Unfortunately, the game makes some really inexplicable missteps which kill it. First and foremost, which had this not been around, could have forgiven everything else. When you die, you are sent back to the beginning of the "dungeon" which might not seem like much, but the combat of the game really isn't strong enough to support doing the same area with the same gimmick over and over. is a hidden gem that truly caught me by surprise with its fun gameplay and different approach to the match three puzzle genre. Its gameplay is half match three and half Minesweeper, with a cute story and pastel pixel graphics. You the player have found a mysterious laptop belonging to a hacker known as “Glitch Witch” who then ask you to help by posing as them online and cleaning up the internet a bit. The story is simple and comes with some colorful dialogue as you progress and speak to different internet users but it’s nothing deep.
The real meat of the game is its gameplay. Your main screen like a computer monitor with many different icons, some lead to files or even internet forums but most are different levels to exploring. Each level has numerous stages where you have to move your avatar along a set of tiles, landing one reveals clues to what the other tiles around it contain. Your goal is to “open the files” along the board to find the exit but along the way there are bombs, shops, treasures and even enemy ambushes. I’ve never been a Minesweeper genius so it took me awhile to get the hang of it and I’m probably not even as good as I could be but I appreciated the challenge this posed to me. There are also useful programs, of sorts, that you collect as you progress through the game which help a lot. The program I found most helpful scans nearby tiles helping to save moves and uncover more tiles at once. Later in the game, saving moves is important because if you use too many you will trigger security attacks.
Along with hidden enemies and the security attacks, there are also enemies that can be seen on the overworld map and landing on their tile will trigger a battle. Battles are where the match three aspect comes in as players are swept off to an entirely different setting filled with colorful blocks. Each one is different, one has a dollar sign others are batteries and much more. Enemies hide under the tiles and you have to set off bombs where they are to defeat them. This may seem simple but you’re also dealing with a limited amount of moves and energy, the energy is used to activate certain blocks like compases. While matching three or more of certain blocks can grant you more moves, energy, and money, once you run out of moves the enemy will attack your health directly. Then the cycle starts over again. Different enemies also have different attack patterns as well as move differently so you’re always kept on your toes.
First impressions count and when I saw the pastel pink screen shots of this game with retro pixel graphics I was certainly enticed. But don’t let the color scheme fool you, this isn’t a game filled with fluff. The main core of this game is the strategy and while I loved the aesthetics, I don’t think you should feel turned off by the cutesy vibe. While the game isn’t an accurate recreation of a computer screen or the internet, it feels enough like one to help players feel immersed and the audio helps too with sound effects like dial up noises and keyboard clicking when characters speak. The music is nice and catchy but it can get a little repetitive and is a bit forgettable, a more varied soundtrack would have been nice.
I had a lot of fun playing
and I think if you like puzzle games you will too. I came mainly for the match three elements but enjoyed the added dimension of the Minesweeper spice, a game I haven’t personally played in a long time. It’s an all around solid experience though it can become repetitive at times. Also, if you lose all of your hearts in a level you have to start the entire level over which can become frustrating so I recommend playing in bursts. There are no Steam cards or achievements and there isn’t much in the way of replay value after beating the main game, but it’s enjoyable and definitely worth playing. The game is ten dollars on Steam, however, is also available on IOS for only four dollars, I however wrote this review having only played the game on Steam so I cannot compare the two.

Nostalgia vs Reality - not a review~
Nostalgia got the better of me and seeing this available on Steam, I just had to install it. This was afterall, the first MMO I ever played back in 2000-2003 and also the first MMO community (twRO) with whom I had the good fortune to go adventuring with. Only five minutes into RO, I was entranced by the comfortable familiarity of it all. -/lazy insert everything I love about RO-
Soon though, the nostalgic glow started to wear off...I missed the feeling of being a wide-eyed newbie, falling down and picking myself up again, bravely exploring a whole new world. I missed the community of twRO, I missed...I missed...
Reality was, the RO of today is somewhat the same but different. Without going into details, some game mechanics are different, simply put. Anyways, my time on RO again after a decade (half of which was subsconsciously spent wishing that I was somehow still playing RO!) was deeply conflicting instead. Also, the awesome fun I had back then in RO also seemed to pale a little in comparison to the 'newer' fun I had in more recent MMOs; what a fickle mistress the human mind is when it comes to comparisons?
The best of nostalgia can only happen when we look back at something and remember only the good but none of the bad and do no comparisons!
My dear RO, I'll stick to remembering that lovely and familiar smile of yours, marvelling at the chemistry we had with each other and the good old times together with that community of twRO. :)
I am not allowing myself to be stuck in the worse, for moving forward is as simple as trying something new: a relationship, creative projects, a new television show or game while holding fast to the firm knowledge that I was fortunate enough to have these fond memories of Ragnarok Online in my lifetime.
tl;dr
***Try it casually if you are new to RO (and to most modern 'action' MMOs) - but don't compare amongst them for RO can come across as antiquated; that won't bode well for the game nor for ya. I also had lag issues with this now and annoying chunky rubberbanding.
***Don't even try RO again, if you had played it before and especially if you had loved it to bits previously. There's no need to make new memories, your old ones of RO are precious enough and good enough forever.

I played local co-op with a friend and it was ample fun.  I can imagine three and four player matches would be equal or (most probably) even more fun!  Playing the solo mode was fine but this game shines in multiplayer mode.

The plastic flying disc originated as an improvised use of pie tin lids with one popular pie and cookie chain lending it's name to the generic term for the  item (which we wont be mentioning here). In any case it's pretty certain that neither the early pioneers, the trade mark holders or partipcants in the ubiquitous college sport "Ultimate [redacted]" had realised the full potential of the flying disc as a versatile weapon.
XMPT games have stepped up and filled that gap, one part damaging projectile, one part deflective shield and one part useful item to trigger things the flying disc is used to it's full potential in the pixelart adventure. Using speed, agility and 3 circular pieces of plastic a range of heroes must defeat hordes of minions, and bosses for some reason that probably isn't important.
With a cool retro style, core mechanics somewhat reminiscent of speedball and a host of level specific special rules I'd reccomend everyone to quit playing catch and start creating some kind of large weather patern of plastic circular things.

DiscStorm has just hit Steam for PC & Mac from Mastertronic and XMPT Games.  After a few teething issues getting into the game, which were quickly sorted out by the extremely impressive response time from the XMPT Games, I stepped into this battle arena having only caught glimpses of a few screenshots beforehand.
DiscStorm attempts to bring an 8-bit Sega Master System/NES feel to its graphics and it achieves this goal extremely well.  I could believe that once again I was sat – near thirty plus years back – in front of my television playing Smash TV with Mario like toons, though admittedly DiscStorm is nowhere near as violent as Smash TV, as here we’re throwing lethal Frisbee’s in this arena.
I’d advise you to take a few moments and jump into the practice Dojo just to get a feel on the controls and movement of the game, as all be it appears to be easy it can be quite tricky and frustrating.   The frustrating element I believe – for myself – lies in the fact I am using a mouse and keyboard and the first screen you meet on DiscStorm in recommends you play this game with a Gamepad, which I don’t; this I believe will hinder the average player.
The single player mode is a series of mobs fights and you can easily path these mobs and bunch them up, bringing them down with one nice throw.  As you pass checkpoint your progress is saved and if you do die you return to said checkpoint,  leaving the game however doesn’t save your progress within the level so you will have to grind through that level again; unless of course you completed the entire level.  Something I found a bit cruel was the lack of health regens that were dropped, after you first encounter with a mid-level boss you’re given one energy bubble back, but you were then expected to proceed through the next round on a heavily depleted life force.
The multiplayer mode is unfortunately only local multiplayer, so there is currently no chance of joining up with three other random’s around the globe to lob discs at their heads.  You can set up a game against bots if you – like me – have no friends, this then immediately shows how hectic the game can become with three other people playing and you realise you need some more training at this game.
The music keeps faithfully in line with the appearance of the game, you would believe that this game has been pulled from a cupboard back in the mid-1980’s.  The developers certainly have their hearts firmly planted in the era of the Sega Master Syst...

That's how a remake of a classic game is done. Everything in the game was given fresh, crisp, high-definition visuals (as opposed to certain other older game re-releases where the old graphics are just passed through some software filter to remove jaggedness), the sound remixes are great, cutscenes and voice acting were added. All the bells and whistles technology in 1989 didn't allow for were put in, while every element that made this an 8-bit gem was kept intact.
If you played it back in the day (I did so avidly, on a rented cartridge from a rental store near my home back in the early '90s) you'll instantly recognize each screen, each enemy, each item, each tune. And even the typical difficulty of late '80s/early '90s Nintendo games is there, so even for those that haven't played this game 25 years ago the challenge is there.
Summing up, I recommend this for both older players (who played the original 8-bit version), as a modern way to relive an old classic, and newer players (who weren't even born when 8-bit consoles waned), because it gives a taste of genuine '80s classic platforming without compromising on audiovisual quality. Congratulations to the producers on this great remake!

I never played the game this is a remake of, but I bought this because the original was considered one of the greatest platformers of all time. So is it still anything special by today's standards? Not really. It's a very basic platformer. But still, what it does, it does very well. And being based off the DuckTales TV show, it turns out to be a pretty cute little game (and I do mean little; it's a very short game). The original had little to no plot, but they came up with a completely new story to tie all the levels together and features several of the characters from the show (my only real issue with the story is that at times Scrooge seems to be a bit more of a jerk than he was on the show). Some reviewers who played the original thought the emphasis on story was a downpoint, but for me that may have been my favorite part. Without it, it's just a generic, if pretty fun platformer. Plus, these days it's getting harder and harder than ever to find someone who wants to make something that's just nice, like a video game that doesn't have bloodletting or edginess to it (ironically, if more people were to make games like this they would be the ones being "edgy"). Hi all,
I liked:
It was hilarious to me that the protagonist Jung, did not have a great deal in common with their programmed Ai girl friend, there was friction, sarcasm and antagonism. Which reminds me of the simple truth that opposites attract and yet such differences also cause friction.
Disliked:
I simply didn't understand why Jung would question, what he was doing with his life after his Ai girl friend crashed. I had noted that Jung appeared to enjoy her company, despite the considerable limitations of their relationship. Why should his relationship as it was, with some manner of synthetic (software) individual be judged as anyway inferior to any other relationship, real or imagined, synthetic or otherwise?
It is evident that many people live their lives in a very lonely fashion, yet PC (Personal Computer) uptake appears to be considerable. Therefore the thought experiment that the game explores, namely human beings developing relationships with Ai software has considerable merit. Many lonely people with access to PCs and such software could develop relationship within the technological constraints of such. I argue then that numerous people's lives could be bettered by the ubiquitous use of such Ai. I suggest that far be it from questioning his own life, Jung, could improve his Ai and eventually with persistence, make a lot of lonely people happier. Maybe even himself.
The implied notion that there is a perfect (or even any) partner just waiting for each of us to approach in real life, is naive and I argue, the greatest fantasy associated with this game.
Good gaming,
Alter
I suggest that we all enjoy our fantasies, they may be all we have, they may be all we will ever have. I recommend against denouncing them as somehow inferior or unworthy and suggest instead embracing them as part of who we are.

Tera will always hold a special place in my heart as one of the greatest MMORPGs ever. I think Tera is a fantastic game, but do I recommend it? No

Hmmm... how to rate this one?  Well, it's got a few fun hours in it, I'll give it that, but it seems less and less fun every time I come back to it.  I will admit though, Tera has the best combat system of all MMOs I've played and that's one major reason why this game even sparks any interest in me anymore.  Aside from that, I really gotta tell ya, En Masse Entertainment has done an absolutely excellent job at eliminating any sort of actual randomness, fun, or individuality from this game.  It's Free to Play so they must also think that means "Free of any fun to play".
I came back this latest time to try out the newest class, the Valkyrie.  The last time I played, I started just as they were introducing the Gunner.  It seems that every time a new class is introduced, it's OP as hell.  So, you can tell that leveling a new Valkyrie was about as fun and challenging as stomping on an ant hill.  I'm still not all the way to 65 with her yet (yes, "her"... the Valkyrie is limited to Castanic females only.... also similar to the Gunner which is limited to Castanic or High Elf females, or the Reaper which is limited to Elin, a race of all females... not sure what to make of these race/gender limited classes yet) but I'm not sure I want to continue.  Things have been so cut and dried in this game it's not really that fun leveling anymore.
For one, there are no random loot drops anymore.  Anything that does drop is either currency, mats for enchanting, and maybe a surprise lock box.  I haven't opened any lock boxes yet because I figure I'm just going to be disappointed... and because the keys aren't cheap.  But the point is that there used to be at least a few gear items that would drop so you could at least swap out pieces of armor or weapons here and there, or even use those weapons and armor to help gear an alt or even use those extra pieces to create a unique look or something.  But nope... all of that's gone and what's left is a field full of cookie cutter sameness amongst everyone leveling.  Boring.  Costumes are available which allow you to turn what you're wearing into something that looks completely different, but most of those are $$$.... did I mention this game was F2P?
There's also the lack of anything to do besides leveling while you're out in the field.  Sure, you can hunt things, but once again... no loot drops... so why?  Well, for that almighty experience that is.  Because the devs want you to get to endgame to do more grinding for actual gear drops in dungeons.  This appeals to me just about as much as sticking icepicks under my fingernails.  Not only because the gameplay has been boiled down to how high you can get your gear score, but because that number is then used by others as some sort of gauge of your skill, which it is not.
Leveling is as simple as "Kill a few of those creatures", "Kill creature for item" or "Talk to that person at that place"... probably to boil down leveling to such basic mundane tasks that you can do these things in as little time as possible.  I mean, hey, it's Free to Play, right?  Why give premium content like "interesting stuff" away for free?  There isn't even any real reason to stop to work on crafting skills because by the time you work your crafting skills up high enough to craft the next level of armor or weapon or whatever, you've out leveled it.  But if you examine the crafting system in depth, it's almost like the game is designed to severely discourage you from crafting in the first place.  You have a daily limit of crafting points (which are used up even for mundane tasks like gathering or mining, as well as the actual crafting of items)... once those are used up, you are disallowed from any further crafting and you have to wait until those points very slowly replenish over the next 24 hours.  But you should know better anyway... the devs have made it clear that crafters are weak and stupid and you should really be out fighting and leveling like a good little drone.
But ya... so if you're one of those "Gotta get to end game so I can group up with other toxic players to repeatedly run dungeons to gear up my character so I can stand around in a group of all similarly geared characters just to be able to run other dungeons and get more gear to look slightly different until everyone has that gear too!" then this game is definitely for you!

What can I say? I'm not a big fan of AC games. I played 1-3 and stopped there.
Nevertheless, I found Assassin's Creed III to be a pleasant enjoyable experience.
The game is set up in a cool historic setting, that isn't used often in games.America of 1754 - 1783, during the French and Indian and American Revolutionary Wars.
The locations are detailed and has a nice atmosphere to them, especially the iconic towns like Boston, Philadelphia and New York. There's also forests and natural terrain that offer unique gameplay and feel, in various weather conditions.
Navigation and movement is enhanced by fluid and beautiful animations and freedom of movement - which isn't restricted to your classic city-parkour: AC's iconic "Free-Running" system works on trees here as well.
The story is decent, especially the main relationship between the two main characters (you and the villain).
The gameplay is quite fun. If a bit too easy, unfortunately. You got a lot of weapons, tricks, slick moves and some equipment to mix it up nicely. You can  disarm and steal weapons and even fight hand-to-hand in a satisfying way.
Connor trades the elegant dance-like combat of AC2 with a much more brutal, wild and aggressive fighting-style. That works really well. Animations are spectacular to watch and take-downs are entertaining to pull off.

A quick, 6-ish hour long RPG. Mediocre visuals and audio, spritework is perfectly acceptable for characters, the backgrounds and animations are all just... there, and functional, while drawing almost no attention, the music works fine but is repetitive and really is just nothing to write home about.
Combat? This is the weakest part of the game by far. Almost every enemy has 2 or 3 times the health they should, making the game hard in an annoying way and an absolute chore. The menu neither looks nor feels nice, there are very few skills and even then a small portion of those feel useful or interesting. The characters are distinct, which is good, but their distinction leaves 2 of your 4 party members feeling absolutely useless once they're out of SP - which happens after your first/second ability of the fight. This is largely why I can't recommend this game, because the part of it that's actually a game is actually really bad. I skipped combat as much as possible in this game, and ended up having to beat the game by cheesing the Cooking system, where you can pretty easily give a character way more ATK than they should have. Even powerlevelling isn't a good option to break past the bad balance because XP gains are bad and combat with mooks takes way too long.
The story, though? Pretty damn good. It feels like an entirely serious version of early Final Fantasy games, in that you have certain tropes used reasonably well with no apologies, bolstered by genuinely well-written dialogue (for the most part), and very nice character interactions. The actual plot is standard stuff, complete with twists and turns you don't expect, much in the vein of FF/Chrono Trigger - nothing that blew my mind, but I did consider them nice. By the end, I genuinely felt for Kenshi, Shinto, the party, and the rest of the lovely people you meet on your journey. The little bits of romance towards the end of the game warmed me.
This is very much a game by a writer, not a game developer, and this means I can't recommend it - it simply isn't fun to play.

This is a mobile game with a stamina system that regens after hours so progression is slow if you are offput by that I recommend not trying this game. End of review for you. Also this is a long review so be warned about that now. It's practically a guide but not focued on being a guide so details will be left out.
However if you are still here let us continue. First off is it pay2win? In my opinion it isn't. It does however have a cash shop that lets you buy boosters that regen stamina and fuel used in PvP as well as Iron used in purchasing equipment and Metal Maids(the units you fight with). You can also buy food used in leveling your maidens.
For starters PvP the biggest P2W problem. Doesn't really matter. All you get is codon(Used in researching tech, combining equipment etc) and a bunch of silver. You will mostly engage in PvP for silver. You steal silver from the enemy player. There is no bonus to being any rank in PvP except for being matched with people with upgraded units and more silver to pillage. You don't steal silver 1:1 it feels more like you take 5% of their total amount and get x10 of that amount in return. How you got more than what they had? Magic! There is also no leaderboard rewards handed out ever so often. so still no incentive to be the best other than braging rights.
2nd P2W aspect. Getting max units from gacha(Or random rewards from a slot machine). Still not a problem. The 3 ranks Blue, Purple, Gold will basically all be the same from the start untill you hit commander rank 25 and can promote them to 2 star(Purple and Gold) or eventually to 3 star(only gold units). Gacha is by far the least effective way to get new maidens(But you should definitly attempt to get them off the start from here). They will be drops for doing missions(Warning:Gold maidens from missions are the same odds of winning the lotto) and purchased at the supply depot. The best way to get a powerful Metal Maiden is via Research and in order to research them you will need blue or purple maidens leveled to specific levels and a motherload of mats. This is a collection game. Go collect! I'm also intentionally leaving out the details that even blue units can hit 3 star because that's advanced stuff and won't be worth your time anyway. But if that blue is really your waifu she can still be used in your main squad.
You can use gold to buy equipment by buying Iron to use in the gacha. The gacha's inventory will expand as you unlock new equipment with your commander level. This in turn will reduce your odds of getting any Gold maidens via having more loot in the draw pool so if that's your interest invest early. It will only give +3 equipment which you can get by combining 9 equipment with codon that is droped by missions so it's not actually alot. Also it's random so no way to get what you want all the time. The gacha however is the only place to get advanced equipment which is exactly the same as normal equipment. Except it's with 50% more stats. so it's basically equipment 1.5, 2.5, 3.5 you get the picture. Regular equipment will be just as powerful and easier to upgrade. Not only that there is a more advanced method to get equipment that doesn't involve missions. But I'm not going to explain it in the review.
But wait doesn't that just sound rather P2W? Well it is but only if you make vast amounts of money and can throw it around. For the common player they have a currency called corn and it is indeed the vegetable. You can trade corn for Stamina and fuel too as well as a few other things. You get corn for doing special missions that reset daily(This isn't the only way but the other method is more advanced). Usually it gives you about as much to restore your stamina for how much you spent doing the mission to get it. Which is a good thing because the missions give materials needed to upgrade and create new Metal maidens. Horde that Corn for special events! But don't shy away from using it too.
Is there anything a paying player can get that a free player can't? Absolutly not. They give you gold (Premium currency) for doing the daily mission and you can use it to buy anything you want in the store. The daily mission only gives 10 gold daily +2 corn. So if time is a problem just be cool and support the game eh? No pressure.
Still around? How about combat? Well combat is very simple. They take turns shooting each other till one side is dead or the 3 combat stages are over. Wait that doesn't sound like a strategy game? It isn't the strategy of the game. The strategy is team building and map awareness. Your maidens aren't going to fight just the enemy they also have to excel at the map they fight on each map has penalties that some Maidens get immunity from. Will a maiden be useless if they get a penalty? No but you will definitly see it hurt your team as a whole. And each map has different attack ranges that change even more with each round of combat. Being that if you are in a field you have 4000m range and end at 300m. In a town you start at 500m end at 50m. This highly impacts accuracy and can be the key to vicotry or defeat.
Remeber the collection bit? It's usually best for you to choose your Research wisely as you will find it will practically double your maidens base stats eventually. But you will run out of resources frequently if you try to work them all. Picking favored maidens and using them in your main team with a few combination off picks will get you far. And not investing in certain ammunitions will get you more resources for a type you actually use. Off the start branch out as things will be cheap and you will probably grab the first tier uprades anyway. I even recommend grabing the first dozen levels in every tree untill you figure out a plan for the future.
Whoa much reading?! Why with the writing?! I was actually just waiting on my building to finish in 2 hours. You also have a base to develop that will give you access to some really nifty stuff. Eventually upgrades will take days. You can also spend gold to complete it instantly. P2W? maybe. But i doupt you will care if you tried the game.

Leveled up to commander rank 104. How much did i spend on the game? Maybe 40$USD and that was because i wanted to support the game. Ragnarok has been my third RPG game that I have probably ever played. The first two, League of Legends and Dofus, really weren't the greatest thing- hence role playing games aren't my selectable game genre. But Ragnarok is quite pleasurable for casual gamers.
The game features the usual Role Playing tactic in which you build your character in your first few levels, then take a pernmament "job" that determines the type of player you play forever. Of course, some people might get bored of their class eventually, but Ragnarok makes up for this lack. Ragnarok allows you to have three character profiles at a time. So if you are willing to start fresh or try another character class, you can! No more having to stick to one destiny for the rest of
E T E R N I T Y .
Ragnarok can be confusing to new players, the game is open freely and vast, and easy to get lost in. you will spawn at first near the heart of the entire game map, from there you can build up your job skill, then be let go into the depths of Ragnarok's world. All areas have different mobs that can be passive or hostile, they also vary by Level everywhere. You can find a relaxing spot here and there with easy passive mobs, or you can run into a mob that is 40 levels HIGHER than you, and it WILL ATTACK you at it's will. This leaves gamers to be adventureous, alert, and competitive. This concept is what probably brings in my attention.
Ragnarok is also fun to play with friends. Beacause it is Free to Play, you can ask your friend to join without any worries. The probable downside is you have to create an account on their website, which shouldn't be too hard if you have spare emails for probable spam.
I highly recommend this game to great RPG players who are looking for challenge, Ragnarok, despite the other RPGs I have played, really adds up to have many differences that give players more freedom. Role Playing Gamers would not be disappointed.
I somewhat recommend this game to those who casually play RPGs, Ragnarok Online is a great game to play on your spare time, but sometimes you can get really lost like me - if that happens.... pray that you'll make it back without dying, or just die and respawn at the heart of the map, you get to keep your stuff, but you loose some of your experience. It's been forever since I've played RO or any of its private server counterparts. To be completely honest, I, taken by nostalgia, wanted to try out RO again solely because I wanted to relive the past. This may sound hypocritical because I'm trying to brag about how great this game is, but RO isn't very exciting compared to all of today's great games. It was the greatest thing in the world 10 years ago, but not the greatest anymore. However, it's not terrible and for veterans it brings a tear to one's eye to hear the old theme song of the capital city playing in the background.
I tried out RO 2 first because I wanted to see what changes were made. To my disappointment some of the game mechanics in RO 2, which worked well for RO, didn't really transition well. So I thought "oh well" and moved onto to RO. It took a little grinding to get started, but I fairly enjoyed it. Some people might find grinding miserable, but after playing years of fast paced games it was suprisingly enjoyable to slow down a bit. The graphics are 2D/3D...and of course it's crap since it was made 10 years ago. (but it was some really great crap back then) The controls consist of the function keys, alt+(letter keys) and just clicking. Moving and attacking are clicking/clicking+holding. Hotkeys are function keys. Very simple~ but it worked fabulously.
The training grounds gave me a bit of a refresher on all the little details and it's a good place to start out as a beginner if you don't know anything at all. This is great because RO can be a bit complicated even for veterans. There are a bunch of requirements you have to meet for certain things and stats you have build on for certain jobs. You might hate tutorials, but trust me... you'll need all the free items, easy levels, and explanations as possible or the beginner stages will be slow and painful. I can't critique on the rest of the game since I haven't gotten too much into it myself, but if memory serves me right this game was well worth my time. Once you make some friends or get into a guild the game will be a little easier to understand and you'll start to play strategically (or not...I prefer strategy). It's a lot more fun to play in parties (especially with experienced players that don't do all the work, but assist the little guys) vs clicking on a bunch of monsters...alone... for hours. Since your characters don't "dodge" (they stand still and exchange blows with the monster you're locked on) the most you can get out of solo playing is really just standing still and hitting monsters. The beauty of rpg's is to figure out (for example) who's going to tank, who's going to heal, who's going to range, etc. And seriously it's going to suck if you solo...
A little tangent here- I loved how the game gave the option of playing the classic RO vs the updated one. When I played in the newer one I couldn't help feel like a total noob because maps were different and monsters had changed levels/locations. The classic RO option let me get used to the game and relive those younger days :D
If you're looking for high end graphics and fast paced gaming... this is not for you. If you're looking to get into an old mmorpg because you want a change of pace, go ahead. If you're a veteran of the game and you haven't played in a while just try it out for a bit. I'm not asking you to commit. It's really hard to start from square one, but playing it once in a while still feels great and you might be able to get serious about it later.

Beglitched is a genuine point of interest in how it manages its systems.
It's a puzzle game about being a hacker, but not in a complex web of newfangled problems. Instead it mixes the logic and feel of old computer games, ones you might find on Windows 95 or in the GAMES section of a Nokia. And that's where it's at its most clever. It borrows without shame, without trickery, in such a way that forms together into one much larger puzzle.
WORLD MAP = Windows Desktop
DUNGEON MAP = Minesweeper + Dungeon Crawler
BATTLE = Bejeweled + Hide & Seek + Resource Management
One warning I should get out of the way is perception. What you might feel in the first parts of the game are misleading.
Beglitched has "dungeons" that you "crawl' through and fight of enemies. This feels like a sort of RPG, or Dungeon Crawler. When you complete the first fight, you think you'll level up, or get a health upgrade. When you get money, you think you can buy better Skills or Permanent Upgrades. When you die you wonder if it's possible to grind.
But no. Get that out of your head right now. This is a puzzle game.
Every "dungeon" is like a level of Mario or Portal. You get better by playing, not by grinding enemies into statistics.
Each dungeon has its own logic. It demands you move and fight in different ways. This is for you to solve. This is where the joy comes from. But you have to fight an urge. You have to realize that attacking an enemy isn't usually the best solution. More often than not, the puzzle is how to AVOID enemy encounters. And when you fight, the puzzle isn't always about winning. Rather, it's about minimizing long-term damage, analyzing how enemies work in that area, and setting up your grid for the next fight if you have to fight it.
The systems explain themselves. Solving how they can be worked around, however, is the fun.
And it's very nice fun. It's light fun. And none of the puzzle outstay their welcome. The concepts used in the SPAM level and the concepts in the CAT level are very different, barely ever bleeding over.
You're given a toolbox of ideas, and each level crafts a way to make you exploit that toolbox differently.
If any of this sounds like your bag of tea, get it! Support these guys! It's a good experience, and worth supporting the devs.

At first glance Beglitched looks like a simple match-3 game with colorful visuals and cutesy sprites, when in fact, is so much more than that.
Beglitched is a puzzle game where you play as the "stranger" who found the "Glitch Witch's" Laptop from a super sekrit hiding place. Congrats. Now you start your adventure by taking the place of the Glitch Witch to bomb hackers, fix forums, run away from dogs and deliver cat pictures, all while learning the secrets of the Glitch Witch in the process.
The "how to play the game" is simple.
You travel around computer networks to dig up for items/rabbits/coins, Minesweeper style.
Battle Mechanic(Match-3):
Activate Computer nodes to find the enemy location. Then blow up the enemy with a bomb.
Sounds easy right?
Now comes in the Energy and Cycle Management.
Each time you move a tile or activate a node/bomb, you consume 1 cycle.
When activating nodes or triggering a bomb, you spend energy.
You lose health when you activated a node with the enemy inside it or when everytime the cycle ends.
I won't go in-depth on this because all these are demonstrated/stated in the tutorial.
All of these become more complex through the course of the game. Complex Puzzles that really make you think. You'll encounter enemies immune to bombs, glitchy computer networks that doesn't seem to have any entry/exit. A bit frustrating at times, but very satisfying when you solve the puzzles, which, I think, is how puzzle games should be.
Another thing worth the praise are the Glitch Witch's secret notes. It tells you how the Glitch Witch spends her free time. From being fascinated from the flushing sound of the toilet, to her opinions about lies in life. This gets you immersed in the story and wonders who the Glitch Witch is, which motivates you to try and attempt to uncover where the Glitch Witch is, and why did she give her job to someone else.
Overall, this is an excellent puzzle game.
Low Replayability. Good soundtracks. Cutesy Visuals.
One of the indie games that, for me, feels "fresh".
Recommended to anyone who likes puzzles or just plain want to try something new. Give it a try.

Beglitched has plenty going for it that goes beyond the cutesy art style, but I’ll never be able to see what it really has to offer since my journey was cut short by how it handles failure. I gave it a good effort which resulted in genuine frustration and the terrible realization that I was just wasting my time without making any sort of progress.
You’re known as The Stranger and you find yourself in a situation where you have to take Glitch Witch’s place while she does other things. You carry out her tasks by cleaning up various networks of its users who tend to be hackers of some sort or the leader. Each network has a boss that has to be defeated in order to complete your task as fake Glitch Witch. By helping her out, you learn a bit more about her and unlock new networks for play.
The gameplay is broken up into two parts, the navigation through the different computers to progress to the next area and the tactical match-3 portion that takes place on a grid. You start off with six hearts that can be depleted by mines when navigating through computer networks or by slowly killing enemies you encounter on those networks. The navigation gameplay involves deciphering what the symbols mean and deducing which computer has what you need be it an exit to the next area, health restoration, or a treasure which can grant money or an item. Enemies are visible on the board and some can be avoided. Other times, you can end up engaging a horde a them in battle. You also unlock abilities that make it slightly easier if you pay the cost. The abilities I used were Scan and Warp. Scan reveals all computers that are connected to the one you’re currently located on instead of having to manually visit each one while warp lets you teleport to an adjacent computer without having to use a turn.
The match-3 portion involves a battle grid and hunting your hacker opponent who is always hiding until you strike them down. You have money sectors (tiles), computer sectors which grant turns aka cycles, bomb and compass sectors that can both be upgraded with a match to become more effective, batteries for energy, and hazard sectors that do their best to interfere with your plans. Energy is used for sectors that have an ability that can be used such as the bomb, computer, or compass sectors. Bombs go boom, computers tell you how far the opponent is from the one you activated, and compasses point in the general direction of the hacker. The battle grid also carries over from battle to battle so manipulating it with extra cycles is a highly recommended strategy. It’s a fairly competent match-3 experience that seems to have issues with difficulty balancing in the later networks. One of my least favorite parts of the match-3 gameplay is how your first sector that you click on has a small chance of being the exact location of the enemy which usually results in a cheap loss of a heart.
Now here is the number one factor that impairs my ability to enjoy this game. If you lose all your hearts at any point, you’re disconnected from the network and have to play it again from the very beginning. The base gameplay isn’t strong enough to keep it from feeling repetitive at all, so beginning the umpteenth attempt for the Catnet and Spamnet networks became more and more tedious in a game that I really wanted to like. I still like Beglitched, but it’s hard to sincerely recommend a game that completely stopped me in my tracks after clearing four out of eight networks that I could see on the desktop.
I think I could handle the difficulty if I didn’t have to go through the same sections over and over again. That part really wore me down and caused me to play even worse as the frustration grows. I’ve lost to the bosses of both network which of course means going back to the beginning. I stopped having fun after spending two hours without having anything to show for it. You don’t gain experience and items only stay within the network being attempted unless it’s a special infinite use one that you’ve unlocked through progression. So I had two hours of fun and two hours of just being stuck which told me that this game was meant for a different kind of player. I’m not sure of the game’s length either since it’s very likely that your mileage may vary depending on your skill level and persistence.
I guess I’ll also mention that I hate enemies that teleport underneath spam sectors since that means I need to have an upgraded bomb prepared and be able to predict which spam tile they’re going to teleport under. Destroying them did me no favors since new ones would just drop down, changing the spawning pattern. I also hated the security dog dudes that only let you start with two cycles and explode when you’re out of them which usually meant one heart gone unless you had spare cash to buy more cycles or a favorable computer sector tile layout. The tutorial is also really vague which might turn off some people.
Beglitched is charming and wonderful, but also brutally punishing and difficult. I might have to say that beginners of turn-based match-3 should give this game a pass. If you’re not good enough, you run the risk of never really seeing the rest of the game. I’ve played some tough games before, but this one knocked me out. I might be missing something. On the other hand, if you’re fairly confident about your abilities and have great planning skills for the persistent battle grid, you’ll probably enjoy yourself and this game.

This is another great indie game that needs better designed marketing. The videos suggest it's just another cutesy match-3 puzzle battle game, albeit one with plot, but it's really much more like a traditional adventure game where instead of verbs and objects, you're solving puzzles through the interface of a match-3 puzzle battler (and minesweeper) game. It's impressive the number of puzzles they've managed to squeeze out of this constraint, and produces a romp that feels constantly fresh and clever. Like traditional adventure games though, much of the playtime is dependent on how fast you can solve the puzzles (which do get fairly obtuse), and in some cases having the board of the match-3 battles work against you even though you know what needs to be done can be frustrating (Tip: do spamnet before catnet). All in all though, a fun and thoughtful crossover game that illustrates the case for having an indie scene in gaming producing original new ideas.

The game itself is well and good, a nice tactical shooter experience the likes of which hasn't been seen since Vegas 2, and during that time the tactical shooter genre was on it's way out - meaning that we had minimal tactical elements and more grey modern military shooter elements encroaching on the game. Siege is the other way around, bringing the elements of modern shooters - that being a more fast-paced experience - into a more tactical playing field. It's a great resurrection of the tactical shooter genre.
That said, I cannot recommend it at the moment. I am prevented from playing this game by a horrible freezing issue which affects me only in this game and Ghost Recon: Wildlands. I have tried every solution under the sun, even going as far as to replace my graphics card and re-format my computer (twice), and I am still burdened by freezing which kicks in randomly for a period of 30-40 seconds. This makes multiplayer impossible as I am dropped due to timeout, and even if I get most of the way through a match before freezing, I tend to get kicked out before the end because I freeze for that long period. I've had this issue since before Operation Health, and it's continued to persist up to now. A couple of my friends I play with have also started reporting this issue when they never had it before. If this problem was fixed, this would be one of my favorite games easily, but as it stands it is unplayable.

Rainbow Six Siege is a tactical shooter like no other FPS.
Comparing this with other well-known shooter titles like Call of Duty and Battlefield, Rainbow Six Siege takes shooter to the next level. Defend the objective by laying out traps, reinforcing walls, or jamming enemy drones. As an attacker, make your way to the objective, throw EMP grenades, breach walls, and overwhelm the enemy with your gadgets. What makes this game more realistic is that the friendly-fire is always on, you don't regenerate health, you must avoid walking and running because the footsteps are easily heard, you have to becareful when entering doorways because there might be a trap in place or a CCTV ready to spot you, and you only have one life. Make your bullets count because there's no such thing as restocking ammo. Accomplish the objective with whatever you got. Be aware of your situation. Make your gadgets count.
What I like best in this game is that you don't just run n gun everyone. I have to pay attention on everything the enemy does on how they work their tactic. Situational awareness is the key to victory.

I never played the game this is a remake of, but I bought this because the original was considered one of the greatest platformers of all time. So is it still anything special by today's standards? Not really. It's a very basic platformer. But still, what it does, it does very well. And being based off the DuckTales TV show, it turns out to be a pretty cute little game (and I do mean little; it's a very short game). The original had little to no plot, but they came up with a completely new story to tie all the levels together and features several of the characters from the show (my only real issue with the story is that at times Scrooge seems to be a bit more of a jerk than he was on the show). Some reviewers who played the original thought the emphasis on story was a downpoint, but for me that may have been my favorite part. Without it, it's just a generic, if pretty fun platformer. Plus, these days it's getting harder and harder than ever to find someone who wants to make something that's just nice, like a video game that doesn't have bloodletting or edginess to it (ironically, if more people were to make games like this they would be the ones being "edgy"). So, ultimately, I'd say DuckTales is a game worth playing, and a kind of game I'd like to see more often.

As someone who grew up playing the original on NES and its cousin on the Game Boy, I was pretty excited for this game, especially when they announced it would be on PC/Steam. Plenty of decent reviews out there, so I'll limit mine to bulleted pros/cons that really stood out for me:
Pros:
-Devs stayed true to the exceptional controls, music, and level design of the original game, and with a facelift that made it look like the cartoon show, it was doubly nostalgic for me. Loved the voice acting.
-The two additional stages from the original game - the Money Bin and Vesuvius - are fun, though the latter far more so than the former. Especially where Vesuvius was concerned though, I wanted more.
-Boss battles were all great fun.
-You can swim in the Money Bin. Not the game's strongest point, but I've wanted to be able to do that since I got the original game when I was 10.
Cons:
-I really would have liked more or different stages. I would hope that if this game is a financial success, that they'd consider making another with more original level designs.
-Cutscenes. I liked the attempt at a bigger story, and that story isn't actually bad, but the cutscenes are long, boring, and with all the wonders they did with the graphics, it would have been nice to seem more gestures, lips moving, etc.
-At an MSRP of $15, it's a little too short, especially since much of the game is material many of us have played before. Might be worth it if you're a big fan, but for the casual platform fan, I'd wait for sales.
Overall, it's worth a look if you're either a huge DuckTales fan, or if it's on sale, looking for a fun game to spend a weekend with.

For starters, I love this game. Years ago when it originally came out, I fell in love with it instantly. It was a childhood dream come true.
At the time, I wasn't allowed to get it, but I did a few years later and it was a blast.
During this recent sale I decided to purchase it, to play it again properly and just enjoy it as I would normally.
Well, let me tell you. If you're playing this on PC, you need a controller.
I'm serious.
The dev's even said when this was being developed that PC players would require a controller to play it properly.
Let me give you a few examples of why you need a controller.
1. Parkour is ridiculous with a keyboard/mouse setup. You can't climb trees and you cant hang onto anything really. Not sure why, but apparently you need a controller to do this.
2. Combat is a bit wonky, moving the camera around while fighting can be very slow.
3. The layout and controls of the game in general on keyboard and mouse just leave much to be desired.
Also, on PC, there seems to be a pretty popular issue, where the screen freaks out and shakes uncontrollaby whenever you do anything in the game. I'm not sure if a controller itself fixes it, but if you make Uplay launch in offline mode while playing it, it works perfectly.
TL;DR
I adore this game, it's so much fun, and it makes me sad that I cannot replay it unless I buy a controller. I don't want to purchase a controller for a single game to never use it again.
If you're not willing to buy a controller as I am, then don't get this game on PC.
For this reason, I cannot reccomend it.. atleast with PC controls.
Either way, still an amazing game, if you can play it right.
Thanks for reading! :]
UPDATE: You can climb trees and free run just fine without a controller. Haytham cannot free run nor climb trees. Get this game, definitely!

DiscStorm is a fast action paced game which will have you flinging frisbee's like it's going out fo fashion. The game play is fast and furious, and the single player campaign is hard. This is a game where you will start off bad, but the mechanics are simple enough that you'll want to get good at it! Fast! Frantic! Fun! FZombies! All in all I highly recommend sitting down with some friends and starting some friendly rivalries.
