I bought starter and have had a very hard time earning Renown to get different items but, for me, it just makes me work for what I've got and it makes everything I have a bit more sentimental to me.
But besides that point, the community is very nice. From my experience, they don't treat you like trash. I've made a few friends that I occasionally see on when I join a match, and it's a friendly competition or alliance that you get to have. You may ask;
''But mate, the toxic players? What about those?''
Well, with every game, and yes, even Euro Truck Simulator 2 (rather suprisingly I might add), there are toxic players. But since Ubisoft has been cracking down on these types of players, I've seen less and less as I level up and progress through the game. It does make me wonder, do I encounter more that just don't use the chat, or are there really less? I'm not too sure, honestly. I never have nor never will use voice chat in-game. So I can't account for those using that means of communication, but I can attest for those using basic chat.
I'll admit: I've got what my friends call ''The craptop''. It was top of the line when it came out, only a few years ago, but it has a bit of trouble running R6S on anything but as-low-as-possible graphics. But, I've realized it has slowly optimized itself and graciously lets me run with minimum resolution (which I would change to 800x600 everytime through the text document in your Documents folder), at well above twelve hundred.
HP, I am appreciative.
That's about all I can add for the 42+ hours I've spent on the game so far.
Oh, yes, while you're here:
I do want do warn you, this is not close to CSGO or CoD in many ways. Yes, people can make it a run and gun but only if they're extremely lucky. Or on Easy mode. Think about where you're going, and please, get in a habit of using your drones.. You have them for a reason. Don't breach like a doofus either. Take your time. If your mates rush you in chat, ignore them. It's better to go through this game slowly and thoughtfully, than to turn a blind eye to a corner and get lit up like a Christmas tree.
To sum this up, I really and truly enjoy this game. It's brought me much fun, some frusturation, and a new enjoyment to FPS games. I highly suggest it, and I hope you enjoy it as well.

Streets of Rogue is a surprisingly deep Rogue-lite action RPG with a tongue-in-cheek sense of humor, cute pixel graphics, and a stellar retro soundtrack. For a game in Early Access, it has a surprising amount of polish and a rather complete feel.
Abundant character options, achievement-based unlocks, and an astounding wealth of weapons and items are par for the course here, and SoR's unique approach to tiny, linked, open levels with randomized layouts and objectives works in its favor to create quite an excellent "anytime" game. The coop mode alone is worth the price of EA admission, and while not perfect, the netcode seems very serviceable and functional. Occasional bugs and crashes are rare, but expected from an unfinished product - we found them to be nearly a non-issue.
Although still in early access and in need of development, Streets of Rogue is blessed with an attentive dev and continual updates.
I've had such a blast with my 10+ hours of gameplay, and eagerly await updates. Highly recommended.

This game has a genuinely interesting concept which could have led to a great game; unfortunately, it feels like the developers took shortcuts that really cut down on my enjoyment with this game. The most glaring issue is the battle system that other reviews have pointed out.
There is nothing wrong with an Active Time Battle System if done correctly, but the user needs to have the option to allow for “waiting”. The Active Time Battle System should be used to give more fine-grained control over how often characters act compared to enemies, not to rush the battle so that the user is constantly using a regular attack or whichever skill catches their eye.
Since well-balanced battles are at the core of any good RPG for me, I cannot in good conscience recommended this game.
Another shortcut that it appears that the developers took was the mapping of towns and dungeons. To give an example, the first town has many houses that the player cannot enter. The only reason given is that the player doesn’t need to enter, but it’s fairly clear that the developers simply didn’t feel like they had time or didn’t need to create those interiors to add to the immersion of the game. There is also a noticeable lack of minor details in the overall mapping.
The dialogue is decent; I didn’t notice any typos while playing. There is certainly some customization made by the developers such as the bamboo text box borders which are nice touch.
I think that’s enough for now. As I said, I cannot recommend this game, but if you don’t care about well-balanced battles and focus only on the story in RPGs, you may enjoy this game.

I've always wanted to know what happens to the circus animals when circus's get boycotted. I now have come to realize that they must somehow retire into game design. Welcome to '1953 KGB Unleashed' where nothing makes sense. Seriously! Nothing!
Before I start on my usual throw this abomination into the 410 shredder let me just say that there will be spoilers in this rant especially regards to the ending. Personally I feel that I am not ruining anything, but saving mankind in general (never thought of me as a saviour did you?) from a fate worse than being locked in a room and forced to watch pride and prejudice.
How about we first start off with the mystery that no one knows even if this is an illegal game on Steam or not? A Russian web site link here provided
claims that '1953 KGB Unleashed' is a pirated renamed English copy of their game 'Phobos 1953' and that they were not paid a single cent for what they are entitled to according to developer George Beloglasov. While other rumours have begun to circulate that the original developing company Phantomery Interactive Studios have since disbanded and again other rumours state that the developers signed over full rights unknowingly to the publishers and have no entitlement. With all that being said, basically no one has any idea what the truth is, as no one has confirmed or denied any of these rumours. In fact some rumours have even stated that the developers knew what a dog’s breakfast this game was and even chose to sell all rights to it. What is the real reason? Only time will tell.
The game advertises itself as a First Person Adventure and I myself personally bought it under this premise. This is very misleading, it's simply a point and click adventure, a 2d game disguised to look like a 3d game. To be even more precise it’s an extremely anal pixel hunter as the frames to click on are often so tiny and obscure, that it will often take you a billion random clicks before you find what your supposed to click on. This is done purposefully as the developers themselves know that the game is extremely short and the amount of puzzles needing to be solved are a handful, so they have evidently chosen to stretch the game out by making it a laborious click and find chore.
The graphic presentation in this game is actually really well done and more often than not it is nearly quite photogenic. The game begins with Moscow as it would appear during that time period with life buzzing around the streets, the camera then pans down through the ground and into a secret bunker under the streets where the character you play begins to gain consciousness with memory loss as to who he in fact is. Paperwork on him suggests that he is some type of maintenance man and he has awoken in a closed section of the bunker with a blaring alarm caused through some type of industrial accident.
It is actually quite an impressive introduction into the game, but unfortunately then the game begins. First your greeted to the sound of an emergency alarm which is more grating than an alarm clock on a new year’s hangover. Seriously it just doesn't shut up, couple this with the fact that you’re in a dark room and you have to find something to click on which is the size of a penny does not make for a fun time.
As you progress further through this bunker your character begins to remember that he was in fact a maintenance man sworn to secrecy not to divulge any secrets about the experimentation's that they were performing here. He was hired on a whims notice given the task to fix certain machinery which was crucial to 'the experiment' before the accident happened and he awoke. Wandering further and further through the small labyrinth of corridors and rooms you learn of the KGB's secret experiments that range from biological to electro-therapy and even into ESP and telekinesis. Here's where things begin to get creepy. Certain documents littered around the floor show that those being interviewed were able to control objects with their mind and even people, forcing them to do things that they normally would not. They claim that in order to do this they have to empty their mind and that sometimes they can even bring a dark presence back with them.
Before you know it, now enters the concept of the supernatural as the 'experiment' that they were fundamentally interested in is communicating with the dead, especially with the people that they had just killed. Your character is then given the task to reproduce the experiment in order to understand fully what was going on.
Before I go on, I forgot to mention that you soon discover the fact that you’re not alone and that there is both someone who is somehow tracking your every movement and communicating to you through the loud speaker. He sounds like Mr Jigsaw from all the 'Saw' movies and talks in riddles as if this is all some sort of test. You further communicate to someone else over the intercom who you find is trapped in another compartment in the bunker.
Ok going back. While you recreate the experiment you discover a door where your E.S.P begins to flare up and tells you that there is something extremely evil on the other side of the door. Don't worry you never find out what it is, it might be more of the mysterious shadows that seem to zoom around and chase you getting your heart all in a flutter.
Anyway, after recreating the experiment successfully you mysteriously black out and awaken in another foreign part of the bunker not far from someone who has been freshly murdered, probably the same person you just saved over the intercom. If someone who was part of the original experiments were forcing you to black out and commit these atrocious acts is never really explained, but it is possible.
So far the story at this point is somewhat semi plausible and interesting, this is the point where as I can tell two things must have happened. 1) The original developing company here disbanded and 2) The circus animals were allowed to take over and finish it off.
Are you seriously ready for this? Your character through the power of his mind he is able to create a subway tunnel to appear in a toilet. Here, he discovers he can do practically anything with the power of his mind given the right fear. In fact he was even able to use a not connected eyeball, place it under the door, and by using the power of his mind, see the lock on the other side of the door, and open it. After creating a whole subway tunnel with the power of his mind, he then goes on to live a normal and happy life. After all this your forced as a gamer to ask yourself 'what the hell is this crap I have just sat through?!'
Would you honestly pay a builder who only builds you half a house? This was an awful lot like that. Why would anyone want to buy this when evidently only half a decent job done and the rest of it is just a rushed, cut every corner you can, story?

Beglitched (as you will have noticed) is a wonderfully bright pink and rather friendly looking game which, if you play, is a tense and demanding beast that asks you to figure out its rules by yourself.
The game actually consists of two different games. As you open up a single level, you're introduced to the first layer: a maze with minesweeper-based puzzles. You move from tile to tile, revealing information about its surrounding tiles. You can 'login' to a tile to unearth what is hidden inside, which has been hinted at you through the other tiles. You'll need to explore whilst avoiding the enemies that are around. Logging in to a tile can provide you resources and most importantly, let you exit to the next floor of the level, but you'll need to avoid hidden enemies and bombs.
Taking steps carefully is vital to completing the level. As the game gets harder, this exploration stage requires more careful thinking, whilst in the beginning, it's a relatively simple piece of the game.
The core is a fighting system where the minesweeper base is married with a not-unlike Puzzle Quest match 3 gameplay.  This layer is a real mix between resource management and a hide and seek. You have a certain number of 'power' and a certain number of actions before the enemies hit you for one damage. Clicking on a tile or 'sector' for your action can activate that tile for a power cost. 'Compass' sectors point at your hidden enemy, another sector gives you the number of tiles away your enemy is. However, even with that information, your real goal is to move a bomb sector to underneath your enemy and then exploding it. Merely clicking on the tile that the enemy is hidden in only informs the enemy that you know where they are and makes them run away to a different tile. As an action, you can drag sectors to match three. Depending on the sectors, they can provide you with more actions or money. Some sectors also level up to become stronger.
Each of the fights last quickly, you NEED them to last quickly. Your health carries over through the whole level and you need to last the however many floors that the level has.
These two gameplay layers marry themselves incredibly well. Since the match 3 board stay the same in between rounds, you're able to anticipate hard matches by playing easy ones to set up your board.
The Glitch Witch wants you to prove yourself. The game tells you very little and you have to figure out each of its rules yourself. You will learn that money doesn't carry over in between levels and as a resource should be used to gain more actions before you get hit. You will learn that if you match the light blue compas sectors, you get a dark blue compass sector which is better at pointing where the enemy is but if you match dark blue compass sectors, you get 4 actions. You will learn about which fights to best avoid, which fights to grind for and which fights you can take to set up your board for the next harder fight.
Even as the game progresses, it difficulty spikes up. It wants you to try, fail, figure it out and try again. Your first foray into a level is to explore the new mechanics as thoroughly as possible, or it will punish you for going so far without understanding its rules.
If you were looking for a puzzle game that tries something new with its gameplay and isn't really afraid to be itself, you should definitely try out Beglitched.

I'm giving this more of a mixed-to-positive recommend.
Writing this at about 4-5 hours in. I like the dense-ness of the ideas: most battles and stages don't feel wasted, there's a bunch of neat twists and small additions to the gameplay with each level. The interface for the level select is neat, as is the ways in which the overworld and in-battle statuses interact. Graphics are clear and mostly understandable, there's a lot of nice graphical polish all over the place here.
That being said, I don't find the handling of difficulty scaling to work particularly well: some levels are fairly unforgiving - think a one-life Mega Man stage, which will completely restart you even if you're 20-30 minutes in and die. It does not help that sometimes new ideas are introduced at the end of stages, giving you one chance to mess up before losing all of your progress. Some of the ideas in the later levels felt obtuse in their more difficult iterations (SquidNet and Egg(?)Net come to mind) - I wasn't sure whether I was winning by luck or not.
I think checkpoints or even mid-stage saves could have helped a lot in this respect: the game seems to be turning into more about learning about these neat tricks and using them, but the context in which they pop up is extremely stressful and so I think that diminishes the game in that respect.
Being able to mark nodes on the maps (not the battle screen) would have been very nice: I think you're really at a disadvantage with this game if you're unable to store a lot of visual information in your head.
Battles become stressful at times because of the aforementioned, the music can become grating at these moments (though for the most part it's fitting).
I can't help but wonder if a keyboard interface for the game would have worked - I find myself wishing I could navigate level selects and battles by using keys rather than having to mouse and click all the time, and it got annoying when replaying stages to have to keep clicking for dialogue to pass.

Highly recommend the game -- so unique and challenging.

Urban Trial Freestyle won't set the world on fire, but I think you still have to play it. It's certenly draws inspiration from Trials, some may say it's copying it and so what? It's good game.
The game is console port and a great one. I even try playing with the keyboard. It's fine, but the prefered method is a controller. And with him playing is great. If you make mistake, it's entirly your fault.
The game have limited video options – resolution, V-sync, Shadow quality and AA. The game is definitely not ugly, it just good, but not great. But so many things happen on screen and you won't notice textures or other things. You will be concentrated over the gameplay mostly. The game may not be the prettiest, but it have so many details on background and foreground. You see lake, big skyscrapers and so on.
Urban Trial Freestyle is side-scroller racing game with a bike. You hate to get from point A to point B, avoiding tons of obstacles. That's it. The level design is great. You will ride through forest, slums, highway with a lot of crashed cars, on top of buildings, high in the sky, on a train, in a train depot, on a dam, through an office and so on. There are some level that feel like you are in a hollywood movie. Police is chasing you, explosions everywhere, highspeed and dangerous jumps. It's like Michael Bay was directing. The thing what I like a lot here is this – there is always something going on on the foreground and background. Worker doing his thing, exploding helicopter, even a train crash. They may distract you, so bear that in mind. Sometimes those events may cause an obsticale to apper or the ground to rise. What i'm trying to tell you is the developer put a lot of thoughts in the level design.
When you finish a track you will be rated with stars and money. Sometimes only when you get 5 you will get cash. For unlocking new tracks you have to gather certain number of stars. Here there are two type of races – time attack and tricks. Tricks are more interesting. You don't race with a clock, although when you finish the race, the remaining time will count as points. Here you have to do highest jump, precise aim, highest speed or rotating the bike. Bigger the achievment, more points you'll get. There is  a green line to show you record for that track, so there is replay value.
You have only one bike, but you can buy upgrades for him. They are pretty straight foreward and all have pluses and minuses. Buy a bigger engine, handling will decrease and so on. You can dress the biker, but i'm not in to this kind of thing.
As far as the sound design, there isn't much to say. The effects are like exploisions, sirens, collapsing road, crashing or crumbling are okay, but I don't like engines. They are weak.
Music is okay. Sometimes it's jazzy, other fast and electronic, but overall you may not notice it that much in the middle of this chaos. I think I won't listening it outside of the game.
When you're done with the main game you can tackle the Challenges. I like the a lot. They are total of 5 and you have to do different things from the main game. Shoot the biker as far as you can, drive as far as possible with limited fuel, platforming with the bike to collect signs for points and my favourite – the track where you can change gravity. There have to be more tracks like this.
The biggest sin here is the lacking of level editor. This is essential for the longevity of the game. It's such a shame. Other small problem is the weird 40-50 fps I get without recording. I have mid-range machine and I think should get more fps. I'm not sure if the problem is on my side or it's the games optimizations. But the fps stay mostly about 50 and they rarely go under 40.
As a whole the game is great. I haven't played Trials and I can't compare them. I supose RedLynx games is superior, but this game is worth playing. If you don't want to deal with Uplay or Trials is pricey for you, jump on here. It took me around 7 h to beat it and here you have enough replay value. If solid controls, good graphics, great level design, and extra challenges sounds good to you, buy it. I definitely recommend it.

My history with this game begins when I was 7 years old.
I did not have a nes as a kid, so I never played the original. I did however play it on the Gameboy, where I was terrible at it, but loved playing it all the same. I watched the Disney afternoon religiously, (except for Talespin, never really got into that as a kid.)
When I bumped into this game, I knew I had to try it, for nostalgias sake.
The graphics are beautifully hand drawn, the backgrounds look amazing and the remixes of the themes are awesome. The thing that amazed me the most was the fact that they got the entire original voice cast back together, including Alan Young ( 91 at the time of making the game,) and June Foray (a whopping 94).
Their participation to me is an amazing gesture of love towards the original fans of the show. In fact, from time to time it actually feels like you are playing a lost episode of Ducktales.
Unfortunately, the developers got so excited by this that they decided to cram a 1 minute cut scene into what feels like every 2 minutes of gameplay, (especially in the Amazon level) which interrupts the play flow. These scenes can be skipped, which is a blessing on the second play through. Less would definitely have been more here.
The gameplay is as fun as I remember and the unlockable extras are an incentive to play through numerous times. Although I wish, they were not tiered. I would have preferred to unlock the soundtrack first thing before background sketches, but this is also a minor gripe.
The controls are a little iffy on the pogo jump at times, but feel right on most of the time. The difficulty is low and consistent, except for in the last level where it spikes up to a “throw-your-controller-across-the-room” hard that the rest of the game did not prepare you for.
Overall, whether or not you enjoy this game will depend on your expectations going in. if you expect an old-school game trip down memory lane you won’t be disappointed, especially if you can find it on sale.

I loved Lemmings, and I wanted to love this. I thought it would be fun and hilarious, but it turned out to be quite frustrating. The learning curve is quite steep due to how easily the sheep die. Traps are everywhere, and you need to have sheep jump over buttons in order to prevent the release of the traps. These buttons are also used to progress, so you need to find a way to manage your sheep getting to the next area before allowing them to progress so that the sheep in front of the group doesn't release a trap killing all the sheep behind it. You also have to hope that the next area doesn't have more traps, otherwise you will need to find a way to let one sheep sacrifice itself first. You have very limited number of 'resources', and if you make one mistake, you've practically failed. There is not too much freedom of choice as to how to solve the very linear puzzles. It's unfortunate that there is also just so much going on at the same time that it becomes almost impossible to save all your sheep on any given level. It's a game of 'how many sheep can I prevent being killed by the traps in their path?', not 'how can I use my resources to overcome a challenging puzzle?'. In Lemmings, you could pause the game to assign commands to the Lemmings. In this game, you cannot. Timing is more important than the puzzles themselves, which is dissapointing. Also, you generally have to assign commands to every single sheep in the line, or else they will die (eg. failing to assign the jump command to every passing sheep will cause them all to fall and die.). You had better hope too that you have enough time to manage the sheep that have jumped already, and on their way to their doom and the sheep that you haven't assigned yet! Completing the early 'puzzles' didn't give me any feelings of joy or achievement, so I stopped playing this game quite early. I may come back again to it... but I'll give it a rest for now.

I found out about this game when I saw a friend play it a few years ago in high school. Our school gave us iPads, so I downloaded it on there and we'd have a fun time playing through the levels and eventually I got all the way up to level 31 and 100%ed the game. Of course, we couldn't keep the iPads, so I downloaded the game on my iPhone and eventaully 100%ed again. After we traded in the iPads for new iPad minis, I got the game again and 100%ed. I have since graduated high school, so I no longer have that iPad either, and I saw that this game was onsale recently, so I decided to buy it and gift a copy to my friend. The steam version is basically the same as the iPhone/iPad, but with the downside of paying money, so if you don't want to pay the 5 dollars, download the app, or play on browsers because it's the exact same experience. This game features 4 unique play areas, and 2 game modes, standard with the 4 maps and battle tanks with 5 new areas which are just floating platforms in the sky with the background of the other levels in the game. This review won't really focus on battle tanks because I don't really play it, so what about this game is fun?
Well, it's a very simple way to pass by time. The controls are pretty good, though with a controller not binded, so if you want to play with a controller you have to figure out how to set everything; however, the keyboard controls are fine so it's not a problem to play with them.
The maps are fun to explore; however, they're all pretty small, so after a few hours of playing it does get a bit bland to be constantly driving in the same area over and over again.
The events are decent, nothing really special, but an easy way to pass by some time.
Sadly, this game suffers from some problems as well.
The biggest problem would have to be dead servers. This game used to have a whole bunch of people; now, you're lucky if there's even 100 players on. Note that this game has all devices on all the servers, so even with people playing on mobile, on tablets, or even browser, there's hardly anyone who plays this game. Fortunately, if you're the only one on a server the game still gives single player events, which is every event but King of the Crown. These dead servers do make some achievements annoying to get like winning a game of King of the Crown, or winning a race with 3 or more people in it.
Another problem is the glitches. This game is at times laughable with how easy it is to break. There's no invisible walls, so escaping the map is easy. If you're going too fast and try to go up a ramp sometimes you'll go through the ramp and it'll crash your car. In the snow level there's a spot where they tried to fix this by removing a bit of the outside part of the map which would send your car flying if hit correctly; however, it's not fixed. If you drive a little bit higher and clip the spot it'll still send you flying all the way across the map. Also, if you're going too fast, you can easily clip through walls, the ground, and props placed throughout the map. These glitches are fun to abuse, but it just shows that the game has a lot of programming errors that have been present for years that haven't been fixed.
Also, the game can become super tedious. The way to 100% the game is by maxing all 30 cars, and completeing various other goals like winning 100 events stuff like that. The problem is, all these cars are simply decals. All of them drive the same, with very small differences that are not noticeable while playing. Also, maxing these cars is done in the exact same way with the exact same stats to max being done in the exact same way 30 times. The only difference is that the cars progressively cost more each time, so you have to earn more money each time you max a car. There's also this feature with this character known as the Shady Dealer. There's 1 of these in every map, so 4 in total. This character is one of the last cars in the game and when you drive up you get the same line of dialogue everytime. The car basically says hey like my car? Well if you want it you must pay me 10 million dollars! Unless, you're willing to make a gamble. If you beat me in a race I'll give you this car, but if I win you owe me 1,000 dollars. However, this isn't exactly true. When you beat the Shady Dealer, you don't unlock the car. Instead, you unlock the ability to buy the car. So you just have to constantly win events, level up the cars, buy the next car, do that 30 times, you 100% if you did all the extra stuff as well. There's no achievements with battle tanks, other than the events won which you can do on the standard game, so what is the point of playing it? You don't get anything from buying the 4 other tanks other than wasting 100,000 dollars of in game money. The default tank is also the all around tank as well, so what's the point in buying the other tanks when the best one is the one you start with?
Lastly, this game is also plauged with hackers. This seems to be a problem with a lot of dead games, but here it's just sad. It's pretty standard stuff like bots that can do events perfectly, and people who level themselves up beyond the cap. The problem is, you don't get the option to report them. It's laughable at how easily I've seen people hack the crap out of this game.
With that being said, why am I recommending this game? Well it's kind of like why I'd recommend movies that are so bad that they're fun to watch. Crash Drive 2 isn't a good game, but it's super fun. I've spent hours of my life having a super fun experience playing this game and I hardly get bored, even with the tedious and unrewarding leveling system. I'd recommend playing this on mobile or browser, or waiting until it's onsale because it is not worth 5 dollars when it's super easy to play the game for free. It's a fun way to pass by time and more of a, "I have nothing else to play" kind of game. Even after 100%ing this game on steam making this the 4th time I've done it, I'd say I still had a fun time even with all of the game's flaws.

This has to be one of the top 10 "way more fun than it sounds like" games of all time.  OK, so you participate in a MP demolition-derby type race in a cartoonish little open world, driving caricature vehicles with crude, basic controls and a flying follow-camera view.  This ain't Euro Truck Simulator by any means.  It has zero realism, a pretty simple campaign (accumulate points and level up), no intellectual challenges or puzzles, controls that many people complain about... it doesn't sound like much.
OTOH, it does have one big thing going for it --  for some reason it's ridiculously fun and addictive  :-)
You roar around in your chosen vehicle, stunting like a deranged superhuman skateboarder in a fancy theme park, using ramps (including a couple of full loop-de-loops) plus the bulging topology to launch yourself from, dodging solid obstacles.   You get points for air time and performing various standard tricks (like in-air somersault or spin).  Various short contests are announced at intervals:  races around a set course, "collect the most coins" derbies, "capture the crown" chase games, "claim objects by stunting on them," "beat the others to this jump" and so on.  You can participate in these or ignore them.  Heavy hints are provided (big green arrow pointing to the current target in chase games).  Here and there little chests of money hang about waiting to be spotted and picked up.  Of course you can use in-game money to buy a fancier car.  And so it goes.
It sounds pretty juvenile and boring.  Well, maybe it is pretty juvenile, but oddly not so boring!  The comical graphics, twitchy race car action, and challenging terrain make it a very pleasant way to waste an hour or so;  and the other players provide some competition, surprises, and additional comedy.   No one gets hurt, you never run out of gas, your car is indestructible, you just bounce off stuff, it's manically cheerful and puts a smile on your face.

You wake up in an underground bunker, the year is 1953. You have no information regarding how you came to be trapped within the cold, concrete walls of this abandoned Soviet project, and you have little memory of your past. Left to uncover the horrors of what occurred here, and you must find a way out. You're alone, or are you? A mysterious voice emanates from an overhead speaker; is he real, or is he in your mind?
The set up to 1953 - KGB Unleashed is promising, and it's a pretty unique concept when it comes to point and click titles. Though the game fails abysmally in every category, making it a "bottom of the barrel" pick for its genre. It also includes a lot of gameplay features that make even veteran fans of point and clicks cringe. Note that the store page says that this game is horror, but there are very little horror elements to be had; a couple of very fleeting moments could be classified as eerie at best. The title functions in a 3D manner, meaning that you can freely pan your mouse around 360 degrees rather than having a stagnant scene like a lot of point and clicks. The visuals are nice, though the bunker looks far too pristine in my opinion. The audio, music specifically, is practically non-existent save for a couple of scenarios. The on-screen inventory system is probably the least complicated feature of the entire game.
The tortuous pixel hunting and terribly ambiguous puzzles are both unforgiving, and unforgivable. Without a guide to follow, most players would likely give up on ever solving the true-to-life KGB mysteries and just resort to a search engine for further historical information. This tedious gameplay mates with excruciatingly dry written text, culminating in an experience that's best left alone entirely. There are tons of documents scattered around the scenes in this game, but many are nefariously long and textbook in quality. You would think learning about the abominable experiments conducted by KGB would be more interesting... but sadly, not in this instance.
It all ends with a very confusing, yet uninspired, scene that contradicts the rest of the game; ultimately, an ending that's not worth the hassle of reaching. If you're using a guide, 1953 - KGB Unleashed will last you anywhere from 1-2 hours. If you're not using one, well then may the gaming gods be with you. Perhaps if you enjoy a story that's as dry as the desert itself, or reading textbook-like documents, as well as clicking on literally everything in sight to find what you've missed so you can progress, then this might be the game for you. If none of that sounds fun, well then we're on the same page. Though the idea could've been phenomenal, this is one game that just fails to deliver in every way imaginable.

I think Cities: Skylines represents what a lot of simulation vetrans wanted to see the SimCity series become, back when Maxis was the behemoth behind everything "Sim" related.  But Colossal Order picked up the reigns that EA dropped and we were given this terrific little edition to the simulation world.
Cities: Skylines builds upon everything gamers have come to love about simulation gaming.  What more is that the community surrounding the game has been quite active and huge swaths of custom buildings and mods can be found in the Steam Workshop.
The graphics are terrific and the ability to zoom seemlessly from a bird's eye view down to the sidewalks cluttered with denizens is a real treat.  During my extensive playtime I have had no real runtime issues nor any noticable performance drops through my build.
The developers behind Skylines, Colossal Order, have a pedigree in transportation simulation and I feel like it is this quality that really makes Skylines shine and excel where other simulations fizzle.  Once you've established the usual foundational elements to your city what really keeps you coming back for more is the transporation and traffic management.  The game could almost be played as a traffic simulator in and of itself.  And I think that's one of the elements that makes this game so special, and especially replayable.  As your city grows so must your transportation infrastructure and it's that sort of micro management that can be seen in other elements of the game, all to bring more depth to a sandbox that already feels alive.
That's ultimately what Skylines does really well.  It's fairly accessible to get a city up and running but the tweaking you can do keeps it highly entertaining for hours and even for the seasoned veteran.
You build a city.  You overcome the obstacles that arise from that venture and fine tune all that is in between.  Loads of fun and a solid entry into the Simulation genre.

This is a tricky game to review, as I don't quite recommend it, but I don't want to give it a thumb down, and imply that it is a bad game, which it isn't. This game is, if you hadn't already made the connection yourself, a poor mans Trials, which is why I felt comfortable reviwing this with so little play time. If you've played any Trials game, you've essentially played this.
It's hard to really mention this game in it's own light without bringing up Trials, as Urban Trial really does nothing to differentiate itself from the game it so clearly apes. The main problem with UBF though, is that it doesn't do anything better than Trials, in fact it does everything worse. The bike controls are vastly inferior, with there being no subtletly in handling and balancing, and you will actually find it very hard to overbalance or even fall off your bike. The track designs are very simple, and repetitive, and do little to challenge anyone coming in from Trials, and I doubt they would even challenge anyone new to the games.
Out of the first two worlds which I completed, (in 45 minutes of play, with there being 5 worlds overall), there were a lot of repeated tracks, which points to this games brevity. Yes, you can go back and replay levels, trying to beat your scores, or 5 star every track, but there is little incentive to do so, when the levels are barely that fun on the first play. There are also 5 challenge modes to unlock, again apeing Trials, but they are very short and not all that interesting.
I state all this but I am still leaving this game a positive review, why? Firstly, no Uplay. Secondly, for the price I picked the game up, I can't say I am too disappointed. The game is cheap, and is very often on sale. At best it's a decent Trials knock off, at worst, a bit boring, definitetly not terrible. If you've played all the Trials games and are looking for more filler, this is worth a shout.

You are born with a mark that allows you to summon, but not until you get proper training, even the king without an heir (his 4 sons died under strange circumstances, and one idiot move), While some argue this is a storyline of many games and movies, I feel this one is very close to how Skyrim is written

The casting of spells have nice animation, and I was pleased to see that most of the A.I. on your team works well. Sometimes you have to make sure they are attacking the right mob, but for the most part they know where to go.
There has been a massive complain that the game runs to fast on modern systems, so with that, I'll post here in this review how to fix that - For $5 its a good buy! Get it.
---- ------------------------------------------------------------
---- SLOW DOWN FIX FOR SUMMONER
---- Tested with Win 7 64bit QUAD Core..
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Win7 64bit QUAD Core - Here is a fix I used. Work very nice
If you have tinkered with the V-Sync then you already know thatt is a hit and miss (system dependent)
Changing the Afinnity will not work either, as these games are made to run on single core (sometimes dual core), and will not recognize anything other than that. So using more cores is impossible
Here is a successful option, that works on many games (and some DOS games as well).
I know it works in win7, if you have another OS and can follow this method - please confirm.
CREATE A NEW POWER MANAGEMENT
Go to control panel: In the search box (upper right) type POWER then click "Choose a power plan"
A new split view will open.
Select "Create a New Power Plan" (left side panel)
Select High Performance
And name it something like "Old Games"
Next
Change both settings in the next view to NEVER
Click "Create"
Now you will see your new power setting (now selected). Click on "Change plan settings"
You'll now have a link that says "Change advanced Power settings"
Scroll down to "Processor Power Management"
Change the Minimum Processor State to 1% (YES ONE PERCENT)
Change the Maximum Processor State to 1% (SAME)
Save it, your done.
NO YOUR COMPUTER WILL NOT RUN AT 1% but it will force it to use the lowest possible processor state as most games are run by state of the processor.
Which this will likely be somewhere between 500-800mhz.
during play there were a few (very rare) minor speed glitches, but they lasted a fraction of a second.. sorta like a hiccup. But it plays nice.
Again, this works on my W7 64bit, Quad Core... results may vary on other systems.
Hope this helped at least ONE person so that they may enjoy this classic!!

Savage is a game about asymmetrical combat, strategic teamplay and raw skill.
Beasts(can leap and are more melee/attack focused) vs Humans(can block and are more ranged/defense focused)
both teams can use various types of ranged weaponry and have a melee attack, this leads to an easy to learn hard to master simplistic combat system that rewards skill and practice.
Each team has a commander that plays in a top down view rts mode that controls the building, tech upgrading, npc workers and overall economy of the team as well as carrying out battle plans/tactics (though you cannot draw on the minimap in this one YET) commanders can assign an officer to give a health regen aura and each team has access to 3 buffs after building the corresponding structures.
Humans get Shield 80% dmg reduction as far as I know, Adrenaline speed boost, and Electricity like x4 melee dmg.
While Beasts get flame shield(dps to enemies around you) rejuvination(full hp, stam, and mana  which acts as ammo for beasts) and Gate, which is basically like a teleporter you can put anywhere on the map for ez back doors etc.
The Savage series has definitely always been one of my very favorite games and this is no different, I love this game and I will be playing it for a very long time!

If you have played the boardgame and like it... what are you waiting for? This is a great adaptation. I can't resist chanting "toad!, toad!, toad!..." every time someone has to roll and may get the infamous one. An "advantage" of a digital version over playing with board and pieces is that it resolves the "rules lawyering"; no more arguments over taking the doppleganger as a trophy or which spells can be cast together. In some cases the reading of the rules may be a little unexpected (deducting the base craft instead of the current craft, for the ninja's secret strike) but I think in the end the designers achieve a good game balance.
If you don't know Talisman but you like turn-based fantasy boardgames that are easy to learn, with games taking a couple of hours, then this is a great choice. The game mechanics are: you compete against 3 othe players, each with different stats and abilities (RPG-like). Move around the board where different events happen, building up your character's abilities. When your abilities are at a good level, try to get to the end game (this is the "inner ring" on the board, for the base game, or it can change depending on expansions). Like the original boardgame, you can add much variety with the expansions, it does not get repetitive. The events are fun and well balanced. Generally you will make progress by making the right choices but... don't get too complacent! Even for the strongest character there is a small random chance of a minor "disaster" that brings your stats down a few notches. By the way, the base game does provide plenty of fun, the expansions are very nice, and I do recommend getting them if they fit into your gaming budget, but the base characters and cards should also provide with a good dose of variety before you need to spice things up. Also regarding the expansions - they are selectable from the options screen, you can try them out and turn them off (e.g., if you want to show the game to a new friend and want the "simpler" game, or if you feel the expansion makes a game longer and you want a quicker game today). For the character packs you can turn them all on or all off.
In terms of bugs the game is quite stable; very rarely I've come across a situation of a missing "continue" button or a seemingly endless loop of questions but it was easily solved by exiting and restarting.
Overall - A great game, and after getting it for myself and playing a couple of games I also bought additional copies as gifts for my friends who I used to play the boardgame with :)

Flockers is an action puzzle game in much the same style as Lemmings, created by Team17, makers of Worms, so you know the pedigree is good.
For those who don't remember the classic Lemmings, it was a game in which a number of "lemmings" (which looked more like human workers to me) were released and would walk through the landscape, following each other like the archetypal lemmings, blindly walking off cliffs to their death. Your job as the player was to guide the lemmings by giving specific instructions to them, for example to build bridges or dig into the landscape, in order to guide as many of them to safety as possible.
Flockers uses essentially the same concept, but with sheep instead of lemmings. Appropriately so, since sheep also have the habit of following one another. This time around, rather than natural landscapes, you have to help them navigate through extremely dangerous factory complexes, filled with saws, spikes, hammers and other nasty objects, often with gory results as your mindless sheep stroll blindly into them.
Each level is a puzzle. They're large, and get progressively more complicated as you progress through them. You can zoom in and out to get a better view of the puzzle you have to solve. Sheep may wander off in different directions, you may meet more sheep along the way, transporters teleport sheep to different locations and it can sometimes be a bit confusing to understand what's going on the first time you try a new level.
As you go through each level, sheep step on buttons which activate machinery, sometimes in a good way, sometimes in a very bad way, so you have to be very careful what you let them step on. They also encounter crates, which when opened give you new abilities that you can assign to your your sheep. It may take a few attempts to figure out how to get through a level.
While you often need to get only one sheep to safety (in the early levels at least), getting more will score you more points, as will doing it in a faster time. You also get a bonus for using fewer abilities. You can retry levels to get a better score, and you can compare your score to your friends.
The levels are very detailed, perhaps overly so, which can make it tricky to figure out how to solve them. But maybe that's the point, distracting you with unimportant details. Fortunately, although it's an action game, you can pause it at any time, giving you the opportunity to study the puzzle at your leisure. You still have to solve it in real time though, giving commands to your sheep as they move. Pressing the right mouse button gives you a bigger "brush", enabling you to give commands to multiple sheep at the same time.
The graphics are very good, and very gory as sheep get smashed and sawed, spiked and gored, with blood splattering everywhere, which is rather amusing if you find that sort of thing funny. For this reason the game has an age rating. But if you don't like that sort of thing, you can simply turn off the gore in the video options.
I haven't played this game for very long yet, but my first impressions are very good. I'm finding it both challenging and amusing, an enjoyable casual way to pass the time. The price is very reasonable and it's on sale at the moment, so this is a great time to grab it if you're interested.

Despite appearances Flockers does not play much like Lemmings.
Lemmings is primarily a puzzle game, not an action game.  Flockers is primarily an action game, not a puzzle game.  The difference is whether you put the emphasis on difficult reasoning or reacting quickly.
Flockers plays more like some sort of strange platformer than a Lemmings clone.  Unlike Lemmings, there is no way to assign tasks while the game is paused or even slowed down.
Assigning tasks is made more unpleasant by the design of flocker tasks.  In Lemmings assigning a single lemming a task typically affected the behavior of the entire stream of lemmings, or terrain, such as blocking their path and turning them around, or building a staircase until an obstacle was struck.  In Flockers you usually need to give the same task to each flocker at the right time.  Too late is fatal.  Too early may also be fatal, depending on the task and environment.  The only concession the controls make for these demands is to allow you to use a larger or smaller 'brush' to assign tasks, and due to the timing constraints a large brush is not very usable.
To make matters worse, there is no way to predict what the level elements will do.  This reduces solving the level to trial and error, rather than planning.
The constant trial and error gameplay is grueling since you will need to start the entire level over if you  mess up badly enough.
If you want to see what it would be like to play Super Mario Bros. with awkward controls, a stream of Marios, and random cheap deaths, then play this.  If you want to play something like Lemmings, you need to look elsewhere.
Some are making comparisons to Worms as well.  There certainly is no similarity between Worms and Flockers gameplay.  Both Lemmings and Worms had destructable environments.  Flockers does not.  While Worms was violent, and Lemmings had a task that made all the lemmings blow themselves up (used to restart the level), the violence was cartoony.  Flockers is gory.  So Flockers is not very comparable to Worms either.

Preface: This review is being written after 17 hours of play, over the course of about 3 days.
The first question on my mind when I downloaded this game was "is it p2w" and/or "how much do they screw the free players". So far, I can say it does not seem to be/do either of those things. Cash shop appears to be mostly cosmetic/mount based, and honestly, there seems to be no real downside to being a non-subscriber. The only significant limiting factor that I've found has been a 2 character limit, which doesn't really affect me as I usually just play one class/character in MMOs. With that out of the way, here's the Pros and Cons:
Pros:
Not P2W
Not garbage F2P system
Actual fun combat system
Fairly quick leveling pace (so far)
Interesting quest/currency/loot loop
The game seems to be a mostly standard MMO, with a few interesting mechanics (most notably, the a true skill based targeting system for the ranged classes). The classes are fairly varied, and the few I've tried have all played completely differently. The brawler was the class I settled on, as it basically plays like a character from Street FIghter or Mortal Combat, complete with juggles and blocks. Its honestly one of the most fun classes I've ever played in an MMO.
Cons:
Super sexualized characters
Elin's
So for me, the biggest reason I waited so long to play this game was because of the character designs. EVERY character (male/female/child race) will be wearing skimpy armor throughout the game. Its actually kind of comical, but keep that in mind when picking a character. You may be looking at a half naked man/woman/child for the whole game. *Note* The animal/golem races don't really have the sexy issue, but...you are an animal or a golem.
When it comes to MMO's, I usually play a male character. With this game, several of the classes (4 or 5 at the time of this writing) are race/gender specific, which means if you want to play as a brawler you will have to play as  a human female. This was almost a deal breaker for me, but since actually sitting down to play I've gotten past it.
With that in mind, there are currently two classes only available to the Elin race, which is depicted as a small, 5 year old girl with animal ears/tail character. Which is sad, as those classes appear to be very interesting, and I will never play one of the child race characters because I think its pretty messed up to be running around looking like a 5 year old in lingerie (regardless of the in-game explaination for it).
TLDR: Its a really fun game if you can get past the armor/character designs.

KGB Unleashed is a horror point and click adventure game, so I'm gonna break this review down by story, puzzles, art direction, and sound design. For those on the fence about buying it, please note that I tried to keep spoilers at a minimum.
The story that's there is fun but incomplete. The story is you're a soviet electrician that wakes up stuck in a bunker. Alarms are going off, so either something really bad happened or it's time for a regulated soviet union smoke break. Either way, you probably want out, so that becomes your drive to rifle through everyone's office supplies to try and figure out what your comrades were up to (not your drive to figure out how to exit the bunker somehow.) 90% of the story is presented through documents just lying around, and the other 10% presents itself through glorious C-tier voice acting. What I could make of the overarching story was good fun, but again, by the end I really felt it wasn't finished and that's really hard to look past. It's unreasonable to expect the game to follow up on every little game world detail, but KGB Unleashed introduced concepts that could have had huge ramifications for soviet electric man, then did nothing with them. The ending doesn't acknowledge or talk about anything in the bunker at all, which soured most of experience for me.
I didn't care too much about the puzzles. They're very cryptic in the "I didn't even realize I could do that with the camera" sort of way. I got stuck in the very first puzzle room for like 30 minutes, so I ended up using a steam guide from then on for the rest of game. That might discredit me quite a lot in talking about this, but having beat it, I can safely guess that I would have given up otherwise. It's a mixed bag of hard puzzles that require ingenuity and puzzles that just require you to figure out what background object isn't just part of the background. The store description for KGB lists "Staggering puzzles and many challenging mind game" as a feature, which is accurate, but I would argue that's not really a good selling point in the way it's executed.
Art in this game is mostly okay with some sparse highs and lows. Before go on, I feel obligated to point out that there are no resolution options or meaningful graphical settings to change. I'm not sure how average that is for these kinds of indie point and clicks, but I thought that was weird. That being said, stylistically it does achieve it's goal of making you feel like you're wandering around a 1950s soviet bunker. It especially excels when it starts getting into some of the later stages of the game because of how much it contributes to accentuating the fact that you're alone and vulnerable. Moments like that where the art lends itself to a greater purpose are few and far between though. As for the lows, I'm just gonna say all in-engine cutscenes.
Sound design is bad. It's really bad in the beginning with the alarm that goes on until you finish the first puzzle. It's nothing I feel that needs in-depth discussion though. Most of the time I didn't think anything of it. In what I felt was this game's highest moment, it opted for no sound.
All that being said, I would not recommend this game. If you're looking for a good point and click or a good horror game, this is not what you're looking for.

I'm generally not a big fan of point-and-click type games, and this experience won't change that. However, I did have a thoroughly enjoyable experience thanks to this game immersing me into a largely suspenseful and paranoia-ridden environment.
__________________________________________________________________________________________
Setting the scene: I wake up in a small room with no memory of how I came to be where I am or any clues as to what my purpose ever was. The only objective being, to escape and find out what happened along the way.
Immediately you'll have to dust off your thinking caps and slam those bad boys on, because puzzle-solving is key here. Observe your surroundings, be perceptive, and try to build up the story behind the place. I honestly went in with no expectations and got a fun 4-5 hours out of it. It might seem a little dull at first, but it gets far more interesting in the second half of the game.
Some puzzles are easy while others require a little more thought put into how they are solved. A couple times I almost gave up because it didn't seem at all logical. But persevere and you'll get your money's worth. I admit, this game could have been made better in regards to finding certain objects that require you to progress further. It just shouldn't be that hard at some points. But it is and can get quite frustrating finding some small object or knowing how to use it. Another thing that I found this game lacked is a little more closure once you neared the end. Some questions were left unanswered and I really wish they hadn't done that, seeing as how I was so drawn in by the atmosphere and dark story-telling.
Overall, I would recommend this to people who enjoy adventure games in general, and to those who love a bit of 1950s Soviet-themed (fake) history with legit themes thrown in. I especially enjoyed reading the patient files and information files on the poisonous gases (they turned out to play a part in the game). The radio puzzle was a nice touch, though I'm not sure if the speeches/songs featured on the device are actual recordings or just created specifically for this game.
Now, for some inexplicable reason, I seem to have a craving for some creepypasta...

My recommendation for you is buying this game when it's heavily discounted, and then finish it by using a walkthrough in your Steam Browser (I used this excellent guide:
. I'm saying this because the puzzles are way, way too hard for a casual gamer or a gamer who doesn't usually play these kind of games (like me). By using a walkthrough, I was able to enjoy the atmosphere and the story to the full extent without beating myself over the puzzles.
The atmosphere is terrific. You can feel the desolation, desperation and hopelessness in the claustophobic environments. The graphics are nice, the sound effects are superb, and the soundtrack fits the game like a glove.
The story is very intriguing, and it has a very big potential but the lackluster (though the word lackluster is a massive understatement here) ending ruins the gravity of the setting. It feels like they had to rush the game at the 90% mark.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, but only if you're willing to play it like I did. If you're going to solve the puzzles yourself, don't bother with buying this game.

I really like the board version of Talisman, so I snatched up this version on a Humble Bundle.  The game is fun, online or offline (but still better with friends).  If you like the board game, you'll probably like this version, as they did a good job getting the basic Talisman experience in here.  The UI can feel kind of awkward sometimes because of weird button placement and the need to click more times than necessary to do certain tasks, but it's possible to get used to and then it stops detracting from the game at all.  The game also has some advantages over the original such as not having to shuffle decks and manage pieces, and letting the computer do the combat math and automatically enforce the rules prevents any player from losing an encounter because they forgot to add an extra strength point from a follower that they lost in their inventory.   It's a more convenient way to play, in several regards.
That's why it's such a shame that the game is so buggy.  Sometimes the game breaks the rules in frustrating ways (spells targeting untargetable opponents, characters being unable to use abilities when they should be able to, cards that should only be used a limited number of times never disappearing from the board, etc.)  So far, every game I've played has had at least one bug that breached the rules.  They can be mildly amusing at best but game-breaking at worst.  The frequency of these bugs is the problem, as they wouldn't be much of an issue if it was just occasional.  But so far it's been every single game.
The bottom line is this: if you like Talisman, this is a pretty good version of it.  It gets all the content even if it lacks some of the streamlining it could have.  However, the frequent bugs are frustrating and having a bug break your game 90 minutes in is enough to make you not want to play again.  If the developers could take care of the bugs, I would definitely recommend getting this game.  Unfortunately, I'd now only recommend getting it on sale.

First off, it's a great concept. It has a decent dodging system implemented that makes it possible to survive in things like Raids. Not only that, but most characters have a block or counter or displacement skill that helps your mistake of not being able to dodge, or for all of the people who go ham. In terms of gameplay, it's actually pretty fun. The map is huge with different varieties of mobs and such. It clearly states which mobs you can wreck and which ones can wreck you. Solo gameplay is a tad bit slow and boring, but most MMORPG's are like that. Playing with a group always makes the experience better. The game itself is grindy, especially for the early levels. When you reach max level on a character, it's just PvP and Raids from then on. The items are definetly worth it.
Now, let's talk a bit about the True Action combat. It's fantastic. The controls and system is fully functional. YOu're in in the attack or not. There's no delay and it adds a little spice to combat. Unlike WoW where there's attacks from bosses you can't dodge or avoid, TERA offers you a chance to either get one-shot or not. You won't get hit by an attack after moving out of the range increment because you were "in the range 2 seconds before it went off". In short, this is a great addition and this is what makes the combat in TERA so good. At least in my opinion.
Graphics: They aren't bad at all. I'd say they're flat out amazing, to be honest. For a free MMO, the animation is quite fluent, the models are well designed, and the environment is something to look at if you jsut want to enjoy nature. In terms of optimization, it's 50-50. This game can be run at a solid 60 fps, but I've heard that people can only run it around 45~ish on the maximum settings, but I've never ran into this problem.
Now we get to bad part fo the game. Yet, this game can be considered a pay-to-win, but only on the European servers. If you're playing basically anywhere else, you're good. Back when this game was still in subscription and a little after that, it was based off of the individuals score. However, in present time, that's been thrown in the past and now it's all about gear score. In the long run, the community itself has turned more toxic than I'd've anticipated. You'll find the occassional hiccup of a good person here and there, but the majority isn't very "new user" friendly, or friendly in general. That being said, it's up to you to decide how you handle the community. From my experience, play Priest. Every raid needs a Priest.
The storyline is, well, lacking, in my opinion. It's your generic MMO storyline. Tragic backstory, tragic events, tragic evil-doers. But, well, every game like this needs an antagonist, so it fits the bill. Another bad thing about this game is the guild system. From my past experiences, if you're not well optimizing your character in an end-game guild, then get prepared to get the boot. Like I said, gear score is everything now.
That's my review and how I feel about the game. I might've missed a few key points here and there, but this sums up my thoughts on the game in general. It's fun to play in groups, grindy as heck early on and lessens up a just a smudge late game, gear score is everything, the shop is overpriced, the community is toxic, combat is nice, and Reaper is the spacebar hero.

I didn't know what I was getting into when I got this game. I had seen it flashing by a couple of times, but I had never felt convinced up until now.
I was in an RPG mood, so I gave it a try (the game was on sale, so I grabbed it).
The story had more depth to it than I expected it would have.
I found the characters likeable. I easily grew fond of them.
This game plays like a very compact, extremely basic and simplistic RPG.
There's no fancy equipment whatsoever. The mobs are quite idiotic (I liked their design, but their battle AI was poor).
The story did make up for all of this. The story is what drove me to finish the game and I'm glad I did - it was rather touching. More so than I had expected!
It's one of those stories where the plot is revealed thru flashbacks - this was done quite well, I must say.
I am content. Glad I played. Lots of time spent going back-and-forth though (way too much time - a lot of it could have been cut down and replaced with more original content).
All-in-all, the game is okay. There were some dull moments, but the story left me in tears nonetheless - ouch!
NB the cover pic for this game is rather misleading - the character in the pic is a Lust Demon (there's only a single apparition of such a demon in game, and it's not even part of the main plot - more like a subplot)
I do not take well to false or misleading advertisement... and I feel like the developers would benefit more if they changed it - it's not exactly representative of what the game is about (I'm hoping they'll change it)

just a note: This is a review being done by someone who never played the original, as I came into gaming late  in the SNES era/early PS era, and am currently on my second play through.
The pros of this game:
The Music- It is stellar.  I wish they would come out with a soundtrack for this game.  The music for the levels are unique and suit the environment and tone of the game.  I can't say whether it is better or worse then the 8Bit rendition.  Thusfar, I've only heard the Amazon level music and the Money bin version, and I don't care for either of those, but that still leaves a few levels worth of music to go.
Voice acting - Getting as many of the original voice actors from the cartoon as they could was a good call.  It made it seem like I was listening to the cartoon.
Level design - Overall was fairly good.  While there was some sticky points that they could have improved on (the finale, for instance), the levels were beautifully designed, appealing to the eye, and offered just enough challenge to keep you from getting bored but not so much that the game was frustrating.  Ending aside.
The Neutrals:
Cut scenes - While I enjoyed watching them generally, they suffered from the fact that the characters were 2D in a 2.5D setting, and as such were limited in what they could do.  Personally, I think the game would have benefitted from cutting down the actual cut scenes to main points (as in, cutting out the ones for individual items) and animating them as 2D cartoons.
Difficulties - There are multiple ones.  Nothing really all that special about it.
The Cons:
Lag - This may have just been an issue with my rig, but there was an odd amount of lag in the game.  While my computer generally is able to handle harder hitting games, it was bogged down by this game, which meant the game hesitated - oddly, this presented as pauses in dialogue and cut scenes, and as slower animation throughout the game, but somehow didn't hinder actual gameplay.
The Gallery - While the gallery as a concept is excellent, and I love the idea of using the money you gain in the levels to buy the extras, the fact you had to unlock so much from one section to unlock the next area to buy from seemed silly.  To me, it seemed like a ploy to force you to replay the game, just to get the content you wanted - which for me was the music and background imagary.
The ending gameplay - While I won't go into what the ending part actually was, I will say this:  In and of itself, the game ending was fairly good story-wise, but the execution of it was terrible when it came to gameplay.  This game had fairly even difficulty throughout, up until this segment - in which the difficulty randomly and suddenly spiked.  The overall design required a level of precision at points that made the game feel near impossible to finish, especially in comparison to the rest of the game.
While the game does have its faults, it's a good game overall.  I bought the game on sale, but likely would have bought it at its full price had I found it at that.  $15 is a steal considering the amount of work that went into making this game, and the sale prices even moreso.  While I can't vouch for the nostalgia of the game, for someone who is a fan of Ducktales and the richest duck in the world, I would definately suggest at least giving this game a shot.

This game is just plain fun!  The player has so much freedom in how to progress in the game.  Essentially there are a few mini objectives to complete in each level, such as destroying a generator, neutralizing a character, or collecting an item.  Naturally there will often be those who get in the way of these objectives to make it harder to complete them.  Now the fun part is determining how to go about accomplishing those objectives; do you use the assassin and cloak yourself and sneak around to backstab people without being caught?  Do you use the doctor to knock somebody out from behind with chloroform?  Do you use the zombie and just infect everyone you see?  You have so many choices on how to go about it, and they also allow you to finish the same objective in numerous different ways, like you can knock on windows to distract or confuse people, turn off power or computers in order to avoid traps, or you can use items or hire people to create diversions.  Choises definitely matter (which is why I nominated it for that category in the Steam Awards for 2017) and make the game so much more fun since it keeps it feeling fresh and new every single time.
Additionally, the game presents randomization with the levels so the maps will always be different, the objectives will be different, and the things you interact with will be different.  That adds a lot to the replayability of the game.  Multiplayer works well with this game and adds even more depth to it, since players can do their own thing in order to accomplish the goals away from each other or they can team up and utilize their specific class' traits to compliment the abilities of each other.
It is fantastic that the developer is updating this game frequently and regularly--there is a lot to do already but this is the type of game that can be expanded upon with the new content that gets added.  I can only imagine what sort of new enemies, new player classes, new items, new missions, etc. will be added as time goes on.  I highly recommend this game.

From the Creators of the award winning 'Lemmings' and 'Worms' Series of games comes another classic in the making from Team 17. I first got to play this awesome and addictive game at 'EGX Rezzed 2014.
If you're a fan of the classic game 'Lemmings' from many moons ago or the recent 'Worms' series of games... then you're in for a treat. Flockers feels like a perfect blend of both styles of game. In Flockers your aim is to guide a flock of sheep to an exit in the safest way possible, along the way you will be met with seemingly impossible obstacles and plenty of gruesome death and you will be laughing all the way! As in 'Worms' you have to collect crate's to aid and help your journey. All in all this makes up for a highly enjoyable and addictive game. Team 17 have not skimped on the gore either this time round and you'll be in stitches and shock at some of the death scenarios. This is already shaping up to be 'Game of the Year' material. The game may still be in 'Early Access' but it doesn't feel that way. It's extremely polished and already has a ton of bonus content with the introducing of 'Steam Workshop' - Highly Recommended!

I like Cardboards and I like Fantasy Settings. This game seems like a pretty good choice.
But it has its flaws. Much unnecessary clicking, many delays. Games turn out to be very slow.
Some people like to click for rolling the dice, but personally if no choices are left other than roll the dice.
Roll dice -> choose destination (necessary) -> Survey the field (take cards) -> Fight the monster -> roll the dice for fight the monster. If only one step in this chain is necessary why not skip the other to speed up the game. I have no other choice to fight this monster so why do I have to tell the game I want to fight it and after that actually fight it with rolling the dice?
There are many Animations (e.g. dice rolling, moving, game effects, battle) and no way to skip them. Try to play a game with AI enemies and after half an hour you get frustrated. You don't want to see them roll the dice. You wait so long for your turn and most of what the AI actions will not even concern you.
But what drives me off most is the game mechanic. Chances for positive Events are not very high, its hard for your character to accumulate progress. And when you finally found items, compagnions you can have bad luck and loose everything by turning into a frog when rolling a bad number in the city. Or an enemy just casts a spell on you to reset your strength to the starting value so you cannot fight most of the monsters anymore.
Of course every game has to have some negativ value to emphasize the positiv values. Its ok to loose an item, healthpoint or to wait one turn. But taking away so much from a player will make you rage. You can be at the very top and in the next moment you loose everything.
This game is far from balanced and although I really like the setting this game is so unforgiving for any awful roles.
I would not recommend it, though the real life version would be possible playable because of its faster pace.
