Audio/SFX - 5/10 - This is probably the worst part, sounds are the same, without any changes on the pitch each time they are played and there is no variety nor anything unique about them, the devs should really put some work on the SFX as the game is in 3D and the sounds don't have the dimansional feel on them(hope this makes sense?).
Settings Menu - 6/10 - Missing a lot of options that should be there. There already are options for SFX volume, resolution, fulscreen/windowed, default directory to show whn you want to select your music, but there are no options for controls. All the menus are kind of confusing at the moment(not too confusing, you will still be able to start playing in less than 30 seconds) but they need to be worked upon.
Overal Score - 8/10 - Will need some more work but it is already pretty good as it is. Definitely a good purchase if you can cope with the speed of the game and you can handle the rage it might drop upon you.

Good and entertaining remake of a classic with some inherited and some added flaws.
The remastered DuckTales
draws you right into the game and you are eager to "press start", though you might encounter the first hurdle here, if you don't have a supported (read an Xbox360) controller. (Installing a utility like x360ce or xPadder helps, the keyboard is also an option on the PC of course.)
The
are great, especially the animated sprites and while some reviewers criticized the comparably small number of different animations, especially noticeable in the cutscenes, I think it's fine for the scope of the project. Talking about the cutscenes, I consider them an added flaw, they are too frequent, interrupt the gameplay unnecessarily and require two button presses to skip them. No need to borrow the weak way of storytelling of a modern FPS in a classic. The voice acting is well done and the cast is mostly from the original TV show.
I like the new 3D backgrounds as well, and I don't see why some reviewers think they wouldn't match with the sprites. The environments are clearly readable, which is important in a game like this.
The uneven
can be considered an inherited flaw, the levels vary greatly in difficulty, and the first on the list, Amazonas, surely isn't the easiest. When you play the game on "Easy" it's not too much of a problem, because you have infinite lives (making the mode arguably "Very Easy"), but beginning on "Normal", it can become frustrating, because if you run out of lives, you have to restart the whole level, all treasure gone. Though if I remember how many times I smashed my NES controller onto the floor, this remake is true to its roots in this aspect.
The game is also really short and most of the playtime can be attributed to the overall unforgiving difficulty once you play on "Normal", "Hard" or the unlockable "Extreme" setting. Gameplay wise, the biggest addition compared to the original is a tutorial level at the beginning.
DuckTales is easy to recommend, not only for the nostalgia, but because it's a very good game for the price. Sure, the cutscenes, will annoy you and the difficulty mixed with occasional hick-ups in the controls will frustrate you from time to time, but hasn't it been like this also 2 decades ago?

- This is the perfect example of a game with so much potential but is ultimately ruined due-to
poor execution. While this game has a deep atmosphere, a dark and intriguing back-story and somewhat realistic graphics, it is all downhill after the first room.
The basics are summed up on the store page so we don't need to go into those little details. The game itself is a Point-&-Click puzzle game, a genre that certainly isn't for everybody but can be very enjoyable if done correctly (see Monkey Island for example),
is not one of those games.
For starters, the interface and menu style feel really amateur when compared to the rest of the games art style. The puzzles that are presented to you almost instantly are either extremely difficult or make little to no sense, the examples I'm about to give may spoil the game for anybody interested in trying it out so read on at your own risk.
One or two of the tasks you have to overcome are relatively easy, such as the voltage puzzle in the first room (even though this involves the dreaded
at first) and there is another puzzle a little bit further in where you have to repair a cable, these are examples of the easier puzzles, and then there are those that make absolutely no sense such as
... yes... seriously... these are the instances I'm talking about that make absolutely no sense.
You get vague instructions and hints from picking up documents and reading notices as you go through the game, plus you have to look very carefully at everything you come across to get hints and pay close attention to the little details of the rooms you are in to acquire certain objects that are important, or again,
, these aspects are interesting but equally annoying. If it wasn't for an online walkthrough I stumbled across, I don't think I could have ever figured out that the radio tuning opened the secret passage. There is also a part where you have to place a certain object in a certain room atop a certain crate, something that you could only figure out purely by chance / trial and error.
Finally, the game is short,
, the hours of play people build up are purley based on the amount of time it takes you to figure out some of the absurd and extremely difficult puzzles, once you are all clued up and give it another play through, it can be completed in no less than 20 minutes.
So that's about it for this game I'm afraid. I don't like giving games negative reviews, really, but all good aspects of this game are hugely overshadowed by all of it's negatives. This could have been something much more, it's a shame. I would say buy it in a sale or a cheap bundle (like I did) if you're still interested in trying it, but it is highly likely that you'll have to consult a walkthrough more than once.

I'm a fan of Point and Clicks, I'm a fan of crazy Russian stuff, I'm also a fan of The X-Files. You'd think KGB 1953 would be really fun to play with all those things considered, but it strangely wasn't. It was actually pretty frustrating.
I'm left wondering just where the story started and at what point it ends. There are plenty of documents and files to read as you progress through the game to flesh out the situation and provide hints and clues to puzzles (and why you're in the bunker) but you never really get any resolve. It's just one big 'what' moment.
One big 'what' moment dotted with lots of smaller 'what' moments in the form of some of the most mind numbingly frantically click and hope puzzles I've experienced in a point and click. Some of them are pretty clever, while the majority rely on you being able to distinguish collectible items from the backgrounds they're hiding in.  So you'll find most of time just clicking and hoping and wondering where the logic/reason was behind the solution.
In the end KGB 1953 is a game that should only be experienced by people who want to experience just how odd this game is. Point and click fans might be disappointed by it, and those new to the genre should avoid this completely.

"1953 - KGB Unleashed" is one of those games that could have been great, but sadly is not. As a point-and-click adventure game, it does create a nice atmosphere. Some of the puzzles did not seem logical to me, so I had to consult outside help (a.k.a. YouTube) to get past them. The voice acting is a bit weak. I expect there was little to no direct given to the actors to let them know the context in which each line would be used in the game. I also had a difficult time understanding one of the voice actors because he was speaking so softly. Curiously, none of the voices have a Russian accent. I noticed several typographical errors in written documents. Given that the game was most likely originally written in Russian and later translated to English, I can understand these mistakes can happen. None of the typos affects the ability to enjoy and play the game, though. The ending is rather abrupt and seems to have been quickly added to complete the game as though finances had ended. Strangely, the ending does not answer any of the questions and seems more like the ending to the film "Raising Arizona" than a game titled "1953 - KGB Unleashed".
All told, I cannot recommend the game at the current price $9.99. I can, however, fully recommend the game if it is on sale or part of a bundle. It is unfortunate that Steam does not have a "Mixed" option for the "Do you recommend this game?" question.
Following is a list of tips that may help you get more enjoyment from the game. Those that do not want help, should skip this section.
1. This is not a hidden object game, so do not try to play that way.
2. The mouse cursor will change when it is over something with which you can interact.
3. If the mouse cursor indicates you can interact with something, but clicking on it does nothing, maybe you need to use something from your inventory.
4. The beginning of the game is very dark and I could see very little. After increasing the brightness setting quite a bit in the game's settings, I was able to proceed with the game.
5. You will need to do some backtracking, but not an excessive amount.
6. Read all of the documents. Not only do they provide a great deal of the post-WWII Russian atmosphere, they also provide clues.

What can I say about Streets of Rogue to someone unacquainted with it?
It's without a doubt, a better than I expected game, it provides a comedic, action-filled romp across a Dystopia, with an active development, and innumerable amount of opportunities to exploit and explore. The standard characters are well augmented by a decent unlock system for items and traits.
Items being utilities or weapons you can find and unlock as either custom character equipment or as mission rewards that cost nuggets (the form of meta-progression system in this game). This goes for traits too, while characters provide good combinations of these traits and trade-offs, like the Gorilla being mega strong and tanky, but lacking the vocal cords to speak english. Characters themselves require the player to achieve goals or challenges to unlock them. Such as destroying graves to unlock the Vampire, freeing a certain amount of Gorillas to unlock the Gorilla, etc.
Overall, I gave this game the "Even Better Than I Expected" award for 2017, overall I wish to see this game make it to release, and I hope that tinyBuild continues to improve and create new content.
tl;dr Much approved, much loved, and needs more attention to it.

Great port of an excellent board game. Everything that's in the board game is here, and is a nifty way to play games without having to keep the board somewhere in reality, as I'm sure any Talisman players will know, games can take a long time. The best way to describe it is a roguelike board game. You have a preset layout of a board, with some set pieces, but everytime someone lands on a square, you draw from the deck on order to determine what happens there. There's a good range of characters to choose from, all with their own special abilites as well as generic RPG stats by any other name. Purchase of the dlc characters is up to you, given the already strong roster and I feel the asking price for those is fair enough.
It's not flashy as a video game, and you pretty much just get a digital representation of the board game, aside from animations for the dice being rolled and a few flashes, there isn't much in the way of graphics. Whether or not you feel the game is worth the admission price depnds on the person. The real life base game plus Reaper and Dungeon expansions will burn a whole in your wallet to the tune of around £80 so this is considerably cheaper than that, but people who are new to board games may be turned off by the asking price, in which case you'd be fair to wait for a sale. But if you like board games, this is an excellent purchase which will do you well.
The dlc works very nicely with other people too; as long as someone has it, everyone in the game can access it, so no worrying about the player base being cut off, I only have the Reaper expansion myself, but that adds a whole new level to the game play on its own, presumebly the other DLC is as high quality.
There's hotseat as well as online, so those with a tablet pc can emulate the real board game even further. However the online is VERY unstable at the moment, so I'd stick to hotseat or LAN till they fix it. If you were planning on only playing online, I'd reccomend holding back on your purchase till that is fixed, otherwise you'll likely get left out in the cold.

I love the Talisman boardgame but the digital edition is a pure stinker! The spell casting mechanic is truly busted. I understand the devs wanted to make sure the game was fast paced when spell casting and that it would not cause people to start guessing when someone wished to cast a spell but the whole mechanic is awful. Here's why:
The only way to cast spells as a reaction is to queue them at which point they will automatically go off regardless if the spell is needed or not. For instance if you have a spell that would give you an edge before a combat roll and you've queued it up, it will automatically be cast at the next combat instance you're in which is a terrible mechanic. And as far as I know you can only queue 1 spell so any other spells you have are worthless if you would normally be able to cast them in a situation that would be helpful.
My recommendation: Stay away from the digital version and buy the actual boardgame.

Good and entertaining remake of a classic with some inherited and some added flaws.
The remastered DuckTales
draws you right into the game and you are eager to "press start", though you might encounter the first hurdle here, if you don't have a supported (read an Xbox360) controller. (Installing a utility like x360ce or xPadder helps, the keyboard is also an option on the PC of course.)
The
are great, especially the animated sprites and while some reviewers criticized the comparably small number of different animations, especially noticeable in the cutscenes, I think it's fine for the scope of the project. Talking about the cutscenes, I consider them an added flaw, they are too frequent, interrupt the gameplay unnecessarily and require two button presses to skip them. No need to borrow the weak way of storytelling of a modern FPS in a classic. The voice acting is well done and the cast is mostly from the original TV show.
I like the new 3D backgrounds as well, and I don't see why some reviewers think they wouldn't match with the sprites. The environments are clearly readable, which is important in a game like this.
The uneven
can be considered an inherited flaw, the levels vary greatly in difficulty, and the first on the list, Amazonas, surely isn't the easiest. When you play the game on "Easy" it's not too much of a problem, because you have infinite lives (making the mode arguably "Very Easy"), but beginning on "Normal", it can become frustrating, because if you run out of lives, you have to restart the whole level, all treasure gone. Though if I remember how many times I smashed my NES controller onto the floor, this remake is true to its roots in this aspect.
The game is also really short and most of the playtime can be attributed to the overall unforgiving difficulty once you play on "Normal", "Hard" or the unlockable "Extreme" setting. Gameplay wise, the biggest addition compared to the original is a tutorial level at the beginning.
DuckTales is easy to recommend, not only for the nostalgia, but because it's a very good game for the price. Sure, the cutscenes, will annoy you and the difficulty mixed with occasional hick-ups in the controls will frustrate you from time to time, but hasn't it been like this also 2 decades ago?
Next stop, Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, WayForward?

I'll be honest and say that I bought 1953: KGB Unleashed thinking it'd be a shooter or a Horror game like "Amnesia: The Dark Descent", so when I found out it was a Point & Click Adventure game, I was a little disappointed and tossed the game aside for nearly a year before giving it a fair shake.
When I finally decided to give this game a go, I was pleaseantly surprised. This game has a great atmosphere, well done (albiet tough to follow) puzzles, and really unnerving documents that fit the setting. You really get the sense that you were left for dead in a old Soviet bunker and you're discovering through rooms and the many found documents of brutal experiments and executions that have taken place there.
If only the game didn't end so abruptly... Just as you find yourself getting deeper and deeper into the bunker, the game is building up to finding some really horrific stuff... A wall blows up and you walk out and the game ends.. And not only that, the character goes on to narrorate that he lives a long and happy life not once even referencing or questioning the events that took place. It comes so sudden, its almost like you can literally see the point where the devs hit the budget limit. Its a real shame.
Regardless of it's awful ending, I do recommend 1953: KGB Unleashed.

I’ll be honest, I’m not the biggest fan of point-and-click games, but I do enjoy them on occasion. In KGB Unleashed it’s the usual journey of solving various puzzles and figuring out the meaning of various objects in each room. This game features more of the latter rather than the former. More often than not, I struggled to progress due to the obscurity of some elements, and despite the fact that I agree with the logic of each puzzle and the idea behind it, I believe it could have been far better designed. Many elements were misleading, or failed to emphasise the reason for its use. There are several examples I could give, one of which was a simple switch in a safe which gave no indication of what it did, yet it unlocked a door in another corridor that I did not realise until I had backtracked through most of the game to try and discover its purpose. In another part of the game, you have to descend a trap hole and there is a crate in the hole. Your cursor highlights to indicate there is something you need to do with the crate, but while I spent almost 10 minutes trying to open it, turns out it was actually where you had to put the tape recorder. Confusion like this could have been easily avoided by making the object anything other than a crate; a crate I had to break open not two rooms before.
I almost quit outright in frustration upon the first 10 minutes of starting the game. I don’t know if it was just my settings, but the initial two rooms are dark, so you have to strain your eyes to hardly see anything and the incessant alarm tone became annoying and headache inducing very quickly, beating the puzzles to the punch. The game significantly lacks any Russian undertones, with the main character voiced with an English accent. Aside from some radio stations and a few scraps of propaganda, the game could be set in the USA or England and you wouldn’t notice any difference.
The ending became downright bizarre, ending very abruptly with little resolution. In the last area, you find a glass (hopefully) eyeball which you roll under a door. You can then look through the eyeball as if by magic and somehow that opens the door. Now here is a big spoiler for you, but the game stops, tells you that guy who has been talking to you is dead and then shoos you out the exit. The exit, by the way, is a subway tunnel that somehow goes directly into a bathroom and the wall just disappears after you pick up a subway token. It almost seems as though the developers gave up at this point, or just didn’t know how to end the game. It was an abrupt and confusing ending that severely jarred the experience.
Aside from me failing at puzzles, the game also failed on technical levels in many places. It’s very slow to load, which is very unusual for my high-end PC. It could take as long as ten seconds to load one room, yet I can load Fallout New Vegas with 50+ mods faster. It only had to do this once per room though, which reduced the annoyance, but it’s still unusual for a game of this era. I also had trouble with sluggish cutscenes that left me locked in the cutscene long after the dialouge ceased. There was also no option for subtitles, which was a bit problem for me when there was poor audio quality dialogue and I couldn’t understand what was said, making me miss what may have been important plot points.
The game looked decent, and the mood was set as it should have been, but it felt empty and void of any character. With constant backtracking to and from rooms, I tired from walking the same slow corridors over and over. It became a grind and that’s no fun at all.
An engine that just isn’t up to scratch, inconsistent gameplay and design ruined this game, which showed great potential. Some may enjoy the puzzles, I know some people who will get more satisfaction from games such as these than I do, but the price, the length of only a mere 2 or 3 hours coupled with all the letdowns made KGB Unleashed a great disappointment.

This is a classic style point and click adventure game. I mean it is just like the old ones that used to be popular in the '90's, right down to a fixed aspect ratio of 4:3, and no High Resolution support, which is pretty inexcusable for a PC game that came out in 2012 (2013 US). It is also very short, easily able to be completed within 4-5 hours. It does feature some interesting atmosphere and story, dealing with a sealed and evacuated KGB bunker, many notes you find providing background, furnishings and propaganda posters you find are evocative of the 1950's. The story ultimately revolves around human experimentation, and features a twist near the end, along with a manufactured and unsatisfying ending that doesn't really come off as believable. The game also suffers from the kind of problem many adventure games have had since the original Myst, namely to advance, sometimes you have to do exactly what the game designers had in mind, using the precise tool on a specific piece of equipment, at the specific time the progression allows it, and not before. More than once I couldn't figure out why perfectly logical combinations didn't work, because only one specific one out of the multiple ones that would have worked was programmed to. Also at least one puzzle I couldn't solve because I was apparently trying to solve too early, the event refusing to work until I ran down other, incorrect leads. All in all, the game has zero replay value, and I would say it is worth playing through once, but only if it can be bought for very cheap, like say less than five dollars.

I must confess that i was not expecting much when i bought this game, frankly, i wouldn't of purchased it if it were not for the extreme reduction of its price during the sale. But, Trials being a fairly successful franchise if you can call it that, i was not worried in the fact of putting some cash down for it, and it was not regretted either.
Trials is a fun arcade styled puzzle game in which you as the player must ride different forms of motorcycles through obstacles, competing for a fast time, and gathering up the much wanted collectibles along the way. Trials has no true depth, but its not supposed to, and that's what makes it a great play. Urban Trials Freestyle is one of those games where you just play for the sake of having some real fun, slowly getting more and more addicted to collecting points, and upgrading your bike. However, being a very repetitive style of game, it does not take long for you as the player to get very bored of the same old Trials gameplay. In fact, as you get further on in the game, i found that it stops getting fun at all, and the game becomes more of a chore or task. I found myself leaving this game because of that very reason, and believe me, once you leave a game like this, you will find it incredibly hard to come back to. The replayability of this game is downright disgraceful, not to mention the lifespan that this game will have in you library, not very long indeed! The game has various levels and stages to get stuck into, and even if you think you will be able to get through all of them and complete it, well i would say good luck to you aha. Its a small game, but Steam only asks you for a small price to pay for it, and so its a reasonable purchase.
Urban Trials Freestyle is a game thats generally going to give you a few hours of fun, but lacks the effort to do further, when you buy this (you should only get this when the price is very cheap), do realise that its a game thats just going to be a few hours of fun.
Overall:
+ Fun game to play for a few hours
+ Can be great for a completionist
+ Good Trials Game
- Very repetitive
- Boring after a few hours of gameplay
- Terrible upgrade system
- Generally becomes a chore to play
Alright 5.5/10
That goes it for my short Urban Trials Freestyle Steam Review.

Tera and I have a longstanding love/hate relationship.  I've played this game since beta, long before it's release on steam.  Having such a long history, I've got a couple of thoughts, so here goes.
Pros
- combat - Amazing is the simplest word.  No matter what drives me away from this game, and no matter where I go, I always breathe a disappointed sigh and think back fondly on the combat of TERA.
- visuals - Tera has a vibrant and unique art style that is just stunning to sit back and look at.  The forsts, the deserts, the snow areas, all have a personality that defines them in a way I've never seen in any other MMO
- community - Aside from the few trolls that love to sit and ruin the day of new players on the various PVP servers, the community is generally positive and most of the guilds out there want to help you.
Cons
- grind - Oh good Lord... Do NOT get me started on the godawful endgame gear grind.  I can't even begin to tell you how punishing the grind for gear, and more recently feedstock, is.  No.  Just no.
- story - Is there even a plot in this game?  for the first 60 levels I wasn't convinced.  Then 61-65 started to get good!  Then endgame happened...  Can anyone explain to me the relation of the various dungeons and characters to the plot?  No?  didn't think so.
- optimization - I can usually get 60+ FPS, but here's why.  I have a 6900k, dual GTX 1070's, 32GB of RAM, and an SSD raid.  Every build before that, I had wretched frame drops all over the game.  Unless you have a supercomputer, do yourself a favor and play on medium, no more.
- classes - Have the devs even considered the legacy players that have warriors, archers, sorcerors and the like?  It's as if they had a meeting with Apple and decided to try there forced obselecense tactics.  Not to mention gender/race locking.
Despite my griping and not recommending this game, I'll probably still continue to play, honestly.  But I can tell you this, it isn't what is used to be.
Here's to the good old days...  *tips hat

Savage: The Battle for Newerth came out some time around in 2003, the game recieved awards and praise from a pretty loyal fan base, in my opinion, the game was revolutionary and original. (I did play it for several years, after all.) We have Savage 2, which was "meh", now we have Savage Resurrection. Savage 2 strayed a little too far off the original's path to some players but was still a decent game.
Savage Resurrection is the original reborn, hence the name, led by the same developer. Now using the Unreal 4 engine, the graphics have improved significantly.
The game is in it's early stages but live true to the original in it's combat, ui, mechanics. There are a lot of odds and ends that need cleaned up, such as shots clipping invisible parts of trees and rocks. There are those getting "Fatal Error" crashes, amongst a few other technical difficulties. However, they're updating rather frequently and I have never been given a reason to not have faith in S2 Games.
Resurrection introduces "Crates & Keys" similar to that of CS:GO. Purely cosmetic.
They've also introduced leaderboard, statistics and things of the sorts.
And now we have not only Casual but Ranked games with leagues like you'd see in League of Legends or Counter Strike. (Well, once it's enabled, that is.)
It's easy to recommend this game to anyone looking for a competitive scene, both 3rd & 1st person. There's even room for those whom enjoy RTS, due to the "Commander" seat which controls workers, construction, resource and research development. The game is solid, even as of now, for it's asking price. It'll only get far better. They intend to introduce new game modes and further improve on what the game once was and it'll be magnificent.

I had my eye on DuckTales Remastered for awhile now, since I loved the NES game so much. Well it was on sale this week so I decided to pick it up and I don't regret it.
It's a great nostalgic throw back to a franchise many of us 80's and 90's children grew up with. The music has been remastered wonderfully and I haven't had any problems with the controls. It's great that they managed to get (most?) of the voice actors back, that only make's it that much more special.
The stages are mostly left the same, with minior changes to make it more action packed or intresting, I haven't had a problem with the stages, in my opinion it simply makes the whole experience more "refreshing".
A complaint that seemed common with people was that the cut scenes cut away from the game and while agree that sometimes there's a little bit TOO much banter interuppting gameplay, it really hasn't been a deal breaker for me and some of the major cutscenes explaining the story and situation has been nice since the original NES game didn't really do too well of a job explaning anything, not that as kids we needed it, ha ha.
To be perfectly honest, the only major grip I have is the art. The character sprites are wonderfully done, except the artists seem to neglect minor touches to the game, such as having the character's mouths move when they talk. The biggest issue I have though is that the sprites look wonderful, as if they were hand drawn and then everything else is a stagnant, ugly, pastel colored 3D rendered. The two styles class horribly and the artists who were doing the background and foreground work didn't even bother to have proper perspective when considering the sprites. In the introduction stage, doors, chairs and other background objects look to be 10 times bigger then character sprites and it's just lame and offputting.
Does that ruin the game for me? No, not really, but it is a little offputting and really made me wish they would have just went that extra mile for attention to details. All in all, I'd pick it up, especally if it's on sale.

Like the original, the music is true, the story and level design are true as well - but it is upgraded to the future with music, voice acting, boss fights, and overrall tweaks that bring DuckTales into a new generation for gamers!

in a nutshell, a mediocre point and click game in a pseudo-3D environment made of panoramic static images. You'll spend hours on this game simply hunting pixels so you can pick up an unusual assortment of items, and then spend hours still researching by means of reading the wealth of written material in this game in order to pick up hints on how to use said-items, in an attempt to escape an underground Soviet bunker.
Potentially quite clever, as it forces you to learn about cold-war-style operations in Russia leading up to Stalin's death, but the inclusion of an all-too-paranormal 'storyline' does little to impress, though to its credit, a couple of scenes are rather dark and intimidating to begin with.
I'd actually advocate the use of a step-by-step guide to finish this game, as you'll get the enjoyment of the good bits, without the laborious hunting for pixels and reading through reams of fictitious documents in order to figure out that you need to tune the radio to a particular frequency so you can open a secret door you had no incentive to hunt for.
Usual thing - pick it up in a bundle or if it's on sale - but get a guide, and play it that way, you'll thank me later.

The completion of this game marks the beginning of a new epoch for me. I have had a bit of a magpie instinct over the last couple of years, and have bought almost every bundle and stockpiled my games. Now my library is quite big with the vast majority of games untouched. I have decided to play through all these games and write a review for each, in order to make sure I do not miss any I will be playing them in alphabetical order. I am likely to keep adding bundles and I don't know if I will ever catch up, but it's going to be a lot of fun!
So 1953 - KGB Unleashed, do I recommend it?
It's only just a yes but with a big asterisk which we will now go into.
I personally really enjoyed this game, but I can imagine that it will not be for everyone. This was a game that I wasn't particularly looking forward to when purchasing the bundle. I was expecting it to be a run of the mill great war first person shooter, but initial impressions and cynicism of the gaming industry can be deceiving! Much to my pleasant surprise. The game is actually a lot more like Myst, a modern first person point and click adventure game.
This game reminds me a lot of Myst 5 I think it was. It has the same pre rendered backdrops and the same “spherical” looking system. Your character will walk forward and stop in certain spots and you can look all around him with the mouse including up and down and a full 360 rotation. If you hold down the mouse button it rotates faster which I found myself doing a lot. It's a single click to interact with the world, move or pick things up. Right click opens your inventory which shows all the items your character is holding and gives you access to all the documents you have read.
The puzzles in this game are very strong. I enjoyed them a lot. Most of the puzzles have quite a cryptic solution, but the documents you read contain clues, and they are just the right balance, the puzzles really are some of the very best I've ever seen in an adventure game as the difficulty to satisfaction ration is spot on. This is a game that will make you think. Which I very much enjoy. There is only one puzzle that relies on trial and error which is kinda a negative however the documents make you aware of this.
So why is this game only getting a slight recommendation? Well there are a few reasons. The graphics are fit for purpose but they're not really anything that special, considering they are pre rendered too, although I don't see this as a bad thing. The game has a very eerie and oppressive nature to it, and as such there is a lot of dark rooms with low lighting which makes finding items annoying. Some rooms I had to enter and leave many many times before finding what was actually quite a big item. This is helped somewhat by a cursor that changes when it is moused over something intractable but you do feel that you are back in the old fashioned pixel hunting days. Although this may not be a bad thing, adventure games need a little bit of frustration otherwise they end up far too easy.
Also the amount of reading you have to do is likely to annoy some gamers, but that kind of gamer probably doesn't like adventure games. I am someone who likes flavour text, I read all the books I found on skyrim and I read mmo quests so this didn't phase me.
Is this game art?
The philosophy behind art is a hard one to pin down on, I used to think that if a game makes you think after you have played it then it qualifies. Something mindless and instant gratification doesn't count using this rule, but can you really say space invaders isn't art? Hmm....well this is a discussion for another time. I do think it is an arty game though! It has a very tense atmosphere and it treats you with respect with its puzzle design. The shadowy operations of the bunker and the more philosophical aspects of this game will give you pause for thought and I expect to take the memories of this game with me for quite some time as I reflect on what was quite a detailed storyline.
I can imagine the people who like this game feel the same way as me and the people who dislike it will really hate it. It was a positive experience.
6/10 Slightly above average - It's certainly worth a play if you already have it like I do.

This game has its good parts and its bad parts, like any other game. However I feel like this game is nowhere near worth what the asking price is, and even though I only got it for a buck or two on sale, I still regret buying it.
I love cold war era stories, and so I thought this game was right up my alley. It's a point and click, and while I'm usually hesitant to BUY point and click games (some of my favorites like Submachine are free) I saw the cold war style and thought it might be worth the couple dollars it was selling for.
Boy was I wrong. This game has a great story (albeit very short) and I thought it was pretty interesting. The puzzles were hard, and kind of abstract, but most point and click games are like that anyways so that's kind of a moot point. The music is pretty awesome, the graphics are beautiful, and the controls are pretty straightforward. The game is pretty reading heavy, and while I'm fine with that, others are not. The biggest gripe I have with this game is the english voice acting, because honestly it's subpar at it's best. You can obviously tell the cinematics are tailored to have the dialogue go on longer, and it seems like the voice actors for the english translation just wanted to get through with it as quickly as possible. The main character had an okay voice, the loudspeaker voice was just laughable because he sounded like he was just reading the lines, and honestly, the best voice actor in the game was the one guy you talk to on the phone for like a minute.
The biggest problem overall is the fact that this is a pirated english version of the Russian game "Phobos 1953". I don't know if the whole quarrel between the Russian developers and the pirates has been settled, but when I learned about this, I felt wrong buying it, even if it was like two bucks. Overall, don't buy this game. If you are so curious, watch a playthrough of it online or something. Just don't buy it, it will be a waste of your money.

Having never played the original board game, I actually just purchased this on a whim.  SOOOOOO glad I did.  My friends and I have a blast playing (I got a four pack) and I absolutely love the myriad of characters/classes.  Playing on random character choice is fun, though the AI has a thing for picking the Exorcist and excelling at it.  I once played a game where I eventually dispatched his Exorcist, forcing him to choose from 3 new classes, but he pratically gave up on his next choice (lasting a total of 3 turns) and the one after that!  His third set of classes included... yep, you guessed it: another Exorcist.  If it wasn't for the fact that I had snatched up all the Talismans, he might have won, garnering a large amount of strength, but after busting through and snatching a talisman from me, he lost his last two lives in the Vampire's lair.  Positioned strongly with a Marter with a massive amount of strength, I destroyed the Ice Queen and finally finished the game.
The computer AI in this game is great, but it seems a little cheap sometimes.  I'd like the ability to tweek the AI (unless I'm missing a portion in the options where you can) and a more stable online multiplayer (I've only had it mess up once for me, but I hear others complaining) but this game was worth every penny, and then some.  I got the Season Pass; all the extra content is great.  I highly recommend this for board game entusiasts or anyone looking for a great game to play, online or against AI.  Don't miss out on getting the season pass, either.  There are a TON of extras included, and it's not even halfway finished with it's "season" (you get every DLC that comes past, present, and future).  With the Highlands coming out (a new region, making a total of two additional regions (dungeon and highlands) on top of the basic board, you won't want to miss out on the extra adventure and danger!  Also, any DLC the host presents in their game, you'll be able to access (this includes characters and extra regions/cards) in their game.  If you plan on hosting games with your friends, DLC is a must have!  Trust me, the game is worth your money, and it's gotten me interested in getting the physical version for pure collection reasons!
EDITS: Grammer (I'm sure there's still some mistakes) and reviews on DLC info.

This AC has made some steps in the right direction. Combat is more engaging thanks to them switching to a hitbox system. The stealth systems are pretty light but things open up once you get more tools. Movement and climbing feel very fluid, and I don't think there was anything I couldn't climb in the game world. They really give you a ton of freedom with how you move around in the game world and it makes exploring very enjoyable. Exploration is more rewarding due to the new loot system, you have more "reasons" to be crawling through tombs or raiding bandit camps etc, but also the world has a stronger sense of mystery than before.
However, the quests get really repetitive. Some are okay, but there's far too many tedious trailing missions and fetch quests that kill the pacing of the game for me.
Honestly, this game is at its best when you just freely roam the world and ignore the main story. Just create your own little adventures.That's when I found I was most engaged. Having a little skirmish with bandits or getting your boat ambushed and sunk by hippos, there's lots of great little moments you can have in the open world. And my god the environment art in this game.There's so many beautiful sights to see, it's almost worth it to get this game for artistic value of this world (if that's something you care about). Many hours of my playthrough are dedicated to just strolling around using photo mode.
At the end of the day, the game has its flaws but I enjoyed my time with it and will probably return to explore more of this gorgeous world. If you like climbing everything you see, Witcher/Dark Souls combat and walking around getting lost in beautiful game worlds, then this might be for you!

My first review...breathe in...and...
TERA, an MMO that my brother told me to look into. So I did, as I'm now 800+ Hours into it and am now typing this review.
Would I suggest you play this game? Well, I'll let you answer that for yourself, and I'll also give you my answer after I break down the things I have witnessed.
-First off, graphically, I LOVE the game, shame my crap laptop (Craptop) can't see the game past the '0' quallity setting.
-Combat wise, it's lovely, shame Craptop and crap connection (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥net as I call it) can't make the game fun, at times I lag everywhere, but that's just ME. Not being able to lock-on to enemies is weird to me, but I got used to it. Controler support's nice, but if you need a better 'shot' (Ranged/Support classes), Mouse/Keyboard is the best. If you're playing physically, go on with the controler.
-There are lots of classes to use with different races to pick from, yes, but that's pushed to the side by the Gender/Racial locked classes (Reaper, Ninja, Gunner, Brawler, Valkyrie [new one from my understanding]). I've found love for the 'Warrior' class in my time, as I heard from players that it's one of the best solo-playing classes in the game to date.
-I haven't payed for anything in the game so far (Got dem priorities, yo) and I've gotten to the end of the game (or close enough), so Pay2Win isn't here, it's Pay2LookPretty. When I say pay, I mean: Drop us a 20, we give you a cosmetic or 2.
So far everything I've typed seem to be a push and pull towards 'Yes' and 'No' on my recommendation. Here's an input from myself, not just what everyone else, and my brother, have said
-The Leveling system...it's ♥♥♥♥ing sad. To progress the story, you HAVE to be a specific level to even SEE the quest. I can also complain about the difficulty curve at specific levels, but that's something I have to be in-game for to get the details on. I got off track a bit, ALL the enimies are either too strong to deal with ALONE, where you need to be 2 levels higher than them to beat properly (Grey name, not white/red), or you need to re-configure your limited Glyphs. Might be MY fault that I'm saying this, but I'm more used to a combat system where BASIC enemies don't have 5-20 thousand HP, and can take away 5% of your HP with a measly little scratch, or the unaviodable magic they cast. This becomes more apparent at level 60+, where they are in many numbers and can, and will, team up on you with their collective power and- *died*
I'm also a SOLO player, as I prefer not to be called a noob, a scrub, useless to the team, and this game has REQUIRED dungeons that NEED parties to progress forward, and the partied players don't understand that some folks NEED to do the story there, and plow through the dungeon without a second thought to the story. Pile that on to MY Craptop and my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥net, I'm the weak-link in a chain that NEEDS to be fully present to make the team progress. So I prefer to play alone, where there's less lag, and no one to let down/let me down.
So in the end, YES, I recomend you play the game, get your own opinion on the game I bash in my solo-player heart. Maybe you'll have a better understanding / better time to a game I love to play with my brother.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege is a great game with many flaws. There are pros and cons to any game but this game... this game is amazing and horrible at the same exact time.
The Pros:
-Good playerbase and there's a way to report players for toxicity if you do find a bad egg
-Good operators (though ubisoft can't seem to balance the new ones)
-Very tactical and really relies on skill than anything else
-Not a pay to win game (For the most part)
-The skins and accessories are pretty cool
-You don't pay to get the Alpha Packs with real money but instead with in game currency A.K.A. Renown. Also you can just earn them
The Cons:
-The players that are toxic can definately ruin the match (From being annoying and rude to straight up team-killing for no reason)
-The newer operators are unlockable but set at a stupidly high price (25,000 in Renown for 1 operator when getting just 2000 renown requires you to play and win at least 9-10 games)
-The game is very, very, VERY graphics intensive and will use and abuse even the higher end systems (I have a Nvidia 1070 GTX, an i7 7700K CPU and 16 GBs of RAM and the game runs at 35-50 FPS on the highest settings)
-You do have to pay to get the secondary in game currency, A.K.A. R6 Credits. Those R6 credits do go towards buying new operators and buying skins and accessories just like with renown. So technically, you have to pay real money to buy any of the better operators... so just buy the DLCs if you have the money.
-Lastly, the year 3 operators are still kinda OP but only if they're being used by people that actually know how to play the game
(I only recommend this game to those with higher end PCs and those who have a ton of spare change to pay for the DLCs)

Soooooo this game is incredible, let me explain >
I've put in 2000+ hours on Guild Wars 2, have every class at max, was an alpha, closed beta, open beta, and pre-release player, and have spent $100's on that game...
This blows it out of the water.
- Graphics are stunning in general. You put it on max settings on a high resolution and you are like "Omg..."
- The combat is super fun, but not overly complex.
- The quests are like generic mmo's but the combat makes it entertaining still, and the occasional super boss is equilalent to GW2's events, but GW2 owns there.
- Characters are unique in their own way. Character customization is in depth but not over the top
- The classes are all unique all with their own builds and are all fun to play
Side note: GW2 got crappy so quickly because up to max level, the only acceptable build for ANY class was a burst dps build. PROS
CONS
A great return to the Assassin's Creed series with an excellent Origin story of "The Creed". Having been a long-time fan, some sections of the story actually did a pretty great job of enciting emotions. This title is fun to play, is built on the tried and true formula of the Assassin's Creed Franchise and it looks gorgeous.
This return to "The Creed" series really shows the merit in developers taking a break from annualised franchises when things become a little stagnant. From the interesting Origin story, to the overhauled combat system, this title should have fans and new players to the series entertained and impressed with the scope of this title.
The gameplay, for me, is what really keeps me coming back to this series, and Assassin's Creed Origins doesn't dissapoint. I found myself traversing the massive Egyptian landscape just to find that next location, complete it's objectives and then ride off into the sunset ready for the next adventure. Of particular note are the encampments, garrisons and hideouts, and I found myself repeatedly infiltrating these when things didn't go as planned and I was discovered. It is extremely satisfying when you can take down one of the larger encampments without the help-signal being lit, and hitting that Centurian in the back of the head with a well-timed arrow as he attempts to get to the beakon is a beautiful thing.
Technical issues aside, the only one true critcism I have with this title is that it really didn't add any dramatically new gameplay features to the series, and the RPG system just lacked a little depth to keep me going onto 100% completion. Having played almost all of the previous entires in the series, and with this title being polished, robust and fairly addictive, I wish I could have taken advantage of all of the content available within the game, however, 62 hours in and with all of the side quests and the main quest completed, along with probably 99% of the open-world locations, I had had enough. Perhaps a statistics or completion progress menu would have helped entice me to the finish line...
All in all, I hope we revisit Egypt in the not-too-distant future.

Tera Online Impressions
Personal Gaming style: PVE only.
To start, I've played WoW from vanilla to Catclysm, then jumping to various MMO's like DC Universe Online, and Guild Wars. Currently, my go to MMO is Guild Wars 2, which is not without its faults. I decided to try out Tera during a dryspell in GW2, but it's hard to recommend this game. It's quite lovely to look at, and you could tell there was a lot of effort in place to build an amazing world, but I'm not sure what happened. When you begin playing, you can tell there is a lot of polishing left to be done, and the overall plot of your main story is severely lacking. By the time I was level 10, I no longer cared about the random NPC quests provided, and simply speed clicked to continue on my way. The gross oversexualization makes picking certain classes an emotional chore. "High fantasy" my♥♥♥♥♥.you don't need undulating boobs everywhere to be high fantasy. Even the little kids in the game can hit the perv radar. However, in saying all that, if you want something free to check out, it does have some pretty nice eye candy in regards to landscapes (and aforementioned boobs, if that's your thing,) and gameplay mechanics.
Pros:
+Free to play.
+Inventive character classes and races.
+Inventive monsters, bosses, etc.
+Gorgeous artwork and landscapes.
+Player modeling very well done.
+Action RPG elements, though slightly clunky, are quite useful.
+You like questing? Several lifetimes of questing.
+Real world purchasable items tend to be costumes and quality of life items.
Cons:
-Storyline is abysmal.
-Too much questing.
-Though voice acting is well done, there is much dialog/story to utilize talent effectively. The lip synching (if lips even move) is horrible.
-Certain classes are racial/sex limited, which if this were any other game, not that big of deal.
-Gratuitous oversexualization. Game may as well be called♥♥♥♥♥& Tittehs.
-Wardrobe, though varied, are only a means of highlightng sexualization of characters.
-The store items are highway robbery. A costume can set you back nearly $20 USD.
-The respawn rate is dialed all the way to 11. I routinely find myself surrounded by the same mob I killed, while picking up loot. It wouldn't be so bad, but the landscape is saturated by these mobs. One or the other...not both.
-Damn near a dead game, but really server dependant.
-The grind is there. In your face. All the time.
-Can I get some armor to cover my gawdamn lady bits, or what?!

What I particularly love about this game is how high the stakes are. This is something completely omitted in the later entries in the series and one of their biggest drawbacks. Two factions in war with each other while an even bigger threat threatens to wipe them both out unless something is done about it. It was the same in the past in the war with the Isu and it's happening again today. It's the same as Game of Thrones in a lot of ways, great lords distracted fighting one another while an apocalyptic threat comes down on them from the north. It's an awesome way to tell a story.
The character development for the villains in this game is great, especially Charles Lee who has a real arc from eager apprentice to evil villain. He also has great lines. The rest of the Templar cohort is also fleshed out rather well before you're given the mission to assassinate them and this was well done and got me more invested in the story. The set piece battles are disappointing and too scripted. Nothing in the trailer can actually be done in the game and it's not unfair to judge the gameplay based on promises a trailer makes. The main character is uncharismatic and dull, especially when viewed in contrast to Ezio. If I had to pick the games biggest flaw that would be it. If we don't like the player character and connect with him then what's left? Maybe he showed a bit humanity in the homestead missions but those missions aren't mandatory and it was very brief as well. I like the slow build-up of the game, taking its time to develop the world and the characters within it. I think this is something rarely done in games and I would like to see more of it. But it loses its impact a bit when we don't have a strong protagonist to relate to.
The multiplayer cutscenes are interesting in this one because they introduced a concept that would be further explored in the Black Flag. The animus as a gaming console used by Abstergo to control the past. After this game you no longer play as a named character in the present day story but rather as yourself, testing the animus console and even though you start to miss a proper protagonist in the later games the concept in itself is interesting. The overarching plot of the templar's goal of releasing humanity's lost potential denied us by the ancients is also explored here and that's genuinely interesting. I just wish they would do more with it in the later installments of the series.
The tailing mission in the "Justice Served" section of The Tyranny of King Washington warrants special mention because it was excellent. All throughout the mission you have to use wolf cloak to stay hidden but you can't use it for too long so you have to look for hiding spots to regain health and there are dogs that smell you along the way so you have to use bait to throw them off. I was never bored during this mission and in a series famous for its boring tailing missions this was truly exceptional. The DLC introduces a series of abilities that affect the meta of the game in several interesting ways and I think it's a very well done expansion. Plus Robin Atkin Downes gives a great performance as Washington and it's always cool to see him in games.
I like the tomahawk quite a lot, it replaced the sword for me in this one because it feels better and more thematically appropriate to use. It handles kind of like the butcher knife in previous games only cooler and more brutal. I found the bow a lot more viable than the crossbow as well because of its thematic importance to the character but also the setting. That and with the new dart arrow you feel like such a badass predator hunting redcoats. Even if the new combat system was a bit simplified I still enjoyed it.

Sadly the game is not without its bugs this time around either, such as NPC's scripting breaking on occasion, causing you to have to reload a checkpoint and and it even snowed indoors once. Although this is annoying I didn't mind as much as I did in Brotherhood and Revelations because of this game's bigger scope. And at least the hidden blade hits the head instead of the air next to it this time. One particularly amusing episode was when I was avoiding guards with Sam Adams and I decided to kill some guards blocking the way to get to my destination faster and while I'm mowing down dozens of redcoats like some native American terminator Sam Adams is yelling "Leave him alone! He's just a child. He's done nothing wrong!"

I'm one of those people who read all of the database entries as I'm playing the game and through playing the series it's gotten me interested in history in a big way. There are literally dozens of us! The database is written by Shaun in the lore of the game and he always adds little jokes and snarky comments directed at Desmond and as an extension, us the player, and this has fallen away in further installments after the third game. Though they're still interesting they don't have the same charm to them but I'm glad they brought it back in Syndicate.

I loved building up the homestead and doing missions for the settlers. It fits the theme of building a new life in a new country and I've always liked having a strong home base in open world games like this. One you enjoy coming back to. It's almost as good as Monteriggioni in Assassin's Creed 2. By the time this game came out Black Flag was well into production and the addition of the naval missions was not only a smart move to prepare us for that game and tie the two of them together more closely but it's also one of the most fun activities in the game. I was surprised to see so many clues to the two next games in the series, several references to the French Revolution and talk of unity between assassins and templars and Connors grandfather and his pirate roots.

Game developers, when you walk along with an NPC to a specific destination and there's a conversation happening, please don't make it so the conversation is cut short because you arrived at the destination too fast! This happens more than once in this game and it's absolutely infuriating. And it's not like I was running to get there as fast as I could, no I was walking slowly next to the NPC. There should be a law against this type of game design. Make it so the conversation doesn't last any longer than the time it takes to get to the destination via the fastest route taken. I hate missing out on plot like this and it made me restart missions because of it. I also don't like the horse for the most part. It's more cumbersome than convenient to use most of the time, especially in the frontier with the amount of obstacles in your way and the lack of a stamina meter for your horse which means you can't maximize your speed.

Your assassin recruits have personalities this time which is great. I loved calling in Stephane to help me out in a scrap. You can also choose between different abilities in your recruits depending on the situation, sniping or assassinating or rioting. I love this and it's a great development of an already good system. Because of their personalities and the nature of the story, fighting a revolution, I was more interested in sending them out on missions in the mini game that's been featured in every game since Brotherhood. The ability to do it from a menu and not having to go to a pigeon coop to send them was very convenient and made me want to do it more.

I like history so i didn't find the game or the story particularly boring but genuinely interesting and I loved learning about the American Revolution through this game. The game also showed us the first and last instance of something I've always wanted to see: modern day assassin gameplay. It's such a shame they didn't explore this further because fighting modern day enemies with a hidden blade was a lot of fun despite how brief it was. I believe the game to be underrated and though some of the criticism towards it is merited I still hold it in high esteem.

Its the final chapter of Five Nights at Freddy's, and by far the most difficult one yet.
Five Nights at Freddy's 4 is the conclusion to the epic story we have slowly learned more and more about over 3 other games. However, it terms of GAMEPLAY, its completely different.
FNAF 1,2,3 all had different gameplay styles, yes. But there was 1 thing that was there every time around.
Security Cameras.
You could see where the animatronics where at pretty much all times. But, in this final chapter, they're GONE. Completely gone. Worse yet, this time around, Freddy, Bonnie, Chica and Foxy are in YOUR HOUSE! Yep, its no longer at Freddy's (well, technically FNAF 3 wasnt at Freddy's either, but...)
Anyway, 2 reccuring themes from the 3 previous games are gone. Now, you must rely on other amtters of defending yourself. Each animatronic has a different way to defend yourself against it.
TO DEFEND AGAINST FREDDY:
You must turn around to your bed every now and then and use your flashlight on his Freddle minions.
TO DEFEND AGAINST BONNIE:
Run to the left door and listen for his breathing. IMPORTANT: IF YOU HEAR BREATHING SHUT THE DOOR WITH SHIFT.
TO DEFEND AGAINST CHICA:
Pretty much just the same thing as Bonnie, but at the right door.
TO DEFEND AGAINST FOXY:
Run to your closet and see if Foxy is there. If he is, shut the door on him. Hold it shut until he turns into a plushie. After that, keep checking back at the closet at various points throughout the night, because he will grow back.
Worse yet, the usual cast are joined by a bunch of new characters, too.
Meet Plushtrap. He is a smaller, cuter and much more evil version of Springtrap from FNAF 3. You will play a minigame with  him inbetween nights. If you win, you get to skip 2 hours on the next night. Baisically, you get to start at 2AM instead of 12AM. Also, remeber the cupcake, Carl? Yeah, well he can kill you now. There are also 2 more antagonists who await you on the later nights, but revealing them to you would be spoilers.
The Atari-style minigames from FNAF 2 and 3 are back. This time, you play them inbetween nights, kinda like the Follow Me ones in FNAF 3. These minigames tell the story of a young boy who gets bullied by his mean brother. A certain incident between these 2 brothers is what starts the events of FNAF 4. I cant tell you anymore than that. (Spoilers, you know.)
Before I write my conclusion, there is some stuff I want to get off my chest about this installement of the franchise.
In my personal opinion, FNAF 4 is the worst of the entire series. It takes away everything that we got used to in the previous games and throws you into something completley different. My least favrioute thing about this game? The fact that it relies on sound cues. Very quiet ones. When you start the game for the first time, you will come to a screen that says "Adjust your volume until you hear the crickets" Do you know how high I had to turn it to hear the crickets? 100. Yep, maximum volume. The problem with this is that FNAF 4 has the LOUDEST jumpscares of them all. So, you can kind of see how mute sound effectss and booming loud jumpscares can be a problem. My solution to this was just turn it up when listening for breathing, and that got me through nights 1-4 just fine. But...
SPOILER ALERT!
On NIght 5, all the animatronics you face on the previous nights disappear completely, and the new character you're facing off against...well...he dosent work like the others. Remember how I said I just turned the sound up for when I was listening for breathing and nothing else? Well, for this new character, you cant do that. You have to have the volume turned up to at least 50 for the whole time. That was bad, and kept me on NIght 5 for awhile. But, I will tell you, finnaly beating a  boss I thought I'd never beat EVER gave me the biggest feeling of acomplishement I've ever felt in gaming.
In conclusion, Five Nights at Freddy's 4 is the worst of the franchise. BUT, dont take that the wrong way. All FNAFs are good games. There is no such thing as a bad FNAF game. Its just I'd reccomend the others alot more than this one. Its completely different and has a bad  way of gameplay. It mixes mute must-hear sound cues with extremely loud jumpscares. Not a good mix. BUT, it is a fun and enjoyable for most of the time, and I'll still recomend it.

This is not a game. It's a utility program that should be reclassified as Software now that Steam has a separate area for that. It's a simulation program for our solar system and the greater universe. It is essentially an educational tool, once part of the now-defunct Steam For Schools programme.
Not having any entertainment value on a platform that was once purely for entertainment, the developer resorted to adding achievements and using them as part of Steam's summer 2011 event. This meant many people started "playing" it, however other achievements are famous for being the most ridiculous on Steam, including starting the program 10,000 times and leaving it running for an actual real-time YEAR.
Though they have since acknowledged these achievements as a mistake, the developer has refused to remove them but instead uses all the topics complaining about them (which are by far the most-discussed topics for the program both on the Steam forums and the developers' own forum) to advertise the game's follow-up in poor taste. And that's before remembering that this follow-up was originally promised to be a free update to owners of this program but now costs twice as much again.
In short: Not a game, not fun, and a great way to ruin your achievement stats. If you joined Steam after 2011 and weren't caught out by this game, avoid it now at all costs.

With a huge library of available experiments to choose from and the ability to create your own using the massive amount of custom options the game offers to you for almost everything I had a lot of fun running simulations and just relaxing.
Fully priced I would have a hard time recommending this title, especially with the better and more updated sequel already on steam but on sale this is a fun little distraction that will help answer a few of those nagging questions in the back of your mind.

Tera is a mixed bag to me. There's a lot of good but some bad to it too. Keep in mind, I'm a vet player who has played on and off, and decided to jump back in recently. My hours played do not reflect my actual game time, as I did have this game before it moved to steam (Selphi, lvl65 slayer, Celestial hills). I won't be talking about the story of this game, as it's apparently been massively changed for the early game (RIP noob island).
Pros - Graphically looks solid. Not the best looking MMO, what with blade and soul, black desert, and others out there, but it looks great. Character models are nice and textures aren't that ugly.
-Some of the best action i've played in an MMO. It's an action-based mmo, meaning there's no targeting, and you gotta aim everything. It brings a strong dynamic to the game in terms of your skills. You gotta be good to play, especially at the end game. It feels a bit odd playing if you're use to tab targetting in mmos like WoW or FFXIV, but you'll get use to it after a bit. Also has controller support, although I wouldn't recommend it for anything other than melee classes.
-Lots to do in the end game. You can gear up and que for dungeons, craft, play the market, do some vanguards, or your dailies.
-This is not a Pay2Win mmo, which is awesome considering it's F2P.
-Post lvl 60 story is pretty awesome.
- AWESOME mounts. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game has some of the best looking mounts imo.
- All of the classes are pretty fun. I've tried out a majority of them, and they're all pretty neat, and do relatively well unless you're a gunner (RIP).
Cons -
-FROM MY EXPERIENCE.. Main scenario questing was painful. Again, apparently this has changed recently, but I'm not sure if the entire main story was overhauled. My guess is that it wasn't, and if that's true, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥was questing a slog in this game. It's all fetch quest or kill x amount of mobs. It's so insanely dull and unappealing.
-The plot is generic. Nothing fantastic. You'll likely forget about it. Some of the end game plot is nice, but again, this game doesn't have anything too deep to revolve around it.
-The shop is too damn expensive. 25 OR MORE Bucks for a decent mount or cosmetic gear is ♥♥♥♥ing atrocious. I'd highly recommend you not buy anything from the shop unless you really wanna support TERA. They're ripping you off otherwise.
- Daily limit on some instances is so stupid. I can understand for some late game, high quality instances, but why is this a thing in the mid tier of the game?
-Some of the dungeons are realllllly difficult. You gotta be really good late game to do well, especially as a healer/tank. Keep in mind if you don't wanna put in that much investment into an MMO.
- The optimization for this game is shotty at best. I have a solid mid range rig and I still cant run this game at max with above 60 fps after YEARS of playing it. They don't intend to optimize it anytme soon either, so good luck if you can run it well. Heavily CPU bound.
-My biggest issue. The amount of "Fanservice" this game offers is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. Elin's are the most popular race, and they're arguably the most hated for their jailbait look. Every female race except for the Aman females are grossly oversexualized. All of the female races have jiggly double d's, generic skimpy end game armor and cosmetics, etc. What's worse is that the new classes they released post release for the game are all female only classes, some being specific to a certain race. This is ridicoulous for people who are not a fan of those specific races, especially the Elen, who received TWO of these classes (Ninja, and Reaper). It's my biggest issue with this game and the reason why I quit. I hated the oversexual look of this game. I really like the esthestic of the castantic race, but I hate how their gear presents them. I wanna look like a armor clad badass, not a hooked with a giant sword. If you like that kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥ then all power to you, i guess.
Basically, if you like really nice action in your mmo, play tera. However, that's one of the ONLY things I like about it. It might seem a little mean, but that's just how I feel. Can't really recommend it past that.

Crash Drive 2 is a disappointing multiplayer game, with repetitive and uninteresting gameplay that is driven entirely by a hollow unlockable/level-up system that sets it down a tragic path that diverges from the fundamental gameplay aspects of it's predecessor, Crash Drive 1.
The gameplay is only half decent, and it relies entirely on levelling up and unlocking new vehicles. Each vehicle is only unique in appearance, since after maxing their levels (which is very easy) they all have virtually the exact same stats. This results in the player having to unlock many, many cars that he/she truly doesn't like or care about until they eventually unlock their favorite car--or maybe even unlock them all--at which point he/she has no reason to ever play with the other cars or really even play the game ever again. This is especially frustrating because the first installment of Crash Drive had totally unique cars with very different stats, and I found myself frequently switching between cars simply for fun. In Crash Drive 2, however, switching between cars is merely a chore that is necessary to continue the unlocking process.
I also found the multiplayer only state of the game to be tedious, since my favorite part of the first Crash Drive game was the solitude of it, doing insane tricks like a child in a sandbox all by yourself without being bothered by anybody. It was peaceful and relaxing, whereas Crash Drive 2's multiplayer focus is almost annoying. Suddenly, the game is all about competition, which ruins what I always thought was the most fundamental part of Crash Drive: the casual gameplay.
I respect Crash Drive 2 for it's ambition, for trying to become something bigger and better, but I don't think the game achieves what it attempts to.
The only saving grace of this game is Tank Battles, which is actually pretty fun and unique. I found it very entertaining for a bit, but it gets boring after not to long. I can't imagine I'll ever return to this game--not for tank battles, and especially not for the main game. After putting this game down, all I can say is that the whole game felt like a job: it kept me playing with the stupid unlockable system, but it never truly entertained me like the first game did. Crash Drive 2 was nothing but a waste of time to me. I disliked the game so much that I can't even imagine giving my free gift copy to a friend, lest I subject them to an equally negative experience.
Overall Rating = 3.3/10

Despite it's name, it's much less of a remastered game than a completely redux of one. A lovley mixture of 2.5D visuals, well done and cartoonish sprites, it's really got Disney written all over it. The music, is wonderful, I could listen to the theme tune all day!
For gameplay, DuckTales: Remastered doesn't have much going for it. Mainly because it's a game targeted at children, so it's understandable why it's easy to use. Simple button controls, jump, hit, brutally murder, the usual.
My one issue with the game, is that it doesn't do much to make me come back, other than improve my rankings on the World Leader Boards. And that final boss battle. It's hard. The story is short and can be completed in 3 hours or so, and of course there are achivements and trading cards that could keep you busy.
All in all, DuckTales is just harmless fun, even if it is a little guilty pleasure game.

Got this on a Humble Bundle, and thats the only time its ever worth considering. It starts as a simple 'bike balance' flash game, but sadly manages to mess up what hundreds of flash games seem to pull off.

All in all, if you want to play a balance game, find a flash game. It'll be a lot cheaper, a lot better, and not have you reaching for headache tablets.
